A Chronological Reference to Every Substantive Person in Scripture

The People
of the Bible

Every person of whom Scripture records something substantive, in chronological order, with what they did right, what they did wrong, and the passages that support it. King James Version.

Books complete: the entire Old Testament, Genesis through Malachi. The chronology continues through the remaining books as they are compiled; see the note at the foot of this page.

The Primeval Period

0

Adam

The first man, formed directly by God from the dust of the ground, and the head of the human race.

Family

No human parents; formed by God (Genesis 2:7). Husband of Eve (Genesis 2:22-25). Father of Cain, Abel, and Seth by name (Genesis 4:1, 4:2, 4:25), and of unnamed sons and daughters (Genesis 5:4). Luke's genealogy calls him the son of God (Luke 3:38), meaning direct origin rather than descent.

Chronology

Lived 930 years (Genesis 5:5) - a figure explicitly stated in Scripture. Anno Mundi 0 to 930 by calculation from Genesis 5; the traditional Ussher equivalent is 4004-3074 BC, which is a seventeenth-century calculation and not a biblical date.

Life Synopsis

Adam was formed of the dust and became a living soul when God breathed into him (Genesis 2:7). He was placed in the garden of Eden to dress it and keep it (Genesis 2:15), and given one prohibition: not to eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, on pain of death (Genesis 2:16-17). He named all the cattle, the fowl, and every beast of the field, and among them no help meet was found for him (Genesis 2:19-20). God then made the woman from his side, and Adam received her with the words "This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh" (Genesis 2:23).

The serpent approached the woman, not Adam. She took of the fruit and ate, "and gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat" (Genesis 3:6). Their eyes were opened, they knew they were naked, and they hid themselves from God among the trees (Genesis 3:7-8). Questioned directly, Adam blamed the woman and, by implication, God who gave her: "The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat" (Genesis 3:12).

God's sentence on Adam names the specific ground: he hearkened to his wife's voice above God's command. The earth was cursed for his sake, and he would eat of it in sorrow and sweat until he returned to the dust (Genesis 3:17-19). After the sentence - and this order matters - Adam named his wife Eve, "because she was the mother of all living" (Genesis 3:20). God clothed them both with coats of skins (Genesis 3:21), then drove the man from the garden and barred the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:22-24).

Outside Eden, Adam fathered Cain and Abel, lived to see one murder the other, and afterward fathered Seth in his own likeness (Genesis 4:25, 5:3). He lived 930 years and died (Genesis 5:5).

What They Did Right

  • Exercised the authority God gave him in naming every creature. Scripture records the act without qualification: Genesis 2:19-20.
  • Received his wife with recognition and welcome rather than indifference: Genesis 2:23.
  • Named his wife Eve, "the mother of all living," after the curse had been pronounced. This appears to indicate some expectation of continued life rather than only death, though Scripture does not state his motive: Genesis 3:20.

What They Did Wrong

  • Ate the forbidden fruit in direct violation of an explicit command. Scripture explicitly condemns this: Genesis 2:16-17; Genesis 3:6; Romans 5:12-14.
  • Hid from God rather than confessing: Genesis 3:8-10.
  • Shifted blame to his wife and implicitly to God: Genesis 3:12.
  • Paul states that Adam was not deceived, distinguishing his transgression from Eve's: 1 Timothy 2:14. His was open-eyed disobedience.

Character Assessment

Scripture treats Adam less as a moral example than as a representative head. No New Testament passage commends his faith; none pronounces his condemnation either. His three recorded good acts are all from before the Fall or immediately after it, and Scripture records no repentance. God's clothing of him in Genesis 3:21 is presented as divine initiative, not as a response to contrition. The text does not specify his eternal state, and this reference does not either.

Significance

Adam is the federal head of the human race. "By one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men" (Romans 5:12). "In Adam all die" (1 Corinthians 15:22). He is "the first man Adam," set deliberately against Christ, "the last Adam" (1 Corinthians 15:45). The whole doctrine of imputed sin and imputed righteousness is argued from the parallel between the two. He also stands at the head of the genealogy of Christ (Luke 3:38) and of the Chronicler's record (1 Chronicles 1:1).

Death / Outcome

Died at 930 years (Genesis 5:5). Last mention in Scripture: Jude 1:14, where Enoch is called "the seventh from Adam."

Scripture References

Genesis 1:26-28; Genesis 2:7-25; Genesis 3:1-24; Genesis 4:1, 4:25; Genesis 5:1-5; 1 Chronicles 1:1; Luke 3:38; Romans 5:12-14; 1 Corinthians 15:22, 15:45; 1 Timothy 2:13-14; Jude 1:14
0

Eve

The first woman, made by God from Adam's side; "the mother of all living."

Also called the woman

Family

Made from Adam (Genesis 2:21-22); wife of Adam; mother of Cain, Abel, and Seth (Genesis 4:1, 4:2, 4:25).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Her creation falls within the Eden narrative, so she is placed at Anno Mundi 0 by context, but Scripture gives no age for her at any point and does not record her death.

Life Synopsis

God declared that it was not good for the man to be alone and made a help meet for him (Genesis 2:18). She was formed from Adam's side while he slept (Genesis 2:21-22). She is called "the woman" throughout the Eden narrative and is not named Eve until after the judgment (Genesis 3:20).

The serpent approached her with a question about God's command. She answered by citing it, but added a clause - "neither shall ye touch it" - which does not appear in the prohibition as God gave it in Genesis 2:16-17 (Genesis 3:2-3). The serpent flatly denied the penalty and impugned God's motive (Genesis 3:4-5). Seeing the tree was good for food, pleasant to the eyes, and desirable to make one wise, she took and ate, and gave to her husband (Genesis 3:6).

Questioned by God, she told the truth without evasion beyond the actual facts: "The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat" (Genesis 3:13). Her judgment was multiplied sorrow in conception and childbearing, and a changed relation to her husband (Genesis 3:16). But the promise of Genesis 3:15 - that the seed of the woman would bruise the serpent's head - is spoken over her, and the whole line of redemption runs from it.

Her two recorded speeches after Eden both credit God. At Cain's birth: "I have gotten a man from the Lord" (Genesis 4:1). After Abel's murder, at Seth's birth: "God, said she, hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel, whom Cain slew" (Genesis 4:25). Scripture does not record her death.

What They Did Right

  • Answered the serpent by citing God's command rather than ignoring it, though she altered it in the citing: Genesis 3:2-3.
  • Told the truth when God questioned her, without shifting blame beyond the facts: Genesis 3:13.
  • Credited the Lord at the birth of Cain: Genesis 4:1.
  • Credited God's appointment at the birth of Seth, after losing two sons in one day: Genesis 4:25.

What They Did Wrong

  • Ate the forbidden fruit and gave it to her husband. Scripture explicitly treats this as transgression: Genesis 3:6; 1 Timothy 2:14.
  • Added to God's command the words "neither shall ye touch it" (Genesis 3:3), which are absent from Genesis 2:16-17. Scripture records the discrepancy without calling it sin; it is noted here as a difference in the text, not as an accusation.
  • Was deceived. Paul states this explicitly and distinguishes it from Adam's transgression: 1 Timothy 2:14; 2 Corinthians 11:3.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents Eve as both the deceived party in the first transgression and the woman through whom the promise runs. She is never condemned by name in the New Testament, though her deception is twice held up as a warning to churches. Both of her recorded utterances after the Fall acknowledge God, which is more than is recorded of Adam.

Significance

The promise of Genesis 3:15 is given with reference to her seed, and it is the first statement of redemption in Scripture. She is the mother of all living (Genesis 3:20) and therefore stands behind every genealogy in the Bible. Paul twice appeals to her experience: to establish an order of creation (1 Timothy 2:13-14) and to warn the Corinthians against subtle corruption of mind (2 Corinthians 11:3).

Death / Outcome

Scripture does not record her death. Last mention: 2 Corinthians 11:3.

Scripture References

Genesis 2:18-25; Genesis 3:1-24; Genesis 4:1-2, 4:25; 2 Corinthians 11:3; 1 Timothy 2:13-14
130

Cain

Firstborn son of Adam and Eve; a tiller of the ground; the first murderer.

Family

Son of Adam and Eve (Genesis 4:1); brother of Abel and Seth. Married; his wife is unnamed and her origin is not stated (Genesis 4:17). Father of Enoch (Genesis 4:17).

Chronology

Primeval; born after the expulsion from Eden, before AM 130. No dates recorded.

Life Synopsis

Brought an offering of the fruit of the ground, which the Lord did not respect (Genesis 4:3–5). Warned directly by God that sin lay at the door and could be mastered (Genesis 4:7). Killed his brother Abel in the field, then denied it: "I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?" (Genesis 4:8–9). Sentenced to be a fugitive; given a protective mark (Genesis 4:11–15). Departed from the Lord's presence, built a city, named it after his son (Genesis 4:16–17).

What They Did Right

  • Brought an offering to the Lord of the fruit of the ground: Genesis 4:3. Scripture records the act but states that the Lord did not respect it, and 1 John 3:12 says his works were evil. It is recorded conduct, not a commendation.
  • Beyond this, no specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Was wroth and his countenance fell when his offering was not respected, after God had reasoned with him directly: Genesis 4:5-7.
  • Murdered his brother Abel. The text notes he first talked with him, indicating premeditation: Genesis 4:8.
  • Lied to God and answered with contempt: "I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?": Genesis 4:9.
  • Explicitly condemned in the New Testament: he was "of that wicked one," and woe is pronounced on those who go in his way: 1 John 3:12; Jude 1:11.

Character Assessment

Condemned. His works were evil (1 John 3:12); woe is pronounced on those who go "in the way of Cain" (Jude 1:11). No repentance is recorded — his reply in Genesis 4:13 laments the sentence, not the sin.

Significance

Cain is the first person born of a woman, the first murderer, and the head of a line that Genesis 4 traces to Lamech's boast of vengeance. He is Scripture's first case of a warning given directly by God and refused (Genesis 4:6-7), and the New Testament uses him three times as a negative pattern.

Death / Outcome

Scripture does not record his death. Last mention: Jude 1:11.

Scripture References

Genesis 4:1–17, 4:25; Hebrews 11:4; 1 John 3:12; Jude 1:11.
130

Abel

Second son of Adam and Eve; a keeper of sheep; the first person murdered and the first declared righteous.

Family

Son of Adam and Eve; younger brother of Cain (Genesis 4:2). No wife or children are mentioned.

Chronology

Primeval; died before AM 130. No dates recorded.

Life Synopsis

Brought the firstlings of his flock and their fat, and the Lord respected his offering (Genesis 4:4). Murdered by Cain (Genesis 4:8); his blood is said to cry from the ground (Genesis 4:10).

What They Did Right

  • Brought the firstlings of his flock and the fat - both the first and the best: Genesis 4:4.
  • Offered by faith a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, and obtained witness that he was righteous: Hebrews 11:4.
  • Called "righteous Abel" by Christ: Matthew 23:35.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. This is an absence of record, not a claim of sinlessness.

Character Assessment

Commended without qualification. He offered "by faith... a more excellent sacrifice" and obtained witness that he was righteous (Hebrews 11:4); Jesus calls him "righteous Abel" (Matthew 23:35). Nothing negative is recorded.

Significance

Abel is the first person in Scripture declared righteous, the first martyr, and the first entry in the roll of faith after creation. Christ measures the whole span of shed innocent blood from Abel onward (Matthew 23:35; Luke 11:51). Hebrews sets his blood against the blood of Christ, which "speaketh better things than that of Abel" (Hebrews 12:24).

Death / Outcome

Murdered by Cain in the field (Genesis 4:8); his blood is said to cry from the ground (Genesis 4:10). Last mention: Hebrews 12:24.

Scripture References

Genesis 4:2–11, 4:25; Matthew 23:35; Luke 11:51; Hebrews 11:4; Hebrews 12:24; 1 John 3:12.
—

Lamech (of the line of Cain)

Fifth from Cain; the first polygamist recorded in Scripture. Distinct from Lamech the father of Noah.

Family

Son of Methusael, fifth in descent from Cain through Enoch, Irad, Mehujael, and Methusael (Genesis 4:17-18). Husband of Adah and Zillah (Genesis 4:19). Father of Jabal, Jubal, Tubal-cain, and Naamah (Genesis 4:20-22).

Chronology

Primeval, pre-Flood. Undatable — the Cainite line carries no ages and no synchronism with Genesis 5.

Life Synopsis

Took two wives, Adah and Zillah (Genesis 4:19). Boasted to them of killing a man who had wounded him, and claimed a vengeance seventy-sevenfold — escalating the sevenfold protection God had given Cain into a personal warrant (Genesis 4:23–24).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Took two wives - the first polygamy recorded in Scripture. Genesis records it without explicit condemnation, but it stands against the pattern of Genesis 2:24, which Christ affirms in Matthew 19:4-6.
  • Boasted to his wives of killing a man for wounding him: Genesis 4:23.
  • Claimed a vengeance seventy-sevenfold for himself, escalating the sevenfold protection God had granted Cain into a personal warrant: Genesis 4:24 compared with Genesis 4:15.

Character Assessment

Nothing commendable is recorded. Genesis reports the polygamy and the boast without explicit condemnation, but the boast is self-evidently a celebration of vengeance, and it stands against the pattern of Genesis 2:24.

Significance

Lamech's boast is the only extended speech recorded from the line of Cain, and Genesis places it as the culmination of that line immediately before returning to Seth and the note that men began to call upon the name of the Lord (Genesis 4:26). The structure sets self-exalting vengeance against the beginning of worship.

Death / Outcome

Scripture does not record his death. Last mention: Genesis 4:24.

Scripture References

Genesis 4:18–24.
—

Adah (wife of Lamech)

One of the two wives of Lamech the Cainite; mother of Jabal and Jubal. Not to be confused with Adah the Hittite wife of Esau (Genesis 36:2), a different woman in a later period.

Family

Wife of Lamech, descendant of Cain (Genesis 4:19); mother of Jabal and Jubal (Genesis 4:20-21).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. The Cainite line carries no ages and no synchronism with the line of Seth, so no chronological placement is possible beyond the pre-Flood period.

Life Synopsis

Scripture records that Lamech took her as one of two wives, that she bore Jabal and Jubal, and that Lamech addressed her by name in his boast about killing a man (Genesis 4:19-23). No words or actions of her own are recorded.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture offers no evaluation of her. She is included because the text records her name, her marriage, her two named sons, and her being addressed directly by name - substantially more than a bare genealogical listing.

Significance

Named as one of the two wives in the first polygamous marriage recorded in Scripture, and mother of the man Genesis credits with originating tent-dwelling and cattle-keeping.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 4:23.

Scripture References

Genesis 4:19-23
—

Zillah

The second wife of Lamech the Cainite; mother of Tubal-cain and Naamah.

Family

Wife of Lamech, descendant of Cain (Genesis 4:19); mother of Tubal-cain and of Naamah (Genesis 4:22).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. As with the whole Cainite line, no ages or synchronisms are given.

Life Synopsis

Scripture records that Lamech took her as his second wife, that she bore Tubal-cain and Naamah, and that Lamech addressed her by name in his boast (Genesis 4:19-23). No words or actions of her own are recorded.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture offers no evaluation of her. She is included on the same basis as Adah: named, married, mother of two named children, and addressed directly by name.

Significance

Mother of Tubal-cain, whom Genesis credits with instructing every artificer in brass and iron, and of Naamah, the only daughter named in the Cainite genealogy.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 4:23.

Scripture References

Genesis 4:19-23
—

Jabal

Son of Lamech by Adah; originator of pastoral nomadism — "the father of such as dwell in tents, and of such as have cattle."

Family

Son of Lamech by Adah; brother of Jubal; half-brother of Tubal-cain and Naamah (Genesis 4:20-22).

Chronology

Primeval, pre-Flood. Undatable.

Life Synopsis

Genesis 4:20, in a single clause.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. Scripture records his cultural achievement without moral evaluation.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the achievement and attaches no moral verdict, favourable or otherwise.

Significance

Named as the originator of a whole way of life - tent-dwelling and cattle-keeping - which becomes the manner of life of the patriarchs themselves.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 4:20.

Scripture References

Genesis 4:20.
—

Jubal

Son of Lamech by Adah; brother of Jabal; originator of music — "the father of all such as handle the harp and organ."

Family

Son of Lamech by Adah; brother of Jabal (Genesis 4:21).

Chronology

Primeval, pre-Flood. Undatable.

Life Synopsis

Genesis 4:21, in a single clause.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. His achievement is recorded without evaluation.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered.

Significance

Named as the originator of music, an art that later fills the worship of Israel.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 4:21.

Scripture References

Genesis 4:21.
—

Tubal-cain

Son of Lamech by Zillah; the first metalworker — "an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron."

Family

Son of Lamech by Zillah; brother of Naamah; half-brother of Jabal and Jubal (Genesis 4:22).

Chronology

Primeval, pre-Flood. Undatable.

Life Synopsis

Genesis 4:22. Note that he is recorded as a teacher of the craft, not merely a practitioner.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered.

Significance

Named as the first metalworker and, notably, as a teacher of the craft rather than merely a practitioner.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 4:22.

Scripture References

Genesis 4:22.
130

Seth

Third named son of Adam and Eve; head of the line through which the genealogy runs to Noah and ultimately to Christ.

Also called Sheth

Family

Son of Adam and Eve (Genesis 4:25); father of Enos (Genesis 5:6) and of unnamed sons and daughters (Genesis 5:7).

Chronology

Born Anno Mundi 130, when Adam was 130 (Genesis 5:3); died Anno Mundi 1042. Scripture explicitly states that he lived 912 years (Genesis 5:8).

Life Synopsis

Seth was born after Abel's murder, and Eve named him with the words, "For God, said she, hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel, whom Cain slew" (Genesis 4:25). Adam begat him "in his own likeness, after his image" (Genesis 5:3) - a statement about human transmission after the Fall rather than a comment on Seth. He fathered Enos, and the note follows immediately: "then began men to call upon the name of the Lord" (Genesis 4:26). He lived 912 years and died.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. What Scripture records is his position rather than his conduct. The clause about men beginning to call upon the name of the Lord (Genesis 4:26) has "men" as its subject, not Seth, and this reference does not credit him with an act the text does not attribute to him.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture assesses Seth by his place in the line rather than by anything he did. He is included in the genealogy of Christ (Luke 3:38) and heads the Chronicler's list after Adam (1 Chronicles 1:1).

Significance

The line of promise runs through Seth rather than Cain, and the genealogy of Genesis 5, of 1 Chronicles 1, and of Luke 3 all pass through him.

Death / Outcome

"And all the days of Seth were nine hundred and twelve years: and he died" (Genesis 5:8).

Scripture References

Genesis 4:25-26; Genesis 5:3-8; 1 Chronicles 1:1; Luke 3:38
235

Enos

A man of the line of Seth; fourth from Adam.

Also called Enosh

Family

Son of Seth; father of Cainan and of unnamed sons and daughters.

Chronology

Born Anno Mundi 235, died Anno Mundi 1140 by calculation from Genesis 5. Scripture explicitly states that he lived 90 years before fathering Cainan, and 905 years in all.

Life Synopsis

Scripture records of him only his place in the line, his age at the birth of Cainan, the further years he lived, and his death. Genesis 4:26 attaches to his birth the note that "then began men to call upon the name of the Lord," but the subject of that clause is men generally, and the text does not specify what part, if any, Enos took in it.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture offers no evaluation of his character. He is included because the text records substantive chronological information about his life - his age at fatherhood and his total lifespan - which is more than a bare name, and which forms part of the chronological framework of the primeval period.

Significance

A link in the line from Adam through Seth to Noah, and so in the genealogy of Christ (Luke 3:36-38).

Death / Outcome

"And all the days of Enos were 905 years: and he died" (Genesis 5).

Scripture References

Genesis 5; 1 Chronicles 1:1-3; Luke 3:36-38

Jared

A man of the line of Seth; seventh from Adam.

Family

Son of Mahalaleel; father of Enoch and of unnamed sons and daughters.

Chronology

Born Anno Mundi 460, died Anno Mundi 1422 by calculation from Genesis 5. Scripture explicitly states that he lived 162 years before fathering Enoch, and 962 years in all.

Life Synopsis

Scripture records of him only his place in the line, his age at the birth of Enoch, the further years he lived, and his death. He is the father of Enoch, but Scripture does not credit him with Enoch's walk with God, and neither does this reference. His 962 years are the second-longest lifespan recorded in Scripture.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture offers no evaluation of his character. He is included because the text records substantive chronological information about his life - his age at fatherhood and his total lifespan - which is more than a bare name, and which forms part of the chronological framework of the primeval period.

Significance

A link in the line from Adam through Seth to Noah, and so in the genealogy of Christ (Luke 3:36-38).

Death / Outcome

"And all the days of Jared were 962 years: and he died" (Genesis 5).

622

Enoch (son of Jared)

Seventh from Adam; prophet; the man who did not die. Distinct from Enoch the son of Cain.

Family

Son of Jared (Genesis 5:18); father of Methuselah (Genesis 5:21) and of unnamed sons and daughters (Genesis 5:22); great-grandfather of Noah.

Chronology

Primeval. Born AM 622, translated AM 987 [traditional: 3382–3017 BC]. 365 years on earth — the shortest span in Genesis 5, and the only one not ending "and he died."

Life Synopsis

Walked with God three hundred years, the phrase repeated for emphasis (Genesis 5:22, 5:24). Taken by God without dying (Genesis 5:24; Hebrews 11:5). Prophesied of coming judgment on the ungodly (Jude 1:14–15).

What They Did Right

  • Walked with God three hundred years - the phrase is stated twice: Genesis 5:22, 5:24.
  • Pleased God, and had that testimony before his translation: Hebrews 11:5.
  • Was translated by faith so that he did not see death: Hebrews 11:5.
  • Prophesied of the Lord's coming in judgment on the ungodly: Jude 1:14-15.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Commended without qualification. He "pleased God" before his translation (Hebrews 11:5). One of only two men in Scripture recorded as not having died.

Significance

One of only two men in Scripture who did not die (with Elijah, 2 Kings 2:11). His translation stands in the middle of a genealogy whose refrain is "and he died," and it is the first indication in Scripture that death is not necessarily the end of a man's walk with God. Jude preserves his prophecy, the earliest recorded prophecy in Scripture.

Death / Outcome

He did not die: "and he was not; for God took him" (Genesis 5:24). Last mention: Jude 1:14-15.

Scripture References

Genesis 5:18–24; 1 Chronicles 1:3; Luke 3:37; Hebrews 11:5; Jude 1:14–15.
687

Methuselah

A man of the line of Seth; ninth from Adam.

Also called Mathusala

Family

Son of Enoch; father of Lamech and of unnamed sons and daughters.

Chronology

Born Anno Mundi 687, died Anno Mundi 1656 by calculation from Genesis 5. Scripture explicitly states that he lived 187 years before fathering Lamech, and 969 years in all.

Life Synopsis

Scripture records of him only his place in the line, his age at the birth of Lamech, the further years he lived, and his death. His 969 years are the longest lifespan recorded in the Bible. By the arithmetic of Genesis 5 his death falls in the year of the Flood, but Scripture does not state whether he died before it or in it, and popular expositions that attach meaning to his name or to this coincidence go beyond the text.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture offers no evaluation of his character. He is included because the text records substantive chronological information about his life - his age at fatherhood and his total lifespan - which is more than a bare name, and which forms part of the chronological framework of the primeval period.

Significance

A link in the line from Adam through Seth to Noah, and so in the genealogy of Christ (Luke 3:36-38).

Death / Outcome

"And all the days of Methuselah were 969 years: and he died" (Genesis 5).

Scripture References

Genesis 5; 1 Chronicles 1:1-3; Luke 3:36-38

Lamech (father of Noah)

Son of Methuselah; father of Noah. Not to be confused with Lamech of the line of Cain.

Family

Son of Methuselah (Genesis 5:25); father of Noah (Genesis 5:28-29) and of unnamed sons and daughters (Genesis 5:30).

Chronology

Born Anno Mundi 874, died Anno Mundi 1651 by calculation - five years before the Flood. Scripture explicitly states that he lived 777 years (Genesis 5:31).

Life Synopsis

Lamech's whole recorded life is one sentence of speech. Naming his son Noah, he said, "This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands, because of the ground which the Lord hath cursed" (Genesis 5:29). He lived 777 years and died.

What They Did Right

  • Named his son with a statement acknowledging the curse on the ground and expressing hope of comfort from it: Genesis 5:29. This appears to indicate awareness of the judgment of Genesis 3:17 and some expectation of relief. Scripture does not label it faith, and neither does this reference.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture offers no direct evaluation. His single recorded utterance is notable for connecting his own generation back to the curse pronounced in Eden, which no one else in Genesis 5 does.

Significance

Father of Noah, and so in the line through which the human race was preserved and through which the genealogy of Christ runs (Luke 3:36).

Death / Outcome

"And all the days of Lamech were seven hundred seventy and seven years: and he died" (Genesis 5:31).

Scripture References

Genesis 5:25-31; 1 Chronicles 1:3; Luke 3:36
1056

Noah

Tenth from Adam; the man through whom the human race and the land animals were preserved through the Flood; the second head of humanity.

Also called Noe

Family

Son of Lamech (Genesis 5:28-29); grandson of Methuselah. His wife is unnamed (Genesis 6:18). Father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth (Genesis 5:32). Eight persons in all were preserved (1 Peter 3:20; 2 Peter 2:5).

Chronology

Born Anno Mundi 1056; 600 years old when the flood came (Genesis 7:6, 7:11); lived 350 years after it; died at 950 (Genesis 9:28-29). Those ages are explicitly stated in Scripture; the Anno Mundi figures are calculated from Genesis 5. Traditional Ussher equivalent 2948-1998 BC.

Life Synopsis

Noah was named by his father Lamech with a hope attached: "This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands, because of the ground which the Lord hath cursed" (Genesis 5:29). He appears in a generation the text describes as filled with violence and corruption, and against that background Scripture says simply, "But Noah found grace in the eyes of the Lord" (Genesis 6:8). He is called "a just man and perfect in his generations," and one who "walked with God" (Genesis 6:9).

God revealed his purpose to destroy the earth and commanded Noah to build an ark to precise specifications (Genesis 6:13-21). Twice the record states his obedience in almost identical words: "Thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he" (Genesis 6:22), and "Noah did according unto all that the Lord commanded him" (Genesis 7:5). Peter adds that he was "a preacher of righteousness" (2 Peter 2:5), and Hebrews that he acted "moved with fear," and by doing so "condemned the world" (Hebrews 11:7).

In his six hundredth year the fountains of the great deep were broken up (Genesis 7:11). He entered the ark with his household and the animals, and the Lord shut him in (Genesis 7:16). After the waters abated he sent out a raven and then a dove three times, reading the state of the earth by what returned (Genesis 8:6-12). On leaving the ark his first recorded act was to build an altar and offer burnt offerings (Genesis 8:20). God responded with the covenant never again to destroy the earth by water, and set the rainbow as its token (Genesis 9:8-17).

Afterward Noah became a husbandman and planted a vineyard. He drank of the wine, was drunken, and lay uncovered in his tent (Genesis 9:20-21). Ham saw and told; Shem and Japheth covered him walking backward (Genesis 9:22-23). On waking he pronounced a curse on Canaan and blessings involving Shem and Japheth (Genesis 9:24-27). He lived 350 years after the flood and died at 950 (Genesis 9:28-29).

What They Did Right

  • Found grace in the eyes of the Lord: Genesis 6:8.
  • Described by God's own record as just, perfect in his generations, and a man who walked with God: Genesis 6:9.
  • Obeyed God's instructions completely, a point the text makes twice: Genesis 6:22; Genesis 7:5.
  • Built an altar and offered burnt offerings immediately on leaving the ark, before any other recorded act: Genesis 8:20.
  • Acted by faith, moved with fear, and became heir of the righteousness which is by faith: Hebrews 11:7.
  • Named by God through Ezekiel, with Daniel and Job, as a byword for personal righteousness: Ezekiel 14:14, 14:20.
  • Called a preacher of righteousness: 2 Peter 2:5.

What They Did Wrong

  • Became drunk on wine from his own vineyard and lay uncovered within his tent: Genesis 9:20-21. Scripture records this plainly but does not explicitly condemn him for it, and does not state whether he understood the effect of the wine. It is a recorded failure whose moral weight the text leaves unstated, and it should not be pressed further than that.

Character Assessment

One of the strongest character commendations in the Old Testament. Every reference to Noah outside Genesis is positive - two in Ezekiel, four in the New Testament - and the drunkenness is never mentioned again in Scripture. Yet Genesis records that failure without softening it, immediately after his greatest deliverance. The honesty of that juxtaposition is characteristic of the biblical record.

Significance

Noah is the second head of humanity; every person alive descends from him and his three sons (Genesis 9:19). The Noahic covenant, with the rainbow as its sign, is the first covenant in Scripture given with an outward token, and it underwrites the stability of the natural order (Genesis 8:22, 9:8-17). Christ uses the days of Noah as the pattern of the world's condition at his coming (Matthew 24:37-38; Luke 17:26-27), and Peter draws from the ark a figure of salvation (1 Peter 3:20-21).

Death / Outcome

Died at 950 years (Genesis 9:29). Last mention: 2 Peter 2:5.

Scripture References

Genesis 5:28-32; Genesis 6:8-22; Genesis 7:1-24; Genesis 8:1-22; Genesis 9:1-29; 1 Chronicles 1:4; Isaiah 54:9; Ezekiel 14:14, 14:20; Matthew 24:37-38; Luke 3:36; Luke 17:26-27; Hebrews 11:7; 1 Peter 3:20; 2 Peter 2:5

Japheth

Son of Noah; ancestor of the peoples of Genesis 10:2–5.

Family

Son of Noah (Genesis 5:32); brother of Shem and Ham. Married; his wife is unnamed and entered the ark (Genesis 7:13). Father of Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras (Genesis 10:2).

Chronology

Born c. AM 1556. No age, lifespan, or death recorded. Genesis 10:21's "Japheth the elder" is ambiguous in the KJV — it may modify Japheth or Shem, and translations differ.

Life Synopsis

With Shem, covered his father's nakedness (Genesis 9:23). Received Noah's blessing: "God shall enlarge Japheth" (Genesis 9:27). Father of seven named sons (Genesis 10:2).

What They Did Right

  • With Shem, covered his father's nakedness, walking backward so as not to look upon him: Genesis 9:23.
  • Received his father's blessing: "God shall enlarge Japheth": Genesis 9:27.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Positive so far as the record goes; blessed rather than cursed, and nothing negative is recorded.

Significance

Ancestor of the peoples listed in Genesis 10:2-5, spread across "the isles of the Gentiles" (Genesis 10:5). Noah's blessing that he would dwell in the tents of Shem has long been read as anticipating Gentile inclusion in the blessings of Shem's line, though Genesis does not state this.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Chronicles 1:5.

Scripture References

Genesis 5:32; Genesis 7:13; Genesis 9:18–27; Genesis 10:1–5; 1 Chronicles 1:4–5.

Shem

Son of Noah; ancestor of the line running to Abraham. Called "Sem" in Luke 3:36.

Family

Son of Noah (Genesis 5:32); brother of Ham and Japheth. Married; his wife is unnamed (Genesis 7:13). Father of Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, and Aram (Genesis 10:22). Called "the father of all the children of Eber" (Genesis 10:21).

Chronology

Born AM 1558 (fixed by Genesis 11:10 — aged 100 two years after the Flood); lived 600 years, dying AM 2158, after Abraham's birth.

Life Synopsis

With Japheth, covered his father's nakedness walking backward so as not to look (Genesis 9:23). Received Noah's pronouncement, framed as praise to God: "Blessed be the Lord God of Shem" (Genesis 9:26). Father of Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, and Aram (Genesis 10:22).

What They Did Right

  • With Japheth, covered his father's nakedness without looking upon him: Genesis 9:23.
  • Received the most emphatic of Noah's pronouncements, framed as praise to God: "Blessed be the Lord God of Shem": Genesis 9:26.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Positive. His one recorded action is honourable; nothing negative is recorded.

Significance

The covenant line runs through Shem to Abraham and to Christ (Genesis 11:10-26; Luke 3:36). Noah's pronouncement over him is framed as a blessing of the Lord himself, which distinguishes it from the words over his brothers.

Death / Outcome

Scripture does not narrate his death, but Genesis 11:10-11 fixes his lifespan at 600 years. Last mention: Luke 3:36.

Scripture References

Genesis 5:32; Genesis 7:13; Genesis 9:18–27; Genesis 10:21–31; Genesis 11:10–11; 1 Chronicles 1:17, 1:24; Luke 3:36.

Ham

Son of Noah, called his "younger son"; father of Cush, Mizraim, Phut, and Canaan.

Family

Son of Noah, called his "younger son" (Genesis 9:24). Married; his wife is unnamed (Genesis 7:13). Father of Cush, Mizraim, Phut, and Canaan (Genesis 10:6).

Chronology

Born c. AM 1556. No age, lifespan, or death recorded.

Life Synopsis

Saw his father's nakedness and told his two brothers outside rather than covering it (Genesis 9:22).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. He entered the ark and was preserved (Genesis 7:13), but the text presents this as God's provision through Noah rather than as a commendation of Ham.

What They Did Wrong

  • Saw his father's nakedness and told his two brothers outside rather than covering it: Genesis 9:22. Scripture presents this as wrong by the contrast immediately drawn with Shem and Japheth (Genesis 9:23) and by the pronouncement that follows. Genesis does not state what he did beyond seeing and telling, and interpretations that go further are inference, not text.

Character Assessment

Negative on the single episode where his conduct is described, by the contrast Genesis draws with his brothers' conduct. Genesis does not state what he did beyond seeing and telling, and readings that go further are inference. The curse of Genesis 9:25 falls on Canaan, not on Ham — Scripture nowhere curses Ham or his other three sons.

Significance

Ancestor of the peoples of Genesis 10:6-20, including Egypt, which the Psalms call "the land of Ham" (Psalms 105:23). It must be stated plainly that the curse of Genesis 9:25 falls on Canaan, and that Scripture nowhere curses Ham or his other three sons. Readings that extend it further have no basis in the text.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention as the man: 1 Chronicles 1:8.

Scripture References

Genesis 5:32; Genesis 7:13; Genesis 9:18–27; Genesis 10:1, 10:6–20; 1 Chronicles 1:4, 1:8.

Canaan

Son of Ham; ancestor of the Canaanite peoples; the man on whom Noah's curse fell.

Family

Son of Ham (Genesis 9:18; Genesis 10:6); grandson of Noah. Father of Sidon his firstborn and of Heth, and progenitor of the Jebusite, Amorite, Girgasite, Hivite, Arkite, Sinite, Arvadite, Zemarite, and Hamathite peoples (Genesis 10:15-18).

Chronology

Post-Flood. No dates recorded.

Life Synopsis

Cursed by Noah: "Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be unto his brethren" (Genesis 9:25), repeated as servitude to Shem and Japheth (Genesis 9:26–27). Father of Sidon his firstborn, Heth, and the peoples of Genesis 10:15–18.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. This deserves emphasis: Scripture records the curse pronounced on him (Genesis 9:25) but attributes the offending act to his father (Genesis 9:22). The text does not specify why the curse fell on the son. Proposed explanations are numerous and none is stated in Scripture; this reference supplies none.

Character Assessment

Nothing is recorded that Canaan himself did. The offending act is attributed to his father (Genesis 9:22), and Scripture does not state why the curse fell on the son. Explanations are numerous and none is biblical.

Significance

Head of the nations later dispossessed from the land promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18-21). The curse of servitude pronounced over him is the first statement of the relation between Israel and the Canaanite peoples.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Chronicles 1:13.

Scripture References

Genesis 9:18, 9:22, 9:25–27; Genesis 10:6, 10:15–19; 1 Chronicles 1:8, 1:13.

Nimrod

Son of Cush; "a mighty one in the earth"; founder of a kingdom in Shinar.

Family

Son of Cush (Genesis 10:8; 1 Chronicles 1:10); grandson of Ham; great-grandson of Noah. No wife or children are named.

Chronology

Post-Flood, plausibly the era of Babel. Undatable — no ages or lifespan recorded.

Life Synopsis

Described as "a mighty hunter before the Lord" (Genesis 10:9). His kingdom began with Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh in Shinar (Genesis 10:10). Micah 5:6 calls Assyria "the land of Nimrod."

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. This needs saying plainly, because a great deal of tradition attaches to Nimrod that Genesis does not support. The text does not say he built the tower of Babel, does not call him a rebel or a tyrant, and does not condemn him. The phrase "a mighty hunter before the Lord" (Genesis 10:9) can be read as commendation or as defiance, and the King James rendering does not settle it. Material from Josephus and from later writers is extra-biblical and is not used here.

Character Assessment

Scripture records no wrongdoing. This needs saying plainly, because tradition supplies a great deal that Genesis does not: the text does not say he built the tower, does not call him a rebel or a tyrant, and does not condemn him. The phrase "before the Lord" can be read as commendation or defiance, and the KJV does not settle it.

Significance

The first man in Scripture described as building a kingdom, and the founder of Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh in Shinar (Genesis 10:10). Assyria is later called "the land of Nimrod" (Micah 5:6). He is the only person in the Table of Nations given a narrative aside.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Micah 5:6.

Scripture References

Genesis 10:8–12; 1 Chronicles 1:10; Micah 5:6.

Peleg

A man of the line of Shem in the generations after the Flood.

Family

Son of Eber; father of Reu and of unnamed sons and daughters.

Chronology

Born Anno Mundi 1757, died Anno Mundi 1996 by calculation from Genesis 11. Scripture explicitly states that he was 30 when he fathered Reu and lived 209 years afterward; the total of 239 years is obtained by addition and is not itself stated in the text.

Life Synopsis

Scripture records of him his place in the line, his age at the birth of Reu, and the years he lived afterward. One substantive statement is made about him, and it is made twice: "in his days was the earth divided" (Genesis 10:25; 1 Chronicles 1:19). Scripture does not specify what this division was. It is commonly connected with the scattering of the nations at Babel (Genesis 11:8-9), which is a reasonable reading given the context, but Genesis does not make the connection explicitly and other explanations have been proposed. The uncertainty lies in the biblical text itself, not merely in later reconstruction.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture offers no evaluation of his character. He is included because the text records substantive chronological information about his life, which is more than a bare name in a list.

Significance

The one recorded fact about him - that in his days the earth was divided - is the only chronological handle Scripture gives for dating the dispersion of the nations, and it is an uncertain one. A link in the line from Shem to Abraham, and so in the genealogy of Christ (Luke 3:34-36).

Death / Outcome

Scripture does not narrate his death, but his lifespan is calculable from Genesis 11.

Terah

Son of Nahor; father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran; began the migration from Ur.

Family

Son of Nahor (Genesis 11:24). Father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran (Genesis 11:26-27); grandfather of Lot, Milcah, and Iscah. His wife is not named in Genesis.

Chronology

Born AM 1878, died in Haran aged 205 [traditional: 2126–1921 BC].

Life Synopsis

Took Abram, Lot, and Sarai from Ur of the Chaldees intending Canaan, but settled in Haran (Genesis 11:31). Died there (Genesis 11:32).

What They Did Right

  • Took Abram, Lot, and Sarai from Ur of the Chaldees with Canaan as the stated destination: Genesis 11:31. The text records the action without commending it, and Acts 7:2-4 indicates the call came to Abram before Haran, so the relative agency is not spelled out.

What They Did Wrong

  • Served other gods. This is Scripture's one explicit evaluation of him, and it is negative: Joshua 24:2.
  • Settled in Haran rather than continuing to Canaan, though Canaan was the stated destination: Genesis 11:31. Scripture does not explicitly call this a failure, and does not state whether it was disobedience, prudence, or circumstance. The moral status is uncertain and is left so here.

Character Assessment

Scripture's one direct verdict is negative: he "served other gods" (Joshua 24:2). Whether stopping short of Canaan was disobedience, prudence, or circumstance, the text does not specify. Acts 7:2–4 indicates God's call came to Abram before Haran, which bears on whose migration it was. He stands in the genealogy of Christ (Luke 3:34).

Significance

Terah stands at the hinge between the postdiluvian genealogy and the call of Abraham, and in the genealogy of Christ (Luke 3:34). His migration begins the movement toward Canaan that his son completes.

Death / Outcome

Died in Haran at 205 years (Genesis 11:32). Last mention: Luke 3:34.

Scripture References

Genesis 11:24–32; Genesis 12:1–5; Joshua 24:2; 1 Chronicles 1:26; Luke 3:34; Acts 7:2–4.

Died in Ur before his father, i.e. before AM 2083. No dates recorded.

Life Synopsis

"And Haran died before his father Terah in the land of his nativity, in Ur of the Chaldees" (Genesis 11:28) — the first son in Scripture recorded as predeceasing his father.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No evaluation is offered.

Significance

Through his son Lot he is the ancestor of Moab and Ammon, and through his daughter Milcah the grandfather of Bethuel and great-grandfather of Rebekah. His death is the first instance in Scripture of a son predeceasing his father.

Death / Outcome

"And Haran died before his father Terah in the land of his nativity, in Ur of the Chaldees" (Genesis 11:28).

Scripture References

Genesis 11:26–31. --- ## PATRIARCHAL PERIOD (Genesis 12–50) Dates in this period rest on the traditional anchor and on the Genesis 11:26 / Genesis 12:4 / Acts 7:4 harmonization that places Abram's birth in Terah's 130th year. All are approximate.

The Patriarchal Period

2008

Abraham

Called out of Ur of the Chaldees; the man to whom God gave the covenant of promise; called the friend of God and the father of all them that believe.

Also called Abram

Family

Son of Terah (Genesis 11:26-27); brother of Nahor and Haran; uncle of Lot. Husband of Sarah, who was also his half-sister, the daughter of his father but not of his mother (Genesis 20:12). Father of Ishmael by Hagar (Genesis 16:15), of Isaac by Sarah (Genesis 21:2-3), and of six sons by Keturah (Genesis 25:1-2).

Chronology

Born Anno Mundi 2008 by calculation; 75 when he departed Haran (Genesis 12:4); 86 at Ishmael's birth (Genesis 16:16); 99 at the covenant of circumcision (Genesis 17:1); 100 at Isaac's birth (Genesis 21:5); died at 175 (Genesis 25:7). The ages are explicitly stated; the Anno Mundi figure depends on reading Genesis 11:26 as a summary, since Genesis 11:32 with Genesis 12:4 and Acts 7:4 require his birth in Terah's 130th year rather than his 70th.

Life Synopsis

God appeared to Abram in Mesopotamia before he dwelt in Haran (Acts 7:2-3) and called him to leave his country, kindred, and father's house for a land he would be shown, with the promise that in him all families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:1-3). He departed Haran at 75, taking Sarai and Lot (Genesis 12:4-5). In Canaan he built altars at Sichem and between Bethel and Hai (Genesis 12:7-8).

A famine drove him to Egypt, where he told Sarai to say she was his sister. Pharaoh took her, was plagued, and sent them away with a rebuke (Genesis 12:10-20). Back in Canaan, strife between herdsmen led Abram to give Lot first choice of the land - the generous act of the weaker claim (Genesis 13:8-9). When Lot was carried off by four kings, Abram armed 318 trained servants, pursued to Hobah, and recovered everyone and everything (Genesis 14:14-16). Returning, he was met by Melchizedek and gave him tithes of all, and refused every thread of the king of Sodom's goods (Genesis 14:18-23).

God brought him out to number the stars, and "he believed in the Lord; and he counted it to him for righteousness" (Genesis 15:5-6) - the verse on which Paul builds the doctrine of justification by faith. Yet at Sarai's suggestion he took Hagar, and Ishmael was born (Genesis 16:1-4, 16:15). At 99 God confirmed the covenant, changed his name from Abram to Abraham, and gave circumcision as its token (Genesis 17:1-14). He interceded for Sodom, pressing from fifty righteous down to ten (Genesis 18:23-33). He repeated the sister deception with Abimelech and was again rebuked by a pagan king (Genesis 20:2-10).

Isaac was born when he was 100 (Genesis 21:5). Then came the hardest command: to offer Isaac as a burnt offering in the land of Moriah. He rose early, went three days' journey, bound his son, and stretched out his hand with the knife before the angel of the Lord stopped him (Genesis 22:1-12). He named the place Jehovah-jireh (Genesis 22:14). He buried Sarah in the cave of Machpelah, which he bought rather than accepted as a gift (Genesis 23:3-20), sent his eldest servant to find a wife for Isaac (Genesis 24:1-9), took Keturah, gave all he had to Isaac, and died at 175, "in a good old age, an old man, and full of years" (Genesis 25:7-8).

What They Did Right

  • Obeyed the call to leave his country for an unnamed land: Genesis 12:1-4; Hebrews 11:8.
  • Believed God's promise, and it was counted to him for righteousness: Genesis 15:6; Romans 4:3, 4:20-22; Galatians 3:6.
  • Gave Lot the first choice of the land, surrendering his own advantage to end strife: Genesis 13:8-9.
  • Risked himself to rescue Lot with a small force: Genesis 14:14-16.
  • Gave tithes to Melchizedek and refused any share of Sodom's spoil, so that no man could say he had made Abram rich: Genesis 14:20-23.
  • Interceded persistently for Sodom: Genesis 18:23-33.
  • Obeyed in offering Isaac, accounting that God was able to raise him up: Genesis 22:1-12; Hebrews 11:17-19; James 2:21-23.
  • Paid the full price for Sarah's burial place rather than take it as a gift: Genesis 23:12-16.

What They Did Wrong

  • Told Sarai to say she was his sister in Egypt, exposing her to Pharaoh's household to protect himself: Genesis 12:11-13. Scripture records Pharaoh's rebuke without recording any defence by Abram.
  • Repeated the same deception with Abimelech years later, and was rebuked again: Genesis 20:2-11. Abimelech's words - "thou hast done deeds unto me that ought not to be done" - are the text's clearest evaluation.
  • Took Hagar at Sarai's suggestion rather than waiting for the promise: Genesis 16:1-4. Genesis records the act and its bitter consequences without an explicit condemnation, so this is recorded conduct with evident consequences rather than a stated sin.
  • Laughed and said in his heart, "Shall a child be born unto him that is an hundred years old?": Genesis 17:17. The text does not label this unbelief, and Romans 4:19-20 says he was not weak in faith. Interpreters differ; the tension is noted rather than resolved.

Character Assessment

Scripture's assessment is high and specific: he is called the friend of God (2 Chronicles 20:7; Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23), the father of all them that believe (Romans 4:11), and the pattern case of justification by faith. It is equally plain about his fear. Twice he endangered his wife to protect himself, and the moral rebuke on both occasions came from a pagan king. Both records stand together, and neither cancels the other.

Significance

The Abrahamic covenant is the hinge of the Old Testament: land, seed, and blessing to all families of the earth (Genesis 12:1-3; Genesis 15:18-21; Genesis 17:1-8). Paul argues from Genesis 15:6 that righteousness was reckoned to Abraham by faith before circumcision and before the law, making him the father of believing Gentiles as well as Jews (Romans 4:9-17; Galatians 3:6-9). Hebrews cites him as the exemplar of pilgrim faith (Hebrews 11:8-19); James cites the offering of Isaac as faith proved by works (James 2:21-23). Christ himself says, "Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day" (John 8:56).

Death / Outcome

Died at 175, and was buried by Isaac and Ishmael together in the cave of Machpelah with Sarah (Genesis 25:7-10).

Scripture References

Genesis 11:26-25:10; 2 Chronicles 20:7; Isaiah 41:8; John 8:56; Acts 7:2-8; Romans 4:1-25; Galatians 3:6-29; Hebrews 11:8-19; James 2:21-23
2018

Sarah

Wife of Abraham; mother of Isaac; the only woman in Scripture whose age at death is recorded.

Also called Sarai

Family

Half-sister of Abraham, daughter of his father but not of his mother (Genesis 20:12). Wife of Abraham (Genesis 11:29). Mother of Isaac (Genesis 21:2-3). Mistress of Hagar (Genesis 16:1).

Chronology

Ten years younger than Abraham (Genesis 17:17); 90 at Isaac's birth (Genesis 17:17, 21:5); died at 127 (Genesis 23:1). Her age at death is explicitly stated - the only such record for a woman in Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Sarai was barren, and the text states it starkly at her introduction: "But Sarai was barren; she had no child" (Genesis 11:30). She left Ur with Terah's household and Haran with Abram (Genesis 11:31; Genesis 12:5). Twice she was taken into a foreign ruler's house on her husband's word that she was his sister - by Pharaoh in Egypt (Genesis 12:14-19) and by Abimelech in Gerar (Genesis 20:2). On both occasions God intervened to protect her.

After ten years in Canaan without a child, she gave Hagar her Egyptian handmaid to Abram, saying, "it may be that I may obtain children by her" (Genesis 16:2-3). When Hagar conceived and despised her, Sarai blamed Abram - "My wrong be upon thee" - and dealt hardly with Hagar until she fled (Genesis 16:5-6).

At 89 her name was changed from Sarai to Sarah, with the promise that she would be a mother of nations and that kings of people would be of her (Genesis 17:15-16). Hearing at the tent door that she would bear a son, she laughed within herself and then denied it out of fear, and was answered: "Is any thing too hard for the Lord?" (Genesis 18:12-15). Isaac was born at the set time, and she said, "God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me" (Genesis 21:6).

At Isaac's weaning feast she saw Ishmael mocking and demanded that Hagar and her son be cast out. The demand grieved Abraham, but God told him to hearken to her voice, "for in Isaac shall thy seed be called" (Genesis 21:9-12). She died at 127 in Hebron, and Abraham mourned and wept for her and bought Machpelah as her burying place (Genesis 23:1-20).

What They Did Right

  • Left Ur and Haran with her husband for an unknown land: Genesis 11:31; Genesis 12:5.
  • Received strength to conceive by faith, judging him faithful who had promised: Hebrews 11:11.
  • Acknowledged God at Isaac's birth rather than claiming the outcome for herself: Genesis 21:6-7.
  • Held up by Peter as an example of a holy woman's trust and conduct: 1 Peter 3:5-6.

What They Did Wrong

  • Proposed that Abram take Hagar rather than wait for the promise: Genesis 16:2. Genesis records the proposal and its consequences without an explicit condemnation.
  • Dealt hardly with Hagar so that she fled, after herself arranging the situation: Genesis 16:5-6. The text records the harshness plainly.
  • Laughed in unbelief at the promise, then denied having laughed because she was afraid: Genesis 18:12-15. The denial is the clearest recorded fault - Scripture notes both the laugh and the lie.

Character Assessment

A mixed and honest record. Scripture does not conceal the scheme with Hagar, the harshness that followed, the laugh, or the lie. Yet Hebrews places her in the roll of faith (Hebrews 11:11), Peter presents her as a pattern for believing women (1 Peter 3:5-6), and Isaiah tells Israel to look to her as the rock from which they were hewn (Isaiah 51:2). God twice defends her honour against her husband's fear, and once directs Abraham to obey her judgment (Genesis 21:12).

Significance

Isaac, the child of promise, is born of her and of no other - the covenant line is defined by her womb, not merely by Abraham's. God's naming of her as a mother of nations and of kings (Genesis 17:15-16) makes her a covenant figure in her own right. Paul builds an allegory of the two covenants on the contrast between Sarah the freewoman and Hagar the bondwoman (Galatians 4:22-31).

Death / Outcome

Died at 127 years in Kirjath-arba, that is Hebron; buried in the cave of Machpelah, the first possession Abraham owned in the land (Genesis 23:1-20).

Scripture References

Genesis 11:29-31; Genesis 12:5-20; Genesis 16:1-8; Genesis 17:15-21; Genesis 18:6-15; Genesis 20:1-18; Genesis 21:1-12; Genesis 23:1-20; Isaiah 51:2; Romans 4:19; Romans 9:9; Galatians 4:22-31; Hebrews 11:11; 1 Peter 3:5-6
—

Lot

Son of Haran and nephew of Abraham; a righteous man who settled in Sodom and lost nearly everything in its destruction.

Family

Son of Haran (Genesis 11:27); nephew of Abraham; brother of Milcah and Iscah. His wife is unnamed (Genesis 19:26). Father of two daughters, unnamed, and through them of Moab and Ben-ammi (Genesis 19:36-38).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He travelled with Terah's household from Ur (Genesis 11:31) and with Abram from Haran (Genesis 12:4-5), so his life runs parallel to Abraham's.

Life Synopsis

Lot left Ur with his grandfather Terah and Haran with Abram (Genesis 11:31; Genesis 12:5). Both men prospered until the land could not bear them and their herdsmen strove. Abram offered Lot first choice, and Lot lifted his eyes, saw the plain of Jordan well watered "even as the garden of the Lord," and chose it, pitching his tent toward Sodom (Genesis 13:5-12). The narrator immediately adds that the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners before the Lord exceedingly (Genesis 13:13). By Genesis 14 he is dwelling in Sodom; by Genesis 19 he sits in its gate.

Captured when four kings sacked the city, he was rescued by Abram (Genesis 14:12-16). When two angels came to Sodom, Lot pressed them to lodge with him rather than in the street, and made them a feast (Genesis 19:1-3). When the men of the city surrounded the house demanding them, he went out, shut the door behind him, pleaded with them not to act so wickedly - and offered them his two virgin daughters instead (Genesis 19:6-8). The angels pulled him inside and struck the crowd with blindness.

Warned to flee, he told his sons in law, "but he seemed as one that mocked" (Genesis 19:14). At dawn he lingered, and the angels took him, his wife, and his daughters by the hand and set them outside the city, "the Lord being merciful unto him" (Genesis 19:16). Told to escape to the mountain, he begged to be allowed the little city of Zoar instead, and it was granted (Genesis 19:18-22). His wife looked back and became a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:26).

Afterward he feared to stay in Zoar and dwelt in a cave with his two daughters. There they made him drink wine on two successive nights and lay with him, and both conceived - the origin of the Moabites and Ammonites (Genesis 19:30-38). Scripture records nothing of Lot after this.

What They Did Right

  • Showed hospitality to strangers at real risk, pressing them into his house and making them a feast: Genesis 19:1-3.
  • Resisted the demand of the men of Sodom and called their intent wicked: Genesis 19:6-7.
  • Peter's evaluation is explicit and would be hard to guess from Genesis alone: he was "just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked," whose righteous soul was vexed from day to day: 2 Peter 2:7-8.

What They Did Wrong

  • Chose the plain of Jordan by sight, moving toward a city Scripture immediately identifies as exceedingly wicked: Genesis 13:10-13. The text records the choice and its context without directly condemning it.
  • Offered his two virgin daughters to the mob: Genesis 19:8. Scripture records this without comment; it stands as one of the most disturbing acts in Genesis attributed to a man the New Testament calls just.
  • Lingered when told to flee, and had to be taken by the hand and pulled out: Genesis 19:16.
  • Argued against the angel's instruction to escape to the mountain, asking for Zoar instead: Genesis 19:18-20.
  • Became drunk on two successive nights, so that he perceived neither when his daughters lay down nor when they arose: Genesis 19:33-35. Genesis places the initiative with the daughters and notes his insensibility; it does not excuse him.

Character Assessment

Genesis records almost nothing to Lot's credit beyond his hospitality, and a great deal that is troubling. Without 2 Peter 2:7-8 a reader would not call him righteous. That passage is therefore essential to any honest assessment: God counted him just and vexed by the wickedness around him, even while his own recorded choices were disastrous. Both testimonies belong in the record, and neither should be used to erase the other.

Significance

Lot is Scripture's standing case study in the cost of choosing by sight. Christ makes his deliverance and his wife's fate a warning about the day of the Son of man: "Remember Lot's wife" (Luke 17:28-32). Peter makes his rescue proof that the Lord knows how to deliver the godly out of temptation (2 Peter 2:6-9). Through his daughters he is the ancestor of Moab and Ammon (Genesis 19:37-38), and so, through Ruth the Moabitess, of David and of Christ (Ruth 4:13-22; Matthew 1:5).

Death / Outcome

Scripture does not record his death. Last appearance: Genesis 19:30-38.

Scripture References

Genesis 11:27-31; Genesis 12:4-5; Genesis 13:1-13; Genesis 14:12-16; Genesis 19:1-38; Deuteronomy 2:9, 2:19; Luke 17:28-32; 2 Peter 2:7-8
—

Pharaoh (of Abram's sojourn in Egypt)

The reigning king of Egypt during Abram's descent in the famine. Unnamed.

Family

Unnamed. The reigning king of Egypt during Abram's descent in the famine. Scripture gives no personal name and this reference assigns none.

Chronology

Patriarchal, early in Abram's sojourn.

Life Synopsis

Took Sarai into his house on Abram's representation that she was his sister, and treated Abram well for her sake (Genesis 12:15–16). Plagued by the Lord, he confronted Abram — "Why saidst thou, She is my sister?" — restored Sarai, and sent them away (Genesis 12:17–20).

What They Did Right

  • Treated Abram well for Sarai's sake: Genesis 12:16.
  • On learning the truth, restored Sarai and did not retaliate: Genesis 12:19-20.
  • Rebuked Abram for the deception - "Why saidst thou, She is my sister?" - which is the moral evaluation the passage offers: Genesis 12:18-19.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He took Sarai into his house, but on Abram's own representation that she was his sister (Genesis 12:19).

Character Assessment

The rebuke in this episode runs from the pagan king to the patriarch, not the reverse. Scripture records no wrongdoing by Pharaoh here.

Significance

The first of two episodes in which a pagan ruler rebukes a patriarch over the same deception, a pattern Genesis repeats with Abimelech twice. The plagues on his house preserve Sarah and so preserve the promised line.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 12:20.

Scripture References

Genesis 12:10–20.

Melchizedek

King of Salem and "the priest of the most high God."

Family

Scripture gives no parentage, birth, or death - an omission Hebrews 7:3 makes deliberate theological use of.

Chronology

Patriarchal; contemporary with Abram. No dates, parentage, birth, or death recorded — an absence Hebrews 7:3 makes theological use of.

Life Synopsis

Brought forth bread and wine to Abram returning from the slaughter of the kings, and blessed him (Genesis 14:18–19). Abram gave him tithes of all (Genesis 14:20).

What They Did Right

  • Brought forth bread and wine to Abram returning from the slaughter of the kings: Genesis 14:18.
  • Blessed Abram in the name of the most high God, possessor of heaven and earth: Genesis 14:19.
  • Blessed God for the victory rather than claiming any part in it: Genesis 14:20.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Wholly positive. Psalms 110:4 makes his priesthood the pattern of the Messiah's; Hebrews 5–7 develops him at length, arguing his superiority to Levi from Abram's tithe.

Significance

One of the most theologically weighted figures in the Old Testament. Psalms 110:4 declares the Messiah "a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek," and Hebrews 5-7 develops the argument at length: his priesthood precedes Levi, and Levi paid tithes in Abraham's loins, so the Melchizedek priesthood is the greater (Hebrews 7:4-10). He is both king and priest, a combination forbidden in Israel and fulfilled in Christ.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Scripture deliberately notes the absence of any record of his beginning or end (Hebrews 7:3).

Scripture References

Genesis 14:18–20; Psalms 110:4; Hebrews 5:6, 5:10; Hebrews 6:20; Hebrews 7:1–21.

Chedorlaomer

King of Elam; head of the four-king coalition that campaigned against the cities of the plain.

Family

King of Elam. Head of the coalition of four kings. No family is recorded.

Chronology

Patriarchal; contemporary with Abram.

Life Synopsis

Held the five cities in subjection twelve years; in the fourteenth year, after their rebellion, he and his allies defeated the Rephaims, Zuzims, Emims, Horites, Amalekites, and Amorites, then the five kings in the vale of Siddim (Genesis 14:4–9). Took Lot captive (Genesis 14:12). Defeated by Abram at night near Damascus (Genesis 14:15–17).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Genesis records his campaign, his subjection of the cities of the plain, and his defeat, without moral evaluation.

Character Assessment

No moral evaluation is offered. He functions in the narrative as the aggressor whose defeat sets up the Melchizedek encounter.

Significance

His campaign carries Lot into captivity and so occasions Abram's rescue, the meeting with Melchizedek, and Abram's refusal of Sodom's goods - the events of Genesis 14 on which Hebrews 7 later builds.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded beyond his defeat by Abram near Damascus (Genesis 14:15-17).

Genesis 14:1–17.

Bera, king of Sodom

King of Sodom at the time of the four kings' campaign.

Family

King of Sodom. No family recorded.

Chronology

Patriarchal; contemporary with Abram.

Joined battle in the vale of Siddim and fled (Genesis 14:8–10). Afterward offered Abram the goods if he would return the persons; Abram refused any part of it, having sworn to take nothing "from a thread even to a shoelatchet... lest thou shouldest say, I have made Abram rich" (Genesis 14:21–23).

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Genesis 13:13 says the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners before the Lord exceedingly, but that is said of the city, not of Bera personally. Scripture records no individual act of his that it condemns.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered on the man. Genesis 13:13 says the men of Sodom "were wicked and sinners before the Lord exceedingly," but that is said of the city, not of Bera personally.

Significance

His offer of the goods to Abram provokes Abram's oath that he would take nothing, "lest thou shouldest say, I have made Abram rich" (Genesis 14:23) - one of the clearest recorded refusals of compromising gain in Scripture.

Mamre, Eshcol, and Aner

Three Amorite brothers, confederate with Abram. Three distinct individuals, recorded only as a group — Scripture gives no separate action to any one of them, so they are entered together rather than split into three near-identical entries.

Family

Three Amorite brothers (Genesis 14:13). These are three distinct individuals; Scripture records no separate action for any one of them, so they are treated together here rather than split into three near-identical entries.

Chronology

Patriarchal; contemporary with Abram.

Life Synopsis

Abram dwelt in the plain of Mamre, named for the eldest (Genesis 14:13). They were "confederate with Abram" (Genesis 14:13) and went with him in the pursuit; Abram, refusing spoil himself, insisted they take their portion (Genesis 14:24).

What They Did Right

  • Were confederate with Abram and went with him in the pursuit of the four kings: Genesis 14:13, 14:24.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered. Their inclusion rests on the confederacy and on Abram's insistence that their claim be honoured.

Significance

Abram dwelt in the plain of Mamre, which is named for the eldest and becomes a fixed landmark of the patriarchal narratives (Genesis 13:18; Genesis 18:1; Genesis 23:17-19). Abram, refusing spoil for himself, insisted their portion be honoured - a distinction between his own vow and what he could impose on others.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 14:24.

Genesis 14:13, 14:24.

Eliezer of Damascus

Steward of Abram's house, and his heir presumptive before Isaac's birth.

Family

Steward of Abram's house and his heir presumptive before Isaac's birth (Genesis 15:2). No family recorded.

Chronology

Patriarchal; before the birth of Ishmael.

Life Synopsis

Named once, in Abram's complaint to God: "what wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless, and the steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus?" (Genesis 15:2).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered. Note a common conflation: the unnamed "eldest servant" who fetches Rebekah in Genesis 24 is widely assumed to be Eliezer, but Genesis never names him, and the two are kept separate here.

Significance

His position illustrates the situation the covenant promise addressed: Abram's estate was set to pass to a servant, not a son. Note carefully that the unnamed "eldest servant" of Genesis 24 is nowhere identified as Eliezer. That identification is traditional, not biblical, and this reference keeps the two separate.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He is named once, in Genesis 15:2.

Hagar

Egyptian handmaid of Sarai; mother of Ishmael; the first person in Scripture recorded as giving God a name.

Family

Egyptian; handmaid of Sarai (Genesis 16:1). Given to Abram as wife (Genesis 16:3). Mother of Ishmael (Genesis 16:15). She took a wife for her son out of Egypt (Genesis 21:21).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Her son Ishmael was born when Abram was 86 (Genesis 16:16), which fixes her position but gives no age of her own.

Life Synopsis

Hagar was Sarai's Egyptian handmaid, given to Abram as wife after ten years of barrenness in Canaan (Genesis 16:1-3). When she conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes; Sarai dealt hardly with her, and she fled into the wilderness (Genesis 16:4-6).

The angel of the Lord found her by a fountain in the way to Shur and addressed her by name and station: "Hagar, Sarai's maid, whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go?" She answered honestly that she was fleeing. She was told to return and submit, and given a promise of her own - that her seed would be multiplied exceedingly - and the name of her son, Ishmael, "because the Lord hath heard thy affliction" (Genesis 16:7-12). She then called the name of the Lord that spake unto her, "Thou God seest me" (Genesis 16:13). No one else in Scripture is recorded doing this. She returned and bore Ishmael (Genesis 16:15).

Years later, after Isaac's weaning feast, Sarah demanded that Hagar and her son be cast out. Abraham rose early, gave her bread and a bottle of water, and sent her away; she wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba (Genesis 21:9-14). When the water was gone she put the child under a shrub and sat a bowshot away, saying, "Let me not see the death of the child," and wept (Genesis 21:15-16). God heard the voice of the lad, and the angel of God called to her out of heaven; God opened her eyes and she saw a well (Genesis 21:17-19). She dwelt in the wilderness of Paran and took an Egyptian wife for her son (Genesis 21:21).

What They Did Right

  • Answered the angel of the Lord truthfully about her flight rather than concealing it: Genesis 16:8.
  • Obeyed the command to return to a mistress who had dealt hardly with her: Genesis 16:9, 16:15.
  • Named God "Thou God seest me" - the only occasion in Scripture where a person gives God a name: Genesis 16:13.

What They Did Wrong

  • When she conceived, her mistress "was despised in her eyes": Genesis 16:4. Scripture records the contempt without further comment; the angel's instruction to submit implies it was not right, but no explicit condemnation is given.

Character Assessment

Scripture treats Hagar with notable tenderness. She is an Egyptian slave woman, twice driven into the wilderness by others' decisions, and on both occasions God meets her there by name and provides. The one fault recorded of her is contempt for her mistress, and even that follows a situation she did not create. God gives her a personal promise (Genesis 16:10), hears her son's voice (Genesis 21:17), and opens her eyes to water.

Significance

She is the mother of Ishmael, from whom twelve princes descend (Genesis 25:12-16), and the recipient of a divine promise in her own right. Paul uses her allegorically in Galatians 4:22-31 to represent the covenant of law and bondage in contrast with Sarah - an interpretive use of her story, expressly identified by Paul as allegory (Galatians 4:24), and not a judgment on Hagar personally.

Death / Outcome

Scripture does not record her death. Last mention: Genesis 21:21; referred to in Galatians 4:24-25.

Scripture References

Genesis 16:1-16; Genesis 21:9-21; Genesis 25:12; Galatians 4:22-31
