Ishmael

Son of Abram by Hagar the Egyptian; ancestor of twelve princes.

Family

Son of Abram by Hagar the Egyptian (Genesis 16:15); half-brother of Isaac. Father of twelve princes (Genesis 25:13-16) and of a daughter Mahalath, whom Esau married (Genesis 28:9).

Chronology

Born when Abram was 86 (Genesis 16:16); died aged 137 (Genesis 25:17).

Life Synopsis

Named before birth by the angel of the Lord, "because the Lord hath heard thy affliction," with the prophecy that he would be a wild man (Genesis 16:11–12). Circumcised at thirteen (Genesis 17:25). Seen mocking at Isaac's weaning feast, prompting Sarah's demand that he be cast out (Genesis 21:9–10). Preserved in the wilderness when God heard his voice (Genesis 21:17–19); became an archer in Paran (Genesis 21:20–21). Joined Isaac in burying Abraham (Genesis 25:9).

What They Did Right

  • Was circumcised at thirteen with all the men of Abraham's house: Genesis 17:23-26.
  • Joined Isaac in burying their father Abraham - the two half-brothers acting together: Genesis 25:9.

What They Did Wrong

  • Was seen mocking at Isaac's weaning feast, which prompted Sarah's demand that he be cast out: Genesis 21:9. Genesis does not characterize the mocking further; Galatians 4:29 later reads the episode as persecution.

Character Assessment

Mixed and sparse. God's promise to make him a great nation is repeated (Genesis 17:20; Genesis 21:13, 21:18), and it is fulfilled (Genesis 25:12–16). The mocking is the only conduct Scripture records against him, and Genesis does not characterize it further; Galatians 4:29 later reads the episode as persecution.

Significance

Ancestor of twelve princes and of a great nation, as God promised both to Hagar and to Abraham (Genesis 17:20; Genesis 21:13, 21:18). Paul uses the contrast between Ishmael, born after the flesh, and Isaac, born by promise, as an allegory of two covenants (Galatians 4:22-31) - expressly identified by Paul as allegory.

Death / Outcome

Died at 137 years; "he gave up the ghost and died; and was gathered unto his people" (Genesis 25:17).

Scripture References

Genesis 16:11–16; Genesis 17:18–26; Genesis 21:9–21; Genesis 25:9, 25:12–18; Galatians 4:29.
—

Lot's wife

Wife of Lot; unnamed.

Family

Unnamed. Wife of Lot; mother of his two daughters (Genesis 19:15).

Chronology

Patriarchal; the destruction of Sodom.

Life Synopsis

Led by the hand out of the city by the angels (Genesis 19:16). "But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt" (Genesis 19:26).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Looked back from behind him during the flight from Sodom, contrary to the express instruction "look not behind thee" (Genesis 19:17), and became a pillar of salt: Genesis 19:26.

Character Assessment

Cited by Jesus as a warning in three words — "Remember Lot's wife" (Luke 17:32) — in a passage about not turning back. Genesis records the act and the consequence without further comment.

Significance

Christ makes her a standing warning in his teaching on the day of the Son of man: "Remember Lot's wife" (Luke 17:32), in a passage about not turning back for what is left behind.

Death / Outcome

"But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt" (Genesis 19:26).

Scripture References

Genesis 19:15–16, 19:26; Luke 17:32.
—

The firstborn daughter of Lot

Elder of Lot's two daughters; mother of Moab.

Family

Unnamed. Elder of Lot's two daughters; mother of Moab (Genesis 19:37).

Chronology

Patriarchal; after the destruction of Sodom.

Life Synopsis

Offered by her father to the men of Sodom (Genesis 19:8) — an act of his, not hers. Afterward, in the cave, she proposed to her sister that they make their father drink wine and lie with him "that we may preserve seed of our father," and did so first (Genesis 19:31–33). Bore Moab, father of the Moabites (Genesis 19:37).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Proposed to her sister that they make their father drink wine and lie with him, and acted first: Genesis 19:31-33. Genesis records the act and the stated motive - to preserve their father's line - without explicit condemnation. The silence should not be read either as approval or as an added charge.

Character Assessment

Genesis records the incest plainly and without explicit condemnation, noting that Lot "perceived not." The stated motive is preservation of the line. Scripture's silence here is notable and should not be filled in either direction.

Significance

Mother of Moab, father of the Moabites (Genesis 19:37). Through the Moabites comes Ruth, and so David and Christ (Ruth 4:13-22; Matthew 1:5).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 19:37.

Scripture References

Genesis 19:8, 19:30–37.
—

The younger daughter of Lot

Younger of Lot's two daughters; mother of Ben-ammi.

Family

Unnamed. Younger of Lot's two daughters; mother of Ben-ammi (Genesis 19:38).

Chronology

Patriarchal; after the destruction of Sodom.

Life Synopsis

Followed her sister's proposal on the second night (Genesis 19:34–35). Bore Ben-ammi, father of the Ammonites (Genesis 19:38).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Followed her sister's proposal on the second night: Genesis 19:34-35. She is recorded as following rather than initiating.

Character Assessment

As above. She is recorded as following rather than initiating.

Significance

Mother of Ben-ammi, father of the children of Ammon (Genesis 19:38).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 19:38.

Scripture References

Genesis 19:8, 19:30–38.
—

Abimelech, king of Gerar (contemporary of Abraham)

Philistine king of Gerar. Possibly distinct from the Abimelech of Genesis 26 — see the note under that entry.

Family

King of Gerar. His wife and maidservants are mentioned but unnamed (Genesis 20:17).

Chronology

Patriarchal; after the destruction of Sodom.

Life Synopsis

Took Sarah on Abraham's representation that she was his sister; warned by God in a dream before touching her, and protested "in the integrity of my heart and innocency of my hands have I done this" — which God confirmed (Genesis 20:2–6). Restored Sarah with gifts and rebuked Abraham: "thou hast done deeds unto me that ought not to be done" (Genesis 20:9, 20:14–16). Later sought a covenant with Abraham at Beer-sheba, acknowledging "God is with thee in all that thou doest" (Genesis 21:22–32).

What They Did Right

  • Had not come near Sarah, and protested his integrity - which God himself confirmed: "I know that thou didst this in the integrity of thy heart": Genesis 20:4-6.
  • Obeyed God's warning at once, rising early and telling all his servants: Genesis 20:8.
  • Restored Sarah with generous gifts and offered Abraham the freedom of his land: Genesis 20:14-15.
  • Rebuked Abraham justly: "thou hast done deeds unto me that ought not to be done": Genesis 20:9.
  • Sought a covenant of peace, acknowledging "God is with thee in all that thou doest": Genesis 21:22-23.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He took Sarah, but on Abraham's own representation that she was his sister, and God explicitly certifies that he acted in integrity of heart (Genesis 20:5-6).

Character Assessment

Treated favourably. God himself certifies his integrity (Genesis 20:6), and the moral rebuke in the episode runs from him to the patriarch. Nothing is recorded against him.

Significance

One of the clearest instances in Genesis of a pagan king behaving better than the patriarch, and of God defending Sarah when her husband would not. God calls Abraham a prophet in this passage - the first use of the word in Scripture (Genesis 20:7).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 21:32.

Scripture References

Genesis 20:1–18; Genesis 21:22–34.
—

Phichol

Chief captain of Abimelech's host.

Family

Chief captain of Abimelech's host (Genesis 21:22). No family recorded.

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Accompanied Abimelech to make covenant with Abraham at Beer-sheba (Genesis 21:22, 21:32), and appears again with Abimelech before Isaac (Genesis 26:26).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered. Note: whether the two appearances are one man or two bearing the same office-title is bound up with the Abimelech question below.

Significance

Present at both covenants at Beersheba, with Abraham and later with Isaac (Genesis 21:22; Genesis 26:26). Whether the two appearances are one man or two holding the same office is bound up with the question of the two Abimelechs, and Scripture does not settle it.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 26:26.

Scripture References

Genesis 21:22, 21:32; Genesis 26:26.
—

Milcah

Daughter of Haran; wife of her uncle Nahor; grandmother of Rebekah.

Family

Daughter of Haran; sister of Lot and Iscah; wife of her uncle Nahor (Genesis 11:29). Mother of eight sons, including Bethuel; grandmother of Rebekah (Genesis 22:20-23).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Married Nahor (Genesis 11:29). Bore him eight sons, named in full — Huz, Buz, Kemuel, Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel — news of which reached Abraham after the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22:20–23). Named repeatedly as Rebekah's grandmother in the betrothal narrative (Genesis 24:15, 24:24, 24:47).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered. Her significance in the narrative is that Bethuel, and so Rebekah, came from Abraham's own kindred rather than from Canaan.

Significance

Her significance in the narrative is genealogical and considerable: through Bethuel she is the grandmother of Rebekah, and it is because Abraham's kindred in Padan-aram descend from her that a wife could be sought for Isaac outside Canaan (Genesis 24:15, 24:24).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 24:47.

Scripture References

Genesis 11:29; Genesis 22:20–23; Genesis 24:15, 24:24, 24:47.
—

Bethuel

Son of Nahor and Milcah; father of Rebekah and Laban; the Syrian of Padan-aram.

Family

Son of Nahor and Milcah (Genesis 22:22-23); father of Rebekah and Laban (Genesis 24:15, 24:29). Called the Syrian of Padan-aram (Genesis 25:20).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

With Laban, answered Abraham's servant: "The thing proceedeth from the Lord: we cannot speak unto thee bad or good" (Genesis 24:50), consenting to Rebekah's departure.

What They Did Right

  • With Laban, acknowledged the Lord's hand in the matter and consented to Rebekah's departure: "The thing proceedeth from the Lord: we cannot speak unto thee bad or good": Genesis 24:50.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered. Note a real oddity: Bethuel speaks once and then vanishes from the negotiation, with Laban and Rebekah's mother acting in his place (Genesis 24:53, 24:55). Genesis does not explain this, and this work does not supply a reason.

Significance

Father of Rebekah, and so of the line through which the covenant continues. A genuine oddity attends him: he speaks once and then disappears from the negotiation, with Laban and Rebekah's mother acting in his place (Genesis 24:53, 24:55). Genesis does not explain this, and no explanation is supplied here.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 28:5.

Scripture References

Genesis 22:22–23; Genesis 24:15, 24:24, 24:47, 24:50; Genesis 25:20; Genesis 28:2, 28:5.
2108

Isaac

Son of Abraham and Sarah; the child of promise; second of the three patriarchs.

Family

Son of Abraham and Sarah (Genesis 21:2-3); half-brother of Ishmael and of Keturah's sons. Husband of Rebekah (Genesis 24:67). Father of the twins Esau and Jacob (Genesis 25:24-26).

Chronology

Born when Abraham was 100 and Sarah 90 (Genesis 21:5; Genesis 17:17); 40 when he married Rebekah (Genesis 25:20); 60 at the birth of his sons (Genesis 25:26); died at 180 (Genesis 35:28). Anno Mundi 2108-2288 by calculation.

Life Synopsis

Isaac was born at the set time God had spoken, when Abraham was 100 years old, and named Laughter (Genesis 21:1-5). He was circumcised at eight days (Genesis 21:4), and at his weaning feast Sarah saw Ishmael mocking and demanded the bondwoman and her son be cast out (Genesis 21:8-10).

The great event of his youth is one in which he is chiefly acted upon. God commanded Abraham to offer him in the land of Moriah. Isaac carried the wood himself and asked the question the narrative turns on: "Behold the fire and the wood: but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?" (Genesis 22:7). He was bound and laid on the altar, and the angel of the Lord stopped his father's hand (Genesis 22:9-12). Scripture does not record that he resisted.

After Sarah's death, Abraham's eldest servant brought Rebekah from Padan-aram. Isaac was meditating in the field at eventide when the camels came; he took her, and she was a comfort to him after his mother's death (Genesis 24:63-67). Rebekah was barren twenty years, and "Isaac intreated the Lord for his wife" - the prayer was answered with twins (Genesis 25:21).

A famine sent him to Gerar, where God forbade him to go down to Egypt and confirmed the covenant to him (Genesis 26:1-5). There he repeated his father's error, telling the men of the place that Rebekah was his sister, until Abimelech saw otherwise and rebuked him (Genesis 26:7-11). He sowed and reaped a hundredfold, grew very great, and the Philistines envied him and stopped his wells (Genesis 26:12-15). His response to repeated strife was to move and dig again - Esek, Sitnah, and finally Rehoboth, "for now the Lord hath made room for us" (Genesis 26:18-22). He built an altar at Beersheba and made covenant with Abimelech (Genesis 26:25-31).

In old age, blind and expecting to die, he called Esau to prepare venison so he might bless him - though God had said the elder should serve the younger (Genesis 25:23; Genesis 27:1-4). Jacob, prompted by Rebekah, deceived him, and Isaac blessed the wrong son. When he discovered it he "trembled very exceedingly," but confirmed the blessing: "yea, and he shall be blessed" (Genesis 27:33). He sent Jacob to Padan-aram for a wife and blessed him again deliberately (Genesis 28:1-4). He died at 180 and was buried by both his sons (Genesis 35:28-29).

What They Did Right

  • Submitted to being bound and laid on the altar; Scripture records no resistance from a young man strong enough to carry the wood: Genesis 22:6-9.
  • Prayed for his barren wife over twenty years of waiting: Genesis 25:21.
  • Obeyed God's command not to go down to Egypt during famine, unlike his father: Genesis 26:2-6.
  • Yielded contested wells repeatedly rather than fight, until strife ceased: Genesis 26:18-22.
  • Built an altar and called on the name of the Lord at Beersheba: Genesis 26:25.
  • Confirmed Jacob's blessing once he understood what had happened, rather than revoking it: Genesis 27:33.
  • Blessed Jacob knowingly and deliberately before sending him away: Genesis 28:1-4; Hebrews 11:20.

What They Did Wrong

  • Told the men of Gerar that Rebekah was his sister out of fear for his life, repeating his father's fault: Genesis 26:7-10. Abimelech's rebuke is the text's evaluation.
  • Loved Esau because he did eat of his venison, while Rebekah loved Jacob - a stated parental favouritism with lasting consequences: Genesis 25:28.
  • Set out to bless Esau despite the oracle that the elder should serve the younger: Genesis 25:23; Genesis 27:1-4. Scripture records the intent without explicitly condemning it, but the oracle had been given.

Character Assessment

The quietest of the three patriarchs, and the one with the least recorded speech. His life is largely a continuation of his father's - the same covenant, the same wells, and the same fear about his wife. What is distinctly his is patience: twenty years of prayer for Rebekah, and a pattern of yielding rather than contending. His clearest failure is favouritism, and it fractured his household. Hebrews commends him for one specific act: blessing his sons concerning things to come (Hebrews 11:20).

Significance

Isaac is the child of promise, the son through whom the covenant line runs, and the proof that the promise depended on God's word rather than natural possibility (Romans 9:7-9). God identifies himself thereafter as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Exodus 3:6; Matthew 22:32). The binding of Isaac in Genesis 22 supplies Scripture's fullest Old Testament picture of a father offering an only son, and Hebrews reads Abraham's faith there as reckoning on resurrection (Hebrews 11:17-19).

Death / Outcome

Died at 180 years, "old and full of days," and was buried by Esau and Jacob (Genesis 35:28-29).

Scripture References

Genesis 17:19-21; Genesis 21:1-12; Genesis 22:1-19; Genesis 24:62-67; Genesis 25:19-28; Genesis 26:1-33; Genesis 27:1-40; Genesis 28:1-5; Genesis 35:27-29; Romans 9:7-10; Hebrews 11:17-20; James 2:21
—

Abraham's eldest servant

The senior servant of Abraham's house, "that ruled over all that he had," sent to find a wife for Isaac. Unnamed in Scripture — see the note under Eliezer.

Family

Unnamed. The senior servant of Abraham's house, "that ruled over all that he had" (Genesis 24:2). Scripture does not name him. He is commonly called Eliezer by tradition, but Genesis makes no such identification, and this reference does not.

Chronology

Patriarchal; after Sarah's death.

Life Synopsis

Sworn by Abraham not to take a wife for Isaac from the Canaanites (Genesis 24:2–9). Prayed for a specific sign at the well and it was answered (Genesis 24:12–21). Worshipped the Lord on the spot (Genesis 24:26–27). Refused to eat before stating his errand (Genesis 24:33). Recounted the whole matter faithfully and pressed for a decision (Genesis 24:34–49).

What They Did Right

  • Bound himself by oath to seek a wife for Isaac from Abraham's kindred rather than the Canaanites: Genesis 24:2-9.
  • Prayed for a specific sign, appealing to God's kindness to his master, and it was answered before he had finished speaking: Genesis 24:12-15.
  • Worshipped the Lord on the spot when the prayer was answered: Genesis 24:26-27.
  • Refused to eat before he had told his errand: Genesis 24:33.
  • Recounted the whole matter faithfully and pressed for a plain decision: Genesis 24:34-49.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Presented favourably throughout — the longest sustained portrait of a servant in Genesis, and one of the few extended examples of petitionary prayer answered in detail. Nothing negative is recorded.

Significance

His prayer at the well and its immediate answer form one of the fullest accounts in Scripture of specific guidance sought and given. He is also the longest sustained portrait of a servant in Genesis, and the whole of Genesis 24 - the longest chapter in the book - turns on his faithfulness.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 24:66.

Scripture References

Genesis 24:1–67.
—

Rebekah

Wife of Isaac; mother of Esau and Jacob; the woman to whom the oracle of the two nations was given.

Family

Daughter of Bethuel, granddaughter of Nahor and Milcah (Genesis 24:15, 24:24); sister of Laban. Wife of Isaac (Genesis 24:67); mother of Esau and Jacob (Genesis 25:24-26).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Isaac was 40 when he married her (Genesis 25:20) and 60 at the birth of their sons (Genesis 25:26), so twenty years passed between. Her age and the date of her death are not recorded.

Life Synopsis

Abraham's eldest servant prayed at the well of Nahor for a specific sign: that the young woman who offered to water his camels would be the one appointed. Before he had finished speaking, Rebekah came out, gave him drink, and said, "I will draw water for thy camels also, until they have done drinking" - watering ten camels by hand (Genesis 24:15-20). When the household hesitated over her departure and was asked directly, she answered in three words: "I will go" (Genesis 24:58). She met Isaac in the field at evening and became his wife, and he was comforted after his mother's death (Genesis 24:64-67).

She was barren twenty years until Isaac's prayer was answered (Genesis 25:21). The children struggled within her, and she went to enquire of the Lord. The answer was an oracle: two nations were in her womb, and "the elder shall serve the younger" (Genesis 25:22-23). Esau and Jacob were born, and the household divided - "Isaac loved Esau, because he did eat of his venison: but Rebekah loved Jacob" (Genesis 25:28).

In Gerar, Isaac passed her off as his sister, and she was exposed to danger until Abimelech discovered the truth (Genesis 26:7-11). When Isaac, old and blind, sent Esau for venison in order to bless him, Rebekah overheard and acted. She directed Jacob to fetch two kids, cooked them as Isaac liked, dressed Jacob in Esau's clothing and put the skins on his hands and neck, and answered his objection by taking the risk on herself: "Upon me be thy curse, my son" (Genesis 27:5-17). The deception succeeded.

When Esau resolved to kill Jacob, she sent Jacob to her brother Laban "for a few days, until thy brother's fury turn away" (Genesis 27:41-45). To Isaac she gave a different reason - weariness at the daughters of Heth (Genesis 27:46). She never saw Jacob again; the twenty years were not a few days. Scripture does not record her death, only that she was buried in the cave of Machpelah (Genesis 49:31).

What They Did Right

  • Offered water for ten camels unasked, going far beyond the request: Genesis 24:18-20.
  • Consented at once to leave her family for a man she had never seen: Genesis 24:58.
  • Enquired of the Lord about the struggle within her rather than merely enduring it: Genesis 25:22.

What They Did Wrong

  • Devised and directed the deception of her blind husband: Genesis 27:5-17. Scripture records the plan in detail and records its cost, though it does not attach an explicit condemnation.
  • Practised open favouritism toward Jacob: Genesis 25:28.
  • Gave Isaac a different reason for sending Jacob away than the real one: Genesis 27:46 compared with Genesis 27:42-45.

Character Assessment

A decisive woman whose decisiveness cut both ways. Her willingness to leave everything on a word is presented admiringly, and her enquiry of the Lord in Genesis 25:22 is the act of someone who takes God seriously. Yet she sought by deception an outcome God had already promised, and she paid for it: the son she favoured fled and did not return in her lifetime. Scripture records both without moralising, and Romans 9:10-13 appeals to the oracle she received - not to her methods - in arguing that God's purpose stands by election rather than by works.

Significance

The oracle of Genesis 25:23 given to Rebekah establishes the reversal of primogeniture that runs through Genesis and is cited by Paul as a foundation of the doctrine of election (Romans 9:10-13). She is the mother of Jacob, and therefore of Israel. Her betrothal narrative is the longest chapter in Genesis, and the servant's answered prayer within it is one of Scripture's fullest accounts of specific guidance sought and given.

Death / Outcome

Scripture does not record her death or her age. Jacob states that she was buried in the cave of Machpelah with Isaac (Genesis 49:31).

Scripture References

Genesis 22:23; Genesis 24:1-67; Genesis 25:19-28; Genesis 26:6-11; Genesis 27:1-46; Genesis 28:5; Genesis 49:31; Romans 9:10-13
—

Keturah

Wife whom Abraham took after Sarah's death; mother of six sons, including Midian.

Family

Wife whom Abraham took after Sarah's death (Genesis 25:1). Mother of Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah (Genesis 25:2). 1 Chronicles 1:32 calls her Abraham's concubine.

Chronology

Patriarchal; after Sarah's death.

Life Synopsis

Bore Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah (Genesis 25:1–2). Her sons received gifts and were sent eastward, away from Isaac, who received all (Genesis 25:5–6). 1 Chronicles 1:32 calls her Abraham's concubine.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered. Note the terminological tension: Genesis 25:1 calls her a wife; Genesis 25:6 refers to "the sons of the concubines," and 1 Chronicles 1:32 names her a concubine. Scripture does not reconcile this.

Significance

Mother of Midian, and so ancestress of the Midianites, among whom Moses later took refuge and found a wife (Exodus 2:15-21). Note a terminological tension the text does not resolve: Genesis 25:1 calls her a wife, Genesis 25:6 refers to "the sons of the concubines," and 1 Chronicles 1:32 names her a concubine.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Chronicles 1:33.

Scripture References

Genesis 25:1–6; 1 Chronicles 1:32–33.
2168

Esau

Elder twin of Isaac and Rebekah; a hunter and a man of the field; father of the Edomites.

Also called Edom

Family

Son of Isaac and Rebekah (Genesis 25:24-26); elder twin of Jacob. Married Judith and Bashemath the Hittites (Genesis 26:34), Mahalath daughter of Ishmael (Genesis 28:9); the list in Genesis 36:2-3 gives different names and parentage, an unresolved discrepancy. Father of Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jaalam, and Korah (Genesis 36:4-5).

Chronology

Born with Jacob when Isaac was 60 (Genesis 25:26); 40 when he married the Hittite women (Genesis 26:34). His death is not recorded.

Life Synopsis

Esau came out first, red and hairy, with Jacob holding his heel (Genesis 25:25-26). He became a cunning hunter, a man of the field, loved by his father for his venison (Genesis 25:27-28). Coming in from the field faint, he asked Jacob for the red pottage, and Jacob demanded the birthright for it. Esau said, "Behold, I am at the point to die: and what profit shall this birthright do to me?" and sold it with an oath. The narrator's verdict is unusually blunt: "thus Esau despised his birthright" (Genesis 25:29-34).

At forty he married two Hittite women, "which were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah" (Genesis 26:34-35). When Isaac sent him for venison in order to bless him, Jacob took the blessing first by deception. Esau returned, and on learning what had happened "cried with a great and exceeding bitter cry," and asked, "Hast thou not reserved a blessing for me?" (Genesis 27:30-38). He received a lesser word from his father, and resolved to kill Jacob after their father's mourning (Genesis 27:41). Learning that his Canaanite wives displeased his parents, he went and took a daughter of Ishmael in addition (Genesis 28:6-9).

Twenty years later Jacob returned in fear, having heard Esau was coming with four hundred men. What followed was not the expected attack: "Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept" (Genesis 33:4). He at first refused Jacob's gift, saying, "I have enough, my brother; keep that thou hast unto thyself" (Genesis 33:9). He offered escort, which Jacob declined, and returned to Seir. The brothers came together once more to bury their father Isaac (Genesis 35:29). Esau settled in mount Seir and became the father of Edom (Genesis 36:8-9).

What They Did Right

  • Reconciled with Jacob, running to meet him, embracing him, and weeping, when he had every opportunity for vengeance: Genesis 33:4.
  • Initially declined Jacob's gift, saying he had enough: Genesis 33:9.
  • Joined Jacob in burying their father: Genesis 35:29.
  • Separated peaceably from Jacob when the land could not bear them both, without recorded strife: Genesis 36:6-8.

What They Did Wrong

  • Despised his birthright, selling it for a single meal. Scripture states the evaluation directly: Genesis 25:34; Hebrews 12:16.
  • Married Hittite women who were a grief of mind to his parents: Genesis 26:34-35.
  • Purposed in his heart to kill his brother: Genesis 27:41.
  • Hebrews describes him as a profane person, and states that afterward, wanting the blessing, "he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears": Hebrews 12:16-17.

Character Assessment

Scripture's judgment on Esau is severe, and it centres on one thing: he treated his covenant inheritance as worth less than a meal. That is the ground of the explicit condemnations in Genesis 25:34 and Hebrews 12:16-17, and of the prophetic word in Malachi 1:2-3 which Paul cites in Romans 9:13. Yet Genesis also records the most generous act of reconciliation in the book, and it is Esau's, not Jacob's. He forgave a brother who had defrauded him twice. Both must be held together: the man who despised eternal things behaved better toward his brother than his brother had toward him.

Significance

Esau is the father of Edom (Genesis 36:8-9), a nation whose long hostility to Israel runs through the prophets and is the entire subject of Obadiah. He is Scripture's standing warning against trading a lasting inheritance for immediate appetite (Hebrews 12:16-17). Paul's citation of Malachi 1:2-3 in Romans 9:13 makes the Jacob-Esau contrast a foundation text for the doctrine of election.

Death / Outcome

Scripture does not record his death. Last appearance: Genesis 36, in the account of his descendants in Seir.

Scripture References

Genesis 25:21-34; Genesis 26:34-35; Genesis 27:1-46; Genesis 28:6-9; Genesis 32:3-8; Genesis 33:1-16; Genesis 35:29; Genesis 36:1-43; Malachi 1:2-3; Romans 9:10-13; Hebrews 12:16-17
2168

Jacob

Son of Isaac and Rebekah; renamed Israel; father of the twelve tribes; third of the patriarchs.

Also called Israel

Family

Son of Isaac and Rebekah (Genesis 25:24-26); younger twin of Esau. Husband of Leah and Rachel, and of their handmaids Bilhah and Zilpah (Genesis 29:23-30; Genesis 30:4, 30:9). Father of twelve sons and of Dinah (Genesis 35:22-26; Genesis 30:21).

Chronology

Born when Isaac was 60 (Genesis 25:26); fled to Padan-aram and served twenty years (Genesis 31:38, 31:41); 130 when he stood before Pharaoh (Genesis 47:9); died at 147 (Genesis 47:28). Anno Mundi 2168-2315 by calculation.

Life Synopsis

Jacob was born holding his brother's heel, and named accordingly (Genesis 25:26). He grew up a plain man dwelling in tents, loved by his mother while Esau was loved by his father (Genesis 25:27-28). He bought Esau's birthright for a mess of pottage when Esau came in faint from the field (Genesis 25:29-34), and later, at Rebekah's direction, deceived his blind father to obtain the blessing intended for Esau (Genesis 27:6-29). Esau resolved to kill him, and he fled to Haran.

At Bethel he dreamed of a ladder reaching to heaven, and God confirmed the covenant to him. He set up the stone, called the place Bethel, and vowed a tenth of all God gave him (Genesis 28:10-22). In Haran he served Laban seven years for Rachel, was given Leah instead, and served seven more (Genesis 29:18-30). Through four women twelve children were born. Laban changed his wages ten times (Genesis 31:7), and after twenty years Jacob left with his family and flocks, pursued and overtaken by Laban, with whom he made covenant at Mizpah (Genesis 31:44-55).

Facing Esau's approach with four hundred men, he divided his company, sent gifts ahead, and prayed a prayer that admits his own unworthiness: "I am not worthy of the least of all the mercies" (Genesis 32:9-12). That night he wrestled with a man until the breaking of the day, refused to let go without a blessing, and had his thigh put out of joint. His name was changed to Israel, "for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed" (Genesis 32:24-30). He met Esau in peace (Genesis 33:1-4).

His later years were heavy. Dinah was defiled and his sons destroyed Shechem, to his open dismay (Genesis 34:30). Rachel died bearing Benjamin (Genesis 35:16-19). Reuben lay with Bilhah (Genesis 35:22). Believing Joseph dead, he refused to be comforted (Genesis 37:34-35). Famine drove him to send his sons to Egypt, and at last to go himself, where God spoke to him in the visions of the night (Genesis 46:2-4). He blessed Pharaoh (Genesis 47:7-10), blessed Joseph's sons crossing his hands to prefer the younger (Genesis 48:13-20), gave prophetic oracles over his twelve sons (Genesis 49:1-28), charged them to bury him at Machpelah, and died at 147 (Genesis 49:29-33).

What They Did Right

  • Vowed and worshipped at Bethel after the vision of the ladder: Genesis 28:16-22.
  • Served fourteen years for Rachel, and twenty in all, through changed wages and hard conditions: Genesis 29:20, 29:30; Genesis 31:38-41.
  • Prayed before meeting Esau, confessing himself unworthy of God's mercies: Genesis 32:9-12.
  • Refused to release the one who wrestled with him until he was blessed, and prevailed: Genesis 32:24-28; Hosea 12:3-4.
  • Put away the strange gods from his household and went up to Bethel as God commanded: Genesis 35:1-4.
  • Blessed Pharaoh - the lesser blessed by the greater, recorded without comment: Genesis 47:7-10.
  • Blessed Joseph's sons by faith, worshipping, leaning on the top of his staff: Genesis 48:13-20; Hebrews 11:21.

What They Did Wrong

  • Exploited his brother's extremity to obtain the birthright: Genesis 25:29-34. Scripture's explicit condemnation here falls on Esau for despising his birthright, not on Jacob for buying it, though the act is plainly opportunistic.
  • Deceived his blind father, using his brother's name and clothing, and lied outright: "I am Esau thy firstborn" (Genesis 27:19). He also invoked God's name in the lie (Genesis 27:20). This is deliberate deception of the most serious kind.
  • Loved Rachel more than Leah, with lasting damage to his household: Genesis 29:30-31.
  • Favoured Joseph openly above his other sons and marked it with a coat, so that his brothers hated him: Genesis 37:3-4.
  • Rebuked Simeon and Levi for Shechem chiefly in terms of the danger to himself: Genesis 34:30. The moral judgment comes later, at his deathbed (Genesis 49:5-7).

Character Assessment

Jacob's record is the most mixed of the patriarchs, and Scripture makes no attempt to smooth it. He is a schemer whose schemes mostly cost him: he deceived his father and lost his home for twenty years; he was himself deceived by Laban over Leah; he favoured one son and was deceived in turn by his other sons over Joseph. Yet he is also the man who wrestled until dawn and would not let go, and Hosea's summary treats that persistence as the key to him: "he had power over the angel, and prevailed: he wept, and made supplication" (Hosea 12:4). Hebrews commends the end of his life, not the middle (Hebrews 11:21). His own verdict was "few and evil have the days of the years of my life been" (Genesis 47:9).

Significance

Jacob is Israel. The twelve tribes descend from his sons, and the nation bears his new name. God's self-identification as "the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob" (Exodus 3:6) makes him one of the three covenant fathers. Paul cites God's choice of him before birth as the pattern case of election not of works (Romans 9:11-13). His oracle over Judah in Genesis 49:10 - that the sceptre shall not depart from Judah until Shiloh come - is a foundational messianic text.

Death / Outcome

Died in Egypt at 147, having blessed his sons; embalmed, carried up to Canaan, and buried in the cave of Machpelah (Genesis 47:28; Genesis 49:33; Genesis 50:1-13).

Scripture References

Genesis 25:21-34; Genesis 27:1-46; Genesis 28:10-22; Genesis 29:1-30; Genesis 30:25-43; Genesis 31:1-55; Genesis 32:1-32; Genesis 33:1-20; Genesis 35:1-29; Genesis 37:1-35; Genesis 42:1-4; Genesis 46:1-47:31; Genesis 48:1-49:33; Hosea 12:2-4; Malachi 1:2-3; Romans 9:10-13; Hebrews 11:21

Abimelech, king of the Philistines (contemporary of Isaac)

Philistine king of Gerar in Isaac's time.

Family

King of Gerar in Isaac's time. No family recorded.

Chronology

Patriarchal; a famine after Abraham's death.

Life Synopsis

Discovered by observation that Rebekah was Isaac's wife, not his sister, and rebuked him: "What is this thou hast done unto us?" (Genesis 26:8–10). Protected them by decree (Genesis 26:11). Later sent Isaac away as too mighty (Genesis 26:16), then sought a covenant with him, acknowledging "the Lord was with thee" (Genesis 26:26–31).

What They Did Right

  • Rebuked Isaac for the sister deception once he discovered it: Genesis 26:9-10.
  • Protected Isaac and Rebekah by public decree on pain of death: Genesis 26:11.
  • Sought a covenant of peace with Isaac, acknowledging "We saw certainly that the Lord was with thee": Genesis 26:26-29.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He sent Isaac away because he had grown too mighty (Genesis 26:16), which Genesis records without condemning.

Character Assessment

Treated favourably; the rebuke again runs from king to patriarch. Identity note: whether this is the same man as the Abimelech of Genesis 20 or a successor is genuinely open. The events are separated by decades, and "Abimelech" may be a dynastic title rather than a personal name. Scripture does not say, and the two are entered separately here rather than merged on an assumption.

Significance

The third instance in Genesis of a pagan ruler rebuking a patriarch over the same deception. Whether he is the same man as the Abimelech of Genesis 20 or a successor is genuinely open - decades separate the events, and Abimelech may be a dynastic title rather than a personal name. Scripture does not say, and the two are kept separate here rather than merged on an assumption.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 26:31.

Scripture References

Genesis 26:1–33.

Judith and Bashemath (wives of Esau)

Hittite wives whom Esau married at forty. Two distinct women, recorded only jointly.

Family

Two distinct women, recorded only jointly. Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite and Bashemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite, both married by Esau at forty (Genesis 26:34).

Chronology

Patriarchal; Esau's fortieth year.

Life Synopsis

"And Esau was forty years old when he took to wife Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Bashemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite: Which were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah" (Genesis 26:34–35).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. The evaluation Scripture gives concerns their effect, not their conduct: they "were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah" (Genesis 26:35). Nothing either woman did or said is recorded.

Character Assessment

The evaluation is of their effect, not their conduct — Scripture records nothing either woman did. The grief is attributed to the marriages, and Rebekah cites the daughters of Heth as her reason for sending Jacob away (Genesis 27:46).

Significance

Their marriages are the stated cause of Rebekah's weariness of life and of her stated reason for sending Jacob to Padan-aram (Genesis 27:46), and so contribute to the separation of the brothers. Note that the list of Esau's wives in Genesis 36:2-3 gives different names and parentage - an unresolved discrepancy in the text, recorded here rather than harmonized.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 26:35.

Scripture References

Genesis 26:34–35; Genesis 27:46. Note: Esau's wives are listed with different names and parentage in Genesis 36:2–3, an unresolved discrepancy.
—

Laban

Son of Bethuel; brother of Rebekah; father of Leah and Rachel; Jacob's father-in-law and employer for twenty years.

Family

Son of Bethuel (Genesis 28:5); brother of Rebekah (Genesis 24:29); father of Leah and Rachel (Genesis 29:16) and of sons (Genesis 31:1). Called the Syrian (Genesis 25:20).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. His dealings with Jacob span twenty years (Genesis 31:38, 31:41).

Life Synopsis

Laban first appears when Abraham's servant comes for Rebekah. He ran out to the man at the well - and the text notes what he had just seen: "when he saw the earring and bracelets upon his sister's hands" (Genesis 24:29-31). He welcomed the servant and, with Bethuel, answered, "The thing proceedeth from the Lord: we cannot speak unto thee bad or good" (Genesis 24:50).

A generation later Jacob arrived fleeing Esau. Laban received him, and after a month proposed wages. Jacob offered seven years for Rachel; Laban agreed, then on the wedding night gave Leah, justifying it afterward by local custom, and required another seven years (Genesis 29:18-28). Over the following years he changed Jacob's wages ten times (Genesis 31:7, 31:41), while his own house prospered - he acknowledged that he had learned by experience that the Lord had blessed him for Jacob's sake (Genesis 30:27).

When Jacob left secretly, Laban pursued him seven days and overtook him in Gilead, having been warned by God in a dream not to speak either good or bad to Jacob (Genesis 31:22-24). He confronted Jacob over the departure and over his stolen images, searched the tents, and found nothing (Genesis 31:26-35). Jacob's answer is the fullest indictment in the passage: twenty years of service, torn beasts borne by himself, frost by night and drought by day, and wages changed ten times (Genesis 31:38-42).

They made a covenant at a heap of stones, called Galeed and Mizpah, agreeing that neither would pass it to harm the other. Laban kissed his sons and daughters, blessed them, and returned to his place (Genesis 31:43-55).

What They Did Right

  • Received Abraham's servant hospitably and acknowledged the Lord's hand in the matter: Genesis 24:31, 24:50.
  • Received Jacob into his house as kin: Genesis 29:13-14.
  • Acknowledged that the Lord had blessed him for Jacob's sake: Genesis 30:27.
  • Obeyed God's warning in the dream and did not harm Jacob: Genesis 31:24, 31:29.
  • Entered a covenant of peace and parted with a blessing on his daughters and grandchildren: Genesis 31:43-55.

What They Did Wrong

  • Substituted Leah for Rachel on the wedding night, a deliberate deception, and used it to extract seven further years of labour: Genesis 29:23-27.
  • Changed Jacob's wages ten times: Genesis 31:7, 31:41. Jacob states this to his face and Laban does not deny it.
  • Kept household images, which his daughter stole and which he pursued Jacob to recover, calling them "my gods": Genesis 31:19, 31:30.
  • Claimed at the parting that everything Jacob had was his own - "all that thou seest is mine" - after twenty years of Jacob's labour: Genesis 31:43.

Character Assessment

Scripture never pronounces a formal verdict on Laban, but the narrative is not neutral. His first recorded action follows the sight of gold; his central act is a deception that cost his son-in-law seven years; and his own daughters say of him, "Are we not counted of him strangers? for he hath sold us, and hath quite devoured also our money" (Genesis 31:14-15). Against this stands genuine hospitality, obedience to God's warning, and a covenant kept. He is not a villain in the text so much as a grasping man whom God restrained.

Significance

Laban is the human instrument by which Jacob the deceiver is himself deceived - the elder daughter substituted for the younger, answering Jacob's own substitution of himself for the elder son. Through his daughters Leah and Rachel, and their handmaids, the twelve tribes of Israel are born. The Mizpah covenant (Genesis 31:49) has passed into common religious usage, often detached from its original setting as a boundary agreement between two men who did not trust each other.

Death / Outcome

Scripture does not record his death. Last appearance: Genesis 31:55, returning to his own place.

Scripture References

Genesis 24:29-60; Genesis 25:20; Genesis 27:43; Genesis 28:2-5; Genesis 29:5-30; Genesis 30:25-43; Genesis 31:1-55
—

Leah

Elder daughter of Laban; Jacob's first wife by Laban's substitution; mother of six of the twelve tribal patriarchs and of Dinah.

Family

Daughter of Laban (Genesis 29:16); elder sister of Rachel. Wife of Jacob (Genesis 29:23-25). Mother of Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, and Dinah (Genesis 29:32-35; Genesis 30:17-21). Mistress of Zilpah (Genesis 30:9).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Her death is not narrated; Jacob states she was buried in the cave of Machpelah (Genesis 49:31).

Life Synopsis

Leah is introduced with a comparison that sets the terms of her life: "Leah was tender eyed; but Rachel was beautiful and well favoured" (Genesis 29:17). Laban gave her to Jacob in place of Rachel on the wedding night, and Jacob discovered it only in the morning (Genesis 29:23-25). The text then states plainly that Leah was hated, and that "when the Lord saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb: but Rachel was barren" (Genesis 29:31).

The names she gave her sons trace her hope and its disappointment. Reuben: "Surely the Lord hath looked upon my affliction; now therefore my husband will love me." Simeon: "the Lord hath heard that I was hated." Levi: "now this time will my husband be joined unto me, because I have born him three sons." Then Judah, where the pattern breaks: "Now will I praise the Lord" (Genesis 29:32-35). She stops asking for her husband's love and praises God.

When she left off bearing she gave Zilpah to Jacob, and two more sons were counted to her (Genesis 30:9-13). She bought a night with Jacob from Rachel for her son's mandrakes and bore Issachar, then Zebulun, and afterward Dinah (Genesis 30:14-21). When Jacob told his wives that God had commanded him to return, she answered with Rachel that they would go (Genesis 31:14-16).

When Esau approached, Jacob arranged his family in order of preference, placing the handmaids first, Leah and her children next, and Rachel and Joseph last (Genesis 33:1-2) - a public ranking she would have understood. Scripture does not narrate her death, but Jacob, dying in Egypt, names Machpelah as the place "where I buried Leah" (Genesis 49:31).

What They Did Right

  • Praised the Lord at the birth of Judah, moving beyond her plea for her husband's affection: Genesis 29:35.
  • Acknowledged God in the naming of each of her sons: Genesis 29:32-35; Genesis 30:18, 30:20.
  • Agreed with Rachel to leave Laban's house at Jacob's word: Genesis 31:14-16.

What They Did Wrong

  • Participated in the wedding-night deception of Jacob: Genesis 29:23-25. Scripture assigns the initiative to Laban and records nothing that Leah said or chose; her degree of responsibility is not stated, and this reference does not assign one.
  • Bargained for a night with her husband using her son's mandrakes, and met him with "thou must come in unto me; for surely I have hired thee": Genesis 30:15-16. The text records it without comment.

Character Assessment

Leah is the unloved wife, and Scripture says so without euphemism. But the record consistently shows God's regard for her precisely in that condition: he saw that she was hated and opened her womb (Genesis 29:31). Six of the twelve tribes come from her, including both the priestly tribe and the royal one. The elders of Bethlehem later bless Ruth by invoking "Rachel and Leah, which two did build the house of Israel" - and they name Rachel first but bless in the line of Leah (Ruth 4:11-12).

Significance

Leah is the mother of Levi, from whom the priesthood came, and of Judah, from whom came David and Christ (Genesis 29:34-35; Matthew 1:2-3). The covenant line runs through the wife Jacob did not choose. She lies in Machpelah with Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, and Jacob (Genesis 49:31), while Rachel is buried by the roadside.

Death / Outcome

Scripture does not narrate her death. Jacob states that he buried her in the cave of Machpelah (Genesis 49:31).

Scripture References

Genesis 29:16-35; Genesis 30:9-21; Genesis 31:4-16; Genesis 33:1-7; Genesis 34:1; Genesis 49:31; Ruth 4:11
—

Rachel

Younger daughter of Laban; the wife Jacob loved; mother of Joseph and Benjamin.

Family

Daughter of Laban (Genesis 29:16); younger sister of Leah; niece of Rebekah. Wife of Jacob (Genesis 29:28). Mother of Joseph and Benjamin (Genesis 30:22-24; Genesis 35:16-18). Mistress of Bilhah (Genesis 30:3-4).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. She died on the way to Ephrath while Jacob was returning from Padan-aram (Genesis 35:16-19). Her age is not recorded.

Life Synopsis

Jacob met Rachel at the well, watered her father's flock, kissed her and wept aloud (Genesis 29:9-11). She was "beautiful and well favoured," and Jacob served seven years for her, "and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her" (Genesis 29:17-20). Laban substituted Leah on the wedding night, and Jacob served another seven years (Genesis 29:23-28).

She was loved but barren while her sister bore sons, and the rivalry between them shapes the whole account. "Give me children, or else I die," she said to Jacob, and his anger was kindled (Genesis 30:1-2). She gave Bilhah her handmaid to him and counted the two sons born as her own victory: "With great wrestlings have I wrestled with my sister, and I have prevailed" (Genesis 30:3-8). She bargained with Leah for her son's mandrakes in exchange for a night with Jacob (Genesis 30:14-16).

At length "God remembered Rachel, and God hearkened to her, and opened her womb," and she bore Joseph, saying, "The Lord shall add to me another son" (Genesis 30:22-24). When Jacob left Padan-aram she stole her father's images and hid them in the camel's furniture, sitting on them while Laban searched - and Jacob, not knowing, had pronounced death on whoever had taken them (Genesis 31:19, 31:32-35).

The second son came at the cost of her life. In hard labour near Ephrath the midwife told her she would have a son; as her soul departed she named him Ben-oni, and his father called him Benjamin. She was buried on the way to Ephrath, and Jacob set a pillar on her grave (Genesis 35:16-20).

What They Did Right

  • Consented to the marriage arrangement and waited through Jacob's years of service: Genesis 29:18-28.
  • Agreed with Leah to leave Laban's house when Jacob told them what God had shown him: Genesis 31:14-16.
  • Named her firstborn Joseph in acknowledgment that God had taken away her reproach: Genesis 30:23-24.

What They Did Wrong

  • Envied her sister: "Rachel envied her sister," the text states directly: Genesis 30:1.
  • Demanded children of Jacob as though he could give them, provoking his anger: Genesis 30:1-2.
  • Stole her father's household images and lied to conceal them: Genesis 31:19, 31:34-35. The theft is stated as fact; the deception of Laban is recorded without comment, but it placed her under Jacob's unwitting curse.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents Rachel as deeply loved and deeply unhappy, and does not hide the envy that ran alongside. Her recorded speech is dominated by rivalry with her sister. Yet the record also shows God remembering her and hearkening to her (Genesis 30:22), and Israel's elders later invoke her and Leah together as the two who built the house of Israel (Ruth 4:11).

Significance

Mother of Joseph and Benjamin, and so of the tribes of Ephraim, Manasseh, and Benjamin. Her tomb near Bethlehem became a landmark (Genesis 35:19-20; 1 Samuel 10:2). Jeremiah pictures her weeping for her children and refusing comfort (Jeremiah 31:15), which Matthew applies to the slaughter of the infants at Bethlehem (Matthew 2:18).

Death / Outcome

Died in hard labour bearing Benjamin, on the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem; buried there under a pillar Jacob set up (Genesis 35:16-20; Genesis 48:7).

Scripture References

Genesis 29:6-30; Genesis 30:1-24; Genesis 31:4-35; Genesis 33:1-7; Genesis 35:16-20; Genesis 48:7; Ruth 4:11; 1 Samuel 10:2; Jeremiah 31:15; Matthew 2:18

Bilhah

Rachel's handmaid, given to Jacob as wife; mother of Dan and Naphtali.

Rachel's handmaid, given to Jacob as wife (Genesis 29:29; Genesis 30:4). Mother of Dan and Naphtali (Genesis 30:5-8).

Given by Rachel to Jacob so that Rachel might "have children by her" (Genesis 30:3–4). Bore Dan and Naphtali (Genesis 30:5–8). Later, Reuben lay with her, and "Israel heard it" (Genesis 35:22).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

No verdict is offered on Bilhah. In both episodes she is acted upon rather than acting, and Scripture records no words of hers.

Significance

Mother of two tribal patriarchs, Dan and Naphtali. Reuben's act with her (Genesis 35:22) is the stated ground of his forfeited birthright (Genesis 49:3-4; 1 Chronicles 5:1).

Leah's handmaid, given to Jacob as wife; mother of Gad and Asher.

Family

Leah's handmaid, given to Jacob as wife (Genesis 29:24; Genesis 30:9). Mother of Gad and Asher (Genesis 30:10-13).

Chronology

Patriarchal; Jacob's years in Padan-aram.

Life Synopsis

Given by Leah to Jacob when Leah left off bearing (Genesis 30:9). Bore Gad and Asher (Genesis 30:10–13).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. She acts nowhere in the narrative and speaks nowhere; the naming of both her sons is Leah's.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered. As with Bilhah, she acts nowhere in the narrative and speaks nowhere — the naming of both sons is Leah's.

Significance

Mother of two tribal patriarchs, Gad and Asher.

Reuben

Firstborn son of Jacob by Leah.

Family

Firstborn son of Jacob by Leah (Genesis 29:32). Father of four sons (Genesis 46:9).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Brought mandrakes to his mother (Genesis 30:14). Lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine (Genesis 35:22). Alone among the brothers, moved to save Joseph — "Let us not kill him... Shed no blood" — intending to return him to his father, and rent his clothes on finding the pit empty (Genesis 37:21–22, 37:29–30). Offered his own two sons as surety for Benjamin (Genesis 42:37).

What They Did Right

  • Alone among the brothers, moved to save Joseph: "Let us not kill him... Shed no blood," intending to return him to his father: Genesis 37:21-22.
  • Rent his clothes on finding the pit empty: Genesis 37:29-30.
  • Offered his own two sons as surety for Benjamin's safe return: Genesis 42:37.
  • Reminded his brothers of their guilt over Joseph rather than concealing it: Genesis 42:22.

What They Did Wrong

  • Lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine: Genesis 35:22. Jacob names this explicitly as the reason for his forfeited pre-eminence: Genesis 49:3-4; 1 Chronicles 5:1.
  • Jacob's verdict is "Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel": Genesis 49:4.

Character Assessment

Mixed, and Scripture is explicit about both sides. Jacob's deathbed verdict names the dignity and the disqualification together: "Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel; because thou wentest up to thy father's bed" (Genesis 49:3–4). His attempts to protect Joseph and Benjamin are recorded without comment but stand in the narrative to his credit.

Significance

The firstborn who lost the birthright, which passed to Joseph's sons (1 Chronicles 5:1-2). His repeated attempts to protect Joseph and Benjamin are recorded without comment but stand to his credit in the narrative, making his record genuinely mixed rather than simply negative.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention in Genesis: Genesis 49:3-4.

Scripture References

Genesis 29:32; Genesis 30:14; Genesis 35:22; Genesis 37:21–30; Genesis 42:22, 42:37; Genesis 49:3–4.
—

Simeon

Second son of Jacob by Leah; head of the tribe of Simeon.

Family

Second son of Jacob by Leah (Genesis 29:33); brother of Levi and Dinah. Father of six sons (Genesis 46:10).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

With Levi, killed all the males of Shechem's city by deceit while they were sore from circumcision, and answered Jacob's rebuke: "Should he deal with our sister as with an harlot?" (Genesis 34:25–31). Bound and held hostage in Egypt by Joseph (Genesis 42:24).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. His answer to Jacob - "Should he deal with our sister as with an harlot?" (Genesis 34:31) - states a genuine grievance, but Scripture does not commend the act it defends.

What They Did Wrong

  • With Levi, deceived the men of Shechem with a proposal of circumcision and killed all the males while they were sore: Genesis 34:13-26.
  • Explicitly condemned by Jacob: "instruments of cruelty are in their habitations... Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel": Genesis 49:5-7. The stated ground is the anger and the cruelty.

Character Assessment

Condemned by Jacob, explicitly and at his deathbed: "instruments of cruelty are in their habitations... Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce" (Genesis 49:5–7). The stated ground is the anger and the cruelty, not the defence of Dinah as such.

Significance

Head of the tribe of Simeon. Jacob's sentence - "I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel" (Genesis 49:7) - is fulfilled in Simeon's inheritance being absorbed within Judah's territory (Joshua 19:1-9). He was the brother Joseph bound and held in Egypt (Genesis 42:24).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention in Genesis: Genesis 49:5-7.

Scripture References

Genesis 29:33; Genesis 34:25–31; Genesis 42:24, 42:36; Genesis 43:23; Genesis 49:5–7.

Levi

Third son of Jacob by Leah; head of the tribe from which Israel's priesthood came.

Family

Third son of Jacob by Leah (Genesis 29:34); brother of Simeon and Dinah. Father of Gershon, Kohath, and Merari (Genesis 46:11).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Acted with Simeon at Shechem (Genesis 34:25–31). Lived 137 years (Exodus 6:16).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • With Simeon, deceived and slaughtered the men of Shechem: Genesis 34:13-26.
  • Explicitly condemned with Simeon at Jacob's deathbed: Genesis 49:5-7.

Character Assessment

Condemned with Simeon in Genesis 49:5–7, and the sentence — "I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel" — is worth noting as a judgment later turned to a different end in the Levites' dispersed priestly settlement. Nothing commendable is recorded of Levi personally.

Significance

Head of the tribe from which Israel's priesthood came. The scattering pronounced as judgment in Genesis 49:7 is turned to a different purpose in the Levites' dispersed priestly settlement throughout Israel (Joshua 21:1-42) - a striking instance of a sentence becoming a service, though Genesis itself does not draw the connection. He lived 137 years (Exodus 6:16).

Death / Outcome

Scripture records his age at death, 137 years (Exodus 6:16), but does not narrate his death.

Scripture References

Genesis 29:34; Genesis 34:25–31; Genesis 49:5–7; Exodus 6:16.

Judah

Fourth son of Jacob by Leah; head of the royal tribe; ancestor of David and of Christ.

Family

Son of Jacob and Leah (Genesis 29:35). Married the daughter of Shuah, a Canaanite (Genesis 38:2). Father of Er, Onan, and Shelah by her, and of the twins Pharez and Zarah by Tamar (Genesis 38:3-5, 38:29-30).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Born in Padan-aram during Jacob's twenty years with Laban; alive at the descent into Egypt (Genesis 46:12, 46:28).

Life Synopsis

Judah was Leah's fourth son, born when she said, "Now will I praise the Lord" (Genesis 29:35). His first significant act is a bad one. When the brothers had cast Joseph into the pit and sat down to eat, it was Judah who proposed selling him: "What profit is it if we slay our brother, and conceal his blood? Come, and let us sell him to the Ishmeelites" (Genesis 37:26-27). The proposal spared Joseph's life and profited the brothers, and it is presented as neither mercy nor justice.

Genesis 38 then interrupts the Joseph narrative for Judah's own story. He went down from his brethren, married a Canaanite woman, and had three sons. Er was wicked and the Lord slew him; Onan refused the levirate duty and was slain also (Genesis 38:6-10). Judah sent his daughter-in-law Tamar home as a widow, promising Shelah when he was grown, and did not give him. Tamar veiled herself and sat by the way; Judah, taking her for a harlot, went in to her and left his signet, bracelets, and staff as pledge (Genesis 38:14-18). When told three months later that she was pregnant by whoredom, he ordered her burnt - until she produced his pledges. His response is the turning point of his life: "She hath been more righteous than I; because that I gave her not to Shelah my son" (Genesis 38:26). He acknowledged the wrong publicly, at his own cost.

The change holds. When famine required Benjamin to go to Egypt, Judah gave himself as surety: "I will be surety for him; of my hand shalt thou require him" (Genesis 43:8-9). When the cup was found in Benjamin's sack, it was Judah who stepped forward with the longest speech in Genesis, recounting the whole matter and offering himself as a slave in his brother's place: "let thy servant abide instead of the lad a bondman to my lord" (Genesis 44:18-34). The man who sold one brother offered himself for another. Jacob sent him ahead to Goshen to prepare the way (Genesis 46:28), and gave him the ruling oracle: the sceptre would not depart from Judah until Shiloh came (Genesis 49:8-12).

What They Did Right

  • Acknowledged his own fault publicly when he could have destroyed the evidence: "She hath been more righteous than I": Genesis 38:26.
  • Became surety for Benjamin with his own life: Genesis 43:8-9.
  • Offered himself as a bondman in Benjamin's place, and made the plea that broke Joseph: Genesis 44:18-34.
  • Was sent ahead by Jacob to prepare the way into Goshen - a mark of trust: Genesis 46:28.

What They Did Wrong

  • Proposed selling Joseph into slavery for profit: Genesis 37:26-27.
  • Married a Canaanite woman: Genesis 38:2. Genesis records this without explicit condemnation, though it stands against the pattern Abraham and Isaac insisted on for their sons (Genesis 24:3; Genesis 28:1).
  • Withheld Shelah from Tamar, leaving her a widow indefinitely, and later admitted it as the wrong it was: Genesis 38:11, 38:26.
  • Went in to a woman he believed to be a harlot: Genesis 38:15-18.
  • Ordered Tamar burnt for the very sin he had himself committed with her: Genesis 38:24.

Character Assessment

One of the clearest arcs of moral change in Genesis. Judah begins by selling a brother for twenty pieces of silver and ends by offering his own freedom to spare another. Between the two stands Genesis 38, where he is confronted with his hypocrisy and does not evade it. Scripture records his failures in unusual detail - the sale, the Canaanite marriage, the harlot, the double standard - and then gives him the royal oracle anyway. The record neither excuses him nor disqualifies him.

Significance

Judah is the royal tribe. Jacob's oracle - "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come" (Genesis 49:10) - is one of the central messianic prophecies of the Old Testament. David descends from him through Pharez and Tamar (Ruth 4:18-22), and so does Christ, who is called the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Matthew 1:2-3; Hebrews 7:14; Revelation 5:5).

Death / Outcome

Scripture does not record his death. Last appearance in Genesis: Genesis 49:8-12, receiving Jacob's blessing.

Scripture References

Genesis 29:35; Genesis 37:26-27; Genesis 38:1-30; Genesis 43:3-10; Genesis 44:14-34; Genesis 46:12, 46:28; Genesis 49:8-12; Ruth 4:12, 4:18-22; Matthew 1:2-3; Hebrews 7:14; Revelation 5:5

Character Assessment

Scripture offers no assessment of him as an individual. He is included because his birth, naming, and the oracle over him are recorded, which is more than a bare name in a list.

Joseph

Eleventh son of Jacob and firstborn of Rachel; sold into Egypt as a slave and raised to be ruler over all the land under Pharaoh.

Also called Zaphnath-paaneah

Family

Son of Jacob and Rachel (Genesis 30:22-24); full brother of Benjamin. Husband of Asenath, daughter of Poti-pherah priest of On (Genesis 41:45). Father of Manasseh and Ephraim (Genesis 41:50-52).

Chronology

Seventeen when sold (Genesis 37:2); thirty when he stood before Pharaoh (Genesis 41:46); died at 110 (Genesis 50:26). These ages are explicitly stated in Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Joseph was seventeen, feeding the flock with his brothers, and brought their father their evil report. Israel loved him more than all his children and made him a coat of many colours, "and when his brethren saw that their father loved him more than all his brethren, they hated him" (Genesis 37:2-4). Two dreams of sheaves and stars, which he told, deepened the hatred (Genesis 37:5-11). Sent to check on them at Dothan, he was stripped, cast into a pit, and sold to Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver; his coat was dipped in goat's blood and carried to his father (Genesis 37:23-33).

In Egypt he served Potiphar, and the Lord was with him so that he was made overseer of the whole house (Genesis 39:1-6). Potiphar's wife solicited him daily; he refused, naming the reason: "how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" When she caught his garment he fled and left it in her hand, and was imprisoned on her false accusation (Genesis 39:7-20). In prison the keeper committed all the prisoners to him (Genesis 39:21-23). He interpreted the dreams of Pharaoh's butler and baker exactly as they fell out, and asked the butler to remember him - who forgot him two full years (Genesis 40:1-23).

When Pharaoh dreamed, the butler remembered. Joseph, brought from the dungeon, disclaimed the ability - "It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace" (Genesis 41:16) - interpreted seven years of plenty and seven of famine, and proposed a plan. Pharaoh set him over all Egypt at thirty (Genesis 41:38-46). He gathered grain, and the famine came.

His brothers came to buy corn and bowed before him without knowing him. Over two visits he tested them - the demand for Benjamin, Simeon held hostage, the money returned, the cup in Benjamin's sack - until Judah offered himself in Benjamin's place. Then Joseph wept aloud and made himself known: "I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt" (Genesis 45:1-4). His interpretation of it all is the theological centre of the story: "be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves... for God did send me before you to preserve life" (Genesis 45:5-8). He brought his father and household into Goshen, sustained Egypt through the famine, and after Jacob's death reassured his frightened brothers: "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good" (Genesis 50:20). He died at 110, having charged them to carry up his bones (Genesis 50:24-26).

What They Did Right

  • Refused Potiphar's wife day after day, naming the sin as against God: Genesis 39:8-10.
  • Fled rather than argue when physically seized, at the cost of his position and his freedom: Genesis 39:12.
  • Served faithfully in every position - Potiphar's house, the prison, and all Egypt - so that each master trusted him completely: Genesis 39:4, 39:22-23; Genesis 41:40-44.
  • Gave God the credit for interpretation rather than claiming it: Genesis 40:8; Genesis 41:16.
  • Wept over his brothers and forgave them, though he had absolute power to destroy them: Genesis 45:1-15; Genesis 50:19-21.
  • Provided for his family and for Egypt through seven years of famine: Genesis 45:9-11; Genesis 47:11-12.
  • Charged his brethren concerning his bones, in faith that God would bring Israel out: Genesis 50:24-25; Hebrews 11:22.

What They Did Wrong

  • Brought his brothers' evil report to their father: Genesis 37:2. Scripture records this without moral comment - whether it was faithfulness or tale-bearing is not stated.
  • Told his dreams to brothers who already hated him, and to his father, who rebuked him for it: Genesis 37:5-11. Again the text records the rebuke without endorsing or condemning Joseph.
  • Scripture records no sin of Joseph. This is an absence of record, not a claim of sinlessness, which Scripture makes of no one but Christ.

Character Assessment

Joseph is one of a very small number of substantial biblical figures of whom no wrongdoing is recorded. His two questionable acts as a boy - the report and the dreams - are set down without moral judgment, and interpreters differ over them. What Scripture does record at length is integrity under injustice: he was sold by his brothers, lied about by his master's wife, and forgotten by a man he had helped, and in none of those does he retaliate. Hebrews commends the last act of his life, his charge concerning his bones (Hebrews 11:22).

Significance

Through Joseph the family of Jacob was preserved alive through famine, and the descent into Egypt took place that set up the Exodus (Genesis 45:5-8; Genesis 50:20). His two sons became two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh, receiving a double portion in place of the birthright forfeited by Reuben (1 Chronicles 5:1-2). His statement in Genesis 50:20 - "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good" - is one of Scripture's clearest expressions of God's providence working through human wrongdoing without excusing it. Stephen recounts his history in his defence before the council (Acts 7:9-18).

Death / Outcome

Died in Egypt at 110 years, was embalmed and put in a coffin, having made Israel swear to carry his bones up (Genesis 50:24-26). His bones were carried out at the Exodus and buried at Shechem (Exodus 13:19; Joshua 24:32).

Scripture References

Genesis 30:22-24; Genesis 37:1-36; Genesis 39:1-23; Genesis 40:1-23; Genesis 41:1-57; Genesis 42:1-45:28; Genesis 46:28-47:31; Genesis 48:1-22; Genesis 50:1-26; Exodus 13:19; Joshua 24:32; Acts 7:9-18; Hebrews 11:22

Benjamin

Youngest son of Jacob, and the only one born in Canaan; Rachel's second son.

Family

Youngest son of Jacob, by Rachel (Genesis 35:18); full brother of Joseph; the only one of Jacob's sons born in Canaan. Father of ten sons (Genesis 46:21).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Born near Ephrath; his dying mother named him Ben-oni and his father renamed him Benjamin (Genesis 35:16–18). Kept back from Egypt by Jacob, who feared losing him (Genesis 42:4, 42:38). Brought at last under Judah's surety (Genesis 43:8–14). Given five times the portion at Joseph's table (Genesis 43:34), and three hundred pieces of silver and five changes of raiment at the reunion (Genesis 45:22). The cup was planted in his sack, precipitating Judah's plea (Genesis 44:2–34).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. Scripture records not one word spoken by Benjamin in the whole of Genesis, though he is central to two chapters. He is the occasion of the test rather than an actor in it.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered. Scripture records not one word spoken by Benjamin in the whole of Genesis, though he is central to two chapters — he is the occasion of the test rather than an actor in it. Jacob's deathbed word is of the tribe: "Benjamin shall ravin as a wolf" (Genesis 49:27).

Significance

Head of the tribe of Benjamin, from which came Saul, Israel's first king (1 Samuel 9:1-2), and Saul of Tarsus, who calls himself of the tribe of Benjamin (Philippians 3:5). His dying mother named him Ben-oni and his father renamed him Benjamin (Genesis 35:18). Jacob's word over him is of the tribe: "Benjamin shall ravin as a wolf" (Genesis 49:27).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention in Genesis: Genesis 49:27.

Scripture References

Genesis 35:16–18, 35:24; Genesis 42:4, 42:36–38; Genesis 43:8–34; Genesis 44:1–34; Genesis 45:12–22; Genesis 46:19–21; Genesis 49:27.

Deborah (Rebekah's nurse)

Nurse to Rebekah, who travelled with her from Padan-aram and remained with the family into Jacob's generation. Distinct from Deborah the judge and prophetess.

Family

Nurse to Rebekah, who travelled with her from Padan-aram (Genesis 24:59) and remained with the household into Jacob's generation. Not to be confused with Deborah the judge and prophetess (Judges 4:4).

Chronology

Patriarchal; died during Jacob's return.

Sent with Rebekah at her betrothal, unnamed there (Genesis 24:59). Named only at her death: "But Deborah Rebekah's nurse died, and she was buried beneath Beth-el under an oak: and the name of it was called Allon-bachuth" (Genesis 35:8). The place-name is generally understood to mean "oak of weeping"; Genesis does not translate it.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered. A servant whose death is marked by a named place and public mourning, which is more honour than Genesis records for most of the free-born.

Significance

A servant whose death is marked by a named place and public mourning - the oak was called Allon-bachuth, and the place-name is generally understood to mean oak of weeping, though Genesis does not translate it. That is more honour than Genesis records for many of the free-born, and it indicates the regard in which she was held.

Death / Outcome

"But Deborah Rebekah's nurse died, and she was buried beneath Bethel under an oak" (Genesis 35:8).

Scripture References

Genesis 24:59; Genesis 35:8.
