Dinah

Daughter of Jacob by Leah.

Family

Daughter of Jacob by Leah (Genesis 30:21); sister of Simeon and Levi.

Chronology

Patriarchal; after Jacob's return to Canaan.

Life Synopsis

Went out to see the daughters of the land; Shechem "took her, and lay with her, and defiled her" (Genesis 34:1–2). Her brothers' revenge followed; she was taken out of Shechem's house (Genesis 34:26). Listed among those who went into Egypt (Genesis 46:15).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. This must be stated carefully. Scripture records nothing that Dinah said and no wrongdoing on her part. The text is explicit that she was defiled - the language of Genesis 34:2 places the act on Shechem. Readings that assign her blame for going out to see the daughters of the land read into Genesis 34:1 something the verse does not say.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing that Dinah said and no wrongdoing on her part. The text is explicit that she was defiled — the language places the act on Shechem. Readings that assign her blame for going out read something into Genesis 34:1 that is not there.

Significance

The violation of Dinah and her brothers' revenge is the occasion of Jacob's rebuke of Simeon and Levi (Genesis 34:30) and of the curse on their anger at his deathbed (Genesis 49:5-7), which in turn determines the scattering of those two tribes in Israel.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 46:15, among those who went into Egypt.

Scripture References

Genesis 30:21; Genesis 34:1–31; Genesis 46:15.
—

Shechem

Son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the country.

Family

Son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the country (Genesis 34:2).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Took Dinah and defiled her (Genesis 34:2). Afterward "his soul clave unto Dinah... and he loved the damsel, and spake kindly" (Genesis 34:3), and sought her in marriage at any price (Genesis 34:11–12). Accepted circumcision and persuaded his city to it (Genesis 34:19–24). Killed by Simeon and Levi (Genesis 34:26).

What They Did Right

  • "He was more honourable than all the house of his father" (Genesis 34:19). Genesis states this without irony, alongside the account of his crime, and both statements stand.
  • Sought to marry Dinah and offered any dowry asked: Genesis 34:11-12.

What They Did Wrong

  • Took Dinah and defiled her. Genesis calls it folly "which thing ought not to be done": Genesis 34:2, 34:7.

Character Assessment

Genesis condemns the act — it "ought not to be done" (Genesis 34:7) — while recording, without irony, that he was "more honourable than all the house of his father" (Genesis 34:19). Both statements stand; the text does not resolve them, and neither should a summary of it.

Significance

His act precipitates the massacre at Shechem, the scattering of Simeon and Levi, and Jacob's fear of the surrounding peoples. The episode is one of the clearest instances in Genesis of a wrong avenged by a greater wrong.

Death / Outcome

Killed by Simeon and Levi with the edge of the sword: Genesis 34:26.

Scripture References

Genesis 34:2–26.
—

Hamor

Hivite prince; father of Shechem.

Family

Hivite prince; father of Shechem (Genesis 34:2, 34:6).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Negotiated with Jacob and his sons for Dinah, proposing intermarriage and shared land (Genesis 34:6–10). Persuaded his city to be circumcised, urging on them the material gain: "Shall not their cattle and their substance and every beast of theirs be ours?" (Genesis 34:20–23). Killed by Simeon and Levi (Genesis 34:26).

What They Did Right

  • Went out to Jacob to commune with him rather than simply seizing what his son wanted: Genesis 34:6, 34:8-10.

What They Did Wrong

  • Urged the circumcision on his townsmen with an acquisitive argument: "Shall not their cattle and their substance and every beast of theirs be ours?": Genesis 34:23. Genesis records the motive without comment.

Character Assessment

No direct verdict is offered on Hamor. The motive he puts to his townsmen is recorded as acquisitive, though the text does not comment.

Significance

Jacob had bought a parcel of ground from the children of Hamor (Genesis 33:19), and that parcel later becomes Joseph's burial place (Joshua 24:32).

Death / Outcome

Killed by Simeon and Levi with the edge of the sword: Genesis 34:26.

Scripture References

Genesis 33:19; Genesis 34:2–26.
—

Timna

Concubine to Eliphaz, Esau's son; mother of Amalek.

Family

Concubine to Eliphaz, Esau's son; mother of Amalek (Genesis 36:12).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

"And Timna was concubine to Eliphaz Esau's son; and she bare to Eliphaz Amalek" (Genesis 36:12).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered. Included because a single verse establishes her position, her relationship, and her son — and that son is the ancestor of a people that becomes a standing adversary of Israel.

Significance

Mother of Amalek, ancestor of the Amalekites, who become a standing adversary of Israel from Exodus 17:8 onward and against whom God declares perpetual war (Exodus 17:16). A single verse establishes her position, her relationship, and her son.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Chronicles 1:39.

Scripture References

Genesis 36:12, 36:22; 1 Chronicles 1:36, 1:39.
—

Anah

Son of Zibeon the Horite; father of Aholibamah, one of Esau's wives.

Family

Son of Zibeon the Horite (Genesis 36:24); father of Aholibamah, one of Esau's wives (Genesis 36:2, 36:25).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

One line, and it is unlike anything else in the chapter: "this was that Anah that found the mules in the wilderness, as he fed the asses of Zibeon his father" (Genesis 36:24). The Hebrew rendered "mules" is uncertain and has been variously translated as hot springs.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered. He is a good illustration of the inclusion standard: nothing hangs on him theologically, but the text singles him out with a specific remembered incident, so he is in.

Significance

Singled out from an otherwise bare genealogy by one remembered incident: "this was that Anah that found the mules in the wilderness, as he fed the asses of Zibeon his father" (Genesis 36:24). The Hebrew word rendered "mules" is uncertain and has also been translated as hot springs. He is a good illustration of the inclusion standard used here: nothing hangs on him theologically, but the text remembers a specific thing about him.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 36:29.

Scripture References

Genesis 36:2, 36:14, 36:20, 36:24–25, 36:29.
—

Hadad son of Bedad

A king who reigned in Edom before any king reigned in Israel.

Family

Son of Bedad; a king who reigned in Edom before any king reigned over Israel (Genesis 36:35).

Chronology

Patriarchal or later; the Edomite king-list of Genesis 36:31–39 is not synchronized with Israel's chronology.

Life Synopsis

"Hadad the son of Bedad, who smote Midian in the field of Moab, reigned in his stead: and the name of his city was Avith" (Genesis 36:35).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered. He is entered while the other Edomite kings are not, because he alone in that list is credited with a specific action.

Significance

The only king in the Edomite list of Genesis 36:31-39 credited with a specific action: he "smote Midian in the field of Moab." His city was Avith. The list itself is notable for the observation that kings reigned in Edom before there were kings in Israel.

Death / Outcome

"And Hadad died" (Genesis 36:36, in the succession formula).

Scripture References

Genesis 36:35; 1 Chronicles 1:46.
—

Er

Firstborn son of Judah by the daughter of Shua; first husband of Tamar.

Family

Firstborn son of Judah by the daughter of Shuah (Genesis 38:3); first husband of Tamar (Genesis 38:6).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

"And Er, Judah's firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the Lord; and the Lord slew him" (Genesis 38:7).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • "Er, Judah's firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the Lord; and the Lord slew him" (Genesis 38:7). Scripture does not state what his wickedness was - only that it was wickedness in the Lord's sight and that it was fatal. Speculation about its nature has no basis in the text.

Character Assessment

Condemned. Scripture does not state what his wickedness was — only that it was wickedness in the Lord's sight and that it was fatal. Speculation about its nature is exactly that.

Significance

His death without issue creates the levirate situation that leads to Onan's sin, Judah's failure with Shelah, and finally Tamar's action - the chain of events producing Pharez, ancestor of David and of Christ.

Death / Outcome

Slain by the Lord for his wickedness (Genesis 38:7). Last mention: 1 Chronicles 2:3.

Scripture References

Genesis 38:3, 38:6–7; Genesis 46:12; Numbers 26:19; 1 Chronicles 2:3.
—

Onan

Second son of Judah; brother of Er.

Family

Second son of Judah (Genesis 38:4); brother of Er and Shelah.

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Directed by Judah to raise up seed to his dead brother by Tamar. "And Onan knew that the seed should not be his," and prevented conception; "the thing which he did displeased the Lord: wherefore he slew him also" (Genesis 38:8–10).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Refused the levirate duty to raise up seed to his dead brother, knowing the child would not be counted his, and prevented conception: Genesis 38:8-9.
  • "The thing which he did displeased the Lord: wherefore he slew him also" (Genesis 38:10). Genesis states the motive explicitly, which locates the offence in the defrauding of his brother's line.

Character Assessment

Condemned. Genesis states the motive explicitly — that the child would not be counted his — which locates the offence in the refusal of the levirate duty and the defrauding of his brother's line.

Significance

His death, with his brother's, leaves Tamar twice widowed and sets up Judah's failure to give her Shelah.

Death / Outcome

Slain by the Lord (Genesis 38:10). Last mention: 1 Chronicles 2:3.

Scripture References

Genesis 38:4, 38:8–10; Genesis 46:12; Numbers 26:19; 1 Chronicles 2:3.
—

Shelah

Third son of Judah. Distinct from Salah/Shelah in the line of Shem.

Family

Third son of Judah by the daughter of Shuah (Genesis 38:5). Not to be confused with Salah son of Arphaxad in the line of Shem (Genesis 11:12).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Promised to Tamar once grown, but withheld — Judah feared he would die like his brothers (Genesis 38:11). Judah later acknowledged the failure: "She hath been more righteous than I; because that I gave her not to Shelah my son" (Genesis 38:26).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. He does nothing in the narrative.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. The wrong in the episode is his father's, who withheld him: Genesis 38:11, 38:26.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered on Shelah, who does nothing in the narrative. The wrong recorded is his father's.

Significance

Head of the Shelanite family of Judah (Numbers 26:20). His being withheld from Tamar is the stated reason Judah pronounced her more righteous than himself.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Chronicles 4:21.

Scripture References

Genesis 38:5, 38:11, 38:14, 38:26; Genesis 46:12; Numbers 26:20; 1 Chronicles 2:3.
—

Tamar

Wife of Er, then of Onan; daughter-in-law of Judah; mother of Pharez and Zarah.

Family

Daughter-in-law of Judah; wife of Er and then of Onan (Genesis 38:6-8); mother of the twins Pharez and Zarah by Judah (Genesis 38:29-30).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Twice widowed and sent to her father's house to wait for Shelah, who was never given her (Genesis 38:6–11, 38:14). Seeing she had been withheld, she veiled herself, sat by the way to Timnath, and conceived by Judah, taking his signet, bracelets, and staff as pledge (Genesis 38:14–18). Condemned to burning when found pregnant, she produced the pledges: "By the man, whose these are, am I with child" (Genesis 38:24–25).

What They Did Right

  • Judah's own verdict is Scripture's verdict on the matter between them: "She hath been more righteous than I; because that I gave her not to Shelah my son": Genesis 38:26.
  • Obeyed Judah's instruction and remained a widow in her father's house as told: Genesis 38:11.
  • Produced the pledges rather than accusing Judah publicly, giving him the opportunity to acknowledge them himself: Genesis 38:25.
  • Invoked as a blessing by the elders of Bethlehem: Ruth 4:12.

What They Did Wrong

  • Disguised herself as a harlot and conceived by her father-in-law: Genesis 38:14-18. Scripture does not commend the means, and Judah's declaration concerns the matter between the two of them rather than a blanket approval of her conduct. The moral status of her action is genuinely debated, and this reference does not resolve it.

Character Assessment

Judah's own verdict is the text's verdict: "She hath been more righteous than I" (Genesis 38:26). Scripture does not commend the means; it records that in the matter between them, the fault was his. She is named in the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:3) and invoked as a blessing at Bethlehem (Ruth 4:12).

Significance

Mother of Pharez, ancestor of David and of Christ (Ruth 4:18-22). She is one of only four women named in Matthew's genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:3). Her insistence on the levirate obligation preserved the line of Judah when Judah himself had let it lapse.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Ruth 4:12; Matthew 1:3.

Scripture References

Genesis 38:6–30; Ruth 4:12; Matthew 1:3.
—

Hirah the Adullamite

Judah's friend and companion.

Family

Judah's friend and companion (Genesis 38:1, 38:12).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Judah "turned in" to him when he went down from his brethren (Genesis 38:1). Went up with him to the sheepshearers (Genesis 38:12), and was sent to deliver the kid and recover the pledge, but could not find the woman (Genesis 38:20–23).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered. Included for a named role in a specific transaction across a chapter.

Significance

Named in a specific role across a chapter: Judah turned in to him, went up with him to the sheepshearers, and sent him to deliver the pledge - a named companion in the events that produced the line of David.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 38:23.

Scripture References

Genesis 38:1, 38:12, 38:20–23.
—

Pharez

Twin son of Judah by Tamar; ancestor of David and of Christ. Also spelled Perez.

Family

Twin son of Judah by Tamar (Genesis 38:29). Father of Hezron and Hamul (Genesis 46:12). Also spelled Perez.

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Born second in the attempt but first in fact, after his brother's hand had been marked: "How hast thou broken forth? this breach be upon thee: therefore his name was called Pharez" (Genesis 38:29). Father of Hezron and Hamul (Genesis 46:12).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered on the man. The line of promise runs through him (Ruth 4:18–22; Matthew 1:3).

Significance

Ancestor of David and of Christ (Ruth 4:18-22; Matthew 1:3; Luke 3:33). The elders of Bethlehem bless Boaz by invoking "the house of Pharez, whom Tamar bare unto Judah" (Ruth 4:12). Born second in the attempt but first in fact - another instance of the Genesis pattern in which the expected order is reversed.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention in the genealogies: Matthew 1:3; Luke 3:33.

Scripture References

Genesis 38:29; Genesis 46:12; Ruth 4:12, 4:18; Matthew 1:3; Luke 3:33.
—

Zarah

Twin brother of Pharez. Also spelled Zerah.

Family

Twin brother of Pharez, son of Judah by Tamar (Genesis 38:30). Also spelled Zerah.

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Put out his hand first in the birth and had a scarlet thread bound on it, then drew it back (Genesis 38:28–30).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered. Entered because the circumstances of his birth are recorded in detail, not merely his name.

Significance

The circumstances of his birth are recorded in unusual detail - the hand put out first, the scarlet thread, the hand drawn back - marking the reversal by which Pharez took precedence.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Chronicles 2:6.

Scripture References

Genesis 38:28–30; Genesis 46:12; 1 Chronicles 2:4, 2:6; Matthew 1:3.
—

Potiphar

An officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard; Joseph's Egyptian master.

Family

An officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard, an Egyptian (Genesis 37:36; Genesis 39:1). Married; his wife is unnamed.

Chronology

Patriarchal; Joseph's servitude.

Life Synopsis

Bought Joseph from the Ishmeelites (Genesis 39:1). Saw that the Lord was with him and made him overseer of all he had, leaving everything in his hand (Genesis 39:3–6). On his wife's accusation, "his wrath was kindled" and he put Joseph in the king's prison (Genesis 39:19–20).

What They Did Right

  • Recognized that the Lord was with Joseph and promoted him accordingly: Genesis 39:3-4.
  • Trusted Joseph so completely that he left everything in his hand and knew nothing he had, save the bread he ate: Genesis 39:6.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He imprisoned Joseph on his wife's false accusation (Genesis 39:19-20). Genesis records his wrath but does not evaluate his judgment, and does not say what he believed. It is worth noting without pressing that the penalty was imprisonment rather than the execution such an accusation would ordinarily have brought.

Character Assessment

No direct verdict is offered. Worth noting: the penalty was imprisonment rather than execution, which the offence as alleged would ordinarily have carried — Genesis does not comment on this, and it should not be pressed further than the silence allows.

Significance

Joseph's service in his house is the first stage of the rise that ends in the preservation of Israel. The prison to which he sent Joseph was "a place where the king's prisoners were bound" (Genesis 39:20), which put Joseph where he would meet Pharaoh's butler.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 39:20.

Scripture References

Genesis 37:36; Genesis 39:1–20.
—

Potiphar's wife

Wife of Joseph's master; unnamed.

Family

Unnamed. Wife of Joseph's master (Genesis 39:7).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Solicited Joseph repeatedly — "she spake to Joseph day by day" (Genesis 39:7–10). Caught him by his garment; when he fled leaving it, she kept it and accused him to the men of the house and then to her husband (Genesis 39:12–18).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Solicited Joseph persistently - "she spake to Joseph day by day": Genesis 39:7-10.
  • Seized him physically: Genesis 39:12.
  • Made a knowingly false accusation against him, first to the men of the house and then to her husband: Genesis 39:13-18. Joseph's own words name the sin she proposed: "how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" (Genesis 39:9).

Character Assessment

Condemned by the narrative, which records both the solicitation and the knowingly false accusation. Joseph's refusal names the offence: "how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" (Genesis 39:9).

Significance

Her accusation sends Joseph to the prison where he meets Pharaoh's officers, and so is the means by which he comes before Pharaoh - one of the clearest instances in Genesis of evil intent serving God's purpose, which Joseph later states as a principle (Genesis 50:20).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 39:19.

Scripture References

Genesis 39:7–20.
—

The keeper of the prison

The officer over the prison where Joseph was held; unnamed.

Family

Unnamed. The officer over the prison where Joseph was held (Genesis 39:21).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Gave Joseph favour and committed all the prisoners to his hand, and "looked not to any thing that was under his hand" (Genesis 39:21–23).

What They Did Right

  • Gave Joseph favour and committed all the prisoners to his hand: Genesis 39:21-22.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered on the man. The text attributes the favour to the Lord's presence with Joseph rather than to the keeper's judgment.

Significance

The text attributes the favour Joseph found to the Lord's presence with him rather than to the keeper's own judgment (Genesis 39:21, 39:23) - the same explanation given for his rise in Potiphar's house and later in Egypt.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 39:23.

Scripture References

Genesis 39:21–23.
—

The chief butler

Pharaoh's chief cupbearer, imprisoned with Joseph; unnamed.

Family

Unnamed. Pharaoh's chief cupbearer, imprisoned with Joseph (Genesis 40:1-2).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Dreamed of a vine with three branches; Joseph interpreted three days to his restoration and asked to be remembered (Genesis 40:9–15). Restored on Pharaoh's birthday exactly as interpreted (Genesis 40:20–21). "Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him" (Genesis 40:23). Two years later, at Pharaoh's dreams, he confessed: "I do remember my faults this day" (Genesis 41:9–13).

What They Did Right

  • Told Joseph his dream when asked: Genesis 40:9.
  • Eventually confessed his failure before Pharaoh: "I do remember my faults this day": Genesis 41:9.
  • Commended Joseph accurately to Pharaoh: Genesis 41:12-13.

What They Did Wrong

  • Forgot Joseph after his restoration, despite being asked to remember him: "Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him" (Genesis 40:23). He himself calls it a fault (Genesis 41:9). Two full years passed (Genesis 41:1).

Character Assessment

The forgetting is recorded pointedly, and he himself calls it a fault. His eventual recollection is what brings Joseph before Pharaoh.

Significance

His forgetting delays Joseph's release by two years, and his remembering brings Joseph before Pharaoh at exactly the moment the dreams required an interpreter. The narrative gives the delay no explanation beyond the fact of it.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 41:13.

Scripture References

Genesis 40:1–23; Genesis 41:9–13.
—

The chief baker

Pharaoh's chief baker, imprisoned with Joseph; unnamed.

Family

Unnamed. Pharaoh's chief baker, imprisoned with Joseph (Genesis 40:1-2).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Dreamed of three baskets with birds eating from the uppermost; Joseph interpreted three days to his execution (Genesis 40:16–19). Hanged on Pharaoh's birthday, "as Joseph had interpreted to them" (Genesis 40:22).

What They Did Right

  • Told Joseph his dream: Genesis 40:16-17.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Genesis 40:1 says both officers had offended the king, without specifying how, and gives no account of what he had done.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered. Genesis 40:1 says both officers had offended the king, without specifying how.

Significance

His execution, exactly as Joseph interpreted, together with the butler's restoration, establishes Joseph's reliability as an interpreter - the credential the butler later reports to Pharaoh (Genesis 41:13).

Death / Outcome

Hanged on Pharaoh's birthday, "as Joseph had interpreted to them" (Genesis 40:22).

Scripture References

Genesis 40:1–22.
—

Pharaoh (of Joseph's elevation)

The reigning king of Egypt through Joseph's rise, the famine, and Jacob's descent. Unnamed.

Family

Unnamed. The reigning king of Egypt through Joseph's rise, the famine, and Jacob's descent. Scripture gives no personal name and this reference assigns none.

Chronology

Patriarchal; Joseph's thirtieth year onward.

Life Synopsis

Troubled by two dreams none could interpret (Genesis 41:1–8). On hearing Joseph, said "Can we find such a one as this is, a man in whom the Spirit of God is?" and set him over all Egypt (Genesis 41:38–44). Gave him Asenath to wife (Genesis 41:45). Received Jacob, who blessed him, and asked his age (Genesis 47:7–10). Settled the family in Goshen and offered them charge of his cattle (Genesis 47:5–6).

What They Did Right

  • Recognized the Spirit of God in Joseph: "Can we find such a one as this is, a man in whom the Spirit of God is?": Genesis 41:38.
  • Acted on the counsel of a foreign slave from the dungeon, setting him over all Egypt: Genesis 41:39-44.
  • Received Jacob and his household generously and offered them the best of the land: Genesis 45:17-20; Genesis 47:5-6.
  • Was blessed by Jacob, and received the blessing without objection: Genesis 47:7-10.
  • Permitted Joseph to go up and bury his father in Canaan with a great company: Genesis 50:4-9.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Treated favourably throughout. He recognizes the Spirit of God in Joseph, and is blessed by Jacob — the lesser blessed by the greater, in a scene Genesis records without comment.

Significance

Under him the family of Jacob is preserved through famine and settled in Goshen, where they become a nation. He is a different Pharaoh from the one "which knew not Joseph" of Exodus 1:8. His scene with Jacob is theologically striking: the patriarch blesses the king, and Genesis records it without comment.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 50:6.

Scripture References

Genesis 41:1–57; Genesis 45:16–20; Genesis 47:1–10; Genesis 50:4–6.
—

Asenath

Daughter of Poti-pherah priest of On; wife of Joseph; mother of Manasseh and Ephraim.

Family

Daughter of Poti-pherah priest of On; given to Joseph as wife by Pharaoh (Genesis 41:45). Mother of Manasseh and Ephraim (Genesis 41:50-52).

Chronology

Patriarchal; married to Joseph before the famine years.

Life Synopsis

Given to Joseph by Pharaoh (Genesis 41:45); bore Manasseh and Ephraim before the famine came (Genesis 41:50–52).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered. Scripture records nothing she said or did, and — notably, given her father's office — makes no comment on her Egyptian and priestly background.

Significance

Mother of two tribal patriarchs, Ephraim and Manasseh, who receive the double portion of the birthright (1 Chronicles 5:1-2). Scripture records nothing she said or did, and - notably, given her father's priestly office in an Egyptian cult - passes no comment whatever on her background.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 46:20.

Scripture References

Genesis 41:45, 41:50; Genesis 46:20.
—

Manasseh

Firstborn son of Joseph by Asenath; head of a tribe. Distinct from King Manasseh of Judah.

Family

Firstborn son of Joseph by Asenath (Genesis 41:51); brother of Ephraim. Father of Machir (Genesis 50:23). Not to be confused with Manasseh king of Judah (2 Kings 21:1).

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Named for forgetting: "For God, said he, hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house" (Genesis 41:51). Presented to Jacob for blessing and placed at Jacob's right hand by Joseph, but Jacob crossed his hands and gave the greater blessing to Ephraim, refusing Joseph's correction: "I know it, my son, I know it" (Genesis 48:13–19). Father of Machir (Genesis 50:23).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. He is acted upon rather than acting.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered. He is acted upon rather than acting.

Significance

Head of a tribe, and one of the two sons of Joseph adopted by Jacob as his own, so receiving a portion in Israel (Genesis 48:5). Jacob deliberately set Ephraim before him, crossing his hands and refusing Joseph's correction: "I know it, my son, I know it" (Genesis 48:19) - a further instance of the younger preferred.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention in Genesis: Genesis 50:23.

Scripture References

Genesis 41:51; Genesis 46:20; Genesis 48:1–20; Genesis 50:23.
—

Ephraim

Second son of Joseph by Asenath; head of a tribe that becomes a name for the northern kingdom.

Family

Second son of Joseph by Asenath (Genesis 41:52); brother of Manasseh.

Chronology

Patriarchal.

Life Synopsis

Named for fruitfulness in affliction (Genesis 41:52). Received the firstborn's blessing from Jacob's right hand though the younger, with the explicit statement that "his younger brother shall be greater than he" (Genesis 48:14, 48:19–20). Joseph saw his children of the third generation (Genesis 50:23).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered on the man. The episode continues Genesis's pattern of the younger preferred, and Hebrews 11:21 counts Jacob's blessing of these two among the acts of faith.

Significance

Head of a tribe that becomes so dominant in the north that Ephraim serves the prophets as a name for the entire northern kingdom (Hosea 5:3-5). Jacob's blessing of him and Manasseh is the act Hebrews singles out from Jacob's whole life as faith (Hebrews 11:21). Joseph saw his children of the third generation (Genesis 50:23).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention in Genesis: Genesis 50:23.

Scripture References

Genesis 41:52; Genesis 46:20; Genesis 48:1–20; Genesis 50:23; Hebrews 11:21.
—

Joseph's steward

The steward of Joseph's house in Egypt; unnamed.

Family

Unnamed. The steward of Joseph's house in Egypt (Genesis 43:16; Genesis 44:1).

Chronology

Patriarchal; the brothers' second visit.

Life Synopsis

Reassured the brothers about the returned money — "Peace be to you, fear not: your God, and the God of your father, hath given you treasure in your sacks" (Genesis 43:23) — and brought out Simeon. Carried out Joseph's instruction to plant the silver cup in Benjamin's sack, then pursued and confronted them (Genesis 44:1–13).

What They Did Right

  • Reassured the frightened brothers about the returned money in words that name their God: "Peace be to you, fear not: your God, and the God of your father, hath given you treasure in your sacks": Genesis 43:23.
  • Brought Simeon out to them: Genesis 43:23.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He planted the cup in Benjamin's sack and made the accusation, but on Joseph's explicit instruction (Genesis 44:1-6).

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered. He acts throughout on Joseph's instruction.

Significance

His words in Genesis 43:23 are the only recorded speech of an Egyptian household servant in Genesis, and they invoke the God of the Hebrews - the text does not explain how he came to speak so.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Genesis 44:13.

Scripture References

Genesis 43:16–24; Genesis 44:1–13.
—

Machir

Son of Manasseh; grandson of Joseph.

Family

Son of Manasseh; grandson of Joseph (Genesis 50:23).

Chronology

Patriarchal; the last generation named in Genesis.

Life Synopsis

"the children also of Machir the son of Manasseh were brought up upon Joseph's knees" (Genesis 50:23) — the closing family scene of the book.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

No verdict is offered.

Significance

His children were brought up on Joseph's knees - the closing family scene of Genesis (Genesis 50:23). His descendants, the Machirites, later take Gilead (Numbers 32:39-40; Joshua 17:1).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention in Genesis: Genesis 50:23.

Scripture References

Genesis 50:23; Numbers 26:29; Joshua 17:1.

—

Job

A man of the land of Uz, perfect and upright, one that feared God and eschewed evil; stripped of children, wealth, and health, and restored at the last.

Family

He had seven sons and three daughters, seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, five hundred she asses, and a very great household (Job 1:2-3). After his restoration he had seven sons and three daughters again, and named the daughters Jemima, Kezia, and Kerenhappuch (Job 42:13-14). His wife is unnamed.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture, and the uncertainty is real. The book gives no synchronism with Israel's history, never mentions the law, the tabernacle, or the exodus, and shows Job sacrificing for his own household as a patriarch would (Job 1:5). His wealth is reckoned in livestock and he lived a hundred and forty years after his restoration (Job 42:16). These features point to the patriarchal period, and he is placed there here - but they are indications, not proof, and Scripture does not date him.

Life Synopsis

"There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job; and that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil" (Job 1:1). He rose early to offer burnt offerings for his children after their feasts, saying, "It may be that my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts. Thus did Job continually" (Job 1:5).

In the heavenly council Satan answered God's commendation of him with a question: "Doth Job fear God for nought? Hast not thou made an hedge about him?" In one day messengers brought word of the loss of his oxen and asses, his sheep, his camels, and all ten of his children. "Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head, and fell down upon the ground, and worshipped, and said, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord. In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly" (Job 1:20-22).

Satan then struck him with sore boils from the sole of his foot to his crown. He sat among the ashes and scraped himself with a potsherd. His wife said, "Dost thou still retain thine integrity? curse God, and die." He answered, "Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh. What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil? In all this did not Job sin with his lips" (Job 2:7-10).

Three friends came and sat with him seven days and seven nights without speaking. Then Job opened his mouth and cursed his day (Job 2:11-3:1). Through the long cycles of speeches he maintained his innocence against their insistence that suffering proves guilt, and grew increasingly direct with God - demanding a hearing, asking why, and finally signing his defence: "Behold, my desire is, that the Almighty would answer me" (Job 31:35).

Elihu answered next, and then "the Lord answered Job out of the whirlwind" - not with an explanation but with a long series of questions about creation that Job could not answer (Job 38:1-41:34). Job replied, "Behold, I am vile; what shall I answer thee? I will lay mine hand upon my mouth," and finally, "I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee. Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes" (Job 40:4; Job 42:5-6).

God then rebuked the three friends: "My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath," and required them to bring offerings and have Job pray for them. "And the Lord turned the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends," and gave him twice as much as he had before (Job 42:7-10). He lived a hundred and forty years afterward and saw four generations.

What They Did Right

  • God's own description of him, given twice: "a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil": Job 1:8; Job 2:3.
  • Offered sacrifices continually for his children in case they had sinned: Job 1:5.
  • Worshipped at the news of total loss and blessed the name of the Lord: Job 1:20-21.
  • "In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly": Job 1:22.
  • Refused his wife's counsel to curse God, and "in all this did not Job sin with his lips": Job 2:10.
  • Held fast his integrity, as God said he would: Job 2:3.
  • Prayed for the three friends who had misrepresented God and accused him: Job 42:10.
  • God's verdict at the end: "ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath": Job 42:7.
  • Named by God through Ezekiel with Noah and Daniel as a byword for personal righteousness: Ezekiel 14:14, 14:20.
  • James cites his endurance and God's end with him: James 5:11.

What They Did Wrong

  • Cursed the day of his birth: Job 3:1-3. Scripture records this after twice stating that he had not sinned, and does not itself call it sin.
  • Charged God with treating him as an enemy and demanded an explanation: Job 13:24; Job 23:3-7; Job 31:35.
  • God's rebuke names the fault as speaking without knowledge: "Who is this that darkeneth counsel by words without knowledge?" and "Wilt thou also disannul my judgment? wilt thou condemn me, that thou mayest be righteous?": Job 38:2; Job 40:8.
  • Job's own final assessment: "I have uttered that I understood not; things too wonderful for me, which I knew not... I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes": Job 42:3-6.

Character Assessment

Scripture's handling of him is unusually careful. It states twice, at the two worst moments, that he did not sin - and then records chapters in which he says things God afterward rebukes as words without knowledge. Both stand. What God does not endorse is the friends' theology, and what he does endorse is Job: "ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath." The book never tells Job why he suffered. The reader is told and Job is not, and his restoration comes after he prays for the men who wronged him.

Significance

The book of Job is Scripture's most sustained treatment of undeserved suffering, and its answer is not an explanation but an encounter. God names him with Noah and Daniel as one of three exemplars of righteousness (Ezekiel 14:14, 14:20), and James makes his endurance the standing example of the Lord's pity and tender mercy (James 5:11). His words "I know that my redeemer liveth" (Job 19:25) are among the most quoted in the Old Testament.

Death / Outcome

"So Job died, being old and full of days" (Job 42:17), after living a hundred and forty years from his restoration and seeing his sons and his sons' sons, even four generations.

Scripture References

Job 1:1-42:17; Ezekiel 14:14, 14:20; James 5:11
—

The wife of Job

Unnamed. Job's wife, who told him to curse God and die.

Family

Wife of Job; mother of his ten children who died (Job 1:2, 1:18-19).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

She had lost ten children in a single day and her household's whole substance. When her husband was struck with boils and sat among the ashes, "then said his wife unto him, Dost thou still retain thine integrity? curse God, and die."

"But he said unto her, Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh. What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?" (Job 2:9-10). She is not mentioned again except in Job's complaint that his breath was strange to his wife (Job 19:17).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Told her husband to curse God and die: Job 2:9. Job's answer is that she spoke as one of the foolish women speaketh - which is a rebuke of the speech, and the text notes carefully that he did not say she was a foolish woman.

Character Assessment

Scripture records one sentence from her and Job's reply, and nothing else. Her losses were his losses, and the account gives her no comfort, no friends who came to sit with her, and no restoration scene. Job's precise wording - you speak as one of the foolish women speaks - is worth noting, and the text passes no further judgment on her.

Significance

Her words put the book's central question in its bluntest form: whether God is worth holding to when the hedge is gone. Job's answer to her is the second of the two statements the narrator uses to certify that he had not sinned.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Job 19:17.

Scripture References

Job 2:9-10; Job 19:17
—

Eliphaz the Temanite

The first and eldest of Job's three friends; argued from a vision and from experience that the innocent do not perish.

Family

A Temanite (Job 2:11); Teman was in Edom, descended from Esau (Genesis 36:11).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

He came with Bildad and Zophar, having made an appointment together to mourn with Job and comfort him. They lifted up their voices and wept, rent their mantles, sprinkled dust on their heads, and "sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great" (Job 2:11-13).

He spoke first, and began gently, recalling that Job had instructed many and strengthened weak hands. Then came the argument: "Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished, being innocent? or where were the righteous cut off?" (Job 4:3-7). He described a night vision in which a spirit passed before his face and a voice asked, "Shall mortal man be more just than God?" (Job 4:12-17).

Across three speeches he hardened. By the end he charged Job with specific crimes he had invented: "Is not thy wickedness great? and thine iniquities infinite? For thou hast taken a pledge from thy brother for nought, and stripped the naked of their clothing... thou hast sent widows away empty, and the arms of the fatherless have been broken" (Job 22:5-9).

At the end the Lord said to him, "My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath." He was told to take seven bullocks and seven rams and let Job pray for him. "So Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite went, and did according as the Lord commanded them: the Lord also accepted Job" (Job 42:7-9).

What They Did Right

  • Came with the others to mourn with Job and comfort him, and sat with him seven days and seven nights in silence: Job 2:11-13.
  • Obeyed the Lord's command at the end and went to Job with the offerings: Job 42:9.

What They Did Wrong

  • Argued that the innocent do not perish, which made Job's suffering evidence of guilt: Job 4:7-8.
  • Invented specific sins to fit his theory - stripping the naked, sending widows away empty, breaking the arms of the fatherless: Job 22:5-9.
  • God's own verdict: he had not spoken of God the thing that was right: Job 42:7.

Character Assessment

Scripture's judgment on him is explicit and comes from God directly. His error was not irreverence but a system: he held that suffering proves sin, and when the facts would not fit he supplied crimes. He began with genuine sympathy and seven days of silence, which the text records to his credit, and his speeches got harsher the longer Job maintained his innocence.

Significance

He is the fullest biblical portrait of a comforter whose theology makes him cruel. Paul quotes his words - "He taketh the wise in their own craftiness" (Job 5:13) - in 1 Corinthians 3:19, which shows that a man rebuked by God may still say true things.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Job 42:9.

Scripture References

Job 2:11-13; Job 4:1-5:27; Job 15:1-35; Job 22:1-30; Job 42:7-9; 1 Corinthians 3:19
—

Bildad the Shuhite

The second of Job's three friends; argued from the tradition of the fathers that God does not pervert judgment.

Family

A Shuhite (Job 2:11); Shuah was a son of Abraham by Keturah (Genesis 25:2).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

He came with the others and sat seven days in silence (Job 2:11-13). His first words to Job are among the harshest in the book: "How long wilt thou speak these things? and how long shall the words of thy mouth be like a strong wind? Doth God pervert judgment? or doth the Almighty pervert justice? If thy children have sinned against him, and he have cast them away for their transgression" - said to a man whose ten children had just been killed (Job 8:2-4).

He appealed to the former age and the search of their fathers, and to the fate of the hypocrite whose hope shall perish (Job 8:8-13). His third speech is only six verses, asking, "How then can man be justified with God? or how can he be clean that is born of a woman?" (Job 25:1-6).

At the end he was included in God's rebuke and took the offerings to Job (Job 42:7-9).

What They Did Right

  • Came to mourn with Job and sat seven days and seven nights in silence: Job 2:11-13.
  • Obeyed the Lord's command and went with the offerings: Job 42:9.

What They Did Wrong

  • Suggested that Job's children died for their own transgression, to a father freshly bereaved of ten: Job 8:4.
  • Argued that if Job were pure and upright God would awake for him - making restoration the proof of innocence: Job 8:5-6.
  • God's verdict: he had not spoken of God the thing that was right: Job 42:7.

Character Assessment

Condemned by God with the others. His distinctive appeal is to tradition - what the fathers searched out - and his distinctive cruelty is in Job 8:4, which the book records without softening. His final speech is the shortest of any of the friends, and after it he has nothing more to say.

Significance

He represents argument from inherited authority, as Eliphaz represents argument from experience and vision. Between them the three exhaust the conventional answers, and God rejects all of them.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Job 42:9.

Scripture References

Job 2:11-13; Job 8:1-22; Job 18:1-21; Job 25:1-6; Job 42:7-9
—

Zophar the Naamathite

The third of Job's three friends; the bluntest of them, who told Job that God exacted of him less than his iniquity deserved.

Family

A Naamathite (Job 2:11).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

He came with the others and sat seven days in silence (Job 2:11-13). He spoke twice, and both speeches are direct accusation. "Should thy lies make men hold their peace? and when thou mockest, shall no man make thee ashamed?... Know therefore that God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth" (Job 11:3-6). He urged Job to put away iniquity and not let wickedness dwell in his tents, promising that then he would lift up his face without spot (Job 11:13-15).

His second speech is a description of the portion of a wicked man from God: he swallows down riches and vomits them up again, the heaven reveals his iniquity, and the increase of his house departs (Job 20:4-29). He does not speak a third time.

He was included in God's rebuke and took the offerings to Job (Job 42:7-9).

What They Did Right

  • Came to mourn with Job and sat seven days and seven nights in silence: Job 2:11-13.
  • Obeyed the Lord's command and went with the offerings: Job 42:9.

What They Did Wrong

  • Called Job's words lies and mockery: Job 11:3.
  • Told a man who had lost everything that God was exacting less than his iniquity deserved: Job 11:6.
  • God's verdict: he had not spoken of God the thing that was right: Job 42:7.

Character Assessment

Condemned by God with the others, and the least restrained of the three. His statement in Job 11:6 is the sharpest single accusation in the book. He also speaks one of its most quoted verses - "Canst thou by searching find out God?" (Job 11:7) - which is true in itself and was used to shut down a suffering man.

Significance

With Eliphaz and Bildad he represents the theology the book exists to refute: that suffering is always the measure of sin. That God required these three to bring offerings and be prayed for by the man they had accused is the book's final judgment on their counsel.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Job 42:9.

Scripture References

Job 2:11-13; Job 11:1-20; Job 20:1-29; Job 42:7-9
—

Elihu

Son of Barachel the Buzite; the young man who waited until the others had finished and then answered both Job and his friends; not included in God's rebuke.

Family

Son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram (Job 32:2). Buz was a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother (Genesis 22:21).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

He appears without introduction after the three friends have ceased to answer, "because he was righteous in his own eyes." His anger was kindled against Job, "because he justified himself rather than God," and against the three friends, "because they had found no answer, and yet had condemned Job" (Job 32:1-3).

He explained his silence: "I am young, and ye are very old; wherefore I was afraid, and durst not shew you mine opinion. I said, Days should speak, and multitude of years should teach wisdom. But there is a spirit in man: and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding. Great men are not always wise: neither do the aged understand judgment" (Job 32:6-9).

His argument differs from the others. He does not accuse Job of hidden crimes but of speaking wrongly in his complaint, and he presents suffering as capable of instruction rather than only of punishment: God "openeth the ears of men, and sealeth their instruction"; he "delivereth the poor in his affliction, and openeth their ears in oppression" (Job 33:16; Job 36:15). He closes with a description of God in the storm - thunder, lightning, snow, and whirlwind - and the whirlwind is what comes next (Job 36:26-37:24).

When the Lord answers out of the whirlwind, Elihu is not addressed. At the end, when God rebukes Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar, Elihu is not named among them.

What They Did Right

  • Waited until his elders had finished before speaking, giving his reason: Job 32:4-7.
  • Was angry both at Job's self-justification and at the friends who condemned him without an answer - the only speaker to see fault on both sides: Job 32:2-3.
  • Refused to give flattering titles or to respect persons: Job 32:21-22.
  • Presented affliction as capable of instructing rather than only of punishing: Job 33:14-30; Job 36:8-10, 36:15.
  • He is not included in God's rebuke of the three friends: Job 42:7-9.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records no verdict on him at all. He is neither commended nor condemned, and God's rebuke names Eliphaz and his two friends without mentioning him. Interpreters differ sharply over whether his speeches are to be taken as sound; the text supplies no answer, and this reference does not supply one.

Character Assessment

The most ambiguous figure in the book, and deliberately so. He appears from nowhere, speaks six chapters, is never answered by Job, is not addressed when God speaks, and is not rebuked when the friends are. That omission is the strongest evidence in his favour, and it is an argument from silence. What can be said is that his diagnosis differs from the others': he charges Job with what he said in his suffering rather than with hidden sin, and his closing description of the approaching storm runs straight into God's own answer out of the whirlwind.

Significance

His speeches introduce the possibility that affliction may instruct rather than merely repay, which is nearer to the book's own frame than anything the three friends say. His absence from the final rebuke has been read for centuries as the text's quiet verdict.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He is not mentioned after Job 37:24.

Scripture References

Job 32:1-37:24

Egypt, the Exodus, and the Wilderness

—

Pharaoh (of the oppression)

Unnamed. The king of Egypt who arose after Joseph's generation, enslaved the Israelites, and ordered the killing of their male children. Scripture gives no personal name and this reference assigns none.

Family

Not recorded. He had a daughter who drew Moses out of the river (Exodus 2:5-10), though Scripture does not say whether she was the daughter of this king or of a successor.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He arose after the death of Joseph's generation (Exodus 1:6-8) and died before Moses returned from Midian (Exodus 2:23). Traditional chronologies place him in the sixteenth or fifteenth century BC, but these rest on external reconstruction, not on Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"Now there arose up a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph" (Exodus 1:8). Seeing the Israelites multiply, he proposed to deal wisely with them lest they join Egypt's enemies, and set taskmasters over them with burdens. The more they were afflicted, the more they multiplied, and the Egyptians were grieved because of them (Exodus 1:9-14).

He then commanded the Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah to kill every male child at birth. They feared God and did not obey. Called to account, they answered that the Hebrew women delivered before the midwives arrived (Exodus 1:15-19). Failing in that, he issued a general charge to all his people: "Every son that is born ye shall cast into the river, and every daughter ye shall save alive" (Exodus 1:22). It is under this decree that Moses was born and hidden.

He died while Moses was in Midian, and it was after his death that Israel's cry came up to God (Exodus 2:23-25).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Enslaved the Israelites and afflicted them with rigorous burdens: Exodus 1:11-14.
  • Commanded the Hebrew midwives to kill every male child at birth: Exodus 1:15-16.
  • When that failed, charged all his people to cast every newborn Hebrew son into the river: Exodus 1:22.
  • Stephen summarises his policy as evil dealing that made the fathers cast out their young children: Acts 7:19.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents him wholly negatively. He is the first ruler in the Bible recorded as attempting the systematic destruction of a people, and the account is careful to note that his measures failed at every stage: the more he afflicted, the more they grew, and the midwives simply refused him.

Significance

His oppression is the setting of the Exodus, and God's covenant with Abraham is explicitly recalled in response to it (Exodus 2:24). His decree against the male children is the reason Moses was placed in the river and so came into Pharaoh's own household - the deliverer raised in the house of the oppressor.

Death / Outcome

"In process of time the king of Egypt died" (Exodus 2:23).

Scripture References

Exodus 1:8-22; Exodus 2:23; Acts 7:17-19
—

Shiphrah

One of the two Hebrew midwives who defied Pharaoh's order to kill the male children at birth.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. She was active shortly before the birth of Moses.

Life Synopsis

Pharaoh spoke directly to the Hebrew midwives, of whom Shiphrah is named first, commanding that every son born to a Hebrew woman be killed at birth and every daughter spared (Exodus 1:15-16). "But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive" (Exodus 1:17). Summoned and questioned, they answered that the Hebrew women were vigorous and delivered before a midwife could reach them (Exodus 1:18-19). God dealt well with them and built them houses of their own (Exodus 1:20-21).

What They Did Right

  • Feared God and refused a direct royal command to commit infanticide: Exodus 1:17.
  • Saved the male children alive: Exodus 1:17.
  • God's own response is the evaluation: "Therefore God dealt well with the midwives... he made them houses": Exodus 1:20-21.

What They Did Wrong

  • Her answer to Pharaoh in Exodus 1:19 is widely regarded as a deception. Scripture records the answer and immediately records that God dealt well with the midwives and blessed them, giving the reason as their fear of God (Exodus 1:21). The text passes no judgment on the words themselves. Whether the reply was a lie, and if so how it stands, is genuinely debated; this reference notes the question rather than settling it.

Character Assessment

One of the clearest instances in Scripture of God commending civil disobedience. Two women named in a book full of unnamed kings defied the most powerful ruler of their world, and God's approval is stated explicitly and materially. Pharaoh is never named; the midwives are.

Significance

Their refusal preserved the generation into which Moses was born. Scripture names them where it leaves Pharaoh anonymous, which is itself a comment on whose actions mattered.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Exodus 1:21.

Scripture References

Exodus 1:15-21
—

Puah

One of the two Hebrew midwives who defied Pharaoh's order to kill the male children at birth.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Active shortly before the birth of Moses.

Life Synopsis

Named with Shiphrah as one of the two Hebrew midwives commanded by Pharaoh to kill every Hebrew male child at birth (Exodus 1:15-16). She feared God and did not obey, saving the children alive, and gave Pharaoh the same answer as her fellow midwife when called to account (Exodus 1:17-19). God dealt well with both and made them houses (Exodus 1:20-21).

What They Did Right

  • Feared God and disobeyed the king's command: Exodus 1:17.
  • Saved the male children alive: Exodus 1:17.
  • Received God's explicit blessing for it: Exodus 1:20-21.

What They Did Wrong

  • As with Shiphrah, the answer given to Pharaoh in Exodus 1:19 raises a question the text does not answer. Scripture records God's blessing on the midwives for fearing him and does not evaluate their words.

Character Assessment

Identical in the record to Shiphrah, and assessed the same way. Scripture treats the two women as a pair and commends them together.

Significance

With Shiphrah, she preserved the generation into which Moses was born.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Exodus 1:21.

Scripture References

Exodus 1:15-21
—

Amram

A man of the house of Levi; father of Aaron, Moses, and Miriam.

Family

Son of Kohath, grandson of Levi (Exodus 6:18). Married Jochebed, his father's sister (Exodus 6:20). Father of Aaron, Moses, and Miriam (Exodus 6:20; Numbers 26:59).

Chronology

Scripture explicitly states that he lived 137 years (Exodus 6:20). The date is not otherwise established.

Life Synopsis

Amram took Jochebed his father's sister to wife, and she bore him Aaron and Moses (Exodus 6:20), and Miriam (Numbers 26:59). Genesis-style narrative is absent: Exodus 2:1 describes him only as "a man of the house of Levi" who took a daughter of Levi. His one recorded act, shared with his wife, is preserved in Hebrews: "By faith Moses, when he was born, was hid three months of his parents, because they saw he was a proper child; and they were not afraid of the king's commandment" (Hebrews 11:23).

What They Did Right

  • With Jochebed, hid the infant Moses three months in defiance of the king's commandment, and Hebrews attributes this to faith and states that they were not afraid: Hebrews 11:23.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records almost nothing of Amram directly, and the one commendation comes from the New Testament rather than from Exodus. Hebrews 11:23 credits both parents jointly with faith and fearlessness, which is the whole of his recorded character.

Significance

Father of the three figures who lead Israel out of Egypt: the lawgiver, the first high priest, and the prophetess. His household is the head of the Amramites among the Levites (Numbers 3:27).

Death / Outcome

Scripture records his age at death, 137 years (Exodus 6:20), but does not narrate his death.

Scripture References

Exodus 2:1; Exodus 6:18-20; Numbers 26:59; 1 Chronicles 6:3; Hebrews 11:23
—

Jochebed

Daughter of Levi; wife of Amram; mother of Aaron, Moses, and Miriam. The woman who hid Moses and then nursed him for Pharaoh's daughter.

Family

Daughter of Levi, born to him in Egypt (Numbers 26:59). Wife and father's sister of Amram (Exodus 6:20). Mother of Aaron, Moses, and Miriam.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Her age is not recorded.

Life Synopsis

Jochebed bore a son and, seeing that he was a goodly child, hid him three months (Exodus 2:2). When she could hide him no longer she made an ark of bulrushes, daubed it with slime and pitch, laid the child in it, and put it among the flags by the river's brink, setting his sister to watch (Exodus 2:3-4). Pharaoh's daughter found the child and had compassion on him; the sister offered to fetch a Hebrew nurse, and brought his own mother. "Take this child away, and nurse it for me, and I will give thee thy wages," said Pharaoh's daughter - and Jochebed was paid to raise her own son (Exodus 2:7-9). When he was grown she brought him back, and he became her son (Exodus 2:10).

What They Did Right

  • Hid her son three months against the king's decree. Hebrews credits both parents with faith and states they were not afraid of the king's commandment: Exodus 2:2; Hebrews 11:23.
  • Made the ark and placed him where he might be found rather than where he would drown: Exodus 2:3.
  • Nursed and raised him in his earliest years, the only period of his upbringing spent among his own people: Exodus 2:9.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records no words of hers and no fault. What it records is a series of deliberate acts under a death decree, and Hebrews 11:23 names the motive as faith. That her son knew he was a Hebrew, and identified with his brethren at forty (Exodus 2:11; Acts 7:23-25), is the one visible fruit of the years she had him.

Significance

Mother of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. One of the very few women in Scripture named as the daughter of a patriarch's son, and the only person recorded as being paid to raise her own child by the household that had decreed its death.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Numbers 26:59.

Scripture References

Exodus 2:1-10; Exodus 6:20; Numbers 26:59; Hebrews 11:23
—

Miriam

Sister of Aaron and Moses; a prophetess; leader of the women of Israel in the song at the sea.

Family

Daughter of Amram and Jochebed (Numbers 26:59); sister of Aaron and Moses. No husband or children are recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. She was old enough to be set to watch the infant Moses (Exodus 2:4), so she was the eldest of the three. She died at Kadesh in the fortieth year of the wilderness period (Numbers 20:1).

Life Synopsis

Miriam is first seen unnamed, standing at a distance to watch what would become of her infant brother in the ark of bulrushes. When Pharaoh's daughter found him, she stepped forward with a question that saved him: "Shall I go and call to thee a nurse of the Hebrew women, that she may nurse the child for thee?" - and fetched his own mother (Exodus 2:4-8).

She is named at the Red Sea, where she is called "Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron." She took a timbrel, and all the women went out after her with timbrels and dances, and she answered them, "Sing ye to the Lord, for he hath triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea" (Exodus 15:20-21).

Her failure is recorded as plainly. With Aaron she spoke against Moses over the Ethiopian woman he had married, and the complaint widened into a claim of equal standing: "Hath the Lord indeed spoken only by Moses? hath he not spoken also by us?" (Numbers 12:1-2). The Lord called all three out, defended Moses, and departed; Miriam was left leprous, white as snow. Aaron pleaded with Moses, and Moses cried, "Heal her now, O God, I beseech thee." She was shut out of the camp seven days, and the people did not journey until she was brought in again (Numbers 12:4-15).

She died at Kadesh in the desert of Zin and was buried there (Numbers 20:1).

What They Did Right

  • Watched over her infant brother and acted decisively to secure his rescue and his nursing by his own mother: Exodus 2:4-8.
  • Led the women of Israel in the song after the crossing of the sea, and is called a prophetess: Exodus 15:20-21.
  • Named by God through Micah as one of the three he sent before Israel: "I sent before thee Moses, Aaron, and Miriam": Micah 6:4.

What They Did Wrong

  • Spoke against Moses with Aaron over his Ethiopian wife: Numbers 12:1.
  • Challenged Moses' unique standing as the Lord's spokesman: Numbers 12:2. The Lord's rebuke is direct and specific (Numbers 12:6-8), and the leprosy fell on her.
  • Israel is told to remember what God did to her by the way, as a standing warning: Deuteronomy 24:9.

Character Assessment

Genuinely mixed, and Scripture gives both sides weight. She is named a prophetess, listed by God himself alongside Moses and Aaron as one of the three sent to lead Israel (Micah 6:4), and credited with the presence of mind that saved her brother's life. She is also the subject of one of the sharpest divine rebukes in the Pentateuch, and Deuteronomy makes her punishment a permanent memorial. Notably, the leprosy fell on her and not on Aaron, though both had spoken - a difference the text records without explaining.

Significance

The first woman called a prophetess in Scripture (Exodus 15:20). Her song at the sea is among the oldest recorded poetry in the Bible. God's own summary of the Exodus leadership in Micah 6:4 places her third alongside her brothers, which is the highest formal standing given to any woman in the Pentateuch.

Death / Outcome

Died at Kadesh in the desert of Zin and was buried there (Numbers 20:1).

Scripture References

Exodus 2:4-8; Exodus 15:20-21; Numbers 12:1-15; Numbers 20:1; Numbers 26:59; Deuteronomy 24:9; Micah 6:4
2430

Aaron

Elder brother of Moses; the first high priest of Israel; spokesman to Pharaoh and to the people.

Family

Son of Amram and Jochebed (Exodus 6:20); brother of Moses and Miriam. Married Elisheba daughter of Amminadab (Exodus 6:23). Father of Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar (Exodus 6:23).

Chronology

Three years older than Moses: he was 83 and Moses 80 when they spoke to Pharaoh (Exodus 7:7). Died at 123 on mount Hor in the fortieth year after the departure from Egypt (Numbers 33:38-39). The Anno Mundi figure rests on the traditional date of the Exodus and on reading Exodus 12:40 as 430 years spent in Egypt, which Galatians 3:17 may not support; see the note on chronology at the foot of this page.

Life Synopsis

Aaron enters when Moses objects at the burning bush that he is not eloquent. God's anger was kindled, and the answer was Aaron: "Is not Aaron the Levite thy brother? I know that he can speak well" (Exodus 4:14-16). He went to meet Moses in the wilderness, kissed him, and together they gathered the elders and went before Pharaoh. His rod became a serpent and swallowed the rods of the magicians (Exodus 7:10-12), and he stretched it out in the first three plagues.

At Rephidim, when Moses' hands grew heavy, Aaron and Hur stayed them up until sunset, and Amalek was defeated (Exodus 17:12). He was left with Hur in charge of the people when Moses went up the mount (Exodus 24:14).

That charge produced his great failure. When Moses delayed, the people demanded gods to go before them. Aaron told them to bring their golden earrings, fashioned a molten calf with a graving tool, built an altar before it, and proclaimed a feast to the Lord (Exodus 32:1-5). Confronted, his account was evasive: he blamed the people, then said, "I cast it into the fire, and there came out this calf" (Exodus 32:22-24). Moses records that the Lord was angry enough with Aaron to destroy him, and that he prayed for him (Deuteronomy 9:20).

He was nevertheless consecrated as high priest with his sons, clothed in the holy garments, anointed, and given the breastplate of judgment with Urim and Thummim (Exodus 28-29; Leviticus 8). He saw two of his sons consumed for offering strange fire, and "Aaron held his peace" (Leviticus 10:1-3). He joined Miriam in speaking against Moses (Numbers 12:1-2), and when the leprosy fell on her he pleaded for her. When Korah challenged the priesthood, Aaron's rod budded, blossomed, and yielded almonds as God's sign (Numbers 17:8), and he stood between the dead and the living with a censer to stay the plague (Numbers 16:47-48). With Moses he was barred from the land for the rebellion at Meribah (Numbers 20:12, 20:24). He died on mount Hor at 123, his garments transferred to Eleazar, and Israel mourned him thirty days (Numbers 20:25-29).

What They Did Right

  • Went to meet Moses at God's word and spoke for him to Israel and to Pharaoh: Exodus 4:27-31.
  • With Hur, held up Moses' hands until the going down of the sun so that Amalek was defeated: Exodus 17:12.
  • Held his peace when fire from the Lord consumed his two eldest sons: Leviticus 10:1-3.
  • Ran into the midst of the congregation with a censer and stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stayed: Numbers 16:47-48.
  • Was chosen by God for the priesthood rather than taking the honour to himself, a point Hebrews makes explicitly: Hebrews 5:4.

What They Did Wrong

  • Made the golden calf at the people's demand, built an altar before it, and proclaimed a feast: Exodus 32:1-5.
  • Gave Moses an evasive and false account of how the calf was made: Exodus 32:22-24.
  • Moses states that the Lord was very angry with Aaron over the calf and would have destroyed him: Deuteronomy 9:20.
  • Joined Miriam in speaking against Moses and questioning his unique standing: Numbers 12:1-2.
  • Rebelled with Moses against God's word at the waters of Meribah, and was barred from the land for it: Numbers 20:10-12, 20:24.

Character Assessment

Aaron's record contains both the founding of Israel's priesthood and its worst single failure. Scripture does not soften the golden calf, and it preserves his evasive answer word for word. Yet the same man was chosen by God for the high priesthood, vindicated by the budding rod, and used to stay a plague at the risk of his own life. His most eloquent moment is silence: after his sons were consumed, "Aaron held his peace" (Leviticus 10:3). Hebrews uses his calling as the pattern of a priesthood no man takes upon himself.

Significance

The first high priest, and the head of the priestly line that served Israel until the destruction of the temple. The Aaronic priesthood, its garments, its sacrifices, and its annual entry into the holy of holies supply the entire framework of the argument of Hebrews, which contrasts it with the priesthood of Christ after the order of Melchizedek (Hebrews 5:1-10; Hebrews 7:11-28). The Aaronic blessing of Numbers 6:24-26 remains in liturgical use.

Death / Outcome

Died at 123 on mount Hor, in the fortieth year after Israel came out of Egypt. Moses stripped him of his garments and put them on Eleazar his son, and Israel mourned him thirty days (Numbers 20:25-29; Numbers 33:38-39).

Scripture References

Exodus 4:14-31; Exodus 7:1-12; Exodus 17:8-13; Exodus 24:14; Exodus 28:1-43; Exodus 32:1-35; Leviticus 8:1-36; Leviticus 10:1-7; Numbers 12:1-15; Numbers 16:41-50; Numbers 17:1-11; Numbers 20:1-29; Numbers 33:38-39; Deuteronomy 9:20; Psalms 106:16; Hebrews 5:1-5; Hebrews 7:11
2433

Moses

The prophet who led Israel out of Egypt, received the law at Sinai, and led the nation through forty years in the wilderness; called the servant of the Lord and the meekest man on earth.

Also called Moshe

Family

Son of Amram and Jochebed (Exodus 6:20); younger brother of Aaron and Miriam. Adopted by Pharaoh's daughter (Exodus 2:10). Married Zipporah daughter of Reuel, priest of Midian (Exodus 2:21); also married an Ethiopian woman (Numbers 12:1). Father of Gershom and Eliezer (Exodus 18:3-4).

Chronology

Forty years in Egypt, forty in Midian, and forty leading Israel: he was 80 when he spoke to Pharaoh (Exodus 7:7) and 120 when he died (Deuteronomy 34:7), and Stephen gives the first two forty-year periods explicitly (Acts 7:23, 7:30). The Anno Mundi figure rests on the traditional date of the Exodus and on a disputed reading of Exodus 12:40; see the chronology note at the foot of this page.

Life Synopsis

Moses was born under Pharaoh's decree that every Hebrew son be cast into the river. His mother hid him three months, then placed him in an ark of bulrushes among the flags, where Pharaoh's daughter found him and raised him as her own son. His own mother was hired to nurse him (Exodus 2:1-10). He was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and mighty in words and deeds (Acts 7:22).

At forty he went out to his brethren, saw an Egyptian smiting a Hebrew, looked this way and that, and killed him. The next day he tried to reconcile two Hebrews and was answered, "Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?" He fled to Midian (Exodus 2:11-15). There he defended Reuel's daughters at a well, married Zipporah, and kept sheep for forty years.

At the burning bush God commissioned him, revealing the name I AM THAT I AM (Exodus 3:14). Moses objected five separate times - who am I, what is thy name, they will not believe me, I am not eloquent, send someone else - until God's anger was kindled and Aaron was given as his mouth (Exodus 3:11-4:16). He returned, confronted Pharaoh through ten plagues, instituted the Passover, and led Israel out. At the sea he stretched out his hand and the waters divided (Exodus 14:21-22).

He went up Sinai and received the law, and came down to find the golden calf. He broke the tables, ground the calf to powder, and then interceded: "Yet now, if thou wilt forgive their sin - ; and if not, blot me, I pray thee, out of thy book" (Exodus 32:32). He asked to see God's glory and was hidden in a cleft of the rock (Exodus 33:18-23), and came down from the mount with his face shining, not knowing it (Exodus 34:29-30).

He led the nation forty years through repeated rebellion, and interceded again and again. His own failure came at Meribah: told to speak to the rock, he struck it twice and said, "Hear now, ye rebels; must we fetch you water out of this rock?" For this he was barred from the land (Numbers 20:10-12). He commissioned Joshua, delivered the addresses of Deuteronomy, blessed the tribes, and went up mount Nebo, where he saw the land and died at 120, his eye not dim nor his natural force abated. God buried him, and no man knows his sepulchre (Deuteronomy 34:1-7).

What They Did Right

  • Refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season: Hebrews 11:24-26.
  • Defended the daughters of Reuel against the shepherds and watered their flock: Exodus 2:17.
  • Obeyed the commission at the bush despite repeated objection, and returned to the country he had fled: Exodus 4:18-20.
  • Interceded for Israel after the golden calf, offering to be blotted out of God's book rather than see them destroyed: Exodus 32:31-32.
  • Interceded again when the people refused the land, appealing to God's own name and character: Numbers 14:13-19.
  • Described by Scripture itself as very meek, above all the men upon the face of the earth: Numbers 12:3.
  • Faithful in all God's house as a servant, a testimony Hebrews sets alongside Christ's: Numbers 12:7; Hebrews 3:2-5.
  • God spoke with him face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend: Exodus 33:11; Deuteronomy 34:10.

What They Did Wrong

  • Killed an Egyptian and hid him in the sand: Exodus 2:11-12. Scripture records the act and the concealment; Stephen frames it as a premature attempt at deliverance his brethren did not understand (Acts 7:24-25), and Exodus does not explicitly condemn or commend it.
  • Objected repeatedly to God's commission until the Lord's anger was kindled against him: Exodus 4:13-14.
  • Broke the tables of the testimony in anger at the foot of the mount: Exodus 32:19. The text records the anger without explicitly condemning it.
  • Struck the rock twice instead of speaking to it, and spoke rashly to the people: Numbers 20:10-11. God's own charge is explicit: "Because ye believed me not, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel" (Numbers 20:12).
  • Psalms 106:32-33 states that it went ill with Moses for the people's sake, "because they provoked his spirit, so that he spake unadvisedly with his lips."

Character Assessment

Scripture's estimate of Moses is higher than that of any figure before Christ: no prophet arose like him, whom the Lord knew face to face (Deuteronomy 34:10); he was faithful in all God's house (Numbers 12:7); he was the meekest man on earth (Numbers 12:3). The record is equally plain that he killed a man, argued with God until the Lord's anger was kindled, and was excluded from the land he had spent forty years walking toward, for a single act of disobedience at a rock. That exclusion is the sharpest demonstration in the Pentateuch that God does not grade leaders on a curve.

Significance

Israel's lawgiver, deliverer, and greatest prophet. Through him came the law (John 1:17), the Passover, the tabernacle, and the covenant at Sinai. He is the standard against which later prophets are measured, and the promise of a prophet like him (Deuteronomy 18:15-18) is applied to Christ in Acts 3:22. He appeared with Elijah at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:3). Hebrews sets his faithfulness as a servant against Christ's as a son (Hebrews 3:5-6), and Revelation names the song of Moses alongside the song of the Lamb (Revelation 15:3).

Death / Outcome

Died in the land of Moab at 120, his eye not dim nor his natural force abated. The Lord buried him in a valley over against Bethpeor, and no man knows his sepulchre (Deuteronomy 34:5-7). Jude 1:9 records a dispute over his body.

Scripture References

Exodus 2:1-40:38; Leviticus 1:1; Numbers 12:1-8; Numbers 14:11-24; Numbers 20:1-13; Deuteronomy 34:1-12; Psalms 106:32-33; Matthew 17:3; John 1:17; Acts 7:20-44; Hebrews 3:1-6; Hebrews 11:23-29; Jude 1:9
