So the plague was stayed" (Numbers 25:7-8). Twenty-four thousand had died.

God's response was explicit: "Phinehas... hath turned my wrath away from the children of Israel, while he was zealous for my sake among them, that I consumed not the children of Israel in my jealousy." He was given a covenant of peace, "even the covenant of an everlasting priesthood; because he was zealous for his God, and made an atonement for the children of Israel" (Numbers 25:11-13).

He went with the army against Midian with the holy instruments and the trumpets (Numbers 31:6). He led the delegation sent to the two and a half tribes over the altar built by Jordan, and accepted their explanation without bloodshed (Joshua 22:13-34). He stood before the ark at Bethel in the days of the judges (Judges 20:28).

What They Did Right

  • Acted decisively at Peor and stayed the plague: Numbers 25:7-8.
  • God's own testimony: he turned away divine wrath and was zealous for God's sake: Numbers 25:11.
  • Went with the holy instruments in the campaign against Midian: Numbers 31:6.
  • Led the delegation to the two and a half tribes and accepted their answer, averting a civil war: Joshua 22:30-32.
  • Psalms records the verdict: "Then stood up Phinehas, and executed judgment: and so the plague was stayed. And that was counted unto him for righteousness unto all generations for evermore": Psalms 106:30-31.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him, and its commendation is emphatic and unusual: his act was counted to him for righteousness, a phrase used elsewhere only of Abraham's faith (Genesis 15:6; Psalms 106:31). His conduct at Joshua 22 is worth setting beside Peor: the same man who acted instantly with a javelin also listened to an explanation and accepted it, preventing a war between the tribes. The record is of decisiveness governed by judgment rather than of violence for its own sake.

Significance

The covenant of an everlasting priesthood given to him fixed the high priestly succession in his line, where it remained (1 Chronicles 6:4-15; Ezra 7:5). His action at Peor is cited in Israel's national confession as the moment judgment was halted (Psalms 106:30-31).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He was buried in a hill that pertained to him in mount Ephraim, where he buried his father (Joshua 24:33). Last appearance: Judges 20:28.

Scripture References

Exodus 6:25; Numbers 25:6-15; Numbers 31:6; Joshua 22:9-34; Joshua 24:33; Judges 20:28; 1 Chronicles 6:4, 6:50; Psalms 106:30-31
—

Zelophehad

A man of the tribe of Manasseh who died in the wilderness leaving five daughters and no sons, and whose case changed the law of inheritance in Israel.

Family

Son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh (Numbers 27:1). Father of Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah (Numbers 26:33).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He died during the wilderness period, before the division of the land.

Life Synopsis

Scripture records that he had no sons but daughters, and names them (Numbers 26:33). What is known of the man himself comes from his daughters' statement before Moses: "Our father died in the wilderness, and he was not in the company of them that gathered themselves together against the Lord in the company of Korah; but died in his own sin, and had no sons" (Numbers 27:3).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. His daughters state that he had no part in Korah's rebellion (Numbers 27:3), which is a specific denial of a specific charge rather than a positive commendation.

What They Did Wrong

  • His daughters say that he "died in his own sin" (Numbers 27:3). Scripture does not say what that sin was. The phrase most likely refers to his sharing in the general unbelief of the generation that perished in the wilderness (Numbers 14:29-35), but the text does not state this, and any more specific charge would be invention.

Character Assessment

An unusual entry, because everything recorded about him comes from his daughters' mouths in a legal petition. They were careful to distinguish him from the rebels and equally careful not to claim he was blameless. The result is one of the more candid family testimonies in Scripture.

Significance

His lack of sons produced the case that established the right of daughters to inherit in Israel, and then the supplementary ruling that such daughters must marry within their father's tribe so that inheritance did not pass between tribes (Numbers 27:6-11; Numbers 36:5-9). His name is preserved because of what his daughters did about it.

Death / Outcome

Died in the wilderness (Numbers 27:3).

Scripture References

Numbers 26:33; Numbers 27:1-11; Numbers 36:1-12; Joshua 17:3-6; 1 Chronicles 7:15
—

The daughters of Zelophehad

Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah - five sisters of the tribe of Manasseh who petitioned Moses for an inheritance and obtained a change in the law. These are five distinct individuals; Scripture records them acting and speaking only together, and names them in the same order four times, so they are entered here as one account rather than five near-identical entries.

Family

Daughters of Zelophehad, son of Hepher, of the family of Manasseh (Numbers 26:33; Numbers 27:1). They had no brothers. They later married their father's brothers' sons (Numbers 36:11).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. They petitioned near the end of the wilderness period and received their inheritance under Joshua.

Life Synopsis

They came and stood before Moses, Eleazar the priest, the princes, and all the congregation, at the door of the tabernacle - a formal approach to the highest authority in Israel. Their case was carefully made: their father died in the wilderness, he was not in Korah's company, he died in his own sin, and he had no sons. "Why should the name of our father be done away from among his family, because he hath no son? Give unto us therefore a possession among the brethren of our father" (Numbers 27:1-4).

Moses did not decide it himself but brought their cause before the Lord. The answer was unambiguous: "The daughters of Zelophehad speak right: thou shalt surely give them a possession of an inheritance among their father's brethren." A general statute followed, governing inheritance where a man dies without a son (Numbers 27:5-11).

The heads of Gilead later raised a difficulty: if the daughters married outside the tribe, the inheritance would pass with them. A supplementary ruling required such daughters to marry within their father's tribe, and the five did so, marrying their cousins (Numbers 36:1-12). Under Joshua they came before Eleazar and Joshua and received their inheritance among their father's brethren, as the Lord had commanded (Joshua 17:3-4).

What They Did Right

  • Brought their case through the proper channel, publicly and respectfully, rather than acting on their own: Numbers 27:1-2.
  • Argued from their father's name and family rather than from personal grievance: Numbers 27:4.
  • God's own verdict is the commendation: "The daughters of Zelophehad speak right": Numbers 27:7.
  • Accepted the supplementary restriction on whom they might marry, and complied: Numbers 36:10-12.
  • Pressed their claim again under Joshua, and it was honoured: Joshua 17:3-4.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against them and one of the plainest divine commendations given to anyone in the Pentateuch. Five women without a male relative to speak for them approached the entire leadership of the nation, and God said they were right. The account is notable for what it shows about the law as well: Moses did not know the answer, enquired, and the statute was framed in response to a petition brought by women.

Significance

Their case established the inheritance rights of daughters in Israel and produced two statutes (Numbers 27:8-11; Numbers 36:6-9). Tirzah's name later attaches to a city that served as a capital of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 15:33). The episode is one of very few in Scripture where existing law is shown being extended in response to a claim of injustice.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Joshua 17:3-4.

Scripture References

Numbers 26:33; Numbers 27:1-11; Numbers 36:1-12; Joshua 17:3-6; 1 Chronicles 7:15

The Conquest and Settlement of the Land

—

Jair (son of Manasseh)

A man of Manasseh who took the country of Argob and the small towns of Gilead and named them after himself. Not to be confused with Jair the Gileadite who judged Israel (Judges 10:3-5), nor with Jair the father of Mordecai (Esther 2:5).

Family

Called the son of Manasseh (Numbers 32:41; Deuteronomy 3:14). 1 Chronicles 2:21-22 traces the descent through Hezron and Segub, with the connection to Manasseh through Machir's daughter, so "son of Manasseh" denotes descent rather than immediate parentage.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He acted during the conquest of the territory east of Jordan, at the end of the wilderness period.

Life Synopsis

"And Jair the son of Manasseh went and took the small towns thereof, and called them Havoth-jair" (Numbers 32:41). Deuteronomy gives the fuller account: "Jair the son of Manasseh took all the country of Argob unto the coasts of Geshuri and Maachathi; and called them after his own name, Bashan-havoth-jair, unto this day" (Deuteronomy 3:14). 1 Chronicles 2:22 records that he had twenty-three cities in the land of Gilead.

What They Did Right

  • Took the territory allotted to his people east of Jordan: Numbers 32:41; Deuteronomy 3:14. Scripture records the conquest without moral evaluation.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records a military achievement and the naming of the towns after himself, and offers no verdict on either. He is included because the acts recorded are specific and substantial, and because he is the only individual Deuteronomy introduces who does not appear elsewhere in the earlier narrative.

Significance

The towns he named, Havoth-jair, remain a fixed geographical reference in Israel long afterward (Joshua 13:30; 1 Kings 4:13; 1 Chronicles 2:23). His conquest helped secure the eastern territory allotted to the half tribe of Manasseh.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Chronicles 2:22-23.

Scripture References

Numbers 32:41; Deuteronomy 3:14; Joshua 13:30; 1 Kings 4:13; 1 Chronicles 2:21-23
—

Rahab

A harlot of Jericho who hid the Israelite spies, was spared at the city's destruction, and is named in the genealogy of Christ.

Also called Rachab

Family

Her father, mother, brethren, and sisters are named as a household but not individually (Joshua 2:13). Matthew 1:5 records that Salmon begat Booz of Rachab, making her the mother of Boaz and an ancestress of David.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. She was living in Jericho at the time of the conquest.

Life Synopsis

Joshua sent two men to spy out Jericho, and they came into the house of a harlot named Rahab. The king of Jericho sent to her demanding the men. She had already taken them up to the roof and hidden them under stalks of flax, and she told the king's messengers that men had come but had gone out at the shutting of the gate, and urged pursuit (Joshua 2:1-7).

She then told the spies why she had done it. Her speech is a confession of faith, and it is the theological centre of the chapter: "I know that the Lord hath given you the land, and that your terror is fallen upon us... for the Lord your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath" (Joshua 2:9-11). She had heard of the Red Sea and of Sihon and Og, and had drawn the conclusion the rest of her city had not.

She asked for a true token that her father's house would be spared. They swore it, on condition that she bind a scarlet line in the window and gather her family inside. She let them down by a cord through the window, her house being on the town wall, told them to hide three days in the mountain, and bound the scarlet line at once (Joshua 2:12-21).

When the city fell, Joshua sent the same two men to bring her out with all she had. "And Joshua saved Rahab the harlot alive, and her father's household, and all that she had; and she dwelleth in Israel even unto this day; because she hid the messengers" (Joshua 6:22-25).

What They Did Right

  • Hid the spies at direct risk of her life: Joshua 2:4-6.
  • Confessed the Lord as God in heaven above and in earth beneath, on the strength of reports she had heard: Joshua 2:9-11.
  • Sought mercy not only for herself but for her whole household: Joshua 2:12-13.
  • Bound the scarlet line in the window immediately, before any army appeared: Joshua 2:21.
  • Hebrews places her in the roll of faith: "By faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace": Hebrews 11:31.
  • James cites her as justified by works: James 2:25.

What They Did Wrong

  • Scripture calls her a harlot in every reference to her, including both New Testament commendations (Joshua 2:1; Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25). It records the fact without narrating any particular act and without a separate condemnation.
  • She told the king's men that the spies had departed when they were on her roof: Joshua 2:4-5. Scripture records the words and then commends her twice in the New Testament, without evaluating the deception itself. Whether it was a lie that stands justified, or a fault covered by faith, is genuinely debated; this reference notes the question rather than settling it.

Character Assessment

Scripture's treatment of Rahab is striking for what it never does: it never removes the word harlot from her name, and it never withholds commendation on that account. Hebrews names her among the faithful; James names her among the justified; Matthew names her in the line of Christ. Her confession in Joshua 2:9-11 is a fuller statement of who God is than anything recorded from Jericho's king or from most of Israel in that generation.

Significance

She is one of four women named in Matthew's genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:5), and through her son Boaz she stands in the line of David. Her deliverance, with the scarlet line in the window and her whole household gathered inside the house, has been read since the earliest Christian writers as a picture of salvation; the text itself makes no such comment. She is one of only two women named in Hebrews 11.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Joshua 6:25 states that she dwelt in Israel. Last mention: James 2:25.

Scripture References

Joshua 2:1-24; Joshua 6:17, 6:22-25; Matthew 1:5; Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25
—

The two spies sent to Jericho

Unnamed. The two men Joshua sent from Shittim to view the land and Jericho; sheltered by Rahab and bound by oath to spare her household. These are two distinct individuals; Scripture records them acting and speaking only together and never names either.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Sent immediately before the crossing of Jordan.

Life Synopsis

Joshua sent them to spy secretly, and they came into Rahab's house. When the king of Jericho sent for them, she hid them under the stalks of flax on the roof and sent the pursuit toward Jordan (Joshua 2:1-7).

Before they lay down she came up to them and made her case, and they swore to her: "Our life for yours, if ye utter not this our business" (Joshua 2:14). They set the terms carefully - a scarlet line in the window, her whole family inside the house, and no blame on them if anyone went into the street (Joshua 2:17-20). She let them down by a cord through the window, and they took her advice to hide three days in the mountain before returning (Joshua 2:15-16, 2:22).

Their report to Joshua reverses the report the ten spies brought a generation earlier: "Truly the Lord hath delivered into our hands all the land; for even all the inhabitants of the country do faint because of us" (Joshua 2:24). When Jericho fell, Joshua sent these same two men to bring Rahab and her household out, and they did (Joshua 6:22-23).

What They Did Right

  • Brought back a report of faith rather than fear, unlike the ten spies of the previous generation: Joshua 2:24; compare Numbers 13:31-33.
  • Swore an oath to a Canaanite harlot and kept it, returning to bring her household out of a city under destruction: Joshua 2:14; Joshua 6:22-23.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against them. The contrast with the twelve spies of Numbers 13 is plainly intentional: same errand, opposite report, opposite outcome. Their keeping of the oath is recorded without comment but is the reason Rahab appears in the genealogy of Christ.

Significance

Their report confirmed to Israel that the land was already given. Their oath to Rahab preserved the household from which Boaz, and so David, descended.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Joshua 6:23.

Scripture References

Joshua 2:1-24; Joshua 6:22-23
—

Achan

A man of Judah who took spoil from Jericho against the ban, bringing defeat on Israel at Ai.

Also called Achar

Family

Son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 7:1). He had sons and daughters (Joshua 7:24). Called Achar in 1 Chronicles 2:7.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He died shortly after the fall of Jericho.

Life Synopsis

Jericho had been placed under a ban: everything in it was accursed and devoted to the Lord (Joshua 6:17-19). "But the children of Israel committed a trespass in the accursed thing: for Achan... took of the accursed thing: and the anger of the Lord was kindled against the children of Israel" (Joshua 7:1). The sin was one man's; the anger fell on the nation.

Israel then attacked Ai with a small force and was routed, and about thirty-six men died. Joshua fell on his face before the ark until evening, and God told him Israel had sinned and could not stand until the accursed thing was removed (Joshua 7:2-13). By lot the tribe, family, household, and finally the man were taken.

Joshua said to him, "My son, give, I pray thee, glory to the Lord God of Israel, and make confession unto him." Achan answered, "Indeed I have sinned against the Lord God of Israel, and thus and thus have I done: When I saw among the spoils a goodly Babylonish garment, and two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold of fifty shekels weight, then I coveted them, and took them; and, behold, they are hid in the earth in the midst of my tent" (Joshua 7:19-21). The sequence he gives - saw, coveted, took, hid - is one of the plainest descriptions of the course of sin in Scripture.

The things were found where he said. He, his sons and daughters, his livestock, his tent, and all he had were taken to the valley of Achor and stoned and burned, and a heap of stones raised over him (Joshua 7:22-26).

What They Did Right

  • Confessed fully and specifically when confronted, concealing nothing and naming exactly what he had taken and where it was: Joshua 7:20-21. Scripture records the confession without stating whether it was repentance or only admission once discovered.

What They Did Wrong

  • Took of the accursed thing in direct violation of the ban: Joshua 7:1, 7:11.
  • Hid the spoil in his tent: Joshua 7:21.
  • His sin brought defeat on the whole nation and the death of about thirty-six men: Joshua 7:5, 7:11-12.
  • Joshua 22:20 recalls the case as the standing example that one man's trespass can bring wrath on the whole congregation: "that man perished not alone in his iniquity."

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned, and the account is unusual in how much attention it gives to the mechanics of the sin. His own confession supplies the anatomy - he saw, he coveted, he took, he hid - and Scripture preserves it as a warning rather than as mitigation. The corporate consequence is the point the rest of Scripture draws from him: Israel's defeat, thirty-six deaths, and a national crisis, all from one concealed theft.

Significance

The valley of Achor, named for the trouble he brought, becomes an image of hope in the prophets: God promises to give "the valley of Achor for a door of hope" (Hosea 2:15; see also Isaiah 65:10). The place named for Israel's worst early failure is the place named for restoration.

Death / Outcome

Stoned and burned with all he had in the valley of Achor, and a great heap of stones raised over him (Joshua 7:25-26).

Scripture References

Joshua 7:1-26; Joshua 22:20; 1 Chronicles 2:7; Hosea 2:15
—

The king of Ai

Unnamed. The king of Ai, whose city defeated Israel at first and was afterward destroyed by ambush.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

The men of Ai defeated Israel's first attack, chasing them from before the gate and killing about thirty-six men, so that the hearts of the people melted (Joshua 7:4-5). That defeat was caused by Achan's sin, not by Ai's strength.

After the matter was dealt with, Joshua set an ambush behind the city and drew the king out by feigning flight. "And it came to pass, when the king of Ai saw it, that they hasted and rose up early, and the men of the city went out against Israel to battle, he and all his people, at a time appointed... but he wist not that there were liers in ambush against him behind the city" (Joshua 8:14). The city was taken and burned, and the king was captured alive and brought to Joshua (Joshua 8:23). "And the king of Ai he hanged on a tree until eventide: and as soon as the sun was down, Joshua commanded that they should take his carcase down from the tree" (Joshua 8:29).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records his defence of his city and his defeat without any moral evaluation of him personally.

Character Assessment

He is recorded as an opponent overcome rather than a man assessed. The one detail Scripture dwells on is his misreading of the situation - he pursued a feigned flight and did not know of the ambush - which the narrative attributes to Joshua's stratagem rather than to any fault of his.

Significance

The taking of his body down from the tree before sunset accords with the law of Deuteronomy 21:22-23, that a hanged body should not remain overnight - a law Paul later applies to the crucifixion of Christ (Galatians 3:13).

Death / Outcome

Hanged on a tree until evening, then taken down and buried under a great heap of stones at the entering of the gate (Joshua 8:29).

Scripture References

Joshua 7:2-5; Joshua 8:1-29; Deuteronomy 21:22-23
—

Adonizedek

King of Jerusalem; formed the coalition of five Amorite kings against Gibeon and was defeated by Joshua.

Also called Adoni-zedek

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He reigned in Jerusalem during the conquest.

Life Synopsis

Adonizedek heard how Joshua had taken Jericho and Ai, and that Gibeon had made peace with Israel. He and his people feared greatly, because Gibeon was a great city and its men were mighty (Joshua 10:1-2). Rather than submit, he sent to four other kings - Hoham of Hebron, Piram of Jarmuth, Japhia of Lachish, and Debir of Eglon - saying, "Come up unto me, and help me, that we may smite Gibeon: for it hath made peace with Joshua and with the children of Israel" (Joshua 10:3-4). The five encamped against Gibeon.

Gibeon sent to Joshua at Gilgal, and he came up all night from Gilgal and fell on them suddenly. The Lord discomfited them, cast down great stones from heaven, and the sun stood still upon Gibeon (Joshua 10:9-13). The five kings fled and hid in a cave at Makkedah. Joshua had great stones rolled on the mouth of the cave until the pursuit was finished, then had them brought out, put the feet of his captains on their necks, slew them, hanged them on five trees until evening, and cast them into the cave with great stones at its mouth (Joshua 10:16-27).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Formed a coalition to attack Gibeon for making peace with Israel: Joshua 10:3-5. Scripture records the campaign without a separate moral verdict on him.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents him as the instigator of the southern coalition and records his fear as the reason. His name means something like lord of righteousness and echoes Melchizedek, king of the same city in Abraham's day (Genesis 14:18); Scripture draws no connection between the two men and none is asserted here.

Significance

His attack on Gibeon precipitated the battle in which the sun stood still and hailstones killed more of the enemy than the sword (Joshua 10:11-14), and it opened the whole southern campaign. Jerusalem, his city, was not taken at this time and remained in Jebusite hands until David (Joshua 15:63; 2 Samuel 5:6-9).

Death / Outcome

Brought out of the cave at Makkedah, slain by Joshua, hanged on a tree until evening, and cast into the cave (Joshua 10:22-27).

Scripture References

Joshua 10:1-27
—

Hoham, Piram, Japhia, and Debir

The four Amorite kings - of Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon - who joined Adonizedek of Jerusalem against Gibeon. Four distinct individuals; Scripture names each with his city but records them acting only as a group.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Adonizedek king of Jerusalem sent to Hoham king of Hebron, Piram king of Jarmuth, Japhia king of Lachish, and Debir king of Eglon, calling them to help him smite Gibeon for making peace with Israel (Joshua 10:3-4). The five kings gathered and encamped against Gibeon.

Joshua marched all night from Gilgal and fell on them suddenly; they were chased along the way to Bethhoron, and more died from the hailstones the Lord cast down than Israel killed with the sword (Joshua 10:9-11). The four fled with Adonizedek to a cave at Makkedah, where they were sealed in, brought out, slain, hanged on five trees until evening, and cast back into the cave (Joshua 10:16-27).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Joined the coalition against Gibeon and made war on Israel: Joshua 10:5. Scripture records the campaign without individual moral evaluation of any of the four.

Character Assessment

Scripture names them, names their cities, and records their common action and common end. Nothing distinguishes one from another in the account, and none is separately assessed.

Significance

Their defeat broke Amorite resistance in the south and is the setting of the long day at Gibeon. Joshua's charge to his captains as they set their feet on the kings' necks - "Fear not, nor be dismayed, be strong and of good courage" - repeats the words God had given him at the start of the book (Joshua 10:25; compare Joshua 1:9).

Death / Outcome

Slain by Joshua, hanged on five trees until evening, and cast into the cave at Makkedah with great stones laid at its mouth (Joshua 10:26-27).

Scripture References

Joshua 10:3-27; Joshua 12:10-12
—

Jabin (king of Hazor)

King of Hazor; formed the northern coalition against Israel and was killed when Hazor was burned. Not to be confused with the later Jabin king of Canaan who oppressed Israel in the days of Deborah (Judges 4:2).

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He reigned during the conquest, after the southern campaign.

Life Synopsis

When Jabin heard of Joshua's victories he sent to Jobab king of Madon, to the kings of Shimron and Achshaph, and to the kings of the north, the plains, the valley, and the borders of Dor, and to the Canaanite, Amorite, Hittite, Perizzite, Jebusite, and Hivite. "And they went out, they and all their hosts with them, much people, even as the sand that is upon the sea shore in multitude, with horses and chariots very many," and pitched at the waters of Merom (Joshua 11:1-5).

The Lord told Joshua not to be afraid of them, and Israel fell on them suddenly and chased them. Joshua houghed their horses and burnt their chariots. He then turned back, took Hazor, and smote Jabin with the sword; Hazor alone of the northern cities was burned, "for Hazor beforetime was the head of all those kingdoms" (Joshua 11:6-13).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Gathered the northern kings to make war against Israel: Joshua 11:1-5. Scripture records the coalition and its defeat without separate moral evaluation of him.

Character Assessment

Presented as the head of the largest confederacy Israel faced in the conquest, and assessed only in that role. Scripture notes his standing - Hazor was the head of all those kingdoms - which explains why his city alone was burned.

Significance

His defeat completed the conquest of the north and effectively ended organised Canaanite resistance in Joshua's campaigns (Joshua 11:16-23). Hazor was later rebuilt, and a later king of the same name oppressed Israel for twenty years until Deborah and Barak (Judges 4:2-3) - a sign that the conquest was not as complete as the summary statements suggest.

Death / Outcome

Smitten with the sword when Joshua took Hazor and burnt it (Joshua 11:10-11).

Scripture References

Joshua 11:1-14; Joshua 12:19
—

Achsah

Daughter of Caleb; given in marriage to Othniel for the taking of Kirjath-sepher; asked her father for springs of water and received them.

Also called Achsa

Family

Daughter of Caleb the son of Jephunneh (Joshua 15:16); wife of Othniel (Joshua 15:17).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. She married during the settlement of the land under Joshua.

Life Synopsis

Caleb offered her in marriage to whoever should take Kirjath-sepher, and Othniel took it (Joshua 15:16-17).

When she came to her husband, she moved him to ask her father for a field. Then she lighted off her ass, and Caleb said, "What wouldest thou?" She answered, "Give me a blessing; for thou hast given me a south land; give me also springs of water." And he gave her the upper springs and the nether springs (Joshua 15:18-19; Judges 1:14-15). The account is repeated word for word in two books, which is unusual for so short an incident.

What They Did Right

  • Asked for what her inheritance actually needed - water for a dry southern land - and asked it directly of her father: Joshua 15:18-19.
  • Scripture records that her request was granted in full, and more than she named: she asked for springs and received both the upper and the nether springs: Joshua 15:19.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her and recounts her one recorded exchange twice. The account presents a woman who understood the value of what she had been given and what it lacked, and who asked plainly. Her father granted it without argument.

Significance

Her request preserved a working inheritance for her household, and the springs are recorded as a fixed feature of Judah's territory. She is one of a small number of women in the historical books whose direct speech is preserved verbatim in two separate books.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Chronicles 2:49.

Scripture References

Joshua 15:16-19; Judges 1:12-15; 1 Chronicles 2:49
—

Othniel

Son of Kenaz, younger brother or kinsman of Caleb; took Kirjath-sepher and won Achsah to wife; the first of the judges of Israel.

Family

Son of Kenaz (Joshua 15:17); called Caleb's younger brother (Judges 1:13). Married Achsah, Caleb's daughter (Joshua 15:17). Father of Hathath (1 Chronicles 4:13).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He took Kirjath-sepher during the settlement under Joshua, and later judged Israel; after his deliverance the land had rest forty years (Judges 3:11).

Life Synopsis

Caleb offered his daughter Achsah to whoever would smite Kirjath-sepher and take it. "And Othniel the son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb, took it: and he gave him Achsah his daughter to wife" (Joshua 15:16-17; Judges 1:12-13).

After Joshua's generation died, Israel served the gods of the land, and the Lord sold them into the hand of Chushanrishathaim king of Mesopotamia, whom they served eight years. "And when the children of Israel cried unto the Lord, the Lord raised up a deliverer to the children of Israel, who delivered them, even Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother. And the Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and he judged Israel, and went out to war... and his hand prevailed against Chushanrishathaim. And the land had rest forty years" (Judges 3:8-11).

What They Did Right

  • Took Kirjath-sepher when Caleb's challenge went out: Joshua 15:17; Judges 1:13.
  • The Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and he judged Israel and went to war: Judges 3:10.
  • Delivered Israel from Chushanrishathaim, and the land had rest forty years: Judges 3:10-11.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him, which is not true of any judge who follows. His account is short and entirely favourable: he answered a challenge, received the Spirit, delivered the nation, and gave it forty years of rest. The book of Judges presents him first, before the pattern of compromised deliverers begins.

Significance

The first of the judges, and the model against which the rest are implicitly measured. He is the only judge of whom no failure is recorded. That he came from Caleb's household connects the first deliverance of the Judges period directly to the faith of the conquest generation.

Death / Outcome

"And Othniel the son of Kenaz died" (Judges 3:11).

Scripture References

Joshua 15:16-19; Judges 1:12-15; Judges 3:8-11; 1 Chronicles 4:13

The Judges

—

Adonibezek

A Canaanite king defeated by Judah at Bezek, who acknowledged that what was done to him was what he had done to others.

Also called Adoni-bezek

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He was defeated at the beginning of the period after Joshua's death.

Life Synopsis

Judah and Simeon found him at Bezek and fought against him. He fled, was caught, and had his thumbs and great toes cut off. His own words are the reason he is remembered: "Threescore and ten kings, having their thumbs and their great toes cut off, gathered their meat under my table: as I have done, so God hath requited me." They brought him to Jerusalem, and there he died (Judges 1:5-7).

What They Did Right

  • Acknowledged the justice of what happened to him, and named God as the one who had requited him: Judges 1:7. Scripture records the admission without commending or condemning the man.

What They Did Wrong

  • Had mutilated seventy kings and kept them under his table: Judges 1:7, by his own account. Scripture records this in his own words rather than as narration, and does not add a separate condemnation.

Character Assessment

Scripture records one act of cruelty on a large scale and one clear-eyed confession that the punishment fit it. He is the only pagan king in Judges recorded as interpreting his own downfall as divine justice. The text does not say whether the acknowledgment was repentance or merely recognition.

Significance

His statement opens the book of Judges with the principle that runs through it: God requites what men do. The mutilation of thumbs and toes disabled a man for both weapon and pursuit, which is why it was done to kings.

Death / Outcome

Brought to Jerusalem, where he died (Judges 1:7).

Scripture References

Judges 1:4-7
—

Chushanrishathaim

King of Mesopotamia; the first oppressor of Israel in the period of the judges.

Also called Chushan-rishathaim

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Israel served him eight years before Othniel delivered them (Judges 3:8).

Life Synopsis

"Therefore the anger of the Lord was hot against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of Chushanrishathaim king of Mesopotamia: and the children of Israel served Chushanrishathaim eight years" (Judges 3:8). When Israel cried to the Lord, he raised up Othniel, the Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and the Lord delivered Chushanrishathaim into his hand (Judges 3:9-10).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records that he oppressed Israel for eight years but frames it as God selling Israel into his hand because of their idolatry, and passes no separate judgment on the king himself.

Character Assessment

He appears only as an instrument of chastening. The text's emphasis falls entirely on Israel's sin and God's response, not on the character of the oppressor.

Significance

The first of the oppressions in Judges, and the one that establishes the book's repeating pattern: Israel does evil, God sells them into an enemy's hand, they cry out, God raises a deliverer, the land has rest.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. His defeat is noted in Judges 3:10.

Scripture References

Judges 3:8-10
—

Eglon

King of Moab; oppressed Israel eighteen years and was killed by Ehud.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Israel served him eighteen years (Judges 3:14).

Life Synopsis

Eglon gathered the children of Ammon and Amalek, smote Israel, and possessed the city of palm trees. Israel served him eighteen years (Judges 3:12-14).

Ehud brought him the tribute, then said he had a secret errand. Eglon dismissed his attendants. Ehud said, "I have a message from God unto thee," and Eglon arose out of his seat. Ehud drew the dagger from his right thigh and thrust it into his belly; the haft went in after the blade and the fat closed on it (Judges 3:19-22). His servants waited outside until they were ashamed, thinking he covered his feet in his summer chamber, and by the time they opened the doors he was dead and Ehud had escaped (Judges 3:24-26).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. Scripture notes that he rose out of his seat when told the message was from God (Judges 3:20), and records nothing further.

What They Did Wrong

  • Oppressed Israel for eighteen years: Judges 3:14. As with the other oppressors in Judges, the text presents this as God strengthening him against Israel because Israel did evil (Judges 3:12), and offers no separate verdict on him.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his oppression, his obesity, and the manner of his death in unusual physical detail. The narrative's interest is in Ehud's stratagem rather than in Eglon's character, and no moral assessment of the man is offered.

Significance

His death began the deliverance under Ehud that gave the land eighty years of rest, the longest period of peace recorded in Judges (Judges 3:30).

Death / Outcome

Killed by Ehud with a two-edged dagger in his summer chamber (Judges 3:21-22).

Scripture References

Judges 3:12-26
—

Ehud

Son of Gera, a Benjamite, left-handed; the second judge, who killed Eglon king of Moab and delivered Israel.

Family

Son of Gera, a Benjamite (Judges 3:15).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. After his deliverance the land had rest eighty years (Judges 3:30).

Life Synopsis

When Israel cried to the Lord under Moab's oppression, he raised up Ehud, "a man lefthanded." Ehud made a two-edged dagger of a cubit's length and girded it under his raiment on his right thigh - the side no one would search on a right-handed man (Judges 3:15-16).

He brought the tribute to Eglon, sent away the men who bore it, then returned from the quarries and said, "I have a secret errand unto thee, O king." Eglon dismissed his attendants. Ehud came to him in the summer parlour and said, "I have a message from God unto thee." As the king rose, Ehud took the dagger with his left hand and thrust it into his belly (Judges 3:17-22).

He went out, shut and locked the doors behind him, and escaped while the servants waited. Reaching Seirath, he blew a trumpet in mount Ephraim, gathered Israel, and took the fords of Jordan against Moab, killing about ten thousand men. "So Moab was subdued that day under the hand of Israel. And the land had rest fourscore years" (Judges 3:26-30).

What They Did Right

  • Was raised up by the Lord as a deliverer when Israel cried out: Judges 3:15.
  • Attributed the deliverance to God when calling Israel to arms: "Follow after me: for the Lord hath delivered your enemies the Moabites into your hand": Judges 3:28.
  • Secured eighty years of rest for the land - the longest peace recorded in Judges: Judges 3:30.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records the deception by which he obtained a private audience and the killing itself without moral comment, and calls him a deliverer raised up by the Lord. The ethics of the stratagem are debated; the text neither defends nor condemns it.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents him wholly as a deliverer. His left-handedness is not a detail of colour but the hinge of the account - it is why the weapon was not found. The narrative's tone toward him is favourable throughout, and it records no failure.

Significance

His deliverance produced the longest period of rest in the book of Judges. He is one of only two judges, with Othniel, of whom no fault is recorded.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded directly; Judges 4:1 notes that Israel again did evil "when Ehud was dead."

Scripture References

Judges 3:12-30; Judges 4:1
—

Shamgar

Son of Anath; slew six hundred Philistines with an ox goad and delivered Israel.

Family

Son of Anath (Judges 3:31).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Deborah's song refers to "the days of Shamgar the son of Anath" as a time when the highways were unoccupied (Judges 5:6).

Life Synopsis

His entire account is one verse: "And after him was Shamgar the son of Anath, which slew of the Philistines six hundred men with an ox goad: and he also delivered Israel" (Judges 3:31). Deborah's song mentions his days as a period when travellers kept to byways and the highways lay empty (Judges 5:6).

What They Did Right

  • Slew six hundred Philistines with an ox goad - a farm implement, not a weapon: Judges 3:31.
  • Scripture states plainly that "he also delivered Israel": Judges 3:31.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

One verse, and it is entirely positive. Scripture records no failure, no oppression preceding him, and no years of rest following him - only the act and the result. He is included because the verse records a specific action, a specific number, a specific instrument, and an explicit statement that he delivered Israel.

Significance

The ox goad has become a standing image of God using what is at hand. Deborah's reference to his days indicates that the Philistine pressure of his time was severe enough to empty the roads.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture References

Judges 3:31; Judges 5:6
—

Deborah

A prophetess and the wife of Lapidoth; the only woman recorded as judging Israel; co-author of the song in Judges 5. Not to be confused with Deborah, Rebekah's nurse (Genesis 35:8).

Family

Wife of Lapidoth (Judges 4:4). She calls herself "a mother in Israel" (Judges 5:7).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. After the victory over Sisera the land had rest forty years (Judges 5:31).

Life Synopsis

"And Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, she judged Israel at that time. And she dwelt under the palm tree of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in mount Ephraim: and the children of Israel came up to her for judgment" (Judges 4:4-5). Israel had been oppressed twenty years by Jabin king of Canaan, whose captain Sisera had nine hundred chariots of iron.

She sent for Barak and delivered a command she attributed directly to God: go to mount Tabor with ten thousand men, and the Lord will draw Sisera to the river Kishon and deliver him into your hand. Barak answered, "If thou wilt go with me, then I will go: but if thou wilt not go with me, then I will not go." She replied, "I will surely go with thee: notwithstanding the journey that thou takest shall not be for thine honour; for the Lord shall sell Sisera into the hand of a woman" (Judges 4:6-9).

She went with him. At her word - "Up; for this is the day in which the Lord hath delivered Sisera into thine hand" - Barak descended from Tabor, and the Lord discomfited Sisera's host (Judges 4:14-15).

She and Barak then sang the song of Judges 5, which recounts the battle, blesses Jael, names the tribes that came and those that did not, and closes: "So let all thine enemies perish, O Lord: but let them that love him be as the sun when he goeth forth in his might" (Judges 5:31).

What They Did Right

  • Judged Israel and gave judgment to those who came to her: Judges 4:4-5.
  • Delivered God's command to Barak plainly and took responsibility for it: Judges 4:6-7.
  • Went with Barak when he would not go alone, while telling him honestly what it would cost him: Judges 4:8-9.
  • Gave the word to advance and credited the victory to the Lord: Judges 4:14.
  • Composed and sang the song recounting the deliverance and giving God the glory: Judges 5:1-31.
  • Named the tribes that failed to come, and those that jeoparded their lives, without flattering either: Judges 5:15-18, 5:23.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her. She is prophetess, judge, and poet, and the only woman in Scripture who held judicial authority over the nation. What is most notable in the record is her clarity: she gives Barak God's word, she tells him the honour will go elsewhere if he insists on her company, and she goes anyway. Her song does not soften the record of the tribes that stayed home.

Significance

The only female judge of Israel, and one of a small number of women called prophetess (with Miriam, Huldah, Noadiah, and Anna). Her song is among the oldest poetry in Scripture. Under her the land had forty years of rest. Notably, Hebrews 11:32 names Barak, not Deborah, in the roll of faith - a fact worth recording without inferring anything the text does not say.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Judges 5:31.

Scripture References

Judges 4:1-24; Judges 5:1-31
—

Barak

Son of Abinoam of Kedeshnaphtali; commanded Israel's forces against Sisera at Deborah's word; named in the roll of faith.

Family

Son of Abinoam, of Kedeshnaphtali (Judges 4:6).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Deborah sent for him and gave him God's command to take ten thousand men to mount Tabor, with the promise that Sisera would be delivered into his hand. He answered, "If thou wilt go with me, then I will go: but if thou wilt not go with me, then I will not go" (Judges 4:6-8). Deborah agreed but warned that the journey would not be for his honour, because the Lord would sell Sisera into the hand of a woman (Judges 4:9).

He gathered ten thousand men and went up. At Deborah's word he came down from Tabor, and the Lord discomfited Sisera and all his chariots; Barak pursued the host to Harosheth and not a man was left (Judges 4:14-16). Coming to Jael's tent in pursuit, he found Sisera already dead (Judges 4:22). He sang the song of deliverance with Deborah (Judges 5:1).

What They Did Right

  • Obeyed the call and gathered ten thousand men: Judges 4:10.
  • Pursued the host until it was destroyed: Judges 4:16.
  • Sang the song of deliverance with Deborah, giving God the glory: Judges 5:1-2.
  • Named in the roll of faith in Hebrews: Hebrews 11:32.
  • Named by Samuel among the deliverers God sent: 1 Samuel 12:11 refers to Bedan, whom many identify with Barak, though the identification is uncertain and Scripture does not make it.

What They Did Wrong

  • Refused to go unless Deborah went with him: Judges 4:8. Scripture records Deborah's response - that the honour of the day would go to a woman - which treats the refusal as a real failing, though it never uses the word sin. Judges 5:15 does record that his conduct in the battle itself was resolute.

Character Assessment

A genuinely mixed record that Scripture holds together without embarrassment. He would not go without the prophetess, and lost the honour of the victory because of it. He also gathered the army, led the charge at the word of command, destroyed the enemy host, and is one of only four judges named in Hebrews 11. The New Testament commendation is not a correction of the Judges account; both stand.

Significance

Under his command Israel broke the twenty-year oppression of Jabin, and the land had forty years of rest (Judges 5:31). He is named in Hebrews 11:32 among those who through faith subdued kingdoms.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Hebrews 11:32.

Scripture References

Judges 4:1-24; Judges 5:1-31; Hebrews 11:32
—

Sisera

Captain of the host of Jabin king of Canaan; commanded nine hundred chariots of iron; killed by Jael.

Family

Not recorded, except that his mother appears in Deborah's song (Judges 5:28).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He oppressed Israel twenty years (Judges 4:3).

Life Synopsis

Sisera dwelt in Harosheth of the Gentiles and had nine hundred chariots of iron, with which he mightily oppressed Israel twenty years (Judges 4:2-3). When Barak came down from Tabor, the Lord discomfited Sisera and all his host before Barak; "Sisera lighted down off his chariot, and fled away on his feet" (Judges 4:15).

He fled to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, because there was peace between Jabin and the house of Heber. Jael invited him in, covered him with a mantle, gave him milk when he asked for water, and agreed to stand at the door and deny that anyone was there. He slept from weariness, and she drove a tent nail through his temples (Judges 4:17-21). Barak, pursuing, found him dead.

Deborah's song closes with a scene at his mother's window: she looks out through the lattice asking why his chariot is so long in coming, and her wise ladies answer that they must be dividing the spoil (Judges 5:28-30).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Mightily oppressed the children of Israel for twenty years: Judges 4:3. As with the other oppressors of Judges, the text frames this within God's selling Israel into their hand for their idolatry, and offers no separate moral verdict on the man.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his power, his oppression, and his end. The narrative gives more attention to his death than to his life, and Deborah's song ends by lingering on his mother waiting at the window - a moment of unexpected pathos in a victory poem, recorded without comment.

Significance

His defeat broke Canaanite power in the north and secured forty years of rest. Psalms 83:9 invokes his fate in a prayer against later enemies.

Death / Outcome

Killed by Jael, who drove a nail of the tent through his temples while he slept (Judges 4:21; Judges 5:26).

Scripture References

Judges 4:2-22; Judges 5:20-30; 1 Samuel 12:9; Psalms 83:9
—

Jael

Wife of Heber the Kenite; killed Sisera with a tent nail and is called blessed above women in Deborah's song.

Family

Wife of Heber the Kenite (Judges 4:17).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Sisera fled on foot to her tent, because there was peace between Jabin king of Hazor and the house of Heber (Judges 4:17). "And Jael went out to meet Sisera, and said unto him, Turn in, my lord, turn in to me; fear not." She covered him with a mantle. He asked for water and she gave him milk. He asked her to stand at the tent door and say no man was there (Judges 4:18-20).

"Then Jael Heber's wife took a nail of the tent, and took an hammer in her hand, and went softly unto him, and smote the nail into his temples, and fastened it into the ground: for he was fast asleep and weary. So he died" (Judges 4:21). When Barak came in pursuit she went out to meet him and showed him the man he sought.

Deborah's song devotes four verses to her: "Blessed above women shall Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite be, blessed shall she be above women in the tent" (Judges 5:24-27).

What They Did Right

  • Deborah's song pronounces her blessed above women, which is the strongest evaluation Scripture offers of anyone in the chapter: Judges 5:24.
  • Her act ended the twenty-year oppression and fulfilled the word that the Lord would sell Sisera into the hand of a woman: Judges 4:9, 4:21.

What They Did Wrong

  • She killed a man who had entered her tent under a truce between his king and her household, after inviting him in, giving him drink, and agreeing to conceal him: Judges 4:17-21. Scripture records every element of that sequence and then blesses her for the outcome, without addressing the breach of hospitality. The tension is real and the text does not resolve it. Readers should note that Judges nowhere states that her method was approved, only that she is blessed for what she accomplished.

Character Assessment

One of the sharpest interpretive difficulties in the book. Scripture's only explicit evaluation of her is superlative praise in an inspired song, and the same Scripture records in detail the deception and the violated hospitality that made the killing possible. This reference sets both down and declines to resolve what the text leaves standing. What the narrative plainly does present is a woman acting decisively where Israel's commander had hesitated.

Significance

Her act completed the deliverance and fulfilled Deborah's word to Barak. She is one of very few individuals in Scripture pronounced blessed above others, a phrase used again of Mary in Luke 1:42.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Judges 5:24.

Scripture References

Judges 4:17-22; Judges 5:6, 5:24-27
—

Heber the Kenite

A Kenite of the children of Hobab, Moses' father in law; separated from his people and pitched his tent near Kedesh; husband of Jael.

Family

Of the children of Hobab, the father in law of Moses (Judges 4:11). Husband of Jael (Judges 4:17).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"Now Heber the Kenite, which was of the children of Hobab the father in law of Moses, had severed himself from the Kenites, and pitched his tent unto the plain of Zaanaim, which is by Kedesh" (Judges 4:11). Scripture also records that there was peace between Jabin king of Hazor and the house of Heber (Judges 4:17), which is why Sisera fled there. It was Heber's household that reported to Sisera that Barak had gone up to Tabor (Judges 4:12).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records his separation from the Kenites and his peace with Jabin without evaluating either.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his lineage, his move, and his treaty, and nothing of his character. He is included because those details are specific and because they are what made Jael's act possible - Sisera came to that tent precisely because Heber's house was at peace with his king.

Significance

His descent from Hobab connects the household to Moses' father-in-law and to the Kenites who came up with Judah (Judges 1:16). His treaty with Jabin is the circumstance on which the whole conclusion of the Sisera narrative turns.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Judges 5:24.

Scripture References

Judges 4:11, 4:17; Judges 5:24
—

The mother of Sisera

Unnamed. The mother of Sisera, pictured in Deborah's song waiting at her window for a son who will not return.

Family

Mother of Sisera (Judges 5:28).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Deborah's song turns at its close from the battlefield to a window in Canaan: "The mother of Sisera looked out at a window, and cried through the lattice, Why is his chariot so long in coming? why tarry the wheels of his chariots? Her wise ladies answered her, yea, she returned answer to herself, Have they not sped? have they not divided the prey; to every man a damsel or two; to Sisera a prey of divers colours..." (Judges 5:28-30). The song then ends abruptly with the prayer that all God's enemies perish.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. The answer she gives herself assumes the division of captured women as spoil (Judges 5:30), which the song records as her expectation rather than her act.

Character Assessment

She acts only in the imagination of the song, and Scripture offers no verdict on her. The passage is included because it is a deliberate and self-contained scene given to a specific identifiable person, and because it is one of the few places in Scripture where a victory poem pauses to picture the grief on the other side.

Significance

The scene supplies the song's final contrast: the mother's confident expectation set against the reader's knowledge that her son is lying dead in a tent with a nail through his temples.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture References

Judges 5:28-31
—

Gideon

Son of Joash the Abiezrite; called by the angel of the Lord to deliver Israel from Midian; destroyed his father's altar of Baal and defeated Midian with three hundred men.

Also called Jerubbaal, Gedeon, Jerubbesheth

Family

Son of Joash the Abiezrite, of Manasseh (Judges 6:11, 6:15). He had many wives and seventy sons (Judges 8:30), including Jether his firstborn (Judges 8:20) and Abimelech by a concubine in Shechem (Judges 8:31).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. After his victory the land was in quietness forty years, and he died in a good old age (Judges 8:28, 8:32).

Life Synopsis

Midian had oppressed Israel seven years, so that Israel made dens in the mountains and Midian destroyed the increase of the earth (Judges 6:1-6). The angel of the Lord found Gideon threshing wheat by the winepress to hide it from the Midianites, and greeted him, "The Lord is with thee, thou mighty man of valour." Gideon's reply was a question: if the Lord is with us, why has all this befallen us? and he protested that his family was poor in Manasseh and he the least in his father's house (Judges 6:11-15).

He asked for a sign, prepared an offering, and saw fire rise out of the rock to consume it (Judges 6:17-21). That night he was told to throw down his father's altar of Baal and the grove beside it. He did it by night, "because he feared his father's household, and the men of the city" - the text records both the obedience and the fear (Judges 6:25-27). When the men of the city demanded his death, his father Joash answered for him: "if he be a god, let him plead for himself." Gideon was named Jerubbaal from that day (Judges 6:28-32).

He asked for two further signs with the fleece, both granted (Judges 6:36-40). Thirty-two thousand men gathered; God said they were too many, "lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me." Twenty-two thousand fearful men left, and the rest were reduced by the manner of their drinking to three hundred (Judges 7:2-7). Fearful still, Gideon went down with Phurah his servant and overheard a Midianite recounting a dream of a barley cake overturning a tent; then he worshipped (Judges 7:9-15). With trumpets, pitchers, and lamps the three hundred routed the host.

Afterward he answered Ephraim's complaint gently and defused it (Judges 8:1-3), but dealt severely with Succoth and Penuel, who had refused bread to his men, tearing the elders of Succoth with thorns and briers and killing the men of Penuel (Judges 8:5-17). When Israel offered him and his sons a dynasty he refused: "I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you: the Lord shall rule over you" (Judges 8:22-23). Then he asked instead for the golden earrings of the spoil, made an ephod of them, and set it in his city, "and all Israel went thither a whoring after it: which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house" (Judges 8:24-27).

What They Did Right

  • Obeyed the command to throw down his father's altar of Baal and cut down the grove, though he did it by night out of fear: Judges 6:25-27.
  • Gathered Israel at the Spirit's coming upon him: Judges 6:34.
  • Accepted the reduction of his army from thirty-two thousand to three hundred: Judges 7:2-8.
  • Worshipped when he heard the Midianite's dream, before the battle was fought: Judges 7:15.
  • Answered Ephraim's angry complaint with a soft answer that turned away their wrath: Judges 8:1-3.
  • Refused the offer of hereditary rule, on the ground that the Lord should rule over Israel: Judges 8:23.
  • Named in the roll of faith: Hebrews 11:32.

What They Did Wrong

  • Repeatedly asked for signs after receiving a clear commission, including the two fleeces: Judges 6:17, 6:36-40. Scripture records God's patience in granting them and does not explicitly rebuke him, but the requests are framed by his own admission of fear.
  • Tore the elders of Succoth with thorns and briers and slew the men of Penuel for refusing bread: Judges 8:16-17. The text records the severity without comment.
  • Made an ephod from the golden earrings of the spoil and set it up in Ophrah: Judges 8:24-27. Here Scripture is explicit: "all Israel went thither a whoring after it: which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house."
  • Had many wives and a concubine in Shechem, whose son Abimelech destroyed his house: Judges 8:30-31.
  • After his death Israel returned to Baalim and showed no kindness to his house: Judges 8:33-35.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents him as a genuinely fearful man whom God used anyway, and it does not hide either the fear or the failure. The commission comes to a man hiding from Midianites; the altar is thrown down at night; the fleeces follow a clear word already given; and the army is cut to three hundred precisely so that no one could claim the victory. His refusal of the crown is one of the finest moments in Judges. His ephod is one of the worst, and the text says so in the plainest terms. Hebrews names him among the faithful without qualifying the record.

Significance

His victory with three hundred men is Scripture's clearest demonstration of the principle God states before the battle: that Israel must not say its own hand had saved it (Judges 7:2). Isaiah 9:4 and Isaiah 10:26 invoke "the day of Midian" as a pattern of deliverance. His refusal of kingship, and his son Abimelech's seizure of it, together frame the book's question about who should rule Israel.

Death / Outcome

Died in a good old age and was buried in the sepulchre of Joash his father in Ophrah (Judges 8:32).

Scripture References

Judges 6:1-8:35; Judges 9:1-57; 1 Samuel 12:11; Psalms 83:11; Isaiah 9:4; Isaiah 10:26; Hebrews 11:32
—

Joash (father of Gideon)

An Abiezrite of Ophrah; owner of the altar of Baal that Gideon destroyed; defended his son against the men of the city. Not to be confused with Joash king of Judah or Joash king of Israel.

Family

Father of Gideon (Judges 6:11).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

The altar of Baal and the grove beside it belonged to Joash (Judges 6:25). When Gideon threw them down by night and the men of the city demanded his death, Joash answered the whole crowd: "Will ye plead for Baal? will ye save him? he that will plead for him, let him be put to death whilst it is yet morning: if he be a god, let him plead for himself, because one hath cast down his altar." From that day Gideon was called Jerubbaal, "Let Baal plead against him" (Judges 6:28-32).

What They Did Right

  • Stood between his son and a crowd demanding his death: Judges 6:31.
  • Made the argument that exposed the whole case: a god who cannot defend his own altar is no god: Judges 6:31.

What They Did Wrong

  • The altar of Baal and the grove were his, standing on his own property: Judges 6:25. Scripture records this as fact and does not separately condemn him for it.

Character Assessment

A brief but pointed record. He kept an altar of Baal, and when it was destroyed he defended the man who destroyed it with an argument against Baal's very existence. Scripture reports both without reconciling them, and Gideon's new name preserved his father's words.

Significance

His defence saved Gideon's life at the outset and gave him the name Jerubbaal, by which he is called throughout the rest of Judges and in 1 Samuel 12:11.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Gideon was buried in his sepulchre in Ophrah (Judges 8:32).

Scripture References

Judges 6:11, 6:25-32; Judges 8:32
—

Phurah

Gideon's servant, who went down with him by night to the edge of the Midianite host.

Also called Purah

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

God told Gideon to go down to the host, and added a provision for his fear: "But if thou fear to go down, go thou with Phurah thy servant down to the host... and afterward shall thine hands be strengthened to go down unto the host. Then went he down with Phurah his servant unto the outside of the armed men that were in the host" (Judges 7:10-11). There they overheard the dream of the barley cake and its interpretation, and Gideon worshipped and returned to raise the camp.

What They Did Right

  • Went with Gideon by night to the edge of an enemy host described as lying along the valley like grasshoppers for multitude: Judges 7:11-12. Scripture records the act without further comment.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing he said and one thing he did. He is included because that act is specific and because the text names him twice in two verses, which it need not have done.

Significance

The provision of a companion for a fearful man is recorded as God's own suggestion, which is the detail most often drawn from the passage.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Judges 7:11.

Judges 7:10-11

Oreb and Zeeb

Two princes of Midian, taken and killed by the men of Ephraim at the rock of Oreb and the winepress of Zeeb. Two distinct individuals, recorded together throughout.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

As Midian fled from Gideon's three hundred, Ephraim took the waters as far as Bethbarah and Jordan. "And they took two princes of the Midianites, Oreb and Zeeb; and they slew Oreb upon the rock Oreb, and Zeeb they slew at the winepress of Zeeb, and pursued Midian, and brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon on the other side Jordan" (Judges 7:25). Gideon later cited their capture in answering Ephraim's complaint: "Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer?" (Judges 8:2).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records their office and their deaths without moral evaluation.

Character Assessment

Named as princes of the enemy and recorded chiefly through the places named after their deaths. No assessment of either man is offered.

Significance

Their capture became a fixed memory in Israel. Psalms 83:11 prays, "Make their nobles like Oreb, and like Zeeb," and Isaiah 10:26 recalls "the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb" as a pattern of God's deliverance.

Death / Outcome

Slain by the men of Ephraim, Oreb at the rock and Zeeb at the winepress afterward named for them (Judges 7:25).

Scripture References

Judges 7:25; Judges 8:3; Psalms 83:11; Isaiah 10:26
—

Zebah and Zalmunna

Two kings of Midian, pursued across Jordan by Gideon and killed by him for the murder of his brothers. Two distinct individuals, recorded together throughout.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

They fled with about fifteen thousand men, all that remained of the hosts of the east. Gideon crossed Jordan with three hundred faint but pursuing men, was refused bread at Succoth and Penuel, and took the two kings at Karkor, discomfiting the whole host (Judges 8:4-12).

He then asked them, "What manner of men were they whom ye slew at Tabor?" They answered, "As thou art, so were they; each one resembled the children of a king." Gideon said, "They were my brethren, even the sons of my mother: as the Lord liveth, if ye had saved them alive, I would not slay you" (Judges 8:18-19). He told Jether his firstborn to kill them, but the youth was afraid. Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, "Rise thou, and fall upon us: for as the man is, so is his strength." Gideon rose and slew them, and took the ornaments from their camels' necks (Judges 8:20-21).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. They answered Gideon's questions directly and, at the end, asked him to do the killing himself rather than leave it to a frightened boy: Judges 8:18-21. Scripture records this without evaluation.

What They Did Wrong

  • They had killed Gideon's brothers at Tabor: Judges 8:18-19, by their own admission.
  • They led the Midianite oppression of Israel: Judges 8:5, 8:12.

Character Assessment

Scripture records their part in the oppression, their admission of the killings at Tabor, and their composed request at the end. No moral verdict on them is offered beyond the facts. Their exchange with Gideon is unusually direct, and it establishes that his pursuit was partly a matter of family blood.

Significance

Their capture completed the defeat of Midian. Psalms 83:11 names them with Oreb and Zeeb in a prayer against Israel's enemies.

Death / Outcome

Slain by Gideon at Karkor after his son Jether would not do it (Judges 8:20-21).

Scripture References

Judges 8:4-21; Psalms 83:11
—

Jether (son of Gideon)

Gideon's firstborn son, told to kill the captured kings of Midian and unable to do it.

Family

Firstborn son of Gideon (Judges 8:20).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He was a youth at the time of the incident.

Life Synopsis

"And he said unto Jether his firstborn, Up, and slay them. But the youth drew not his sword: for he feared, because he was yet a youth" (Judges 8:20). Zebah and Zalmunna then asked Gideon to do it himself, and he did.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture states plainly that he did not draw his sword because he feared, and immediately supplies the reason: he was yet a youth. The text explains rather than condemns.

Character Assessment

One verse, and Scripture's handling of it is notably gentle. It records the failure and in the same breath gives the excuse. He is presumably one of the seventy sons later killed by Abimelech at Ophrah (Judges 9:5), though he is not named there.

Significance

The incident marks the point at which Gideon began treating his household as a royal line - assigning the execution of captured kings to his firstborn, which is a king's prerogative, not a judge's.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded by name. Judges 9:5 records that Abimelech slew seventy of Gideon's sons at Ophrah, of whom only Jotham escaped.

Scripture References

Judges 8:20; Judges 8:30; Judges 9:5
—

Abimelech (son of Gideon)

Son of Gideon by a concubine of Shechem; killed his seventy brothers and made himself king; died at Thebez when a woman cast a millstone on his head. Not to be confused with the Abimelechs of Gerar in Genesis.

Family

Son of Gideon by his concubine in Shechem (Judges 8:31); half-brother of Gideon's seventy sons, including Jotham.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He reigned three years over Israel (Judges 9:22).

Life Synopsis

After Gideon's death Abimelech went to Shechem to his mother's brethren and put a question to the men of the city: was it better for them to be ruled by seventy men, or by one - "remember also that I am your bone and your flesh" (Judges 9:1-2). They gave him seventy pieces of silver from the house of Baalberith, with which he hired vain and light persons who followed him. "And he went unto his father's house at Ophrah, and slew his brethren the sons of Jerubbaal, being threescore and ten persons, upon one stone: notwithstanding yet Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left; for he hid himself" (Judges 9:4-5). He was then made king by the men of Shechem.

Jotham stood on mount Gerizim and told the parable of the trees seeking a king, ending with a curse conditional on their treachery (Judges 9:7-20). After three years God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem, "that the cruelty done to the threescore and ten sons of Jerubbaal might come" (Judges 9:23-24).

Gaal son of Ebed came to Shechem and led a revolt. Zebul, Abimelech's officer, secretly informed him, and Abimelech destroyed Gaal's force, took the city, beat it down, sowed it with salt, and burned about a thousand men and women in the hold of the house of their god (Judges 9:26-49).

He then went to Thebez and took the city, but the people fled into a strong tower. As he approached the door to burn it, "a certain woman cast a piece of a millstone upon Abimelech's head, and all to brake his skull." He called his armourbearer and said, "Draw thy sword, and slay me, that men say not of me, A woman slew him." His young man thrust him through and he died (Judges 9:50-54).

The narrator supplies the verdict: "Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren: and all the evil of the men of Shechem did God render upon their heads: and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal" (Judges 9:56-57).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Murdered seventy of his brothers on one stone: Judges 9:5.
  • Hired vain and light persons with silver taken from the house of Baalberith: Judges 9:4.
  • Made himself king over Israel by conspiracy: Judges 9:1-6.
  • Destroyed Shechem, beat down the city, and sowed it with salt: Judges 9:45.
  • Burned about a thousand men and women in the hold of the house of their god: Judges 9:49.
  • Scripture's own verdict is explicit: "Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech": Judges 9:56.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned, and the condemnation is stated by the narrator rather than left to inference. He is the one figure in Judges who seizes rule rather than being raised up, and the whole account is constructed to show the outcome. Judges never calls him a judge; it says he reigned. His father had refused a dynasty on the ground that the Lord should rule Israel; his son murdered seventy men to take one.

Significance

His three-year reign is the book's demonstration of what happens when a man makes himself king in Israel by force. Jotham's parable of the trees, told against him, is the earliest fable in Scripture. His death by a woman's millstone was still cited as a proverbial warning generations later, when Joab recalled it at the siege of Thebez (2 Samuel 11:21).

Death / Outcome

Struck on the head by a millstone dropped by a woman at Thebez, and finished off at his own request by his armourbearer (Judges 9:53-54).

Scripture References

Judges 8:31; Judges 9:1-57; 2 Samuel 11:21
—

Jotham (son of Gideon)

Youngest son of Gideon; the only one of the seventy to escape Abimelech; spoke the parable of the trees from mount Gerizim. Not to be confused with Jotham king of Judah.

Family

Youngest son of Gideon (Judges 9:5).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

When Abimelech killed the seventy sons of Gideon on one stone, "yet Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left; for he hid himself" (Judges 9:5).

When Shechem made Abimelech king, Jotham went and stood on the top of mount Gerizim, lifted up his voice, and told the parable of the trees: the olive, the fig, and the vine each refused the crown because they would not leave their fatness, sweetness, and wine to be promoted over the trees; only the bramble accepted, offering shade it could not give and threatening fire if they refused (Judges 9:7-15). He applied it directly: if they had dealt truly with Jerubbaal's house, let them rejoice in Abimelech; if not, let fire come out from Abimelech and devour them, and from them and devour Abimelech (Judges 9:16-20). "And Jotham ran away, and fled, and went to Beer, and dwelt there, for fear of Abimelech his brother" (Judges 9:21).

Three years later, when Abimelech and Shechem destroyed each other, the narrator records that "upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal" (Judges 9:57).

What They Did Right

  • Spoke publicly against a usurper who had murdered his seventy brothers, from a hillside above the city that crowned him: Judges 9:7-20.
  • His words were vindicated: Scripture records that his curse came upon Abimelech and Shechem: Judges 9:56-57.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. He hid to survive, spoke once with great courage, and fled. His parable is a shrewd piece of political speech: the useful trees will not abandon their work to rule, and only the worthless one wants the crown. The narrator's closing note treats his words as prophecy fulfilled.

Significance

The parable of the trees is the first fable in Scripture and one of the sharpest critiques of kingship in the Old Testament, spoken generations before Israel asked Samuel for a king.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He dwelt at Beer for fear of Abimelech (Judges 9:21).

Scripture References

Judges 9:5-21, 9:56-57
