A man who came to Shechem with his brethren, won the confidence of the city, and led a failed revolt against Abimelech.

Family

Son of Ebed (Judges 9:26); he had brethren and a father named Ebed, and Zebul is called his adversary.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. During Abimelech's three-year reign.

Life Synopsis

"And Gaal the son of Ebed came with his brethren, and went over to Shechem: and the men of Shechem put their confidence in him" (Judges 9:26). At a vintage festival in the house of their god, with wine and cursing of Abimelech, he said, "Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him?... would to God this people were under my hand! then would I remove Abimelech" (Judges 9:27-29).

Zebul, the ruler of the city and Abimelech's officer, was angry and sent word secretly to Abimelech, advising him to lie in wait by night. In the morning Gaal stood in the gate and saw people coming down from the mountains. Zebul mocked him: "Thou seest the shadow of the mountains as if they were men." When it was undeniable, Zebul turned on him: "Where is now thy mouth, wherewith thou saidst, Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?" Gaal went out and fought, was chased, and many fell; Zebul then thrust him and his brethren out of the city (Judges 9:30-41).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Made a drunken boast at a festival and led a revolt he could not sustain: Judges 9:27-29, 9:39-40. Scripture records the boast, the failure, and his expulsion without a separate moral verdict.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents him as an opportunist whose talk exceeded his capacity. The narrative gives his boast in full and then gives Zebul's answer in full, and the contrast is the whole assessment the text offers.

Significance

His revolt provoked Abimelech's destruction of Shechem, which was the first half of the fulfilment of Jotham's curse.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He was thrust out of Shechem by Zebul (Judges 9:41).

Zebul

Abimelech's officer and the ruler of Shechem; informed against Gaal and drove him out.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Zebul was Abimelech's officer and the ruler of the city (Judges 9:28, 9:30). Hearing Gaal's words, his anger was kindled and he sent messengers to Abimelech privily, with a plan: come by night, lie in wait in the field, and fall on the city in the morning (Judges 9:30-33).

When Gaal saw the approaching force, Zebul kept him talking - "Thou seest the shadow of the mountains as if they were men" - until it was too late to prepare. Then he goaded him into battle: "Where is now thy mouth... go out, I pray now, and fight with them" (Judges 9:36-38). After Gaal's defeat, Zebul thrust him and his brethren out of Shechem (Judges 9:41).

  • No specific commendation is recorded. He was loyal to Abimelech, but Scripture presents Abimelech's cause as wicked and offers no commendation of that loyalty.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records his deception of Gaal and his service to a usurper without explicit condemnation of him personally.

Character Assessment

Scripture records competence and cunning in the service of a murderer, and passes no verdict. He is the most effective actor in Judges 9 and one of the least examined.

Significance

His intelligence and his delaying tactic gave Abimelech the victory over Gaal, which drew Abimelech into the destruction of Shechem and so into the working out of Jotham's curse.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Judges 9:41.

Unnamed. The woman who dropped a piece of a millstone from the tower of Thebez and broke Abimelech's skull.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Abimelech took Thebez, but all the men and women of the city fled into a strong tower, shut it, and got up to the top. He came to the tower door to burn it with fire. "And a certain woman cast a piece of a millstone upon Abimelech's head, and all to brake his skull" (Judges 9:50-53). Abimelech called his armourbearer and asked to be run through so that it should not be said a woman killed him.

What They Did Right

  • Acted to defend her city against a man about to burn the tower with everyone in it: Judges 9:52-53. Scripture records the act without moral comment.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records one act and nothing else, not even her name. The narrative makes clear that her stone accomplished what Israel's armies had not, and that Abimelech's last recorded concern was that people would find out who did it. Joab's recollection generations later shows they did (2 Samuel 11:21).

Significance

Her act ended Abimelech's three-year reign and completed Jotham's curse. It became a proverbial military lesson about approaching a wall too closely, cited by Joab in advising the messenger who reported Uriah's death (2 Samuel 11:21).

Not recorded. Last mention: Judges 9:53.

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"Then he called hastily unto the young man his armourbearer, and said unto him, Draw thy sword, and slay me, that men say not of me, A woman slew him. And his young man thrust him through, and he died" (Judges 9:54).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He killed his master at his master's explicit command. Scripture records the act without evaluating it.

One verse. Scripture records the order and the obedience and passes no judgment. The episode is recorded chiefly for what it shows about Abimelech, whose final concern was his reputation.

His act completed the death Scripture attributes to God's rendering of Abimelech's wickedness (Judges 9:56), and the attempt to conceal the manner of it failed, as 2 Samuel 11:21 shows.

Not recorded.

Son of Puah, the son of Dodo, of the tribe of Issachar (Judges 10:1).

Chronology

Judged Israel twenty-three years (Judges 10:2). The date is not otherwise established.

Life Synopsis

"And after Abimelech there arose to defend Israel Tola the son of Puah, the son of Dodo, a man of Issachar; and he dwelt in Shamir in mount Ephraim. And he judged Israel twenty and three years, and died, and was buried in Shamir" (Judges 10:1-2). No oppression, deliverance, or battle is recorded in his time.

What They Did Right

  • Arose to defend Israel and judged twenty-three years: Judges 10:1-2. Scripture records the service without further detail.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Two verses, entirely neutral to favourable. He is one of the judges sometimes called minor, of whom Scripture records the tribe, the dwelling, the length of service, and the burial place, but no exploit. The absence of any recorded crisis in twenty-three years is not nothing.

Significance

He follows immediately after Abimelech's destructive reign, and Scripture says he arose "to defend Israel" - a deliberate contrast with the man who had ruled by murder.

Death / Outcome

Died and was buried in Shamir (Judges 10:2).

Jair (the Gileadite)

A Gileadite who judged Israel twenty-two years; had thirty sons who rode on thirty ass colts and had thirty cities. Not to be confused with Jair the son of Manasseh (Numbers 32:41) or Jair the father of Mordecai (Esther 2:5).

Family

Father of thirty sons (Judges 10:4).

Chronology

Judged Israel twenty-two years (Judges 10:3).

Life Synopsis

"And after him arose Jair, a Gileadite, and judged Israel twenty and two years. And he had thirty sons that rode on thirty ass colts, and they had thirty cities, which are called Havothjair unto this day, which are in the land of Gilead. And Jair died, and was buried in Camon" (Judges 10:3-5).

What They Did Right

  • Judged Israel twenty-two years: Judges 10:3.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. The detail of thirty sons on thirty ass colts with thirty cities is recorded without comment. It indicates considerable wealth and a dynastic style of household, which some read as a criticism in the pattern of Judges; the text itself says nothing.

Character Assessment

Three verses, with no crisis, no deliverance, and no failure recorded. The account is chiefly notable for the household it describes.

Significance

The Havothjair he is associated with carry the name of the earlier Jair of Numbers 32:41 and Deuteronomy 3:14, and Scripture does not explain the relation between the two men beyond the shared name and region.

Death / Outcome

Died and was buried in Camon (Judges 10:5).

Scripture References

Judges 10:3-5
—

Jephthah

A Gileadite, son of a harlot, driven out by his brothers and later called back to lead Gilead against Ammon; judge of Israel; made a vow concerning his daughter.

Also called Jephthae

Family

Son of Gilead by a harlot (Judges 11:1); half-brother of Gilead's legitimate sons, who drove him out. Father of one daughter, an only child (Judges 11:34).

Chronology

Judged Israel six years (Judges 12:7). The date is not otherwise established.

Life Synopsis

"Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty man of valour, and he was the son of an harlot." His half-brothers thrust him out, saying he would not inherit in their father's house, and he fled to the land of Tob, where vain men gathered to him (Judges 11:1-3).

When Ammon made war, the elders of Gilead came to fetch him. He asked the obvious question - "Did not ye hate me, and expel me out of my father's house? and why are ye come unto me now when ye are in distress?" - and made them agree that if he prevailed he would be their head. He spoke all his words before the Lord in Mizpeh (Judges 11:4-11).

He then sent a long diplomatic message to the king of Ammon, reviewing the history of Israel's passage around Edom and Moab and the defeat of Sihon, and arguing that Israel had not taken Ammonite land and that Ammon had made no claim for three hundred years. The king would not hear it (Judges 11:12-28).

The Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and he vowed: "If thou shalt without fail deliver the children of Ammon into mine hands, then it shall be, that whatsoever cometh forth of the doors of my house to meet me... shall surely be the Lord's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering" (Judges 11:29-31). He defeated Ammon with a very great slaughter. Returning to Mizpeh, "behold, his daughter came out to meet him with timbrels and with dances; and she was his only child." He rent his clothes: "I have opened my mouth unto the Lord, and I cannot go back" (Judges 11:34-35). She asked two months to bewail her virginity, and returned, "and he did with her according to his vow which he had vowed: and she knew no man" (Judges 11:39).

Ephraim then quarrelled with him as they had with Gideon, but the outcome was different. Jephthah fought them, took the fords of Jordan, and tested each man by asking him to say Shibboleth; those who said Sibboleth were killed. Forty-two thousand Ephraimites fell (Judges 12:1-6). He judged Israel six years and died (Judges 12:7).

What They Did Right

  • Spoke all his words before the Lord at Mizpeh when accepting the command: Judges 11:11.
  • Attempted a long and reasoned diplomatic settlement with Ammon before fighting: Judges 11:12-28.
  • Appealed to God as judge between the parties: Judges 11:27.
  • The Spirit of the Lord came upon him: Judges 11:29.
  • Kept his vow at enormous personal cost when he could have broken it: Judges 11:35.
  • Named in the roll of faith: Hebrews 11:32; and named by Samuel among the deliverers God sent: 1 Samuel 12:11.

What They Did Wrong

  • Made a rash and open-ended vow, promising as a burnt offering whatever came out of his doors: Judges 11:30-31. Scripture records the vow without commanding or approving it, and the law it appears to invoke expressly forbade human sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31; Leviticus 18:21).
  • Killed forty-two thousand Ephraimites in an inter-tribal war, where Gideon in a similar quarrel had answered softly and averted bloodshed: Judges 12:1-6; compare Judges 8:1-3.

Character Assessment

One of the most difficult figures in Judges, and Scripture leaves the difficulty standing. He is named in Hebrews 11 among those who through faith subdued kingdoms, and named by Samuel among the deliverers God sent. He is also the man who made a vow he should never have made and then kept it. What was actually done to his daughter is genuinely disputed. Judges 11:39 says he did with her according to his vow and adds, "and she knew no man," and the following verse records an annual four-day lamentation by the daughters of Israel. Some read this as a burnt offering; others as perpetual virginity and dedication, pointing to the emphasis on her virginity rather than her death. The Hebrew of the vow itself can be read either as "shall surely be the Lord's and I will offer it up" or "shall surely be the Lord's or I will offer it up." This reference sets out the alternatives and does not decide between them, because the text does not.

Significance

His diplomatic message to Ammon in Judges 11:15-27 is the longest historical argument in the book and preserves a summary of the wilderness itinerary. His life is also the book's clearest case of a man used by God whose theology of God was defective: he treated the Lord as a deity to be bargained with by vow, in the manner of the nations around him. The word Shibboleth has passed into general use for a test of belonging.

Death / Outcome

Died and was buried in one of the cities of Gilead (Judges 12:7).

Scripture References

Judges 10:6-12:7; 1 Samuel 12:11; Hebrews 11:32
—

The daughter of Jephthah

Unnamed. The only child of Jephthah, who met him with timbrels and dances on his return from defeating Ammon and became the subject of his vow.

Family

Only child of Jephthah; "beside her he had neither son nor daughter" (Judges 11:34).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

She came out of the doors of her father's house to meet him with timbrels and with dances - the customary welcome for a victorious commander. He rent his clothes and told her of the vow. Her answer is the most striking speech in the chapter: "My father, if thou hast opened thy mouth unto the Lord, do to me according to that which hath proceeded out of thy mouth; forasmuch as the Lord hath taken vengeance for thee of thine enemies, even of the children of Ammon" (Judges 11:34-36).

She asked only for two months to go up and down upon the mountains and bewail her virginity with her companions. She returned at the end of two months, and he did with her according to his vow, "and she knew no man." It became a custom in Israel that the daughters of Israel went yearly to lament her four days in a year (Judges 11:37-40).

What They Did Right

  • Submitted to her father's vow without resistance or reproach, and credited the Lord with the victory in the same breath: Judges 11:36.
  • Returned at the end of the two months rather than staying away: Judges 11:39.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her and gives her one of the most composed speeches in Judges. Her request concerns her virginity rather than her life, which is one of the reasons the nature of the vow's fulfilment is disputed (see Jephthah's entry). Whatever was done, the text presents her as consenting to it and honours her with an annual memorial - the only such memorial in Scripture for a woman.

Significance

The four-day yearly lamentation by the daughters of Israel is the only recorded annual commemoration of an individual in the Old Testament outside the appointed feasts. Her story is Scripture's sharpest illustration of the cost of a rash vow, and Ecclesiastes 5:4-5 states the principle directly: better not to vow than to vow and not pay.

Death / Outcome

Scripture states that her father did with her according to his vow, and that she knew no man (Judges 11:39). What this means is disputed; see the entry for Jephthah.

Scripture References

Judges 11:29-40; Ecclesiastes 5:4-5

Father of thirty sons and thirty daughters; he sent his daughters abroad and brought in thirty wives for his sons (Judges 12:9).

Judged Israel seven years (Judges 12:9).

Life Synopsis

"And after him Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel. And he had thirty sons, and thirty daughters, whom he sent abroad, and took in thirty daughters from abroad for his sons. And he judged Israel seven years. Then died Ibzan, and was buried at Bethlehem" (Judges 12:8-10).

What They Did Right

  • Judged Israel seven years: Judges 12:9.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. The marriages arranged abroad for all sixty children are recorded without evaluation. Whether "from abroad" means outside his clan or outside Israel is not stated, and this reference does not assume the latter.

Character Assessment

Three verses. Scripture records the service, the household, and the burial, and offers no verdict.

Significance

One of the judges of whom no military action is recorded. His extensive marriage alliances suggest a period of consolidation rather than crisis.

Death / Outcome

Died and was buried at Bethlehem (Judges 12:10).

Not recorded.

Judged Israel ten years (Judges 12:11).

"And after him Elon, a Zebulonite, judged Israel; and he judged Israel ten years. And Elon the Zebulonite died, and was buried in Aijalon in the country of Zebulun" (Judges 12:11-12).

What They Did Right

  • Judged Israel ten years: Judges 12:11.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Two verses recording tribe, length of service, death, and burial place. Scripture offers nothing further.

Significance

One of the judges from a northern tribe, indicating that the office was not confined to any one region.

Death / Outcome

Died and was buried in Aijalon in Zebulun (Judges 12:12).

Son of Hillel the Pirathonite (Judges 12:13); father of forty sons, with thirty nephews (Judges 12:14).

Chronology

Judged Israel eight years (Judges 12:14).

Life Synopsis

"And after him Abdon the son of Hillel, a Pirathonite, judged Israel. And he had forty sons and thirty nephews, that rode on threescore and ten ass colts: and he judged Israel eight years. And Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite died, and was buried in Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the mount of the Amalekites" (Judges 12:13-15).

What They Did Right

  • Judged Israel eight years: Judges 12:14.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Significance

The last judge named before Samson. The note that Pirathon lay "in the mount of the Amalekites" is a quiet indication of how incomplete the conquest remained.

—

Manoah

A Danite of Zorah; father of Samson; twice sought instruction from the angel of the Lord about how to raise the child.

Family

Of the family of the Danites, of Zorah (Judges 13:2). His wife is unnamed. Father of Samson (Judges 13:24).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Manoah's wife was barren. The angel of the Lord appeared to her and told her she would bear a son who was to be a Nazarite to God from the womb, and who would begin to deliver Israel out of the hand of the Philistines (Judges 13:2-5).

She told her husband. Manoah entreated the Lord: "Let the man of God which thou didst send come again unto us, and teach us what we shall do unto the child that shall be born." God hearkened, and the angel came again to the woman in the field; she ran and fetched her husband (Judges 13:8-11). Manoah's question was practical: "How shall we order the child, and how shall we do unto him?" He then pressed the visitor to stay for a kid, and asked his name, and was told, "Why askest thou thus after my name, seeing it is secret?" (Judges 13:12-18).

When the flame went up from the altar and the angel ascended in it, Manoah fell on his face and said, "We shall surely die, because we have seen God." His wife answered with better reasoning: if the Lord had meant to kill them, he would not have received an offering from their hands, nor shown them all these things, nor told them such things as these (Judges 13:19-23).

What They Did Right

  • Prayed that the messenger be sent again to teach them how to raise the child - a request Scripture says God hearkened to: Judges 13:8-9.
  • Asked how to order the child rather than for a sign or a blessing: Judges 13:12.
  • Offered a burnt offering unto the Lord: Judges 13:19.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. His fear that they would die is recorded, and his wife's answer corrects it, but the text does not call it sin: Judges 13:22-23.

Character Assessment

Scripture records a man taking the announcement seriously and asking the right practical question, and it also records that his wife saw the situation more clearly than he did at both key moments - she received the message first, and she reasoned rightly when he feared death. The account is notably even-handed, and neither is disparaged.

Significance

The annunciation to Manoah's wife is one of a series of births to barren women in Scripture, and the fullest such account before the Gospels. The instruction that the child be a Nazarite from the womb (Judges 13:5) sets the terms by which Samson's life is later judged.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded directly. Samson was buried between Zorah and Eshtaol "in the buryingplace of Manoah his father" (Judges 16:31).

Scripture References

Judges 13:1-25; Judges 16:31
—

The wife of Manoah

Unnamed. The barren wife of Manoah, to whom the angel of the Lord appeared twice; mother of Samson.

Family

Wife of Manoah of Zorah (Judges 13:2); mother of Samson (Judges 13:24).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

The angel of the Lord appeared to her and told her that though she was barren she would conceive and bear a son. She was charged to drink no wine or strong drink and to eat nothing unclean, because the child would be a Nazarite to God from the womb, and would begin to deliver Israel out of the hand of the Philistines (Judges 13:3-5).

She told her husband accurately, including that she had not asked the visitor's name or origin (Judges 13:6-7). When the angel came again, it was again to her, and she ran to fetch Manoah (Judges 13:9-10).

When Manoah concluded they would die because they had seen God, she answered him: "If the Lord were pleased to kill us, he would not have received a burnt offering and a meat offering at our hands, neither would he have shewed us all these things, nor would as at this time have told us such things as these" (Judges 13:23). She bore the child and called his name Samson (Judges 13:24).

What They Did Right

  • Received the message and reported it accurately to her husband: Judges 13:6-7.
  • Reasoned soundly from what God had done to what God intended, correcting her husband's fear: Judges 13:23.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her, and her one extended speech is a piece of clear theological reasoning that steadies her husband. She is the one to whom the angel came, both times.

Significance

Mother of Samson, and the recipient of one of the fullest birth announcements in the Old Testament. Her argument in Judges 13:23 - that God's past acceptance is evidence of his present intention - is among the clearest statements of that principle in Scripture.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Judges 14:5-6.

Scripture References

Judges 13:2-24; Judges 14:2-6
—

Samson

Son of Manoah of Zorah; a Nazarite from the womb; judged Israel twenty years and fought the Philistines alone; betrayed by Delilah and died pulling down the house of Dagon.

Family

Son of Manoah and his unnamed wife, of the tribe of Dan (Judges 13:2, 13:24). Married a Philistine woman of Timnath (Judges 14:1-2). No children are recorded.

Chronology

Judged Israel twenty years in the days of the Philistines (Judges 15:20; Judges 16:31).

Life Synopsis

Samson was announced before his birth as a Nazarite to God from the womb, who would begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines (Judges 13:5). "And the child grew, and the Lord blessed him. And the Spirit of the Lord began to move him at times" (Judges 13:24-25).

He saw a woman of Timnath and told his parents, "Get her for me; for she pleaseth me well." They objected; the narrator adds that they did not know it was of the Lord, who sought an occasion against the Philistines (Judges 14:1-4). On the way he killed a lion with his bare hands, and later took honey from its carcase - and gave some to his parents without telling them where it came from (Judges 14:5-9). At the wedding feast he set a riddle; his wife wept before him seven days until he told her, and she told her people. His answer to them - "If ye had not plowed with my heifer, ye had not found out my riddle" - was followed by his killing thirty men of Ashkelon for their garments (Judges 14:10-19).

When his wife was given to his companion, he caught three hundred foxes, tied firebrands between their tails, and burned the Philistine harvest. The Philistines burned his wife and her father. He smote them hip and thigh, was bound by his own countrymen of Judah and handed over, and then broke the cords when the Spirit came on him and killed a thousand men with the jawbone of an ass (Judges 15:1-16). Afterward he was sore athirst and called on the Lord, who split a hollow place and gave him water (Judges 15:18-19).

He went in to a harlot in Gaza and carried off the city gates (Judges 16:1-3). Then he loved Delilah in the valley of Sorek. The Philistine lords offered her eleven hundred pieces of silver each to learn the secret of his strength. Three times he lied to her; three times she used the answer against him. "And it came to pass, when she pressed him daily with her words, and urged him, so that his soul was vexed unto death," he told her all his heart (Judges 16:4-17). His hair was shaven, "and he wist not that the Lord was departed from him" (Judges 16:20). The Philistines put out his eyes, bound him with fetters of brass, and set him to grind in the prison house.

"Howbeit the hair of his head began to grow again after he was shaven" (Judges 16:22). At the feast of Dagon they called him out to make sport. He asked the lad who held him to let him feel the pillars, and prayed, "O Lord God, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once, O God, that I may be at once avenged of the Philistines for my two eyes." He bowed himself with all his might, and the house fell on the lords and all the people. "So the dead which he slew at his death were more than they which he slew in his life" (Judges 16:25-30).

What They Did Right

  • The Spirit of the Lord came upon him repeatedly, and by it he tore the lion, broke his bonds, and struck the Philistines: Judges 14:6, 14:19; Judges 15:14.
  • Called on the Lord when he was sore athirst, acknowledging that God had given the deliverance by his servant's hand: Judges 15:18.
  • Prayed at the last, appealing to God rather than to his own strength: Judges 16:28.
  • Judged Israel twenty years: Judges 15:20; Judges 16:31.
  • Named in the roll of faith: Hebrews 11:32.

What They Did Wrong

  • Pursued a Philistine wife against his parents' objection on the ground that she pleased him well: Judges 14:1-3. The narrator adds that it was of the Lord, who sought an occasion against the Philistines (Judges 14:4) - a statement about God's purpose, not an approval of Samson's motive.
  • Took honey from the carcase of the lion and ate it, and gave it to his parents without telling them: Judges 14:8-9. Contact with a dead body violated the Nazarite separation (Numbers 6:6), which Scripture leaves the reader to observe rather than stating.
  • Killed thirty men of Ashkelon to pay a wager: Judges 14:19.
  • Went in to a harlot at Gaza: Judges 16:1.
  • Told Delilah the secret of his strength after she had already used three previous answers against him: Judges 16:16-17.
  • The gravest note is the quietest: "he wist not that the Lord was departed from him": Judges 16:20.

Character Assessment

Samson's record is the most self-contradictory in Judges. He was set apart from the womb, endowed with the Spirit repeatedly, and named in Hebrews 11 among the faithful. He was also driven throughout by appetite and injury - what pleased him, what was owed him, what had been done to his eyes - and his recorded prayers are two, one for water and one for vengeance. He never leads an army; every victory is personal. Scripture presents him as a deliverer whom God used despite himself, and reserves its most devastating line for the moment his strength failed: he did not know the Lord had departed.

Significance

He began the deliverance from the Philistines that Samuel continued and David completed. His life is Scripture's fullest illustration of gifting without self-government. The Nazarite vow of Numbers 6, taken by his parents on his behalf before birth, supplies the standard by which each of his failures is measured. He is named in Hebrews 11:32 among those who through faith out of weakness were made strong.

Death / Outcome

Died pulling down the house of Dagon on the Philistine lords and about three thousand men and women on the roof. His brethren brought him up and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the buryingplace of Manoah his father (Judges 16:29-31).

Scripture References

Judges 13:1-16:31; Hebrews 11:32
—

The wife of Samson

Unnamed. A Philistine woman of Timnath whom Samson married; pressed him for the answer to his riddle and was afterward given to his companion.

Family

A daughter of the Philistines of Timnath (Judges 14:1). Her father is unnamed (Judges 15:1-2).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Samson saw her at Timnath and demanded that his parents get her for him. At the seven-day marriage feast he set a riddle to thirty companions with a wager of thirty sheets and thirty changes of garments. On the fourth day they threatened her: "Entice thy husband, that he may declare unto us the riddle, lest we burn thee and thy father's house with fire" (Judges 14:15).

She wept before Samson the seven days of the feast, saying he hated her and had not told her. On the seventh day he told her, and she told the children of her people (Judges 14:16-17). Her father then gave her to Samson's companion, supposing Samson hated her, and offered her younger sister instead (Judges 14:20; Judges 15:1-2). When Samson burned the Philistine harvest in revenge, the Philistines burned her and her father with fire (Judges 15:6).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Pressed her husband for the riddle and disclosed it to her countrymen: Judges 14:16-17. Scripture records that she did so under a threat to burn her and her father's house (Judges 14:15), and passes no verdict on her.

Character Assessment

Scripture records her actions and the coercion behind them, and gives no evaluation. She is threatened with burning to obtain the riddle, betrays her husband to avoid it, is given away to another man, and is burned in the end anyway. The narrative records this sequence without comment, and it is one of the bleakest in the book.

Significance

The riddle and its betrayal set off the cycle of reprisals that occupied Samson's public life and, in the narrator's framing, gave the occasion God sought against the Philistines (Judges 14:4).

Death / Outcome

Burned with fire by the Philistines, together with her father (Judges 15:6).

Scripture References

Judges 14:1-20; Judges 15:1-6
—

Delilah

A woman of the valley of Sorek whom Samson loved; took money from the Philistine lords to discover the secret of his strength and betrayed him.

Family

Not recorded. Scripture does not state her nationality.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"And it came to pass afterward, that he loved a woman in the valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah" (Judges 16:4). The lords of the Philistines came to her: "Entice him, and see wherein his great strength lieth... and we will give thee every one of us eleven hundred pieces of silver" (Judges 16:5).

She asked him directly, three times, and three times he lied - seven green withs, new ropes, the web of his hair - and each time she applied the answer and called the Philistines, and each time he broke free. Her reproach after the third: "How canst thou say, I love thee, when thine heart is not with me? thou hast mocked me these three times" (Judges 16:15).

"And it came to pass, when she pressed him daily with her words, and urged him, so that his soul was vexed unto death; that he told her all his heart" (Judges 16:16-17). She made him sleep upon her knees, called for a man to shave off the seven locks, and cried, "The Philistines be upon thee, Samson." He awoke not knowing the Lord had departed from him (Judges 16:19-20). The Philistines took him, put out his eyes, and bound him.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Took money from the Philistine lords to entrap the man she was with: Judges 16:5.
  • Used each of his three false answers against him immediately, so that he knew exactly what she was doing, and continued: Judges 16:8-14.
  • Pressed him daily until his soul was vexed to death, then betrayed the answer: Judges 16:16-19.

Character Assessment

Uniformly negative in the record, though Scripture never pauses to condemn her - the account simply lays out what she did and what she was paid. What the narrative emphasises is not her cunning but Samson's persistence: he watched her hand him over three times and stayed. Note that Scripture does not say she was a Philistine, only that she lived in the valley of Sorek; it also does not call her a harlot, and this reference does not.

Significance

Her name has become proverbial for betrayal through intimacy. The episode is the turning point of Samson's life and the occasion of the most sobering line in the book: "he wist not that the Lord was departed from him" (Judges 16:20).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Judges 16:19-20.

Micah (of mount Ephraim)

A man of mount Ephraim who stole and returned eleven hundred shekels from his mother, made a house of gods with the silver, and hired a Levite as his private priest. Not to be confused with Micah the prophet.

Family

His mother is unnamed (Judges 17:2). He had sons, one of whom he first consecrated as priest (Judges 17:5).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Judges places the account in the period when "there was no king in Israel" (Judges 17:6).

Life Synopsis

Micah told his mother that he had taken the eleven hundred shekels of silver she had cursed over, and restored them. She said, "Blessed be thou of the Lord, my son," and dedicated the silver to the Lord "to make a graven image and a molten image" - and gave two hundred shekels of it to a founder, who made them (Judges 17:1-4).

"And the man Micah had an house of gods, and made an ephod, and teraphim, and consecrated one of his sons, who became his priest." The narrator adds the refrain: "In those days there was no king in Israel, but every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judges 17:5-6).

A young Levite from Bethlehemjudah came by seeking a place. Micah hired him for ten shekels a year, a suit of apparel, and his victuals, and said, "Now know I that the Lord will do me good, seeing I have a Levite to my priest" (Judges 17:7-13).

Six hundred armed Danites, seeking territory, came and took the graven image, the ephod, the teraphim, and the molten image, and persuaded the Levite to come with them - "Is it better for thee to be a priest unto the house of one man, or that thou be a priest unto a tribe and a family in Israel?" Micah gathered his neighbours and pursued them, but was told to hold his peace lest angry fellows fall on him. "And Micah saw that they were too strong for him, and turned and went back unto his house" (Judges 18:14-26).

What They Did Right

  • Confessed to his mother that he had taken the silver, and restored it: Judges 17:2. Scripture records the restitution as fact and does not commend it further.

What They Did Wrong

  • Stole eleven hundred shekels of silver from his own mother: Judges 17:2.
  • Made a house of gods with graven and molten images, an ephod, and teraphim - a direct breach of the second commandment: Judges 17:4-5; compare Exodus 20:4.
  • Consecrated his own son as priest, and later hired a Levite, having no authority to appoint either: Judges 17:5, 17:12.
  • Assumed that possessing a Levite would secure God's favour: Judges 17:13.

Character Assessment

Scripture never states a verdict on Micah in so many words; it does something more damaging, which is to record his words and let them stand. He and his mother both invoke the Lord's name while commissioning idols. He believes hiring a Levite guarantees prosperity. The narrator's only comment is the refrain about every man doing what was right in his own eyes, placed immediately after the description of his shrine.

Significance

His household shrine became the cult of the tribe of Dan, which continued "all the time that the house of God was in Shiloh" (Judges 18:31) and marks the beginning of the idolatry for which Dan is later notorious. The account is the book's clearest picture of religion conducted entirely on private judgment.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Judges 18:26.

Scripture References

Judges 17:1-18:31
—

The mother of Micah

Unnamed. The woman whose eleven hundred shekels her son stole, who blessed him when he returned them, and who dedicated the silver to make a graven image.

Family

Mother of Micah of mount Ephraim (Judges 17:2).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

She had cursed over the loss of eleven hundred shekels of silver. When her son admitted taking them and restored them, she said, "Blessed be thou of the Lord, my son." Then: "I had wholly dedicated the silver unto the Lord from my hand for my son, to make a graven image and a molten image." She took two hundred shekels and gave them to a founder, who made them, and they were in the house of Micah (Judges 17:2-4).

What They Did Right

  • Blessed her son rather than pressing the curse when he confessed and restored the silver: Judges 17:2.

What They Did Wrong

  • Dedicated silver to the Lord for the express purpose of making a graven and a molten image, in direct breach of the second commandment: Judges 17:3-4; compare Exodus 20:4-5.
  • Kept back nine hundred of the eleven hundred shekels she said she had wholly dedicated: Judges 17:3-4. Scripture records both figures and leaves the discrepancy without comment.

Character Assessment

Scripture offers no explicit verdict, but the account is constructed so that the contradictions speak: she blesses in the name of the Lord, dedicates wholly, gives less than a fifth, and commissions idols. She is included because her words and acts are recorded in detail and because they set the whole Micah narrative in motion.

Significance

The silver she dedicated became the images that were carried off by the Danites and established the tribal shrine at Dan (Judges 18:30-31).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Judges 17:4.

Scripture References

Judges 17:1-5
—

Jonathan (son of Gershom)

A young Levite of Bethlehemjudah who became Micah's private priest and then priest to the tribe of Dan; named at the close of the account.

Family

Named in Judges 18:30 as "Jonathan, the son of Gershom, the son of Manasseh." The King James Version reads Manasseh; the Hebrew text carries a well-known irregularity at this word which has long been understood to point to Moses, making Jonathan a grandson of Moses through Gershom. This is a textual question of long standing. This reference follows the King James reading and notes the alternative without adopting it.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. His descendants served as priests to Dan "until the day of the captivity of the land" (Judges 18:30).

Life Synopsis

He was a young man of Bethlehemjudah, a Levite, who sojourned there and left to find a place. He came to Micah's house in mount Ephraim, and Micah hired him for ten shekels of silver a year, a suit of apparel, and his food. "And the Levite was content to dwell with the man; and the young man was unto him as one of his sons" (Judges 17:7-11). Micah consecrated him and said, "Now know I that the Lord will do me good, seeing I have a Levite to my priest" (Judges 17:12-13).

When five Danite spies passed by, they asked him to enquire of God for them, and he told them to go in peace (Judges 18:5-6). Later six hundred armed Danites took Micah's images, and the priest asked what they were doing. They told him to hold his peace and put his hand on his mouth, and offered him a larger post: better to be priest to a tribe than to one man's house. "And the priest's heart was glad, and he took the ephod, and the teraphim, and the graven image, and went in the midst of the people" (Judges 18:18-20).

The account closes by naming him: "And the children of Dan set up the graven image: and Jonathan, the son of Gershom, the son of Manasseh, he and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan until the day of the captivity of the land" (Judges 18:30).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Served as priest at a shrine of graven and molten images, which no Levite had any warrant to do: Judges 17:12; Judges 18:30.
  • Gave an oracle - "Go in peace: before the Lord is your way wherein ye go" - on his own authority: Judges 18:6.
  • Abandoned his employer for a better position without hesitation, and Scripture records his gladness at the offer: Judges 18:20.

Character Assessment

Scripture withholds his name until the last possible moment, and then supplies a genealogy that makes the failure worse. He is a Levite by descent and, on the reading many take of Judges 18:30, a direct descendant of Moses - and he became the founding priest of an idolatrous shrine that lasted until the captivity. The narrative offers no verdict beyond the facts, but the placement of the genealogy at the end is not accidental.

Significance

His line served the Danite shrine "until the day of the captivity of the land" (Judges 18:30), making a single hired appointment the origin of centuries of tribal idolatry.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Judges 18:30.

Scripture References

Judges 17:7-13; Judges 18:3-6, 18:14-31
—

The Levite of Gibeah

Unnamed. A Levite sojourning in mount Ephraim whose concubine was abused to death at Gibeah, and who divided her body and sent the pieces through Israel.

Family

His concubine was of Bethlehemjudah; her father is unnamed (Judges 19:1-3).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Judges places the events in the period when there was no king in Israel (Judges 19:1).

Life Synopsis

His concubine left him for her father's house. After four months he went after her "to speak friendly unto her, and to bring her again." Her father detained him with hospitality for five days, and he set out late on the fifth (Judges 19:1-10).

He refused to lodge in Jebus because it was a city of strangers, and pressed on to Gibeah of Benjamin. No one took them in until an old man of mount Ephraim brought them to his house (Judges 19:11-21). Then men of the city beset the house demanding the Levite. The old man offered his own virgin daughter and the concubine instead. "So the man took his concubine, and brought her forth unto them: and they knew her, and abused her all the night until the morning" (Judges 19:22-25).

At dawn she fell down at the door. He rose in the morning to go on his way, opened the door, and said, "Up, and let us be going. But none answered." He put her on the ass, took her home, divided her into twelve pieces, and sent them into all the coasts of Israel (Judges 19:26-29). His account to the assembled tribes omitted that he had put her out himself: he said the men of Gibeah sought to kill him and forced his concubine so that she died (Judges 20:4-6).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Put his concubine out of the door to a mob to save himself: Judges 19:25.
  • Rose in the morning and prepared to leave without looking for her: Judges 19:27-28.
  • Divided her body into twelve pieces and sent them through Israel: Judges 19:29.
  • Gave the tribes an account that omitted his own part in what happened: Judges 20:4-6 compared with Judges 19:25.

Character Assessment

Scripture offers no verdict on him in words, and the omission is itself striking in a book that elsewhere states its judgments. What the narrative does is set his account in Judges 20 beside what actually happened in Judges 19 and let the reader compare them. He is the last major figure in the book, and the account of him is the book's demonstration of what Israel had become.

Significance

His action provoked the war against Benjamin in which the tribe was nearly destroyed (Judges 20:1-48). Hosea twice refers to this era - "they have deeply corrupted themselves, as in the days of Gibeah" (Hosea 9:9; Hosea 10:9). The book ends four verses later with the refrain: "In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judges 21:25).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Judges 20:6.

Scripture References

Judges 19:1-20:7; Hosea 9:9; Hosea 10:9
—

The concubine of the Levite

Unnamed. The concubine of the Levite of mount Ephraim, abused to death by the men of Gibeah.

Family

Of Bethlehemjudah; her father took her back into his house (Judges 19:1-3).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

She played the whore against her husband and went from him to her father's house in Bethlehemjudah, and was there four whole months (Judges 19:2). Her husband came after her to speak friendly to her and bring her back, and her father received him gladly and detained him five days (Judges 19:3-9).

At Gibeah, when the men of the city beset the house, her husband brought her out to them, "and they knew her, and abused her all the night until the morning: and when the day began to spring, they let her go." She came and fell down at the door of the house where her lord was, and lay there till it was light. He opened the door in the morning and told her to get up, "But none answered" (Judges 19:25-28).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Judges 19:2 states that she played the whore against her husband and left him. Scripture records this and nothing else against her, and the record of what was done to her is set out at far greater length than the record of what she did.

Character Assessment

Scripture gives her no name, no words, and no verdict beyond the single clause in Judges 19:2. What it gives instead is the most detailed account of an atrocity in the Old Testament, told without commentary. The final image - her hands on the threshold of the door - is left to speak for itself.

Significance

Her death provoked the war that nearly destroyed the tribe of Benjamin and brought the book of Judges to its close. Scripture treats the whole episode as the measure of how far Israel had fallen, and the prophets afterward use Gibeah as shorthand for national corruption (Hosea 9:9; Hosea 10:9).

Death / Outcome

Abused all night by the men of Gibeah and found dead at the door in the morning; her body was divided into twelve pieces and sent through Israel (Judges 19:25-29).

Scripture References

Judges 19:1-30; Judges 20:4-6
—

The old man of Gibeah

Unnamed. An old man of mount Ephraim sojourning in Gibeah, who took the Levite and his concubine into his house and then offered his own daughter to the mob.

Family

He had a virgin daughter (Judges 19:24).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

The Levite and his party sat down in the street of Gibeah because no man took them into his house. An old man came from his work in the field at evening - he was of mount Ephraim, sojourning in Gibeah, while the men of the place were Benjamites. He said, "Peace be with thee; howsoever let all thy wants lie upon me; only lodge not in the street." He brought them in, gave the asses fodder, and they washed their feet and ate and drank (Judges 19:15-21).

When the men of the city beset the house demanding the Levite, he went out and pleaded: "Nay, my brethren, nay, I pray you, do not so wickedly; seeing that this man is come into mine house, do not this folly. Behold, here is my daughter a maiden, and his concubine; them I will bring out now, and humble ye them, and do with them what seemeth good unto you: but unto this man do not so vile a thing" (Judges 19:22-24).

What They Did Right

  • Took in travellers whom no one else in the city would receive, and provided for them fully: Judges 19:20-21.
  • Named the mob's intent as wickedness and folly and refused to give up his guest: Judges 19:23.

What They Did Wrong

  • Offered his own virgin daughter and his guest's concubine to the mob: Judges 19:24. Scripture records the offer without comment. It closely parallels Lot's offer at Sodom (Genesis 19:8), and as there, the text neither approves nor condemns it.

Character Assessment

A man whose hospitality was genuine and whose solution was monstrous, recorded without any authorial verdict. He is the only person in Gibeah who behaves decently at all, which is part of the point the narrative is making about the city.

Significance

The deliberate echo of Lot at Sodom is one of the strongest signals in Judges about Israel's condition: a city of Israel behaving as Sodom did, with an Ephraimite sojourner playing Lot's part.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Judges 19:24.

Scripture References

Judges 19:16-24; compare Genesis 19:1-8

Ruth and the House of Bethlehem

—

Elimelech

A man of Bethlehemjudah who took his family to Moab during a famine and died there.

Family

Husband of Naomi; father of Mahlon and Chilion; an Ephrathite of Bethlehemjudah (Ruth 1:2). Kinsman of Boaz (Ruth 2:1, 2:3).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. "In the days when the judges ruled" (Ruth 1:1).

Life Synopsis

A famine drove him from Bethlehem - the house of bread - to sojourn in the country of Moab with his wife and two sons. "And Elimelech Naomi's husband died; and she was left, and her two sons" (Ruth 1:1-3). His land in Bethlehem remained, and its redemption is the legal matter Boaz settles at the gate years later (Ruth 4:3-9).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records the move to Moab and his death there without evaluating either. Interpreters have often read the departure as a failure of faith, but the text makes no such statement, and this reference does not.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his name, his town, his family, his sojourn, and his death, and offers no verdict. He is included because those facts drive the whole book: his death and his land are what the story must resolve.

Significance

His parcel of land is the property Boaz redeems, and his name is the name raised up upon the inheritance through Ruth's son (Ruth 4:5, 4:9-10).

Death / Outcome

Died in Moab (Ruth 1:3).

Scripture References

Ruth 1:1-3; Ruth 2:1, 2:3; Ruth 4:3-10
—

Naomi

Wife of Elimelech; bereaved of her husband and both sons in Moab; returned to Bethlehem with Ruth and became nurse to Obed.

Also called Mara

Family

Wife of Elimelech; mother of Mahlon and Chilion; mother in law of Ruth and Orpah (Ruth 1:2-4).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

After ten years in Moab her husband and both sons were dead, "and the woman was left of her two sons and her husband" (Ruth 1:4-5). Hearing that the Lord had visited his people with bread, she set out to return, and urged both daughters in law to go back to their mothers' houses, arguing plainly that she had no more sons to give them (Ruth 1:6-13).

Orpah kissed her and went; Ruth clave to her. Arriving in Bethlehem, the city was moved, and she answered them: "Call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me. I went out full, and the Lord hath brought me home again empty" (Ruth 1:19-21).

She directed Ruth's gleaning and, learning it was Boaz's field, blessed him and identified him as one of their near kinsmen (Ruth 2:19-20). She then devised the plan at the threshingfloor, instructing Ruth exactly what to do (Ruth 3:1-4). At the end the women of the neighbourhood said, "There is a son born to Naomi," and she took the child and laid him in her bosom and became nurse to him (Ruth 4:16-17).

What They Did Right

  • Urged both daughters in law to return to their own people rather than bind them to her poverty: Ruth 1:8-13.
  • Blessed Boaz and recognised the Lord's kindness in the gleaning: Ruth 2:20.
  • Sought a secure home for Ruth rather than for herself: Ruth 3:1.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Her charge that the Almighty had dealt bitterly with her and brought her home empty (Ruth 1:20-21) is recorded as honest lament, not as sin, and Scripture does not rebuke it.

Character Assessment

Scripture treats her bitterness with respect and without correction. She says God has afflicted her, and the book does not argue; it simply keeps going until the women of Bethlehem tell her that her daughter in law is better to her than seven sons. The movement of the book is from her emptiness to the child in her lap.

Significance

Her return brought Ruth to Bethlehem, and the redemption of Elimelech's land raised up the line that runs to David. The women's blessing over Obed - "a restorer of thy life, and a nourisher of thine old age" (Ruth 4:15) - answers her complaint of emptiness directly.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Ruth 4:17.

Scripture References

Ruth 1:1-4:17
—

Mahlon

Elder son of Elimelech and Naomi; husband of Ruth; died in Moab.

Family

Son of Elimelech and Naomi (Ruth 1:2); brother of Chilion. Boaz names him as Ruth's husband (Ruth 4:10).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He died after about ten years in Moab (Ruth 1:4-5).

Life Synopsis

He went to Moab with his parents and took a wife of the women of Moab. Ruth 4:10 identifies her as Ruth. He died there without children, after the family had dwelt in Moab about ten years (Ruth 1:4-5).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He married a Moabitess. Scripture records the marriage without condemning it, and Deuteronomy 23:3 bars a Moabite from the congregation to the tenth generation - a tension the book of Ruth raises and never explicitly addresses. This reference notes it rather than resolving it.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his name, his marriage, and his death. His significance is entirely posthumous: his name is the one Boaz undertakes to raise up upon the inheritance.

Significance

Boaz's stated purpose in the redemption was "to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance" (Ruth 4:10), naming Mahlon specifically.

Death / Outcome

Died in Moab without children (Ruth 1:5).

Scripture References

Ruth 1:2-5; Ruth 4:9-10
—

Chilion

Younger son of Elimelech and Naomi; husband of Orpah; died in Moab.

Family

Son of Elimelech and Naomi (Ruth 1:2); brother of Mahlon. Ruth 4:9 names him among the dead whose property Boaz redeemed. By elimination his wife was Orpah (Ruth 1:4; Ruth 4:10).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

He went to Moab with his family, married a woman of Moab, and died there without children after about ten years (Ruth 1:4-5). His property was among that which Boaz redeemed at the gate (Ruth 4:9).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his name, his marriage, and his death, and nothing further. He is included because his death and his estate are part of the legal situation the book resolves.

Significance

His name appears in Boaz's public declaration of what he purchased at the gate of Bethlehem (Ruth 4:9).

Death / Outcome

Died in Moab without children (Ruth 1:5).

Scripture References

Ruth 1:2-5; Ruth 4:9
—

Orpah

A Moabitess; daughter in law of Naomi; wept, kissed her, and returned to her own people.

Family

Moabitess; wife of one of Naomi's sons, by elimination Chilion (Ruth 1:4; Ruth 4:10).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

She set out with Naomi and Ruth toward Judah. Naomi urged them twice to return; they wept, and Orpah wept again and kissed her mother in law, "but Ruth clave unto her" (Ruth 1:8-14). Naomi said, "Behold, thy sister in law is gone back unto her people, and unto her gods: return thou after thy sister in law" (Ruth 1:15). Scripture records nothing further of her.

What They Did Right

  • Set out with Naomi in the first place, and wept at parting: Ruth 1:7, 1:14. Scripture records her affection without commending or blaming her decision.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. She did exactly what Naomi twice urged her to do. Scripture does not condemn her, and Naomi's description of her returning to her people and her gods (Ruth 1:15) is a statement of fact rather than a rebuke. Readings that treat Orpah as a negative example go beyond what the text says.

Character Assessment

Scripture offers no verdict on her at all. She is present chiefly as a contrast that makes Ruth's choice visible: two women in the same position, both urged to leave, one of whom did what was asked and one who would not.

Significance

Her departure sets the terms of Ruth's declaration in the next verses, which is the theological centre of the book.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Ruth 1:14-15.

Scripture References

Ruth 1:4-15
—

Ruth

A Moabitess; widow of Mahlon; refused to leave Naomi, gleaned in the field of Boaz, and became his wife and the great-grandmother of David.

Family

A woman of Moab (Ruth 1:4); widow of Mahlon (Ruth 4:10); daughter in law of Naomi. Married Boaz; mother of Obed, father of Jesse, father of David (Ruth 4:13-17).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. "In the days when the judges ruled" (Ruth 1:1).

Life Synopsis

Widowed in Moab, she set out with Naomi. When Naomi urged her to return, she answered with the words the book is remembered for: "Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God: where thou diest, will I die, and there will I be buried: the Lord do so to me, and more also, if ought but death part thee and me" (Ruth 1:16-17). Naomi stopped urging her.

In Bethlehem she asked leave to glean, and her lot fell on the part of the field belonging to Boaz. He had already heard about her: "It hath fully been shewed me, all that thou hast done unto thy mother in law since the death of thine husband: and how thou hast left thy father and thy mother, and the land of thy nativity, and art come unto a people which thou knewest not heretofore" (Ruth 2:11). He blessed her under the wings of the God of Israel and gave her protection and extra grain (Ruth 2:12-17).

At Naomi's direction she went to the threshingfloor at night, uncovered his feet, lay down, and when he woke asked him to spread his skirt over her, "for thou art a near kinsman." Boaz answered, "Blessed be thou of the Lord, my daughter: for thou hast shewed more kindness in the latter end than at the beginning, inasmuch as thou followedst not young men, whether poor or rich... all the city of my people doth know that thou art a virtuous woman" (Ruth 3:6-11).

After the nearer kinsman declined, Boaz took her to wife. She bore Obed, and the women said to Naomi that her daughter in law "which loveth thee, which is better to thee than seven sons, hath born him" (Ruth 4:13-17).

What They Did Right

  • Refused to leave Naomi and bound herself to Naomi's people and God: Ruth 1:16-17.
  • Worked from morning until evening in the field to support her mother in law: Ruth 2:7, 2:17-18.
  • Boaz's own testimony: she left her father, mother, and homeland for a people she did not know: Ruth 2:11.
  • Sought a kinsman-redeemer rather than young men, which Boaz calls greater kindness than her first: Ruth 3:10.
  • Called a virtuous woman by the report of the whole city: Ruth 3:11.
  • Judged by the women of Bethlehem to be better to Naomi than seven sons: Ruth 4:15.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her and commends her repeatedly - by Boaz, by the elders at the gate, and by the women of the town. She is a Moabitess, of a people barred from the congregation to the tenth generation (Deuteronomy 23:3), and the book neither hides that nor explains it away; it simply records that she came under the wings of the God of Israel and was received.

Significance

Great-grandmother of David (Ruth 4:17, 4:21-22) and one of four women named in Matthew's genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:5). The elders' blessing set her with Rachel and Leah, "which two did build the house of Israel" (Ruth 4:11). Her book stands in the middle of the period of the judges as evidence that ordinary faithfulness continued while the nation did what was right in its own eyes.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Matthew 1:5.

Scripture References

Ruth 1:4-4:22; Matthew 1:5
—

Boaz

A mighty man of wealth of Bethlehem, kinsman of Elimelech; redeemed the inheritance and married Ruth.

Also called Booz

Family

Of the family of Elimelech; called "a mighty man of wealth" (Ruth 2:1). Son of Salmon by Rahab (Matthew 1:5; Ruth 4:21). Husband of Ruth; father of Obed (Ruth 4:13, 4:21).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Boaz came from Bethlehem and greeted his reapers, "The Lord be with you," and they answered, "The Lord bless thee" (Ruth 2:4). Learning who the gleaning woman was, he told her to stay in his field, charged the young men not to touch her, gave her water and food, and told the reapers to let handfuls fall on purpose for her (Ruth 2:8-16).

When she came to the threshingfloor at night he did not take advantage of the situation. He blessed her, promised to do all she required, told her to lie down till morning and to leave before she could be recognised, and sent her away with six measures of barley so that she would not go to her mother in law empty (Ruth 3:10-17).

He went up to the gate, seated ten elders, and put the matter to the nearer kinsman publicly and in the right order - first the land, then the obligation to Ruth. When the man declined, Boaz declared before all the people that he had purchased the inheritance of Elimelech, Chilion, and Mahlon, and had bought Ruth to wife "to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance" (Ruth 4:1-10). He married her, and Obed was born.

What They Did Right

  • Greeted his workers in the name of the Lord and was answered in kind: Ruth 2:4.
  • Protected a foreign widow gleaning in his field and provided for her beyond the law's requirement: Ruth 2:8-16.
  • Blessed her at the threshingfloor and sent her away untouched and unshamed: Ruth 3:10-14.
  • Acknowledged the prior claim of the nearer kinsman and settled the matter publicly and lawfully rather than simply taking what he wanted: Ruth 3:12-13; Ruth 4:1-6.
  • Redeemed the inheritance and took Ruth to wife to raise up the name of the dead: Ruth 4:9-10.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. What is most notable is his restraint at the threshingfloor and his insistence on doing the redemption in the open, at the gate, before ten elders, when the nearer kinsman's claim could easily have been ignored. He is one of the few men in this period of Scripture whose dealings are entirely above board.

Significance

Great-grandfather of David (Ruth 4:21-22) and an ancestor of Christ (Matthew 1:5; Luke 3:32). His role as kinsman-redeemer is the fullest working example in Scripture of the law of redemption (Leviticus 25:25) and of the levirate obligation (Deuteronomy 25:5-10). His mother, on Matthew's genealogy, was Rahab of Jericho - so a man raised by a Canaanite convert married a Moabitess.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Luke 3:32.

Scripture References

Ruth 2:1-4:21; Matthew 1:5; Luke 3:32
—

The near kinsman

Unnamed. The kinsman nearer than Boaz, who was willing to redeem the land until he learned the obligation to Ruth came with it, and then declined.

Family

A kinsman of Elimelech, nearer than Boaz (Ruth 3:12; Ruth 4:1).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Boaz sat him down at the gate before ten elders and set out the matter: Naomi was selling the parcel of land that was Elimelech's, and he had the first right to redeem it. He said, "I will redeem it."

Then Boaz added the rest: "What day thou buyest the field of the hand of Naomi, thou must buy it also of Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of the dead, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance." He answered, "I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I mar mine own inheritance: redeem thou my right to thyself; for I cannot redeem it" (Ruth 4:1-6). He drew off his shoe, which was the manner of attesting in Israel, and the right passed to Boaz (Ruth 4:7-8).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. He acted lawfully throughout and settled the matter honestly in public. Scripture records this without commendation.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He declined an obligation he was entitled to decline, and gave his reason: it would mar his own inheritance. Scripture records the reason without condemning it.

Character Assessment

Scripture gives him no name and no verdict, only his words. The contrast the narrative draws is quiet: he was willing to take the land and unwilling to take the widow, and Boaz took both. That his name is not preserved, while Boaz's is in the genealogy of Christ, is an irony the text leaves entirely unstated.

Significance

His refusal cleared the way for Boaz, and the account of the shoe preserves a legal custom of attestation that the narrator says was already obsolete by his own time (Ruth 4:7).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He is never named.

Scripture References

Ruth 3:12-13; Ruth 4:1-8
—

Obed

Son of Boaz and Ruth; father of Jesse; grandfather of David.

Family

Son of Boaz and Ruth (Ruth 4:13, 4:17); father of Jesse (Ruth 4:22).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"So Boaz took Ruth, and she was his wife: and when he went in unto her, the Lord gave her conception, and she bare a son." The women said to Naomi, "Blessed be the Lord, which hath not left thee this day without a kinsman... he shall be unto thee a restorer of thy life, and a nourisher of thine old age." Naomi took the child and laid him in her bosom and became nurse to him, and the neighbours named him Obed. "He is the father of Jesse, the father of David" (Ruth 4:13-17).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his birth, his naming by the women of the neighbourhood, and his descendants. Nothing he said or did is recorded. He is included because the circumstances of his birth are recorded in detail and because the line runs through him.

Significance

Grandfather of David and an ancestor of Christ (Ruth 4:17, 4:21-22; Matthew 1:5; Luke 3:32). His birth is the resolution of Naomi's emptiness and of Elimelech's failed line.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Luke 3:32.

Scripture References

Ruth 4:13-22; 1 Chronicles 2:12; Matthew 1:5; Luke 3:32

Samuel, Saul, and David

—

Elkanah

An Ephrathite of Ramathaimzophim in mount Ephraim; husband of Hannah and Peninnah; father of Samuel.

Family

Son of Jeroham, of the hill country of Ephraim, of Levitical descent through Kohath (1 Samuel 1:1; 1 Chronicles 6:27, 6:34). Husband of Hannah and Peninnah; father of Samuel and of other children (1 Samuel 1:2; 1 Samuel 2:21).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

He went up yearly out of his city to worship and sacrifice at Shiloh, where Eli's two sons were priests (1 Samuel 1:3). He had two wives; Peninnah had children and Hannah had none. To Hannah he gave a worthy portion, "for he loved Hannah: but the Lord had shut up her womb" (1 Samuel 1:5).

Seeing her weeping and not eating, he asked, "Hannah, why weepest thou? and why eatest thou not? and why is thy heart grieved? am not I better to thee than ten sons?" (1 Samuel 1:8). When she vowed the child to the Lord and proposed not to go up until he was weaned, he agreed: "Do what seemeth thee good; tarry until thou have weaned him; only the Lord establish his word" (1 Samuel 1:22-23). He went up with her to present the child, and worshipped there (1 Samuel 1:24-28).

What They Did Right

  • Went up yearly to worship and sacrifice at Shiloh: 1 Samuel 1:3.
  • Loved Hannah and gave her a worthy portion despite her barrenness: 1 Samuel 1:5.
  • Sought to comfort her rather than reproach her: 1 Samuel 1:8.
  • Consented to her vow and committed the matter to the Lord: 1 Samuel 1:23.

What They Did Wrong

  • He had two wives, and the rivalry between them is the setting of the whole chapter: 1 Samuel 1:2, 1:6-7. Scripture records the polygamy without explicit condemnation, but the provocation Hannah suffered is a direct consequence of it.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents him favourably in everything he says and does, while recording without comment the arrangement that made Hannah's life miserable. His question - am not I better to thee than ten sons - is kindly meant and beside the point, and the narrative lets that stand.

Significance

Father of Samuel, and a Levite of the family of Kohath, which places Samuel's later ministry within a legitimate line (1 Chronicles 6:33-38).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Samuel 2:20-21.

Scripture References

1 Samuel 1:1-2:21; 1 Chronicles 6:27, 6:33-34
—

Hannah

Barren wife of Elkanah; vowed her son to the Lord and gave him up; mother of Samuel; author of the song in 1 Samuel 2.

Family

Wife of Elkanah (1 Samuel 1:2); mother of Samuel and afterward of three sons and two daughters (1 Samuel 2:21).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Hannah was barren, and her rival Peninnah "provoked her sore, for to make her fret" year after year at the house of the Lord, so that she wept and would not eat (1 Samuel 1:6-7).

In bitterness of soul she prayed and wept and vowed: if the Lord would give her a man child, she would give him to the Lord all the days of his life, and no razor would come on his head. She spoke in her heart, only her lips moving, and Eli took her for drunk and rebuked her. She answered, "No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit... I have poured out my soul before the Lord." Eli blessed her, and "her countenance was no more sad" (1 Samuel 1:9-18).

She bore Samuel, and did not go up to Shiloh again until he was weaned. Then she brought him with sacrifices and gave him to Eli: "For this child I prayed; and the Lord hath given me my petition which I asked of him: therefore also I have lent him to the Lord as long as he liveth" (1 Samuel 1:24-28).

Her song follows: "My heart rejoiceth in the Lord, mine horn is exalted in the Lord... The Lord killeth, and maketh alive: he bringeth down to the grave, and bringeth up. The Lord maketh poor, and maketh rich: he bringeth low, and lifteth up" (1 Samuel 2:1-10). She brought him a little coat every year when she came up with her husband, and the Lord visited her with five more children (1 Samuel 2:19-21).

What They Did Right

  • Took her grief to the Lord in prayer rather than retaliating against Peninnah: 1 Samuel 1:10-11.
  • Answered Eli's false accusation with respect and honesty: 1 Samuel 1:15-16.
  • Kept her vow and gave up the son she had prayed for: 1 Samuel 1:24-28.
  • Rejoiced in God rather than in the child, in a song that is almost entirely about God's reversals: 1 Samuel 2:1-10.
  • Continued to care for him, bringing a little coat year by year: 1 Samuel 2:19.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her. Her prayer is the fullest example in the Old Testament of a vow made in extremity and kept at cost, and her song shows where her hope actually rested: not one line of it is about having a son to silence Peninnah.

Significance

Mother of Samuel, the prophet who anointed Israel's first two kings. Her song is the clearest Old Testament anticipation of the Magnificat, which follows it closely in structure and theme (Luke 1:46-55), and it ends with the first mention in Scripture of the Lord's anointed - his king and his Messiah (1 Samuel 2:10).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Samuel 2:21.

Scripture References

1 Samuel 1:1-2:21; Luke 1:46-55
—

Peninnah

The second wife of Elkanah, who had children and provoked the barren Hannah.

Family

Wife of Elkanah; mother of sons and daughters (1 Samuel 1:2, 1:4).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"And he had two wives; the name of the one was Hannah, and the name of the other Peninnah: and Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children" (1 Samuel 1:2). "And her adversary also provoked her sore, for to make her fret, because the Lord had shut up her womb. And as he did so year by year, when she went up to the house of the Lord, so she provoked her; therefore she wept, and did not eat" (1 Samuel 1:6-7).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Provoked Hannah year after year to make her fret, and did so at the house of the Lord: 1 Samuel 1:6-7. Scripture calls her Hannah's adversary and records the provocation as deliberate and sustained.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing in her favour and one sustained cruelty, described in unusually direct language. She is the adversary against whom Hannah does not retaliate, which is the point the narrative makes with her.

Significance

Her provocation drove Hannah to the vow that produced Samuel. Hannah's song answers her directly in its opening lines about the barren bearing seven and the mother of many children waxing feeble (1 Samuel 2:5).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Samuel 1:4.

Scripture References

1 Samuel 1:2-7
—

Eli

Priest and judge at Shiloh; raised Samuel; failed to restrain his sons and died when the ark was taken.

Family

Father of Hophni and Phinehas (1 Samuel 1:3). His house was of the line of Ithamar (1 Chronicles 24:3, where Ahimelech of his house is so identified).

Chronology

He judged Israel forty years and died at ninety-eight (1 Samuel 4:15, 4:18).

Life Synopsis

Eli was priest at Shiloh when Hannah came to pray. He mistook her for a drunken woman and rebuked her, then blessed her when she explained (1 Samuel 1:12-17). He received the weaned Samuel and raised him.

His sons were "sons of Belial; they knew not the Lord." They took the sacrificial meat by force before the fat was burned, and lay with the women that assembled at the door of the tabernacle (1 Samuel 2:12-17, 2:22). Eli heard of it and remonstrated - "Why do ye such things? for I hear of your evil dealings by all this people" - but did no more, and they did not listen (1 Samuel 2:23-25).

A man of God came with a heavy word: God had chosen his father's house for the priesthood, and now asked, "Wherefore kick ye at my sacrifice and at mine offering... and honourest thy sons above me?" Both sons would die in one day (1 Samuel 2:27-34). The word was confirmed to the boy Samuel, who told him everything, and Eli answered, "It is the Lord: let him do what seemeth him good" (1 Samuel 3:11-18).

When the ark was taken and both sons killed, Eli was sitting by the wayside watching, "for his heart trembled for the ark of God." At the news of the ark he fell backward off his seat by the gate and broke his neck, "for he was an old man, and heavy" (1 Samuel 4:13-18).

What They Did Right

  • Blessed Hannah and asked God to grant her petition: 1 Samuel 1:17.
  • Raised Samuel and taught him to answer the Lord: 1 Samuel 3:8-9.
  • Submitted to the judgment when Samuel reported it: "It is the Lord: let him do what seemeth him good": 1 Samuel 3:18.
  • His heart trembled for the ark of God: 1 Samuel 4:13.

What They Did Wrong

  • Falsely accused Hannah of drunkenness: 1 Samuel 1:13-14.
  • Restrained his sons with words only and did not remove them from office: 1 Samuel 2:23-25; 1 Samuel 3:13, where God states the charge exactly: "because his sons made themselves vile, and he restrained them not."
  • Honoured his sons above God, in God's own words: 1 Samuel 2:29.
  • Shared in the profit of his sons' extortion: "to make yourselves fat with the chiefest of all the offerings": 1 Samuel 2:29.

Character Assessment

A genuinely mixed record, and Scripture states the central failure precisely rather than leaving it to inference. He was a priest who trembled for the ark, raised Samuel well, and accepted God's judgment without complaint - and he was also a father who spoke to his sons and did nothing else while they made the sacrifices of the Lord abhorred. The indictment in 1 Samuel 2:29 and 3:13 is not that he was ignorant but that he preferred them.

Significance

The fall of his house ended the priesthood in his line as God had said, fulfilled first in the deaths of his sons, then in the slaughter at Nob, and finally when Solomon put out Abiathar (1 Samuel 2:31-36; 1 Kings 2:27). His forty years as judge close the era of the judges, and Samuel's rise under his roof marks the transition to the prophets and the monarchy.

Death / Outcome

Fell backward from his seat by the gate and broke his neck on hearing that the ark of God was taken; he was ninety-eight and had judged Israel forty years (1 Samuel 4:15-18).

Scripture References

1 Samuel 1:9-4:18; 1 Samuel 14:3; 1 Kings 2:27
—

Hophni

A son of Eli; priest at Shiloh; described as a son of Belial; killed on the day the ark was taken.

Family

Son of Eli; brother of Phinehas (1 Samuel 1:3).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He died on the day the ark was captured.

Life Synopsis

Hophni and Phinehas were priests at Shiloh. "Now the sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they knew not the Lord" (1 Samuel 2:12). Their custom was to send a servant with a fleshhook while the meat was seething and take whatever it brought up, and to demand raw flesh before the fat was burnt, taking it by force if refused. "Wherefore the sin of the young men was very great before the Lord: for men abhorred the offering of the Lord" (1 Samuel 2:13-17).
