They also lay with the women that assembled at the door of the tabernacle (1 Samuel 2:22).

They would not hearken to their father's remonstrance, "because the Lord would slay them" (1 Samuel 2:25). Both were killed in one day at the battle of Aphek, where they had carried the ark into the camp (1 Samuel 4:4, 4:11).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Knew not the Lord, though he served as priest: 1 Samuel 2:12.
  • Took the offerings by force and before the fat was burnt, so that men abhorred the offering of the Lord: 1 Samuel 2:13-17.
  • Lay with the women that assembled at the door of the tabernacle: 1 Samuel 2:22.
  • Would not hearken to his father's reproof: 1 Samuel 2:25.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned. Scripture's charge is unusually severe: his sin was very great before the Lord, and it made ordinary Israelites despise the sacrificial system itself.

Significance

His death with his brother in a single day was the first fulfilment of the word against Eli's house (1 Samuel 2:34), and the loss of the ark on the same day ended Shiloh as Israel's sanctuary - a judgment Jeremiah later invokes against Jerusalem (Jeremiah 7:12-14).

Death / Outcome

Slain at the battle against the Philistines, the same day the ark was taken (1 Samuel 4:11, 4:17).

Scripture References

1 Samuel 1:3; 1 Samuel 2:12-25, 2:34; 1 Samuel 4:4-17
—

Phinehas (son of Eli)

A son of Eli; priest at Shiloh; killed on the day the ark was taken; father of Ichabod. Not to be confused with Phinehas the son of Eleazar.

Family

Son of Eli; brother of Hophni (1 Samuel 1:3). His wife is unnamed; father of Ichabod and of Ahitub, whose descendants included Ahimelech and Abiathar (1 Samuel 4:19-21; 1 Samuel 14:3).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

He acted throughout with his brother Hophni in the corruptions of the priesthood at Shiloh (1 Samuel 2:12-25). He carried the ark of the covenant into the camp at Ebenezer with his brother, and both were killed the same day (1 Samuel 4:4, 4:11). His wife, near her time, went into labour at the news and died bearing a son she named Ichabod (1 Samuel 4:19-22).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Shared in taking the offerings by force and in lying with the women at the door of the tabernacle: 1 Samuel 2:12-25.
  • Carried the ark into battle as though it were a talisman: 1 Samuel 4:3-4. Scripture records the act and its outcome without a separate rebuke of him.

Character Assessment

Identical in the record to his brother, and assessed the same way. Scripture treats them as a pair throughout.

Significance

His line nevertheless continued through Ahitub to Ahimelech and Abiathar, and so carried Eli's doomed priesthood down to Solomon's reign (1 Samuel 14:3; 1 Kings 2:27).

Death / Outcome

Slain the same day as his brother, when the ark was taken (1 Samuel 4:11, 4:17).

Scripture References

1 Samuel 1:3; 1 Samuel 2:12-34; 1 Samuel 4:4-22; 1 Samuel 14:3
—

The wife of Phinehas

Unnamed. The wife of Phinehas son of Eli, who died in childbirth on hearing that the ark was taken and named her son Ichabod.

Family

Wife of Phinehas son of Eli; mother of Ichabod (1 Samuel 4:19).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

She was with child and near to be delivered. "And when she heard the tidings that the ark of God was taken, and that her father in law and her husband were dead, she bowed herself and travailed; for her pains came upon her." As she died the women told her she had borne a son, "but she answered not, neither did she regard it." She named the child Ichabod, saying, "The glory is departed from Israel: because the ark of God was taken, and because of her father in law and her husband" (1 Samuel 4:19-22).

What They Did Right

  • Her dying words fix on the right thing: she names the loss of the ark twice and the deaths of her husband and father in law once, and the name she gives her son is about the glory of God departing, not about her own bereavement: 1 Samuel 4:21-22.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her. Her one recorded utterance is a theological judgment on the whole disaster, delivered as she died, and it is the sharpest assessment of the day's events that anyone in the chapter offers.

Significance

The name Ichabod - the glory is departed - became the epitaph of Shiloh and of the house of Eli.

Death / Outcome

Died in childbirth at the news of the ark's capture (1 Samuel 4:20).

Scripture References

1 Samuel 4:19-22
—

Ichabod

Son of Phinehas son of Eli, born as his mother died; named for the departure of the glory from Israel.

Family

Son of Phinehas, grandson of Eli (1 Samuel 4:21); brother of Ahitub (1 Samuel 14:3).

Chronology

Born on the day the ark was taken. His death is not recorded.

Life Synopsis

"And she named the child Ichabod, saying, The glory is departed from Israel: because the ark of God was taken, and because of her father in law and her husband" (1 Samuel 4:21). He is mentioned once more, as the brother of Ahitub, in identifying Ahiah the priest who was with Saul (1 Samuel 14:3).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Nothing he said or did is recorded. He is included because the circumstances of his birth and the meaning of his name are recorded in full, and because Scripture uses him afterward to identify a priestly line.

Significance

His name is Scripture's summary of the fall of Shiloh, and it has passed into general use for the loss of a former glory.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Samuel 14:3.

Scripture References

1 Samuel 4:19-22; 1 Samuel 14:3
—

Samuel

Son of Hannah; prophet, priest, and the last judge of Israel; anointed both Saul and David.

Family

Son of Elkanah and Hannah (1 Samuel 1:20); of Levitical descent through Kohath (1 Chronicles 6:27-28, 6:33-34). Father of Joel and Abiah (1 Samuel 8:2).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He judged Israel all the days of his life (1 Samuel 7:15) and died before Saul (1 Samuel 25:1).

Life Synopsis

Given to the Lord in fulfilment of his mother's vow, Samuel ministered before Eli as a child, girded with a linen ephod (1 Samuel 2:11, 2:18). "And the word of the Lord was precious in those days; there was no open vision." The Lord called him by night three times; Eli understood and told him to answer, "Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth." The first message he received was the judgment on Eli's own house, and he told Eli every whit (1 Samuel 3:1-18). "And all Israel from Dan even to Beersheba knew that Samuel was established to be a prophet of the Lord" (1 Samuel 3:20).

He called Israel to put away their strange gods and gathered them to Mizpeh, where he judged them and prayed, and the Philistines were subdued. He set up the stone Ebenezer, "Hitherto hath the Lord helped us" (1 Samuel 7:3-12). He judged Israel all his days, going in circuit yearly to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpeh (1 Samuel 7:15-17).

When he was old he made his sons judges, and they took bribes and perverted judgment. The elders used this to demand a king. "But the thing displeased Samuel... And Samuel prayed unto the Lord" (1 Samuel 8:1-6). God told him the rejection was of God, not of him, and had him warn the people what a king would do (1 Samuel 8:7-18). He anointed Saul, presented him to the nation, and at his farewell challenged Israel to accuse him of any wrong: "Whose ox have I taken? or whose ass have I taken? or whom have I defrauded?" They answered that he had taken nothing (1 Samuel 12:3-5). He added, "God forbid that I should sin against the Lord in ceasing to pray for you" (1 Samuel 12:23).

He confronted Saul twice - at Gilgal for the unlawful sacrifice, and after Amalek for sparing Agag and the spoil, where he spoke the words that define the book: "Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams" (1 Samuel 13:13-14; 1 Samuel 15:22-23). He hewed Agag in pieces himself. He mourned for Saul, and came no more to see him (1 Samuel 15:33-35).

Sent to Bethlehem, he was corrected over Eliab - "the Lord seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart" - and anointed David (1 Samuel 16:1-13). He died, and all Israel lamented him and buried him at Ramah (1 Samuel 25:1). Saul afterward sought him through the woman at Endor, and Samuel appeared and pronounced Saul's doom (1 Samuel 28:11-19).

What They Did Right

  • Answered God's call and told Eli the whole judgment without softening it, though Eli had raised him: 1 Samuel 3:10-18.
  • Called Israel to put away strange gods and prepare their hearts for the Lord: 1 Samuel 7:3-4.
  • Prayed for Israel and cried unto the Lord for them: 1 Samuel 7:5-9.
  • Judged Israel honestly all his life, and was publicly cleared of taking anything from anyone: 1 Samuel 12:3-5.
  • Regarded ceasing to pray for a people who had rejected his counsel as a sin against the Lord: 1 Samuel 12:23.
  • Rebuked Saul plainly on both occasions, at cost to himself: 1 Samuel 13:13-14; 1 Samuel 15:16-23.
  • Mourned for Saul rather than gloating over his fall: 1 Samuel 15:35; 1 Samuel 16:1.
  • Named among those who called upon God's name and were answered: Psalms 99:6; Jeremiah 15:1; and in the roll of faith: Hebrews 11:32.

What They Did Wrong

  • Made his sons judges over Israel, and they turned aside after lucre, took bribes, and perverted judgment: 1 Samuel 8:1-3. Scripture records the appointment and the outcome without stating a charge against Samuel, but the parallel with Eli's sons is unmistakable and the elders cite it as their reason for demanding a king.
  • Feared to go to Bethlehem lest Saul kill him: 1 Samuel 16:2. The text records the fear and God's provision for it without rebuke.

Character Assessment

One of the most consistently upright figures in the Old Testament. God names him with Moses as an intercessor whose prayer carried weight (Jeremiah 15:1), and his public clearing in 1 Samuel 12 is unique - no other leader in Scripture invites the nation to accuse him and is acquitted. The one shadow is his sons, and Scripture places their corruption immediately before the demand for a king without comment. That silence is itself notable in a book that elsewhere states its judgments plainly.

Significance

The last judge and the first of the line of prophets that runs to the exile (Acts 3:24; Acts 13:20). He anointed both Saul and David, and so presided over the founding of the monarchy he had opposed. His words in 1 Samuel 15:22 are the Old Testament's clearest statement that obedience outweighs sacrifice, taken up by the prophets and by Christ.

Death / Outcome

Died, and all Israel gathered and lamented him and buried him at Ramah (1 Samuel 25:1; 1 Samuel 28:3).

Scripture References

1 Samuel 1:20-25:1; 1 Samuel 28:3-20; 1 Chronicles 6:27-33; Psalms 99:6; Jeremiah 15:1; Acts 3:24; Acts 13:20; Hebrews 11:32
—

Joel and Abiah

The two sons of Samuel, made judges in Beersheba, whose corruption prompted Israel's demand for a king. Two distinct individuals, recorded only together.

Family

Sons of Samuel (1 Samuel 8:2). 1 Chronicles 6:28 names Samuel's firstborn Vashni and the second Abiah; 1 Chronicles 6:33 names Joel. The discrepancy between the lists is unresolved and is noted here rather than harmonized.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"And it came to pass, when Samuel was old, that he made his sons judges over Israel. Now the name of his firstborn was Joel; and the name of his second, Abiah: they were judges in Beersheba. And his sons walked not in his ways, but turned aside after lucre, and took bribes, and perverted judgment" (1 Samuel 8:1-3). The elders of Israel came to Samuel at Ramah and said, "Behold, thou art old, and thy sons walk not in thy ways: now make us a king to judge us like all the nations" (1 Samuel 8:5).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Walked not in their father's ways: 1 Samuel 8:3.
  • Turned aside after lucre, took bribes, and perverted judgment - a direct breach of the law given to judges: 1 Samuel 8:3; compare Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned in the one verse that describes them. Scripture names the three faults precisely and offers nothing on the other side.

Significance

Their corruption was the occasion Israel used to demand a king, which God told Samuel was a rejection of his own kingship (1 Samuel 8:7). The monarchy therefore begins from a failure of succession in the house of the last judge, as the priesthood at Shiloh had failed in the house of Eli.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Chronicles 6:33.

Scripture References

1 Samuel 8:1-5; 1 Chronicles 6:28, 6:33
—

Kish

A Benjamite, a mighty man of power; father of Saul.

Family

Son of Abiel, of the tribe of Benjamin (1 Samuel 9:1); father of Saul (1 Samuel 9:2).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"Now there was a man of Benjamin, whose name was Kish, the son of Abiel... a mighty man of power. And he had a son, whose name was Saul, a choice young man, and a goodly: and there was not among the children of Israel a goodlier person than he: from his shoulders and upward he was higher than any of the people" (1 Samuel 9:1-2). The asses of Kish were lost, and he sent Saul with a servant to seek them - the errand on which Saul met Samuel and was anointed (1 Samuel 9:3-4). Saul and Jonathan were later buried in his sepulchre at Zelah (2 Samuel 21:14).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his tribe, his standing as a mighty man of power, his son, and his lost asses, and offers no verdict on him.

Significance

The search for his stray animals is the occasion of Saul's meeting with Samuel and of the founding of the monarchy - a point the narrative makes without comment. Paul names him when recounting Israel's history: "God gave unto them Saul the son of Cis" (Acts 13:21).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. His sepulchre at Zelah received the bones of Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 21:14).

Scripture References

1 Samuel 9:1-3; 1 Samuel 10:11, 10:21; 1 Samuel 14:51; 2 Samuel 21:14; Acts 13:21
—

Saul

Son of Kish, of Benjamin; the first king of Israel; rejected by God for disobedience; died by his own hand on mount Gilboa. Not to be confused with Saul of Tarsus.

Also called Cis's son

Family

Son of Kish (1 Samuel 9:1). Wife Ahinoam daughter of Ahimaaz (1 Samuel 14:50); concubine Rizpah (2 Samuel 3:7). Father of Jonathan, Ishui, Melchishua, Abinadab, and Ishbosheth, and of Merab and Michal (1 Samuel 14:49; 1 Samuel 31:2; 2 Samuel 2:8). Abner was his cousin and captain (1 Samuel 14:50).

Chronology

Reigned over Israel; Acts 13:21 gives the length as forty years. He died with three sons at Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:6).

Life Synopsis

Saul was a head taller than any Israelite and was seeking his father's lost asses when Samuel anointed him privately (1 Samuel 9:2, 9:15-10:1). The Spirit of God came upon him and he prophesied; God gave him another heart (1 Samuel 10:6-9). At his public selection by lot he had hidden among the stuff (1 Samuel 10:21-22). He held his peace when worthless men despised him, and when the Spirit came on him he delivered Jabeshgilead, then refused to execute those who had opposed him: "There shall not a man be put to death this day" (1 Samuel 11:6-13).

The decline is recorded in two decisive failures. At Gilgal, waiting for Samuel and watching his army scatter, he offered the burnt offering himself. Samuel told him his kingdom would not continue: "the Lord hath sought him a man after his own heart" (1 Samuel 13:8-14). Then, commanded to destroy Amalek utterly, he spared Agag and the best of the sheep and oxen. Confronted, he claimed he had performed the commandment, then blamed the people, then said the spoil was for sacrifice. Samuel answered, "Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice... Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king" (1 Samuel 15:9-23). Saul's confession followed, but with a request: "honour me now, I pray thee, before the elders of my people" (1 Samuel 15:30).

The Spirit of the Lord departed from him and an evil spirit troubled him, and David was brought in to play the harp (1 Samuel 16:14-23). After David killed Goliath and the women sang that Saul had slain his thousands and David his ten thousands, "Saul eyed David from that day and forward" (1 Samuel 18:6-9). He threw a javelin at him twice, set him in dangerous commands, offered his daughters as a snare, and pursued him for years through the wilderness. When David twice spared his life in the cave and at Hachilah, Saul wept and blessed him and went home, and then resumed the pursuit (1 Samuel 24:16-22; 1 Samuel 26:21-25).

He had killed eighty-five priests at Nob, with the whole city, for helping David (1 Samuel 22:16-19). At the end, with Samuel dead and God not answering him by dreams, Urim, or prophets, he sought a woman with a familiar spirit at Endor - having himself put such people out of the land - and was told he and his sons would be with Samuel the next day (1 Samuel 28:3-19). Wounded by archers at Gilboa, he asked his armourbearer to kill him; the man would not, so Saul fell on his own sword (1 Samuel 31:1-6).

What They Did Right

  • Held his peace and made no reprisal against those who despised him at the start of his reign: 1 Samuel 10:27.
  • Delivered Jabeshgilead when the Spirit of God came upon him: 1 Samuel 11:6-11.
  • Refused to execute his early opponents on the day of victory, crediting the deliverance to the Lord: 1 Samuel 11:12-13.
  • Fought valiantly against Israel's enemies on every side, and delivered them out of the hands of their spoilers: 1 Samuel 14:47-48.
  • Twice acknowledged his wrong to David and blessed him: 1 Samuel 24:16-21; 1 Samuel 26:21, 26:25.
  • David's lament honours him without irony: "Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives": 2 Samuel 1:23.

What They Did Wrong

  • Offered the burnt offering himself at Gilgal rather than waiting for Samuel: 1 Samuel 13:8-13.
  • Made a rash oath that nearly cost Jonathan his life: 1 Samuel 14:24, 14:44.
  • Spared Agag and the best of the spoil against an explicit command, then claimed obedience, blamed the people, and offered the spoil as a religious excuse: 1 Samuel 15:9-21.
  • Cared more for honour before the elders than for the rejection itself: 1 Samuel 15:30.
  • Sought repeatedly to kill David, whom he knew to be innocent: 1 Samuel 18:10-11; 1 Samuel 19:9-10; 1 Samuel 23:14-15.
  • Ordered the slaughter of eighty-five priests and of the whole city of Nob, men, women, children, and sucklings: 1 Samuel 22:16-19.
  • Sought a woman with a familiar spirit, having himself cut off such from the land: 1 Samuel 28:3, 28:7.
  • The Chronicler's summary is explicit: he died "for his transgression which he committed against the Lord... and also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it; and enquired not of the Lord": 1 Chronicles 10:13-14.

Character Assessment

Scripture's account of Saul is a study in decline. He begins modest, generous, and Spirit-filled, and ends consulting a medium the night before his death. The two acts that cost him the kingdom were both religious in form - a sacrifice offered and a sacrifice proposed - which is the sharpest thing the narrative says about him: his failures were not irreligion but disobedience dressed as devotion. He confesses repeatedly and changes nothing. The slaughter at Nob is the moral floor of his reign, and Scripture records that he ordered it while sparing Agag whom he had been told to kill. David's lament and the men of Jabeshgilead's rescue of his body show that he was genuinely mourned.

Significance

Israel's first king, given in answer to a demand God called a rejection of himself (1 Samuel 8:7). His reign establishes the standard by which every later king is judged, and his rejection introduces the phrase "a man after his own heart" that Scripture applies to David (1 Samuel 13:14; Acts 13:22). Paul cites his forty years and his removal in the synagogue at Antioch (Acts 13:21-22).

Death / Outcome

Wounded by archers at Gilboa, he fell on his own sword rather than be taken; three of his sons died the same day. The men of Jabeshgilead took his body from the wall of Bethshan and buried his bones under a tree, and David later gathered them to the sepulchre of Kish (1 Samuel 31:1-13; 2 Samuel 21:12-14).

Scripture References

1 Samuel 9:1-31:13; 2 Samuel 1:1-27; 1 Chronicles 10:1-14; Acts 13:21-22
—

Jonathan (son of Saul)

Eldest son of Saul; heir to the throne; David's covenant friend, who defended him against his own father. Not to be confused with Jonathan the son of Gershom, or Jonathan the son of Abiathar.

Family

Son of Saul (1 Samuel 13:16); brother of Ishui, Melchishua, Abinadab, Merab, and Michal. Father of Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 4:4).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He died with his father at Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:2).

Life Synopsis

Jonathan smote the Philistine garrison at Geba, beginning the war (1 Samuel 13:3). At Michmash he crossed with only his armourbearer to a Philistine garrison, on a principle he stated first: "there is no restraint to the Lord to save by many or by few" (1 Samuel 14:6). They killed about twenty men and the ground trembled, and the Philistine host melted away.

Not knowing of his father's rash oath, he ate honey and was condemned to die by it; the people rescued him, saying he had wrought with God that day (1 Samuel 14:24-45).

After David killed Goliath, "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." He stripped off his robe, garments, sword, bow, and girdle and gave them to David - the heir handing over the tokens of his position (1 Samuel 18:1-4). He spoke for David to Saul and turned him from killing him (1 Samuel 19:1-7). He made covenant with the house of David, warned him of Saul's intent at the risk of a javelin thrown at himself, and they wept together (1 Samuel 20:1-42).

He went to David in the wood at Ziph "and strengthened his hand in God," and said, "Fear not: for the hand of Saul my father shall not find thee; and thou shalt be king over Israel, and I shall be next unto thee" (1 Samuel 23:16-18). It is the last recorded meeting between them.

He died with his father and two brothers at Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:2). David's lament mourned him: "I am distressed for thee, my brother Jonathan: very pleasant hast thou been unto me: thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of women" (2 Samuel 1:26).

What They Did Right

  • Attacked a Philistine garrison with only his armourbearer, resting on the sufficiency of God to save by many or by few: 1 Samuel 14:6-14.
  • Loved David as his own soul and gave him his own robe, sword, bow, and girdle: 1 Samuel 18:1-4.
  • Spoke for David to Saul and turned his father from killing an innocent man: 1 Samuel 19:4-6.
  • Warned David at personal risk, his father casting a javelin at him for it: 1 Samuel 20:32-33.
  • Strengthened David's hand in God, and accepted that David would be king in his own place: 1 Samuel 23:16-18.
  • Stayed with his father to the end and died in battle beside him: 1 Samuel 31:2.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He ate the honey in ignorance of his father's oath, and Scripture presents this as Saul's fault rather than his: 1 Samuel 14:27, 14:45.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. He is one of a small number of substantial figures in the Old Testament with an unblemished record, and the most striking thing about it is what he gave up: he was the crown prince, he knew David would take the throne, and he assisted him in it. His loyalty to his father and his loyalty to David were both real and cost him both.

Significance

His covenant with David governed David's treatment of Saul's house for the rest of his reign, and it is the reason Mephibosheth ate at David's table (2 Samuel 9:1-7) and was spared when Saul's other descendants were not (2 Samuel 21:7). His friendship with David is Scripture's fullest portrait of covenant loyalty between two men.

Death / Outcome

Slain by the Philistines at mount Gilboa with his father and two brothers; his body was fastened to the wall of Bethshan and recovered by the men of Jabeshgilead (1 Samuel 31:2, 31:8-13; 2 Samuel 21:12-14).

Scripture References

1 Samuel 13:2-14:49; 1 Samuel 18:1-4; 1 Samuel 19:1-7; 1 Samuel 20:1-42; 1 Samuel 23:16-18; 1 Samuel 31:2; 2 Samuel 1:17-27; 2 Samuel 9:1-7; 2 Samuel 21:7
—

Jonathan's armourbearer

Unnamed. The young man who went with Jonathan alone against the Philistine garrison at Michmash.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Jonathan proposed crossing to the Philistine garrison with no one but him, saying that God could save by many or by few. The armourbearer answered, "Do all that is in thine heart: turn thee; behold, I am with thee according to thy heart" (1 Samuel 14:6-7). They climbed up on hands and feet, and "they fell before Jonathan; and his armourbearer slew after him" - about twenty men within about half an acre of land (1 Samuel 14:13-14).

What They Did Right

  • Committed himself wholly to his master's purpose in a plainly desperate undertaking: 1 Samuel 14:7.
  • Climbed up after Jonathan on hands and feet and fought beside him: 1 Samuel 14:13.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records one speech and one action, both wholly favourable. His answer is one of the shortest and most complete expressions of loyalty in the Old Testament.

Significance

The attack he shared in threw the Philistine host into a trembling that became a rout, and it is contrasted with Saul, who was sitting under a pomegranate tree at Migron with six hundred men while it happened (1 Samuel 14:2, 14:15-16).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Samuel 14:17.

Scripture References

1 Samuel 14:1-17
—

Merab

Elder daughter of Saul; promised to David and given to another man.

Family

Elder daughter of Saul (1 Samuel 14:49); sister of Jonathan and Michal. Given to Adriel the Meholathite (1 Samuel 18:19); mother of five sons (2 Samuel 21:8).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Saul offered her to David as wife on condition that he fight the Lord's battles, "for Saul said, Let not mine hand be upon him, but let the hand of the Philistines be upon him" (1 Samuel 18:17). David demurred that his family was too lowly. "But it came to pass at the time when Merab Saul's daughter should have been given to David, that she was given unto Adriel the Meholathite to wife" (1 Samuel 18:19). Her five sons were later given up by David to the Gibeonites and hanged (2 Samuel 21:8-9).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Nothing she said or did is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records only what was done with her and to her family. She is included because her promised marriage, her actual marriage, and the fate of her sons are all recorded and all bear on the narrative.

Significance

Saul's use of his daughters as a snare for David is recorded twice, and she is the first instance. Her five sons died in the reprisal for Saul's slaughter of the Gibeonites (2 Samuel 21:8-9), which is one of the darkest passages in David's reign.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Samuel 21:8.

Scripture References

1 Samuel 14:49; 1 Samuel 18:17-19; 2 Samuel 21:8
—

Michal

Younger daughter of Saul; David's first wife; loved him, saved his life, was given to another man, restored to him, and despised him at the return of the ark.

Family

Daughter of Saul (1 Samuel 14:49); sister of Jonathan and Merab. Wife of David (1 Samuel 18:27), then given to Phalti of Gallim (1 Samuel 25:44), then restored to David (2 Samuel 3:14-16).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"And Michal Saul's daughter loved David" - the only place in Scripture that says a woman loved a particular man (1 Samuel 18:20). Saul used it, demanding a hundred Philistine foreskins as dowry, hoping David would fall; David brought two hundred (1 Samuel 18:21-27).

When Saul sent messengers to kill David in the morning, she let him down through a window, put an image in the bed with a pillow of goats' hair, and told the messengers he was sick. Challenged by her father, she said David had threatened to kill her (1 Samuel 19:11-17).

In David's absence Saul gave her to Phalti the son of Laish. Years later David demanded her back as a condition of treating with Abner, and she was taken from her husband, "and her husband went with her along weeping behind her to Bahurim," until Abner sent him back (1 Samuel 25:44; 2 Samuel 3:14-16).

When David brought the ark up to Jerusalem dancing before the Lord with all his might, "Michal Saul's daughter looked through a window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before the Lord; and she despised him in her heart." She met him with contempt: "How glorious was the king of Israel to day, who uncovered himself to day in the eyes of the handmaids of his servants." David answered that he had done it before the Lord and would be yet more vile. "Therefore Michal the daughter of Saul had no child unto the day of her death" (2 Samuel 6:16-23).

What They Did Right

  • Loved David: 1 Samuel 18:20.
  • Saved his life at real risk, letting him down through a window and deceiving her father's messengers: 1 Samuel 19:11-14.

What They Did Wrong

  • Despised David in her heart and reproached him for dancing before the ark: 2 Samuel 6:16, 6:20. The narrative sets her childlessness immediately after the exchange, though it does not state a causal connection in so many words.
  • She kept an image, a teraphim, in the house, which she used in the deception: 1 Samuel 19:13. Scripture records its presence without comment.

Character Assessment

A life shaped almost entirely by other people's decisions, and Scripture records the cost. She loved David and saved him; she was used as bait by her father, given away to another man, taken back as a political counter while that man wept behind her, and finally set aside. The narrator pointedly calls her "Michal the daughter of Saul" rather than the wife of David in the final scene. Her contempt at the ark is recorded as fault, and it is her only recorded fault; the rest is what was done to her.

Significance

Her marriage tied David to Saul's house, and her return was the price of Abner's negotiation and of David's claim to the northern tribes. Her childlessness meant no descendant of Saul sat on David's throne.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded directly; 2 Samuel 6:23 refers to the day of her death. Last mention: 2 Samuel 21:8.

Scripture References

1 Samuel 14:49; 1 Samuel 18:20-28; 1 Samuel 19:11-17; 1 Samuel 25:44; 2 Samuel 3:13-16; 2 Samuel 6:16-23
—

Abner

Son of Ner; Saul's cousin and captain of his host; made Ishbosheth king after Saul's death, then defected to David and was murdered by Joab.

Family

Son of Ner, Saul's uncle (1 Samuel 14:50-51); cousin of Saul and captain of his army.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Abner was captain of Saul's host throughout his reign, sitting by him at meat and leading the pursuit of David (1 Samuel 14:50; 1 Samuel 20:25; 1 Samuel 26:5). When David called across the valley of Hachilah, mocking him for failing to guard the king, Abner had no answer (1 Samuel 26:13-16).

After Saul's death he took Ishbosheth and made him king over Israel, and there was long war between the house of Saul and the house of David (2 Samuel 2:8-10; 2 Samuel 3:1). At Gibeon he proposed that young men "play before us"; twenty-four died and a general battle followed. Fleeing, he was pursued by Asahel, warned him twice to turn aside, and finally struck him through with the hinder end of his spear (2 Samuel 2:14-23).

When Ishbosheth accused him over Rizpah, Abner was furious and swore to transfer the kingdom to David. He negotiated with the elders of Israel and came to Hebron with twenty men, and David made him a feast (2 Samuel 3:6-21). Joab, returning, warned David he had come to deceive him, then sent for Abner privately and "smote him there under the fifth rib, that he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother" (2 Samuel 3:26-27).

David mourned him publicly, followed the bier, wept at the grave, and fasted; and "the king said unto his servants, Know ye not that there is a prince and a great man fallen this day in Israel?" (2 Samuel 3:31-38).

What They Did Right

  • Warned Asahel twice to turn aside before killing him, and only struck when he would not: 2 Samuel 2:21-22.
  • Called for an end to the fighting between the tribes: "Shall the sword devour for ever? knowest thou not that it will be bitterness in the latter end?": 2 Samuel 2:26.
  • Acknowledged that God had sworn to give the kingdom to David, and worked to bring it about: 2 Samuel 3:9-10, 3:17-19.
  • David's own verdict: "a prince and a great man fallen this day in Israel": 2 Samuel 3:38.

What They Did Wrong

  • Set up Ishbosheth as king over Israel in the knowledge that God had sworn the kingdom to David - which he admits himself: 2 Samuel 3:9-10; 2 Samuel 2:8-9.
  • Proposed the deadly contest at Gibeon that began the war between the houses: 2 Samuel 2:14-17.
  • Went in to Rizpah, Saul's concubine - an act with dynastic implications, though he denied wrongdoing: 2 Samuel 3:7-8.
  • Changed sides only after a personal quarrel over his own honour, not out of conviction: 2 Samuel 3:8-10.

Character Assessment

An able and formidable man whose loyalties were finally to himself. Scripture records that he knew what God had sworn about David and set up a rival king anyway, and that he changed sides when his honour was slighted rather than when he learned the truth. Yet David's lament over him is genuine and public, and the text lets both stand: he was a great man, and he was murdered treacherously by a man taking private vengeance.

Significance

His defection would have delivered the northern tribes to David peacefully; his murder delayed it and left David publicly disavowing the deed - "I am this day weak, though anointed king; and these men the sons of Zeruiah be too hard for me" (2 Samuel 3:39). David charged Solomon with the account of his blood at the end of his life (1 Kings 2:5-6).

Death / Outcome

Murdered by Joab at the gate of Hebron, struck under the fifth rib, in revenge for Asahel (2 Samuel 3:27).

Scripture References

1 Samuel 14:50-51; 1 Samuel 17:55-57; 1 Samuel 26:5-16; 2 Samuel 2:8-32; 2 Samuel 3:6-39; 1 Kings 2:5, 2:32
—

Jesse

A Bethlehemite, son of Obed; father of David and of seven other sons.

Family

Son of Obed, grandson of Boaz and Ruth (Ruth 4:17, 4:22). Father of eight sons, of whom David was the youngest, and of Zeruiah and Abigail (1 Samuel 16:10-11; 1 Chronicles 2:13-16).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He was already old in Saul's days (1 Samuel 17:12).

Life Synopsis

Samuel was sent to Bethlehem to anoint a king from among his sons. Jesse brought seven of them before Samuel, and none was chosen; it was over Eliab that God said, "Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature... for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart" (1 Samuel 16:1-10). Samuel asked whether these were all his children; Jesse said the youngest was keeping the sheep. "And Samuel said unto Jesse, Send and fetch him: for we will not sit down till he come" (1 Samuel 16:11-13).

He sent David with provisions to his brothers in Saul's army (1 Samuel 17:17-18). When David fled from Saul, he brought his father and mother to the king of Moab for safety: "Let my father and my mother, I pray thee, come forth, and be with you, till I know what God will do for me" (1 Samuel 22:3-4).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. Scripture records his actions without moral evaluation.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He did not think to include his youngest son when a prophet came to see his children (1 Samuel 16:11). The text records this without comment, and it is part of the passage's point about outward appearance rather than an accusation against Jesse.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his household, his obedience to Samuel's summons, and his errands, and passes no verdict on him. His significance is entirely in his son and in his line.

Significance

Father of David, and the name by which the messianic line is repeatedly identified: "there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse" (Isaiah 11:1, 11:10, quoted in Romans 15:12). David is called "the son of Jesse" throughout Scripture, sometimes with respect and sometimes, in the mouths of his enemies, as a slight (1 Samuel 20:27; 2 Samuel 20:1).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Samuel 22:3-4.

Scripture References

Ruth 4:17, 4:22; 1 Samuel 16:1-13; 1 Samuel 17:12-20; 1 Samuel 22:3-4; 1 Chronicles 2:12-16; Isaiah 11:1, 11:10; Romans 15:12
—

Eliab

Eldest son of Jesse; passed over at David's anointing; rebuked David at the valley of Elah.

Family

Eldest son of Jesse (1 Samuel 16:6; 1 Chronicles 2:13); brother of David.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

When Samuel came to Bethlehem and saw Eliab, "he said, Surely the Lord's anointed is before him. But the Lord said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the Lord seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart" (1 Samuel 16:6-7).

He was with Saul's army at Elah. When David asked the men about Goliath, "Eliab's anger was kindled against David, and he said, Why camest thou down hither? and with whom hast thou left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know thy pride, and the naughtiness of thine heart; for thou art come down that thou mightest see the battle." David answered, "What have I now done? Is there not a cause?" (1 Samuel 17:28-29).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Accused his younger brother of pride and naughtiness of heart for asking a question, in front of the men: 1 Samuel 17:28. Scripture records the accusation and David's mild reply, and the reader already knows from 1 Samuel 16:7 whose heart God had actually assessed.

Character Assessment

Scripture uses him to make a point rather than to assess him. He was the obvious candidate by appearance and was refused on the ground of the heart; he then charged his brother with a bad heart. The narrative places the two scenes a chapter apart and says nothing further.

Significance

God's words over him in 1 Samuel 16:7 are among the most quoted in Scripture on the difference between human and divine assessment. His daughter Abihail married Rehoboam (2 Chronicles 11:18).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 11:18.

Scripture References

1 Samuel 16:6-7; 1 Samuel 17:13, 17:28-29; 1 Chronicles 2:13; 2 Chronicles 11:18
—

Goliath

The Philistine champion of Gath, six cubits and a span in height; defied the armies of Israel and was killed by David.

Family

Of Gath (1 Samuel 17:4). 2 Samuel 21:19 records the slaying of a Goliath the Gittite by Elhanan; 1 Chronicles 20:5 says Elhanan slew Lahmi the brother of Goliath. The relation between the two passages is a long-standing textual question, noted here rather than resolved.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

He came out from the camp of the Philistines at Ephesdammim, armed with a helmet of brass, a coat of mail weighing five thousand shekels, greaves of brass, a target of brass, and a spear whose staff was like a weaver's beam and its head six hundred shekels of iron. He challenged Israel to send out a man to fight him, and defied them morning and evening for forty days (1 Samuel 17:4-16).

When David came, Goliath disdained him "for he was but a youth," cursed him by his gods, and said he would give his flesh to the fowls of the air. David answered, "Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied... that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel" (1 Samuel 17:41-46). David struck him in the forehead with a stone from his sling and cut off his head with his own sword (1 Samuel 17:49-51).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Defied the armies of the living God for forty days: 1 Samuel 17:10, 17:26.
  • Cursed David by his gods: 1 Samuel 17:43.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his stature, his armour, his challenge, and his defiance, and offers no assessment beyond the terms David uses: he defied the armies of the living God. His contempt for David's youth is recorded as the immediate prelude to his death.

Significance

His defeat established David publicly and became the standing image in Scripture and beyond of the weak overcoming the strong by faith. His sword was kept at Nob wrapped behind the ephod, and David later took it (1 Samuel 21:9).

Death / Outcome

Struck in the forehead by a stone from David's sling and beheaded with his own sword (1 Samuel 17:49-51).

Scripture References

1 Samuel 17:4-58; 1 Samuel 21:9; 1 Samuel 22:10; 2 Samuel 21:19; 1 Chronicles 20:5
—

David

Youngest son of Jesse; shepherd, musician, and warrior; second king of Israel; the man after God's own heart, and the ancestor of Christ.

Family

Youngest of the eight sons of Jesse of Bethlehem (1 Samuel 16:10-11); brother of Eliab, Abinadab, Shammah and others, and of Zeruiah and Abigail (1 Chronicles 2:13-16). Wives included Michal, Ahinoam of Jezreel, Abigail, Maacah, Haggith, Abital, Eglah, and Bathsheba (1 Samuel 18:27; 1 Samuel 25:42-43; 2 Samuel 3:2-5; 2 Samuel 11:27). Father of Amnon, Chileab, Absalom, Adonijah, Shephatiah, Ithream, Solomon, Tamar, and others (2 Samuel 3:2-5; 2 Samuel 5:13-16; 2 Samuel 13:1).

Chronology

Thirty years old when he began to reign, and reigned forty years - seven and a half in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:4-5). He died at a good old age (1 Chronicles 29:28).

Life Synopsis

David was keeping the sheep when Samuel came to Bethlehem, and was not thought worth bringing in until the prophet asked. He was ruddy, of a beautiful countenance, and goodly to look to; Samuel anointed him, "and the Spirit of the Lord came upon David from that day forward" (1 Samuel 16:11-13). He was brought to Saul's court to play the harp when an evil spirit troubled him.

At Elah he heard Goliath's defiance and asked what would be done for the man who removed the reproach from Israel. He refused Saul's armour, took five stones from the brook, and answered the giant's curses: "I come to thee in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied" (1 Samuel 17:45). He killed him with a sling and a stone.

Saul's jealousy followed the women's song, and David spent years as a fugitive - at Nob, at Gath feigning madness, in the cave of Adullam with four hundred distressed and discontented men, at Keilah, in the wilderness of Ziph and Maon and Engedi. Twice he had Saul at his mercy and would not touch him: "The Lord forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the Lord's anointed" (1 Samuel 24:6; 1 Samuel 26:9-11). He was turned from killing Nabal's household only by Abigail. He lived sixteen months as a Philistine vassal at Ziklag, deceiving Achish about his raids, and was spared having to fight Israel only because the Philistine lords distrusted him.

On Saul's death he executed the Amalekite who claimed to have killed him, and lamented Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:1-27). He reigned in Hebron seven and a half years while Ishbosheth held the north, and then over all Israel. He took Jerusalem from the Jebusites, brought up the ark with dancing and sacrifice, and proposed to build a house for God - and was told instead that God would build him a house, and establish his throne for ever (2 Samuel 5:6-9; 2 Samuel 6:12-15; 2 Samuel 7:1-16). He showed kindness to Jonathan's crippled son Mephibosheth for the covenant's sake.

Then, at the time when kings go forth to battle, he stayed at Jerusalem, saw Bathsheba, sent for her, and lay with her. When she conceived, he recalled Uriah and tried twice to get him to go home; when Uriah would not, David sent him back carrying his own death warrant, with orders to Joab to set him in the forefront of the battle and retire from him. "But the thing that David had done displeased the Lord" (2 Samuel 11:1-27). Nathan came with the parable of the ewe lamb, and David condemned himself before he understood it. His confession was immediate - "I have sinned against the Lord" - and the sentence was that the sword would never depart from his house (2 Samuel 12:1-14).

It did not. Amnon raped Tamar and David was very wroth but did nothing; Absalom killed Amnon and fled; Absalom returned, stole the hearts of Israel, and drove his father out of Jerusalem barefoot and weeping; and David charged his commanders to deal gently with the young man, and wept for him when Joab killed him: "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee" (2 Samuel 13:1-18:33). He faced Shimei's cursing without reprisal, put down Sheba's revolt, and near the end numbered the people against Joab's advice and brought a plague on Israel, buying Araunah's threshingfloor at full price rather than offer to God what cost him nothing (2 Samuel 24:1-25).

He made the preparations for the temple he was not permitted to build, charged Solomon, and died, "and was buried in the city of David" (1 Kings 2:1-10).

What They Did Right

  • Killed Goliath in the name of the Lord of hosts, that all the earth might know there was a God in Israel: 1 Samuel 17:45-47.
  • Twice refused to harm Saul when he had him at his mercy, on the ground that he was the Lord's anointed: 1 Samuel 24:4-7; 1 Samuel 26:8-11.
  • Accepted Abigail's rebuke and blessed her for keeping him from avenging himself: 1 Samuel 25:32-33.
  • Encouraged himself in the Lord his God at Ziklag when his own men spoke of stoning him: 1 Samuel 30:6.
  • Lamented Saul and Jonathan without a word of triumph over the man who had hunted him: 2 Samuel 1:17-27.
  • Brought up the ark with rejoicing and danced before the Lord with all his might, and answered Michal's contempt without retracting: 2 Samuel 6:14-22.
  • Sought out Jonathan's surviving son and restored him for the covenant's sake: 2 Samuel 9:1-7.
  • Confessed at once when Nathan confronted him, without excuse or delay: 2 Samuel 12:13; Psalms 51:1-4.
  • Refused to take Araunah's threshingfloor as a gift: "neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the Lord my God of that which doth cost me nothing": 2 Samuel 24:24.
  • Prepared abundantly for the temple he was not allowed to build: 1 Chronicles 22:1-19; 1 Chronicles 29:1-9.
  • God's own testimony, repeated in the New Testament: "I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after mine own heart, which shall fulfil all my will": Acts 13:22; compare 1 Samuel 13:14.

What They Did Wrong

  • Lied to Ahimelech at Nob, saying the king had sent him, and afterward acknowledged that he had occasioned the death of the priests and their whole city: 1 Samuel 21:2; 1 Samuel 22:22.
  • Deceived Achish about the object of his raids and left no survivors to contradict him: 1 Samuel 27:8-12.
  • Set out to destroy Nabal's entire household over an insult, and was stopped only by Abigail: 1 Samuel 25:13, 25:21-22, 25:32-34.
  • Took multiple wives and concubines, against the law given for kings: 2 Samuel 3:2-5; 2 Samuel 5:13; compare Deuteronomy 17:17.
  • Committed adultery with Bathsheba: 2 Samuel 11:2-4.
  • Arranged the death of Uriah, a loyal soldier, using Joab and the enemy's sword to do it: 2 Samuel 11:14-17. Scripture's verdict is explicit: "the thing that David had done displeased the Lord" (2 Samuel 11:27), and Nathan's charge was that he had despised the commandment of the Lord and killed Uriah with the sword of the children of Ammon (2 Samuel 12:9).
  • Did nothing when Amnon raped his daughter Tamar, though he was very wroth: 2 Samuel 13:21.
  • Numbered Israel against Joab's protest, and afterward acknowledged that he had sinned greatly and done very foolishly: 2 Samuel 24:1-10.
  • 1 Kings 15:5 gives the summary judgment of his reign with its one stated exception: he did right in the eyes of the Lord all the days of his life, "save only in the matter of Uriah the Hittite."

Character Assessment

No figure in the Old Testament is presented with a fuller record of both faith and failure. Scripture calls him a man after God's own heart and then narrates his adultery and his murder of a loyal soldier at greater length than almost any other episode in his reign. It does not resolve the tension by minimising either. What distinguishes him from Saul in the text is not the gravity of the sin but the response: Saul confessed and asked to be honoured before the elders; David confessed and wrote Psalm 51. The consequences fell anyway - the child died, and the sword did not depart from his house, working out through Amnon, Tamar, Absalom, and Adonijah. The summary in 1 Kings 15:5 is Scripture's own balance, and it names the exception.

Significance

The central human figure of the Old Testament after Moses. The covenant given him in 2 Samuel 7:12-16 - that God would establish his throne for ever - is the foundation of messianic expectation, and Christ is called the son of David throughout the Gospels (Matthew 1:1; Matthew 21:9; Romans 1:3; Revelation 22:16). He is credited with the organisation of temple worship and with a large part of the Psalter. Jerusalem is called the city of David, and his name is invoked as the standard by which every later king of Judah is measured (1 Kings 15:11; 2 Kings 18:3; 2 Kings 22:2).

Death / Outcome

Died after reigning forty years, and was buried in the city of David; Peter notes that his sepulchre remained in Jerusalem (1 Kings 2:10-11; Acts 2:29).

Scripture References

1 Samuel 16:1-1 Kings 2:11; 1 Chronicles 11:1-29:30; Psalms 51:1-19; Matthew 1:1, 1:6; Acts 2:25-31; Acts 13:22-23; Romans 1:3; Hebrews 11:32; Revelation 22:16
—

Ahimelech

Priest at Nob; gave David the shewbread and Goliath's sword; killed with eighty-four other priests by Doeg at Saul's command.

Family

Son of Ahitub, of the house of Eli (1 Samuel 22:9, 22:20); father of Abiathar.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

David came to Nob alone, and Ahimelech was afraid at the meeting. David told him the king had sent him on urgent business. Having no common bread, the priest gave him the hallowed shewbread on being assured the young men were clean, and gave him the sword of Goliath, which was kept there wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod (1 Samuel 21:1-9). Doeg the Edomite was there that day.

Doeg reported it, adding that Ahimelech had enquired of the Lord for David. Summoned before Saul and accused of conspiracy, Ahimelech answered without retracting: "And who is so faithful among all thy servants as David, which is the king's son in law, and goeth at thy bidding, and is honourable in thine house? Did I then begin to enquire of God for him? be it far from me: let not the king impute any thing unto his servant" (1 Samuel 22:11-15). Saul ordered his death and the death of all his father's house; the footmen would not lay hands on the priests, so Doeg killed eighty-five persons wearing a linen ephod, and struck the city of Nob with the edge of the sword (1 Samuel 22:16-19).

What They Did Right

  • Provided for David in need, giving the hallowed bread when there was no other: 1 Samuel 21:4-6.
  • Defended David's character to Saul's face when accused of treason for helping him: 1 Samuel 22:14.
  • Christ himself cites the incident approvingly in defending his disciples: Matthew 12:3-4; Mark 2:25-26.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He was deceived by David, who told him the king had sent him (1 Samuel 21:2). David later acknowledged responsibility for the outcome: "I have occasioned the death of all the persons of thy father's house" (1 Samuel 22:22).

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him and one act of mercy that cost him his life and the lives of his household. His answer to Saul is notable for what it does not do: he does not disown David or plead ignorance, but states plainly that David was the most faithful of the king's servants.

Significance

The giving of the shewbread became the precedent Christ used to defend his disciples plucking corn on the sabbath, arguing that need takes precedence over ceremonial restriction (Matthew 12:3-4; Mark 2:25-26; Luke 6:3-4). The massacre at Nob fulfilled part of the word spoken against the house of Eli (1 Samuel 2:31-33).

Death / Outcome

Killed by Doeg at Saul's command, with eighty-four other priests, at Nob (1 Samuel 22:18).

Scripture References

1 Samuel 21:1-9; 1 Samuel 22:9-23; Matthew 12:3-4; Mark 2:25-26; Luke 6:3-4
—

Doeg

An Edomite, chief of Saul's herdmen; informed against Ahimelech and killed eighty-five priests when Saul's own footmen refused.

Family

An Edomite (1 Samuel 21:7).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"Now a certain man of the servants of Saul was there that day, detained before the Lord; and his name was Doeg, an Edomite, the chiefest of the herdmen that belonged to Saul" (1 Samuel 21:7). He saw David come to Ahimelech.

When Saul complained that no one told him anything, Doeg answered and reported what he had seen, adding that Ahimelech had enquired of the Lord for David and given him victuals and Goliath's sword (1 Samuel 22:9-10). Saul summoned the priests and ordered their death. "But the servants of the king would not put forth their hand to fall upon the priests of the Lord. And the king said to Doeg, Turn thou, and fall upon the priests. And Doeg the Edomite turned, and he fell upon the priests, and he slew on that day fourscore and five persons that did wear a linen ephod." He then destroyed Nob entirely - men, women, children, sucklings, oxen, asses, and sheep (1 Samuel 22:17-19).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Informed against Ahimelech in terms that made an act of hospitality look like conspiracy: 1 Samuel 22:9-10.
  • Killed eighty-five priests of the Lord when the king's own footmen refused to do it: 1 Samuel 22:18.
  • Destroyed the whole city of Nob, including women, children, and sucklings: 1 Samuel 22:19.
  • Psalm 52 is titled with reference to him and describes a man who loves evil more than good and lying rather than righteousness, and whose tongue devises mischiefs like a sharp razor: Psalms 52:1-4.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned, and one of very few individuals in Scripture against whom a whole psalm is directed. The narrative marks the moment precisely: Saul's Israelite servants would not touch the priests of the Lord, and the Edomite would. Scripture records that he was "detained before the Lord" at the sanctuary on the day he saw David, which makes his subsequent action worse rather than better.

Significance

The slaughter at Nob destroyed the priestly settlement and drove Abiathar, the sole survivor, to David - so that the surviving line of Eli's house served David instead of Saul. Psalm 52 preserves David's judgment on him.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Samuel 22:22; Psalms 52 title.

Scripture References

1 Samuel 21:7; 1 Samuel 22:9-22; Psalms 52:1-9
—

Abiathar

Son of Ahimelech; sole survivor of the massacre at Nob; priest to David throughout his reign; deposed by Solomon for supporting Adonijah.

Family

Son of Ahimelech, of the house of Eli (1 Samuel 22:20); father of Jonathan (2 Samuel 15:27).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He served David from the flight at Nob until Solomon's accession.

Life Synopsis

"And one of the sons of Ahimelech the son of Ahitub, named Abiathar, escaped, and fled after David." David said, "I have occasioned the death of all the persons of thy father's house. Abide thou with me, fear not... with me thou shalt be in safeguard" (1 Samuel 22:20-23). He brought the ephod with him, and David enquired of the Lord through him repeatedly during the years of flight (1 Samuel 23:6-12; 1 Samuel 30:7-8).

He served as priest through David's reign alongside Zadok (2 Samuel 8:17). When Absalom rebelled, he and Zadok carried the ark out of the city and were sent back by David to act as his informants, their sons Ahimaaz and Jonathan carrying messages (2 Samuel 15:24-36; 2 Samuel 17:15-21).

At the end of David's life he supported Adonijah rather than Solomon (1 Kings 1:7). Solomon spared his life for the ark he had borne and the afflictions he had shared, but removed him from the priesthood and sent him to his fields at Anathoth, "that he might fulfil the word of the Lord, which he spake concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh" (1 Kings 2:26-27).

What They Did Right

  • Fled to David with the ephod after the massacre and served him through the years of exile: 1 Samuel 22:20-23; 1 Samuel 23:6.
  • Carried the ark out of Jerusalem in the rebellion and then returned at David's word to serve as his informant at personal risk: 2 Samuel 15:24-29.
  • Solomon's own testimony: he bore the ark of the Lord God before David and was afflicted in all wherein David was afflicted: 1 Kings 2:26.

What They Did Wrong

  • Followed Adonijah in his attempt on the throne, against David's declared purpose for Solomon: 1 Kings 1:7, 1:19.

Character Assessment

A long and largely faithful service ending in a single decisive misjudgment. Scripture records both fully and lets Solomon's sentence express the balance: his life was spared for what he had been, and his office was taken for what he had done. The narrator adds the theological note that his removal fulfilled the word spoken against Eli's house generations earlier.

Significance

His removal ended the priestly line of Eli and established Zadok's line in its place (1 Kings 2:27, 2:35), a change that shapes the priesthood for the rest of the Old Testament. Christ refers to "the days of Abiathar the high priest" in citing the incident of the shewbread (Mark 2:26), a reference that raises a well-known difficulty since the priest at Nob was his father Ahimelech; the question is noted here and not resolved.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He was sent to Anathoth (1 Kings 2:26).

Scripture References

1 Samuel 22:20-23; 1 Samuel 23:6-12; 1 Samuel 30:7-8; 2 Samuel 8:17; 2 Samuel 15:24-36; 2 Samuel 17:15-21; 1 Kings 1:7, 1:19; 1 Kings 2:26-27, 2:35; Mark 2:26
—

Nabal

A rich man of Maon whose possessions were in Carmel; churlish and evil in his doings; refused David's request and died ten days after his wife averted the reprisal.

Family

Of the house of Caleb (1 Samuel 25:3); husband of Abigail.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"The man was very great, and he had three thousand sheep, and a thousand goats... Now the name of the man was Nabal; and the name of his wife Abigail: and she was a woman of good understanding, and of a beautiful countenance: but the man was churlish and evil in his doings" (1 Samuel 25:2-3).

David's men had protected his shepherds in the wilderness and taken nothing. At sheepshearing David sent ten young men to ask for whatever came to hand. Nabal answered, "Who is David? and who is the son of Jesse? there be many servants now a days that break away every man from his master. Shall I then take my bread, and my water, and my flesh that I have killed for my shearers, and give it unto men, whom I know not whence they be?" (1 Samuel 25:10-11). David girded on his sword and set out with four hundred men.

Abigail met him with provisions and turned him back. "And it came to pass in the morning, when the wine was gone out of Nabal, and his wife had told him these things, that his heart died within him, and he became as a stone. And it came to pass about ten days after, that the Lord smote Nabal, that he died" (1 Samuel 25:36-38).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Churlish and evil in his doings, in the narrator's own words: 1 Samuel 25:3.
  • Returned insult for protection, denying that he knew who David was: 1 Samuel 25:10-11.
  • His own servant's assessment: "he is such a son of Belial, that a man cannot speak to him": 1 Samuel 25:17.
  • Held a feast like a king and was very drunken on the night his household stood in danger: 1 Samuel 25:36.

Character Assessment

Uniformly negative, and unusually so - the narrator, his servants, and his wife all assess him the same way. Abigail's summary plays on his name: "as his name is, so is he; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him" (1 Samuel 25:25). Scripture attributes his death directly to the Lord.

Significance

The episode is the occasion of one of David's clearest recorded restraints from private vengeance, and of Abigail's speech reminding him that he should not have the shedding of innocent blood on his conscience when God made him ruler (1 Samuel 25:30-31).

Death / Outcome

"The Lord smote Nabal, that he died" - about ten days after his heart died within him (1 Samuel 25:38).

Scripture References

1 Samuel 25:2-39
—

Abigail

Wife of Nabal, and after his death a wife of David; a woman of good understanding who averted a massacre by her own initiative. Not to be confused with Abigail the sister of David and mother of Amasa (1 Chronicles 2:16-17).

Family

Wife of Nabal of Carmel (1 Samuel 25:3); afterward wife of David (1 Samuel 25:42); mother of Chileab, also called Daniel (2 Samuel 3:3; 1 Chronicles 3:1).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Described as "a woman of good understanding, and of a beautiful countenance" while her husband was churlish and evil (1 Samuel 25:3). A servant told her what had happened and what was coming, and "she made haste" - loading two hundred loaves, two bottles of wine, five sheep ready dressed, parched corn, raisins, and figs on asses, and going down without telling her husband (1 Samuel 25:18-19).

Meeting David, she fell at his feet and took the blame on herself, described her husband accurately, and made the argument that turned him back: that the Lord had kept him from avenging himself with his own hand, that his life was bound in the bundle of life with the Lord, and that when God had made him ruler over Israel this would be no grief to him, "that thou hast shed blood causeless, or that my lord hath avenged himself" (1 Samuel 25:23-31).

David answered, "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me: and blessed be thy advice, and blessed be thou, which hast kept me this day from coming to shed blood, and from avenging myself with mine own hand" (1 Samuel 25:32-33). She told Nabal in the morning, and he died ten days later. David then sent for her and she became his wife (1 Samuel 25:36-42).

What They Did Right

  • Acted immediately and decisively when told what was coming: 1 Samuel 25:18-19.
  • Took the blame on herself and pleaded for a household that did not deserve it: 1 Samuel 25:24-28.
  • Reasoned with David from what God had promised him, not from her own danger: 1 Samuel 25:28-31.
  • David's own verdict: blessed be the Lord who sent her, blessed be her advice, and blessed be she: 1 Samuel 25:32-33.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. She acted without her husband's knowledge (1 Samuel 25:19). Scripture records this as fact and the outcome as blessed, and passes no judgment on the concealment.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her and one of the most effective speeches in the Old Testament. She is the only person in Scripture whose counsel David is recorded as blessing in those terms. What she prevented was not merely a massacre but a stain on the reign that had not yet begun, and she argued it on exactly that ground.

Significance

Her intervention kept David from shedding innocent blood in private vengeance during the years before his accession - a restraint that becomes significant when set beside his later conduct toward Uriah. She became his wife and the mother of his second son.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. She was taken captive at Ziklag and recovered (1 Samuel 30:5, 30:18). Last mention: 1 Chronicles 3:1.

Scripture References

1 Samuel 25:3-42; 1 Samuel 27:3; 1 Samuel 30:5, 30:18; 2 Samuel 2:2; 2 Samuel 3:3; 1 Chronicles 3:1
—

Achish

King of Gath; David took refuge with him twice, first feigning madness and later serving him as a vassal.

Family

Son of Maoch (1 Samuel 27:2).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

David fled to Achish the first time alone. The servants of Achish identified him as the king of the land of whom they sang that he had slain his ten thousands. David was sore afraid, changed his behaviour, feigned madness, scrabbled on the doors of the gate and let his spittle fall on his beard. Achish said, "Have I need of mad men, that ye have brought this fellow to play the mad man in my presence?" and sent him away (1 Samuel 21:10-15).

Later David came again with six hundred men and dwelt at Ziklag a year and four months as Achish's vassal. He raided the Geshurites, Gezrites, and Amalekites, leaving none alive to report, and told Achish he had raided Judah - "And Achish believed David, saying, He hath made his people Israel utterly to abhor him; therefore he shall be my servant for ever" (1 Samuel 27:1-12).

When the Philistines gathered against Israel, Achish told David he would go with him to battle. The other Philistine lords objected and demanded his removal. Achish defended him warmly: "I have found no fault in him since he fell unto me unto this day," and told him, "thou hast been upright, and thy going out and thy coming in with me in the host is good in my sight: for I have not found evil in thee since the day of thy coming unto me unto this day: nevertheless the lords favour thee not" (1 Samuel 29:3-9).

What They Did Right

  • Gave refuge to a fugitive and dealt honourably with him: 1 Samuel 27:5-6.
  • Defended David's character to the other Philistine lords and spoke to him with unusual warmth and candour when sending him away: 1 Samuel 29:3, 29:6-9.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him and a good deal in his favour. He is repeatedly deceived by David and repeatedly generous. His declaration that he had found no evil in David is ironic in context - it was true of David's conduct toward him and untrue of David's words to him - and the narrative records the irony without comment.

Significance

His protection preserved David through the last and most dangerous phase of Saul's pursuit, and the removal of David from the Philistine army by the other lords kept him from having to fight against Israel at Gilboa.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. A king of Gath named Achish son of Maachah appears in Solomon's reign (1 Kings 2:39-40); whether this is the same man is not stated.

Scripture References

1 Samuel 21:10-15; 1 Samuel 27:1-12; 1 Samuel 28:1-2; 1 Samuel 29:1-11; 1 Kings 2:39-40; Psalms 34 title
—

The woman of Endor

Unnamed. A woman with a familiar spirit at Endor, consulted by Saul the night before his death.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. The night before the battle of Gilboa.

Life Synopsis

Samuel was dead and Saul had put those with familiar spirits out of the land. Facing the Philistine host and receiving no answer from the Lord by dreams, Urim, or prophets, he disguised himself and went by night to a woman at Endor (1 Samuel 28:3-8).

She was cautious: "Behold, thou knowest what Saul hath done, how he hath cut off those that have familiar spirits... wherefore then layest thou a snare for my life?" He swore to her by the Lord that no punishment would come. She asked whom to bring up, and he said Samuel. "And when the woman saw Samuel, she cried with a loud voice: and the woman spake to Saul, saying, Why hast thou deceived me? for thou art Saul" (1 Samuel 28:9-12). Samuel pronounced Saul's doom.

Saul fell full length on the earth, having eaten nothing all day. She came to him and said she had obeyed him at the risk of her life, and asked him to eat. When he refused, she and his servants pressed him; she killed a fat calf, baked unleavened bread, and set it before him and his men, and they went away that night (1 Samuel 28:20-25).

What They Did Right

  • Showed real compassion to Saul when he collapsed, killing her only fat calf and pressing food on him: 1 Samuel 28:21-25. Scripture records this without comment, and it is the last kindness anyone does for him.

What They Did Wrong

  • She practised divination with a familiar spirit, which the law forbade on pain of death: 1 Samuel 28:7-9; compare Leviticus 20:27; Deuteronomy 18:10-12. Scripture records her trade plainly. The narrative's condemnation, however, falls on Saul for consulting her rather than on her for existing: 1 Chronicles 10:13-14.

Character Assessment

Scripture records her occupation, her fear, her shock when Samuel appeared, and her kindness afterward. What actually happened at Endor - whether Samuel truly appeared, and by what means - is much debated; the text simply says the woman saw Samuel and that Samuel spoke, and does not explain it. This reference reports what the text says and does not go beyond it.

Significance

The Chronicler names Saul's consultation of her as one of the two reasons for his death (1 Chronicles 10:13-14), which makes the episode the formal end of his reign in Scripture's own accounting.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Samuel 28:25.

Scripture References

1 Samuel 28:3-25; 1 Chronicles 10:13-14
—

Agag

King of the Amalekites, spared by Saul against God's command and executed by Samuel.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Saul was commanded to smite Amalek and utterly destroy all they had. "But Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep, and of the oxen, and of the fatlings, and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them" (1 Samuel 15:9).

After Samuel had pronounced Saul's rejection, he called for Agag. "And Agag came unto him delicately. And Agag said, Surely the bitterness of death is past. And Samuel said, As thy sword hath made women childless, so shall thy sword be childless among women. And Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before the Lord in Gilgal" (1 Samuel 15:32-33).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Samuel's sentence names the charge: his sword had made women childless: 1 Samuel 15:33. Scripture gives no other detail of his conduct.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his sparing, his brief speech, and his execution. The one charge against him is stated by Samuel at the moment of judgment, and no other account of his reign is given.

Significance

His sparing was the specific disobedience for which Saul lost the kingdom, and Samuel's words on that occasion - that to obey is better than sacrifice - are among the most quoted in the Old Testament. Haman the enemy of the Jews is called an Agagite (Esther 3:1), which Scripture states without explaining the connection.

Death / Outcome

Hewn in pieces by Samuel before the Lord in Gilgal (1 Samuel 15:33).

Scripture References

1 Samuel 15:8-33; Esther 3:1
—

The armourbearer of Saul

Unnamed. Saul's armourbearer at Gilboa, who refused to kill him and then fell on his own sword.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Wounded by the archers, Saul said to his armourbearer, "Draw thy sword, and thrust me through therewith; lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and abuse me. But his armourbearer would not; for he was sore afraid. Therefore Saul took a sword, and fell upon it. And when his armourbearer saw that Saul was dead, he fell likewise upon his sword, and died with him" (1 Samuel 31:4-5).

What They Did Right

  • Refused to lift his hand against the Lord's anointed, even at the king's own command: 1 Samuel 31:4. Scripture gives the reason as fear rather than principle, and offers no commendation.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his refusal, the reason for it, and his death, and offers no verdict. His refusal stands in deliberate contrast with the Amalekite who shortly afterward claimed to David that he had done exactly what this man would not do.

Significance

His account is the true version against which the Amalekite's claim in 2 Samuel 1:6-10 is measured, and the difference between the two accounts is the reason David executed the Amalekite.

Death / Outcome

Fell on his own sword and died with Saul at Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:5).

Scripture References

1 Samuel 31:4-6; 1 Chronicles 10:4-5
—

The Amalekite who claimed to have killed Saul

Unnamed. A young man, the son of a stranger, an Amalekite, who came to David with Saul's crown and bracelet claiming to have killed him.

Family

"I am the son of a stranger, an Amalekite" (2 Samuel 1:13).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Three days after Saul's death.

Life Synopsis

He came to David at Ziklag with earth on his head and clothes rent, reporting that Israel had fled and that Saul and Jonathan were dead. Asked how he knew, he said he had come by chance on mount Gilboa and found Saul leaning on his spear, who asked him to kill him, "So I stood upon him, and slew him, because I was sure that he could not live after that he was fallen: and I took the crown that was upon his head, and the bracelet that was on his arm, and have brought them hither" (2 Samuel 1:1-10). His account contradicts 1 Samuel 31:4-5, which records that Saul killed himself.

David asked, "How wast thou not afraid to stretch forth thine hand to destroy the Lord's anointed?" and commanded one of his young men to kill him, saying, "Thy blood be upon thy head; for thy mouth hath testified against thee" (2 Samuel 1:14-16).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Claimed to have killed the Lord's anointed: 2 Samuel 1:10. Whether he actually did so, or invented the story hoping for reward, Scripture does not say; the account in 1 Samuel 31:4-5 indicates Saul died by his own hand. David's sentence rested on his own testimony rather than on independent evidence: 2 Samuel 1:16.
  • Stripped the crown and bracelet from the body and carried them to Saul's rival: 2 Samuel 1:10.

Character Assessment

Scripture sets his story beside the account already given and lets the reader see the difference. Whether he was a killer or a liar, he was executed on the strength of his own words - which is exactly how David framed the sentence.

Significance

His execution established at the outset of David's reign that David would not profit from Saul's death or countenance a hand raised against the Lord's anointed - a position he had maintained twice when he could have killed Saul himself.

Death / Outcome

Killed at David's command at Ziklag (2 Samuel 1:15).

Scripture References

2 Samuel 1:1-16; compare 1 Samuel 31:1-6
—

Ishbosheth

A son of Saul, set up by Abner as king over Israel after Gilboa; reigned two years and was murdered in his own house.

Also called Eshbaal

Family

Son of Saul (2 Samuel 2:8); called Eshbaal in 1 Chronicles 8:33 and 1 Chronicles 9:39.

Chronology

"Ishbosheth Saul's son was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and reigned two years" (2 Samuel 2:10).

Life Synopsis

Abner took him to Mahanaim and made him king over Gilead, the Ashurites, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all Israel, while Judah followed David (2 Samuel 2:8-10). There was long war between the two houses, "but David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker" (2 Samuel 3:1).

He accused Abner of going in to Rizpah, his father's concubine. Abner was enraged and swore to transfer the kingdom to David, "And he could not answer Abner a word again, because he feared him" (2 Samuel 3:7-11). He surrendered Michal to David on demand (2 Samuel 3:14-15). When he heard that Abner was dead, "his hands were feeble, and all the Israelites were troubled" (2 Samuel 4:1).

Two of his own captains, Baanah and Rechab, came into his house at noon while he lay on his bed, killed him, cut off his head, and carried it to David at Hebron expecting reward. David had them executed and buried Ishbosheth's head in Abner's sepulchre (2 Samuel 4:5-12).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records that he accepted a crown God had promised to David, but the initiative is attributed throughout to Abner, who took him and made him king (2 Samuel 2:8-9). The text records nothing he did on his own account beyond the accusation against Abner.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents him as a man moved by others. Abner set him up; Abner turned on him and he could not answer a word; and when Abner died his hands were feeble. His one recorded initiative was an accusation that cost him his kingdom. The narrative's judgment falls on those who used him and on those who murdered him rather than on him.

Significance

His two-year reign was the last of Saul's house. His murder removed the final obstacle to David's rule over all Israel, and David's public execution of the murderers made clear he had not sought it that way.

Death / Outcome

Murdered on his bed at noon by Baanah and Rechab, who beheaded him; David executed them and buried the head in Abner's sepulchre in Hebron (2 Samuel 4:5-12).

Scripture References

2 Samuel 2:8-4:12; 1 Chronicles 8:33; 1 Chronicles 9:39
—

Zeruiah

Sister of David; mother of Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Her sons are named by her rather than by their father throughout Scripture.

Family

Daughter of Jesse and sister of David and Abigail (1 Chronicles 2:16); mother of Abishai, Joab, and Asahel.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Scripture never records anything she said or did. It names her repeatedly, always as the mother of her three sons: "the sons of Zeruiah" is the standing phrase, used even by David - "what have I to do with you, ye sons of Zeruiah?" and "these men the sons of Zeruiah be too hard for me" (2 Samuel 3:39; 2 Samuel 16:10; 2 Samuel 19:22). 1 Chronicles 2:16 establishes that she was David's sister. Asahel was buried "in the sepulchre of his father, which was in Bethlehem" (2 Samuel 2:32), but her husband is never named.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.
