What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Nothing of her own conduct is recorded. She is included because Scripture identifies three of the most consequential men of David's reign by her name rather than their father's - an unusual pattern the text never explains - and because her relation to David establishes that his commanders were his nephews.

Significance

Her three sons commanded David's armies and shaped his reign for good and ill. That Joab and Abishai were David's own nephews explains much about why he could not remove them.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. She is never described as acting or speaking.

Scripture References

1 Samuel 26:6; 2 Samuel 2:18; 2 Samuel 3:39; 2 Samuel 16:10; 2 Samuel 19:22; 1 Chronicles 2:16
—

Joab

Son of Zeruiah, David's sister; captain of David's host for most of his reign; a formidable and ruthless commander whom David could neither do without nor control.

Family

Son of Zeruiah, David's sister (1 Chronicles 2:16); brother of Abishai and Asahel; nephew of David.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He served from the war with Ishbosheth until Solomon's accession.

Life Synopsis

Joab led David's men at Gibeon, where his brother Asahel was killed by Abner in flight (2 Samuel 2:12-23). When Abner later came to Hebron to hand the kingdom to David, Joab rebuked the king to his face, then sent for Abner privately and killed him under the fifth rib "for the blood of Asahel his brother" (2 Samuel 3:24-27). David disavowed it and said, "these men the sons of Zeruiah be too hard for me" (2 Samuel 3:39).

He took the stronghold of Zion and became chief (1 Chronicles 11:6). He commanded at Rabbah, and he carried out the order to place Uriah where he would be killed - and coolly instructed the messenger how to break the news to a king who might be angry (2 Samuel 11:14-21). He then summoned David to take the city himself so that it should not be called by Joab's name (2 Samuel 12:26-28).

He engineered Absalom's recall through the woman of Tekoah, and set his field on fire when Absalom would not see him (2 Samuel 14:1-31). Yet when Absalom rebelled and David charged the commanders to deal gently with him, it was Joab who thrust three darts through his heart as he hung in the oak, and Joab who afterward told the weeping king to get up and speak comfortably to his servants or lose the kingdom - harsh counsel, and correct (2 Samuel 18:9-14; 2 Samuel 19:5-8).

David replaced him with Amasa; Joab took Amasa by the beard as if to kiss him and struck him under the fifth rib (2 Samuel 20:9-10). He put down Sheba's revolt by negotiating with the wise woman of Abel (2 Samuel 20:16-22). He protested against the numbering of Israel and was overruled (2 Samuel 24:3-4). At the end he supported Adonijah, and Solomon, following David's charge, had him killed at the altar (1 Kings 2:5-6, 2:28-34).

What They Did Right

  • Fought David's wars with success over a long career and took the stronghold of Zion: 2 Samuel 10:7-14; 1 Chronicles 11:6.
  • Refused to let the credit for taking Rabbah fall to himself rather than the king: 2 Samuel 12:26-28.
  • Told David the truth about his mourning for Absalom when no one else would: 2 Samuel 19:5-7.
  • Protested against the numbering of Israel before carrying it out: 2 Samuel 24:3.
  • Spared the city of Abel when the wise woman offered terms, rather than destroying it: 2 Samuel 20:20-22.

What They Did Wrong

  • Murdered Abner in time of peace under pretence of a private word, in revenge for Asahel: 2 Samuel 3:27; 1 Kings 2:5.
  • Carried out the killing of Uriah and managed the report of it: 2 Samuel 11:14-21.
  • Killed Absalom in direct disobedience to the king's explicit charge: 2 Samuel 18:5, 18:14.
  • Murdered Amasa with the same treachery he had used on Abner: 2 Samuel 20:9-10; 1 Kings 2:5.
  • Supported Adonijah against Solomon: 1 Kings 1:7; 1 Kings 2:28.
  • David's own charge names the shedding of the blood of war in peace as his guilt: 1 Kings 2:5-6.

Character Assessment

One of the most capable and least governable men in Scripture. He was loyal to David's throne throughout and repeatedly acted against David's stated wishes when he judged the king wrong - sometimes disastrously, as with Absalom, and sometimes rightly, as with the mourning that was demoralising the army. His three murders were all committed on personal grounds and all by the same method, a private approach and a thrust under the fifth rib. Scripture credits his military service fully and condemns his blood-guilt explicitly, and David's dying charge treats the account as unsettled.

Significance

He was the instrument of both David's greatest victories and his greatest crime. His career is the clearest illustration in Scripture of a subordinate whose competence made him untouchable, and David's admission that the sons of Zeruiah were too hard for him is a rare acknowledgment of a king's practical limits.

Death / Outcome

Killed by Benaiah at Solomon's command, holding the horns of the altar in the tabernacle, and buried in his own house in the wilderness (1 Kings 2:28-34).

Scripture References

2 Samuel 2:13-3:39; 2 Samuel 10:1-14; 2 Samuel 11:1-25; 2 Samuel 12:26-31; 2 Samuel 14:1-33; 2 Samuel 18:1-19:8; 2 Samuel 20:1-23; 2 Samuel 24:1-9; 1 Kings 1:7; 1 Kings 2:5-6, 2:28-34; 1 Chronicles 11:6
—

Abishai

Son of Zeruiah; brother of Joab and Asahel; one of David's chief warriors, repeatedly restrained by David from killing his enemies.

Family

Son of Zeruiah, David's sister; brother of Joab and Asahel (1 Chronicles 2:16).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Abishai went down with David by night into Saul's camp at Hachilah and offered to pin the sleeping king to the earth with one stroke of the spear. David forbade it: "Destroy him not: for who can stretch forth his hand against the Lord's anointed, and be guiltless?" (1 Samuel 26:6-9).

He pursued Abner with Joab and shared in his death (2 Samuel 3:30). He commanded a wing against the Ammonites and Syrians, with the agreement that whichever brother was hard pressed the other would help (2 Samuel 10:9-11). When Shimei cursed David on the flight from Absalom, Abishai said, "Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? let me go over, I pray thee, and take off his head," and David again refused (2 Samuel 16:9-11). He made the same offer again after the return, and was refused again (2 Samuel 19:21-22).

He saved David's life when Ishbibenob, a giant of the sons of the giant, thought to have killed him (2 Samuel 21:15-17). He was chief of the three, and slew three hundred with his spear, and had a name among the mighty men (2 Samuel 23:18-19).

What They Did Right

  • Volunteered to go down alone with David into the enemy camp by night: 1 Samuel 26:6-7.
  • Saved David's life in battle against a Philistine giant: 2 Samuel 21:17.
  • Chief among the mighty men, having slain three hundred with his spear: 2 Samuel 23:18.
  • Fought loyally under his brother's command and offered mutual support in battle: 2 Samuel 10:9-11.

What They Did Wrong

  • Shared in the killing of Abner: 2 Samuel 3:30.
  • Twice proposed executing men summarily, and was twice refused by David: 1 Samuel 26:8; 2 Samuel 16:9; 2 Samuel 19:21.

Character Assessment

A brave and wholly loyal soldier whose instinct in every recorded disagreement was to kill someone. David restrained him three times, and each restraint is recorded as the right decision. Scripture credits his courage and his rescue of the king without softening the pattern.

Significance

His repeated offers and David's repeated refusals form one of the running threads of the narrative and illustrate David's own principle about the Lord's anointed. He is listed among the chief of the mighty men.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Chronicles 18:12; 2 Samuel 23:18-19.

Scripture References

1 Samuel 26:6-9; 2 Samuel 2:18-24; 2 Samuel 3:30; 2 Samuel 10:9-14; 2 Samuel 16:9-11; 2 Samuel 18:2, 18:5; 2 Samuel 19:21-22; 2 Samuel 21:15-17; 2 Samuel 23:18-19; 1 Chronicles 18:12
—

Asahel

Son of Zeruiah; brother of Joab and Abishai; light of foot as a wild roe; killed by Abner while pursuing him.

Family

Son of Zeruiah; brother of Joab and Abishai (2 Samuel 2:18).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"And there were three sons of Zeruiah there, Joab, and Abishai, and Asahel: and Asahel was as light of foot as a wild roe" (2 Samuel 2:18). After the fight at Gibeon he pursued Abner and would not turn aside to the right hand or the left.

Abner warned him twice: "Turn thee aside to thy right hand or to thy left, and lay thee hold on one of the young men, and take thee his armour... Turn thee aside from following me: wherefore should I smite thee to the ground? how then should I hold up my face to Joab thy brother?" He refused to turn, and Abner struck him with the hinder end of the spear under the fifth rib, so that it came out behind him, and he died on the spot; and all who came to the place stood still (2 Samuel 2:19-23).

What They Did Right

  • Pursued the enemy commander with singular determination: 2 Samuel 2:19. Scripture records the courage without commending the judgment.
  • Named among David's thirty mighty men: 2 Samuel 23:24.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He refused two warnings and pressed a pursuit he could not win. Scripture records the warnings and the outcome without calling the refusal a fault.

Character Assessment

Scripture records speed, courage, and a fatal unwillingness to turn aside, and passes no verdict. Abner's reluctance to kill him is recorded in unusual detail, which matters because Joab afterward treated the death as murder rather than as a battle casualty.

Significance

His death was the stated ground of Joab's murder of Abner, which delayed the reunification of the kingdom and left a blood-guilt David charged Solomon to settle (2 Samuel 3:27; 1 Kings 2:5).

Death / Outcome

Killed by Abner with the hinder end of his spear at Gibeon, and buried in his father's sepulchre at Bethlehem (2 Samuel 2:23, 2:32).

Scripture References

2 Samuel 2:18-32; 2 Samuel 3:27, 3:30; 2 Samuel 23:24; 1 Chronicles 11:26
—

Rizpah

Concubine of Saul; the occasion of the quarrel between Abner and Ishbosheth; kept watch over the bodies of her two sons and five others until they were buried.

Family

Daughter of Aiah; concubine of Saul (2 Samuel 3:7); mother of Armoni and Mephibosheth by Saul (2 Samuel 21:8).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Her vigil lasted from the beginning of barley harvest until rain fell (2 Samuel 21:10).

Life Synopsis

Ishbosheth accused Abner of going in to her, and Abner's fury at the accusation moved him to transfer the kingdom to David (2 Samuel 3:7-10).

Later, a three-year famine was attributed to Saul's slaughter of the Gibeonites, and the Gibeonites demanded seven of Saul's descendants. David gave them her two sons and the five sons of Merab, and they were hanged in the hill before the Lord in the days of harvest (2 Samuel 21:1-9).

"And Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth, and spread it for her upon the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon them out of heaven, and suffered neither the birds of the air to rest on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night." When David was told what she had done, he gathered the bones of Saul and Jonathan and of the seven, and buried them all in the sepulchre of Kish (2 Samuel 21:10-14).

What They Did Right

  • Kept watch over the exposed bodies of her sons and their kinsmen for months, driving off birds by day and beasts by night: 2 Samuel 21:10. Scripture records this without comment, and records that it moved the king to act.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her and one act of endurance that shamed a kingdom into doing what should have been done at once. She had no power to prevent the executions and no standing to demand burial; what she had was the ability to stay on the rock, and it worked.

Significance

Her vigil brought about the burial of Saul and Jonathan in their family sepulchre, closing the account of Saul's house. The episode is one of the most troubling in David's reign, and the narrative gives the last word not to the king but to a concubine on a rock.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Samuel 21:11.

Scripture References

2 Samuel 3:7-11; 2 Samuel 21:1-14
—

Mephibosheth

Son of Jonathan; lamed at five years old when the news of Gilboa came; brought to David's table for Jonathan's sake.

Also called Meribbaal

Family

Son of Jonathan, grandson of Saul (2 Samuel 4:4); father of Micha (2 Samuel 9:12). Called Meribbaal in 1 Chronicles 8:34. Not to be confused with Rizpah's son Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 21:8).

Chronology

Five years old when Saul and Jonathan died (2 Samuel 4:4).

Life Synopsis

"And Jonathan, Saul's son, had a son that was lame of his feet. He was five years old when the tidings came of Saul and Jonathan out of Jezreel, and his nurse took him up, and fled: and it came to pass, as she made haste to flee, that he fell, and became lame" (2 Samuel 4:4).

David asked whether any of Saul's house was left "that I may shew him kindness for Jonathan's sake," and Ziba named him. Brought to the king, he fell on his face; David told him not to fear, restored to him all Saul's land, and set him to eat at the king's table continually. He answered, "What is thy servant, that thou shouldest look upon such a dead dog as I am?" (2 Samuel 9:1-13).

When Absalom rebelled, Ziba met David with provisions and said Mephibosheth had stayed in Jerusalem hoping to be given his grandfather's kingdom; David gave Ziba all his property (2 Samuel 16:1-4). On David's return Mephibosheth came down, having neither dressed his feet nor trimmed his beard nor washed his clothes since the king left, and said Ziba had slandered him and had refused to saddle his ass. David divided the land between them. Mephibosheth answered, "Yea, let him take all, forasmuch as my lord the king is come again in peace unto his own house" (2 Samuel 19:24-30). He was spared when the Gibeonites took seven of Saul's descendants, for the oath between David and Jonathan (2 Samuel 21:7).

What They Did Right

  • Received David's kindness with humility rather than entitlement: 2 Samuel 9:8.
  • Mourned for the king throughout the rebellion, neglecting his own person from the day David left until he returned in peace: 2 Samuel 19:24.
  • Surrendered his whole claim to the property without complaint when the king's own judgment went against him: 2 Samuel 19:30.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Ziba accused him of hoping to recover Saul's kingdom (2 Samuel 16:3), and Mephibosheth denied it and accused Ziba of slander (2 Samuel 19:26-27). Scripture reports both accounts and does not say which was true. David's division of the land settled the matter without resolving the question, and this reference does not resolve it either.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents him sympathetically throughout and never settles the one accusation against him. What it does record is his condition when David returned - unwashed and unkempt for the whole period of the rebellion - which is evidence a reader can weigh, and his willingness to give up everything so long as the king was safe.

Significance

His restoration is the fulfilment of the covenant Jonathan made with David, and Scripture makes the motive explicit each time: for Jonathan's sake, and for the Lord's oath between them (2 Samuel 9:1, 9:7; 2 Samuel 21:7). It is one of the clearest pictures in the Old Testament of kindness shown on the strength of a covenant with someone else.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Samuel 21:7.

Scripture References

2 Samuel 4:4; 2 Samuel 9:1-13; 2 Samuel 16:1-4; 2 Samuel 19:24-30; 2 Samuel 21:7; 1 Chronicles 8:34
—

Ziba

A servant of the house of Saul; steward of Mephibosheth's restored lands; brought provisions to David in the rebellion and accused his master.

Family

A servant of the house of Saul, with fifteen sons and twenty servants (2 Samuel 9:2, 9:10).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Called before David, he identified Mephibosheth as Jonathan's surviving son, and was appointed with his sons and servants to till the land for him: "Thou therefore, and thy sons, and thy servants, shall till the land for him... but Mephibosheth thy master's son shall eat bread alway at my table" (2 Samuel 9:2-11).

When David fled from Absalom, Ziba met him with two saddled asses, two hundred loaves, a hundred bunches of raisins, a hundred summer fruits, and a bottle of wine. Asked where his master's son was, he said, "Behold, he abideth at Jerusalem: for he said, To day shall the house of Israel restore me the kingdom of my father." David said, "Behold, thine are all that pertained unto Mephibosheth" (2 Samuel 16:1-4).

On David's return Mephibosheth said Ziba had deceived him and slandered him, having refused to saddle an ass for a lame man. David divided the land between them (2 Samuel 19:26-29).

What They Did Right

  • Brought substantial and timely provision to David and his household in flight: 2 Samuel 16:1-2.

What They Did Wrong

  • Mephibosheth accused him of slander and of refusing to saddle his ass so that he could go with the king: 2 Samuel 19:26-27. Scripture records the accusation without confirming or denying it. Ziba's report gained him his master's whole estate, which is a fact the reader is left to weigh.

Character Assessment

Scripture gives two irreconcilable accounts and adjudicates neither. What it records plainly is that Ziba profited by his report, that David's first judgment was made on one side of the story only, and that his second judgment split the difference rather than establishing the truth.

Significance

The episode is one of the few in Scripture where a king's judgment is shown to be uncertain and is left uncorrected. It also illustrates how far the rebellion had disordered ordinary justice.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Samuel 19:29.

Scripture References

2 Samuel 9:2-12; 2 Samuel 16:1-4; 2 Samuel 19:17, 19:26-29
—

Uriah the Hittite

A Hittite; one of David's thirty mighty men; husband of Bathsheba; killed at David's order to conceal the king's adultery.

Family

A Hittite (2 Samuel 11:3); husband of Bathsheba the daughter of Eliam. Listed among David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:39).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He died during the siege of Rabbah.

Life Synopsis

While Uriah was with the army at Rabbah, David saw Bathsheba, sent for her, and lay with her; she conceived (2 Samuel 11:1-5). David recalled him from the front on a pretext, asked after the war, and told him to go down to his house and wash his feet. "But Uriah slept at the door of the king's house with all the servants of his lord, and went not down to his house." Asked why, he answered: "The ark, and Israel, and Judah, abide in tents; and my lord Joab, and the servants of my lord, are encamped in the open fields; shall I then go into mine house, to eat and to drink, and to lie with my wife? as thou livest, and as thy soul liveth, I will not do this thing" (2 Samuel 11:6-11).

David kept him another day and made him drunk, and still he would not go home. Then David wrote to Joab, "Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle, and retire ye from him, that he may be smitten, and die" - and sent the letter by Uriah's own hand (2 Samuel 11:12-15). Joab did it, and Uriah died with others at the wall (2 Samuel 11:16-17, 11:24).

What They Did Right

  • Refused the comfort of his own house while the ark and the army were in the field, and swore he would not do it: 2 Samuel 11:11.
  • Kept that resolve even when made drunk by the king: 2 Samuel 11:13.
  • Carried his own death warrant without suspicion, and is named among David's thirty mighty men: 2 Samuel 11:14; 2 Samuel 23:39.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him and sets his integrity in deliberate contrast with the king's. The soldier would not go to his own wife while the army was in the field; the king had taken that soldier's wife while the army was in the field. Uriah is a Hittite - a foreigner - and he is the only man in the chapter who behaves honourably.

Significance

His death is the crime by which David's reign is finally measured. Nathan's charge names it directly: "thou hast killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword" (2 Samuel 12:9), and 1 Kings 15:5 makes it the single stated exception to David's lifelong obedience. He is named in the genealogy of Christ - not by name, but as the marker of Bathsheba: "her that had been the wife of Urias" (Matthew 1:6).

Death / Outcome

Killed at the wall of Rabbah, deliberately exposed at David's written order (2 Samuel 11:17, 11:24).

Scripture References

2 Samuel 11:1-27; 2 Samuel 12:9-10; 2 Samuel 23:39; 1 Kings 15:5; Matthew 1:6
—

Bathsheba

Daughter of Eliam and wife of Uriah the Hittite; taken by David; mother of Solomon.

Also called Bathshua

Family

Daughter of Eliam (2 Samuel 11:3); called the daughter of Ammiel in 1 Chronicles 3:5. Wife of Uriah, then of David. Mother of an unnamed child who died, and of Solomon, Shimea, Shobab, and Nathan (2 Samuel 12:24; 1 Chronicles 3:5).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

David saw her washing from the roof of the king's house, and enquired. "And David sent messengers, and took her; and she came in unto him, and he lay with her... and she returned unto her house." She sent word that she was with child (2 Samuel 11:2-5). After her husband was killed and she had mourned for him, David sent and fetched her to his house and she became his wife (2 Samuel 11:26-27).

The child born of the adultery fell sick and died despite David's fasting. "And David comforted Bathsheba his wife, and went in unto her, and lay with her: and she bare a son, and he called his name Solomon: and the Lord loved him" (2 Samuel 12:15-24).

When Adonijah moved to take the throne, Nathan sent her to David to remind him of his oath that Solomon should reign, and she did so; David swore it again, and Solomon was made king (1 Kings 1:11-31). She later carried Adonijah's request for Abishag to Solomon, who reacted with fury and had Adonijah killed (1 Kings 2:13-25).

What They Did Right

  • Interceded successfully for Solomon's succession at Nathan's prompting, and reminded David of his own oath: 1 Kings 1:15-21.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture assigns the initiative in the adultery entirely to David - he saw, he enquired, he sent, he took (2 Samuel 11:2-4) - and Nathan's parable casts her as the poor man's one ewe lamb, taken from him (2 Samuel 12:1-4). Nothing she said or did in the episode is recorded, and no charge is laid against her anywhere in Scripture. Interpreters have debated her degree of complicity; the text does not raise the question.

Character Assessment

Scripture is notably restrained about her. In the whole account of the adultery she has no recorded words except the four that announce her pregnancy, and every active verb belongs to David. Nathan's parable, which is God's own framing of the matter, treats her as the thing taken and Uriah as the man robbed. Her later appearances show a woman capable of decisive action on her son's behalf.

Significance

Mother of Solomon, and an ancestress of Christ - named in Matthew's genealogy, though by reference to her first husband: "of her that had been the wife of Urias" (Matthew 1:6). Psalm 51 is titled as David's psalm "when Nathan the prophet came unto him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba."

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Kings 2:19.

Scripture References

2 Samuel 11:2-27; 2 Samuel 12:24; 1 Kings 1:11-31; 1 Kings 2:13-19; 1 Chronicles 3:5; Psalms 51 title; Matthew 1:6
—

Nathan (the prophet)

A prophet in David's reign; brought the covenant promise of an everlasting throne and afterward the rebuke over Uriah; secured Solomon's succession. Not to be confused with Nathan the son of David.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He served from before the temple proposal until Solomon's accession.

Life Synopsis

When David proposed to build a house for the ark, Nathan at first said, "Go, do all that is in thine heart; for the Lord is with thee." That night the word of the Lord came to him with a different message, and he delivered it exactly: David would not build the house; God would build David a house, and establish the throne of his kingdom for ever (2 Samuel 7:1-17).

After Uriah's death "the Lord sent Nathan unto David." He told the parable of the rich man who took the poor man's one ewe lamb, and David's anger was greatly kindled: "the man that hath done this thing shall surely die." Nathan answered, "Thou art the man," and delivered the charge and the sentence - the sword would never depart from his house, and evil would be raised up against him out of his own house. When David said, "I have sinned against the Lord," Nathan replied that the Lord had put away his sin, but that the child would die (2 Samuel 12:1-14). He also named the child Solomon Jedidiah, beloved of the Lord (2 Samuel 12:25).

When Adonijah moved to seize the throne, Nathan took the initiative: he sent Bathsheba to David and came in after her to confirm her words, and secured the oath that put Solomon on the throne. He went with Zadok and Benaiah to anoint Solomon at Gihon (1 Kings 1:11-45).

What They Did Right

  • Corrected his own first answer when the word of the Lord came, and delivered the message God actually gave: 2 Samuel 7:3-17.
  • Rebuked the king to his face for adultery and murder, at obvious personal risk: 2 Samuel 12:1-12.
  • Told him the sin was put away as soon as he confessed, without withholding the consequences: 2 Samuel 12:13-14.
  • Acted decisively to secure the succession David had sworn: 1 Kings 1:11-27.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. His initial encouragement of the temple plan was given before he had the word of the Lord and was corrected the same night (2 Samuel 7:3-4). Scripture records the correction without rebuking him.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His confrontation of David is the model instance in the Old Testament of a prophet holding a king to account, and its method is as notable as its courage: he told a story that made the king pronounce his own sentence before he knew what he was doing. He also kept a working relationship with David afterward and was trusted with the succession.

Significance

Through him came the Davidic covenant of 2 Samuel 7:12-16, the foundation of messianic hope. He is named among those who recorded the acts of David (1 Chronicles 29:29) and of Solomon (2 Chronicles 9:29), and had a hand in the ordering of temple music (2 Chronicles 29:25).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 29:25.

Scripture References

2 Samuel 7:1-17; 2 Samuel 12:1-25; 1 Kings 1:8-45; 1 Chronicles 17:1-15; 1 Chronicles 29:29; 2 Chronicles 9:29; 2 Chronicles 29:25; Psalms 51 title
—

Amnon

David's firstborn; raped his half-sister Tamar and was killed two years later by her brother Absalom.

Family

Firstborn of David by Ahinoam of Jezreel (2 Samuel 3:2); half-brother of Absalom and Tamar.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He was killed two full years after the rape (2 Samuel 13:23).

Life Synopsis

Amnon loved Tamar, his half-sister, and fell sick with frustration because she was a virgin and he could do nothing to her. His cousin Jonadab, "a very subtil man," advised him to feign illness and ask that Tamar be sent to prepare food for him (2 Samuel 13:1-5).

David sent her. When she brought the cakes, Amnon sent everyone out and took hold of her. She pleaded: "Nay, my brother, do not force me; for no such thing ought to be done in Israel... whither shall I cause my shame to go? and as for thee, thou shalt be as one of the fools in Israel. Now therefore, I pray thee, speak unto the king; for he will not withhold me from thee." He would not listen, and forced her (2 Samuel 13:6-14).

"Then Amnon hated her exceedingly; so that the hatred wherewith he hated her was greater than the love wherewith he had loved her." He had her put out and the door bolted after her, ignoring her protest that this wrong was greater than the other (2 Samuel 13:15-18).

David was very wroth but did nothing. Absalom said nothing to Amnon, good or bad, but hated him. Two years later, at a sheepshearing feast, Absalom's servants killed Amnon at his command when his heart was merry with wine (2 Samuel 13:21-29).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Forced his half-sister, refusing her plea, in an act Scripture describes as folly that ought not to be done in Israel: 2 Samuel 13:12-14.
  • Hated her afterward more than he had loved her, and had her thrown out and the door bolted: 2 Samuel 13:15-17.
  • Refused to hear her protest that putting her away was a greater evil than what he had already done: 2 Samuel 13:16.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned. Scripture gives the account in unusual detail and gives Tamar's arguments in full, so that the reader sees exactly what he refused to hear. The observation that his hatred afterward exceeded his love is one of the sharpest psychological notes in the Old Testament.

Significance

His crime is the first working out of Nathan's sentence that the sword would not depart from David's house and that evil would be raised up out of it (2 Samuel 12:10-11). David's failure to act on it drove Absalom to act instead, which led directly to the rebellion.

Death / Outcome

Killed by Absalom's servants at the sheepshearing in Baalhazor, at Absalom's command (2 Samuel 13:28-29).

Scripture References

2 Samuel 3:2; 2 Samuel 13:1-39; 1 Chronicles 3:1
—

Tamar (daughter of David)

Daughter of David and full sister of Absalom; raped by her half-brother Amnon and left desolate. Not to be confused with Tamar the daughter-in-law of Judah.

Family

Daughter of David; full sister of Absalom, both children of Maacah (2 Samuel 13:1; 2 Samuel 3:3). Absalom later named his own daughter after her (2 Samuel 14:27).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

She was a fair virgin, sister to Absalom. Sent by David at Amnon's request, she made cakes in his sight and brought them to his chamber. When he took hold of her she reasoned with him at length - that no such thing ought to be done in Israel, that it was folly, that she would have nowhere to carry her shame, and that if he asked the king she would not be withheld from him. "Howbeit he would not hearken unto her voice: but, being stronger than she, forced her" (2 Samuel 13:1-14).

When he then ordered her out, she said, "There is no cause: this evil in sending me away is greater than the other that thou didst unto me." He would not hear her and had the door bolted. She put ashes on her head, rent her garment of divers colours - the dress of the king's virgin daughters - laid her hand on her head, and went crying. Absalom told her to hold her peace and not regard it, "So Tamar remained desolate in her brother Absalom's house" (2 Samuel 13:15-20).

What They Did Right

  • Resisted and reasoned at length before being overpowered, naming the act as folly and appealing to what ought not to be done in Israel: 2 Samuel 13:12-13.
  • Protested the second wrong as greater than the first: 2 Samuel 13:16.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records nothing against her. The text is explicit that she was forced by a man stronger than she, after refusing him.

Character Assessment

Scripture gives her more recorded speech than most women in the historical books, and every word of it is an argument against what was done to her. It then records that her father was angry and did nothing, and that her brother told her to be quiet, and that she remained desolate. The narrative offers no verdict, but it lets the sequence stand: she was the only person in the account who said the right thing at the time.

Significance

The wrong done to her set in motion Amnon's murder, Absalom's exile, and the rebellion that nearly cost David his throne - the working out of Nathan's word. Absalom named his only daughter Tamar, which is the one memorial Scripture records of her (2 Samuel 14:27).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Samuel 13:20, remaining desolate in Absalom's house.

Scripture References

2 Samuel 13:1-22; 2 Samuel 14:27
—

Jonadab

Son of Shimeah, David's brother; a very subtle man; advised Amnon how to get Tamar alone, and afterward reassured David that only Amnon was dead.

Family

Son of Shimeah, David's brother (2 Samuel 13:3); cousin of Amnon, Absalom, and Tamar.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"But Amnon had a friend, whose name was Jonadab, the son of Shimeah David's brother: and Jonadab was a very subtil man." Seeing Amnon lean and asking why, he heard that Amnon loved Tamar, and gave him the plan: lie down, feign sickness, and ask the king to send Tamar to make him food (2 Samuel 13:3-5).

After Absalom killed Amnon, a report reached David that all the king's sons were dead. Jonadab said, "Let not my lord suppose that they have slain all the young men the king's sons; for Amnon only is dead: for by the appointment of Absalom this hath been determined from the day that he forced his sister Tamar." He was right, and the sons arrived as he spoke (2 Samuel 13:32-35).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. He gave David accurate information in a panic. Scripture records that it was correct without commending him for it.

What They Did Wrong

  • Supplied the plan by which Amnon got Tamar alone: 2 Samuel 13:5. Scripture calls him subtil and records the advice without an explicit condemnation, but the whole crime followed from it.
  • His speech after the murder shows he had known Absalom's intention from the day of the rape: 2 Samuel 13:32. He had said nothing to anyone for two years.

Character Assessment

Scripture describes him in three words - a very subtil man - and then shows exactly what that meant. He devised the means of the rape and he knew of the coming murder for two years and warned no one, and he is present at court afterward with useful information. No verdict is stated. None is needed.

Significance

His advice is the hinge on which the whole collapse of David's household turns.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Samuel 13:35.

Scripture References

2 Samuel 13:3-5, 13:32-35
—

Absalom

Third son of David; killed Amnon for the rape of Tamar; rebelled against his father, drove him from Jerusalem, and was killed by Joab.

Family

Son of David by Maacah daughter of Talmai king of Geshur (2 Samuel 3:3); full brother of Tamar. Father of three sons and a daughter named Tamar (2 Samuel 14:27).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He fled to Geshur for three years, spent two more in Jerusalem before seeing the king, and rebelled after forty years - a figure disputed in the manuscripts (2 Samuel 13:38; 2 Samuel 14:28; 2 Samuel 15:7).

Life Synopsis

"In all Israel there was none to be so much praised as Absalom for his beauty: from the sole of his foot even to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him" (2 Samuel 14:25).

After Amnon raped Tamar, Absalom said nothing to him, good or bad, and took his sister into his house. Two years later he had Amnon killed at a sheepshearing feast and fled to his grandfather in Geshur for three years (2 Samuel 13:20-38). Joab engineered his recall through the woman of Tekoah, but David would not see him for two more years. Absalom set Joab's barley field on fire to force a meeting, and was at last kissed by the king (2 Samuel 14:1-33).

He then prepared chariots and horsemen and fifty men to run before him, rose early to stand beside the gate, and intercepted everyone with a suit. "Absalom said moreover, Oh that I were made judge in the land, that every man which hath any suit or cause might come unto me, and I would do him justice!" He kissed those who bowed to him. "So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel" (2 Samuel 15:1-6).

He had himself proclaimed king at Hebron, and David fled Jerusalem barefoot and weeping. On Ahithophel's counsel he went in to his father's concubines on the roof in the sight of all Israel (2 Samuel 15:7-16:22). He then took Hushai's advice over Ahithophel's, which cost him the war. In the battle in the wood of Ephraim his head caught in an oak and the mule went from under him; Joab, told of it, thrust three darts through his heart while he was still alive, disregarding David's charge to deal gently with the young man (2 Samuel 17:1-18:15).

He was cast into a pit in the wood and a great heap of stones laid on him. He had built himself a pillar in the king's dale in his lifetime, "for he said, I have no son to keep my name in remembrance" (2 Samuel 18:17-18). David's cry when the news came is one of the most quoted in Scripture: "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!" (2 Samuel 18:33).

What They Did Right

  • He sheltered his violated sister in his own house: 2 Samuel 13:20. Scripture records the act without stating a motive.
  • Beyond this, no specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Murdered Amnon by ambush at a feast, having planned it for two years: 2 Samuel 13:28-29.
  • Stole the hearts of the men of Israel by systematic flattery and by implying his father's justice was unavailable: 2 Samuel 15:2-6.
  • Rebelled against his father and the Lord's anointed, and drove him from Jerusalem: 2 Samuel 15:10-14.
  • Went in to his father's concubines publicly on the roof, fulfilling Nathan's word: 2 Samuel 16:21-22; compare 2 Samuel 12:11.
  • Sought his father's life: 2 Samuel 17:1-4.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents him as gifted, handsome, patient, and entirely without scruple. His one arguably creditable act - sheltering Tamar - is recorded in the same breath as the two years of silence in which he planned a murder. What the narrative emphasises is his method: he did not seize the kingdom by force at first but by standing at the gate every morning being sympathetic. The judgment on him is left largely to events, and to the father who mourned him past all propriety.

Significance

His rebellion is the fullest working out of Nathan's sentence on David's house, including the specific word about the concubines (2 Samuel 12:11-12; 2 Samuel 16:22). Several psalms are associated with the flight, notably Psalm 3, titled as David's psalm when he fled from Absalom his son. David's mourning for him, and Joab's rebuke of it, is one of the sharpest treatments of grief and duty in Scripture.

Death / Outcome

Caught by his head in an oak in the wood of Ephraim and killed by Joab with three darts; buried under a heap of stones in the wood (2 Samuel 18:9-17).

Scripture References

2 Samuel 3:3; 2 Samuel 13:1-19:8; 1 Chronicles 3:2; Psalms 3 title
—

Ahithophel

David's counsellor, whose advice was esteemed as the oracle of God; joined Absalom's rebellion and hanged himself when his counsel was rejected.

Family

The Gilonite, of Giloh (2 Samuel 15:12). His son Eliam was one of the mighty men (2 Samuel 23:34), and Bathsheba was the daughter of Eliam (2 Samuel 11:3), which would make Ahithophel her grandfather - a connection Scripture states in pieces without drawing it together, and which is likely but not certain.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"And the counsel of Ahithophel, which he counselled in those days, was as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God: so was all the counsel of Ahithophel both with David and with Absalom" (2 Samuel 16:23).

He was with Absalom at Hebron when the conspiracy began, and David's response on hearing it was to pray, "O Lord, I pray thee, turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness" (2 Samuel 15:12, 15:31). He advised Absalom to go in to his father's concubines publicly, to make himself abhorred of his father and strengthen his followers (2 Samuel 16:20-22).

He then advised an immediate pursuit with twelve thousand men that night, to strike David while he was weary and weak-handed, kill the king alone, and bring the people back. "And the saying pleased Absalom well, and all the elders of Israel." But Absalom called for Hushai, who argued for delay - and "the Lord had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that the Lord might bring evil upon Absalom" (2 Samuel 17:1-14).

"And when Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his ass, and arose, and gat him home to his house, to his city, and put his household in order, and hanged himself, and died, and was buried in the sepulchre of his father" (2 Samuel 17:23).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. His counsel is described as being like the oracle of God (2 Samuel 16:23), which is a statement about its quality and reputation rather than a commendation of the man.

What They Did Wrong

  • Betrayed David and joined Absalom's conspiracy: 2 Samuel 15:12, 15:31.
  • Advised Absalom to take his father's concubines publicly: 2 Samuel 16:21.
  • Advised the immediate killing of the king he had served: 2 Samuel 17:1-3.
  • Took his own life when his advice was set aside: 2 Samuel 17:23.

Character Assessment

A man whose judgment was the best in the kingdom and whose loyalty failed completely. Scripture never states his motive; the possible family connection through Bathsheba has often been proposed as an explanation and is not asserted in the text. His end is recorded with unusual procedural calm - he saddled the ass, went home, set his house in order, and hanged himself - which reads as the act of a man who knew exactly what the rejection of his counsel meant.

Significance

His defection is treated in the Psalms as the type of betrayal by a trusted friend: "Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me" (Psalms 41:9), which Christ applies to Judas (John 13:18). He is one of only two people in Scripture recorded as taking their own life by hanging, the other being Judas (Matthew 27:5).

Death / Outcome

Hanged himself at his house in Giloh after his counsel was rejected, and was buried in his father's sepulchre (2 Samuel 17:23).

Scripture References

2 Samuel 15:12, 15:31; 2 Samuel 16:20-23; 2 Samuel 17:1-23; 2 Samuel 23:34; 1 Chronicles 27:33-34; Psalms 41:9; Psalms 55:12-14
—

Hushai

The Archite, David's friend; sent back to Absalom to defeat Ahithophel's counsel, and did so.

Family

An Archite (2 Samuel 15:32); called "the king's friend" (2 Samuel 15:37; 1 Chronicles 27:33).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

He met David at the top of the mount with his coat rent and earth on his head. David told him he would be a burden if he came along, but could serve by returning to the city and saying to Absalom, "I will be thy servant," so as to defeat Ahithophel's counsel, passing word through Zadok and Abiathar (2 Samuel 15:32-36).

He went to Absalom and declared, "God save the king." Absalom challenged him - is this thy kindness to thy friend? - and Hushai answered that he would serve whom the Lord and the people chose (2 Samuel 16:16-19).

When Ahithophel advised immediate pursuit, Absalom called for Hushai's opinion. He argued that David and his men were mighty and chafed in their minds like a bear robbed of her whelps, that David was a man of war who would not lodge with the people, and that a defeat at the outset would be catastrophic; instead all Israel should be gathered first, with Absalom himself going to battle. "And Absalom and all the men of Israel said, The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel" (2 Samuel 17:5-14). He sent word to David by Zadok and Abiathar to cross Jordan that night.

What They Did Right

  • Went back into danger at David's word rather than taking the easier course of accompanying him: 2 Samuel 15:34.
  • Gave counsel that saved David's life and the kingdom: 2 Samuel 17:7-14.
  • Sent immediate warning to David to cross Jordan without delay: 2 Samuel 17:15-16.

What They Did Wrong

  • He deceived Absalom, professing loyalty he did not have: 2 Samuel 16:16-19. Scripture records the deception as David's plan and as the means by which the Lord defeated Ahithophel's counsel (2 Samuel 17:14), and passes no separate judgment on the ethics of it.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his loyalty and his effectiveness, and attributes the outcome directly to God: the Lord had appointed to defeat Ahithophel's counsel. The deception is treated as part of that appointment rather than as a fault, and this reference notes that the text takes no separate position on the method.

Significance

His counsel saved David's life at the point where Ahithophel's plan would have ended the reign that night. He is listed among David's officials as the king's companion (1 Chronicles 27:33). His son Baana was one of Solomon's officers (1 Kings 4:16).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Samuel 17:15.

Scripture References

2 Samuel 15:32-37; 2 Samuel 16:16-19; 2 Samuel 17:5-16; 1 Chronicles 27:33
—

The woman of Tekoah

Unnamed. A wise woman of Tekoah, sent by Joab with a feigned case to move David to recall Absalom.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Joab perceived that the king's heart was toward Absalom and fetched a wise woman from Tekoah, telling her to feign mourning and putting words in her mouth (2 Samuel 14:1-3).

She told David she was a widow whose two sons had fought in the field with none to part them, so that one killed the other; and now the family demanded the survivor for the avenger of blood, which would quench her one remaining coal and leave her husband neither name nor remainder. David promised to protect the son. She then turned the case on him: "Wherefore then hast thou thought such a thing against the people of God?... For we must needs die, and are as water spilt on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again; neither doth God respect any person: yet doth he devise means, that his banished be not expelled from him" (2 Samuel 14:4-14).

David asked, "Is not the hand of Joab with thee in all this?" She acknowledged it: "as thy soul liveth, my lord the king, none can turn to the right hand or to the left from ought that my lord the king hath spoken: for thy servant Joab, he bade me" (2 Samuel 14:18-20). David then sent Joab to bring Absalom back.

What They Did Right

  • Delivered a difficult argument with skill and, when challenged, admitted at once who had sent her: 2 Samuel 14:19-20.

What They Did Wrong

  • She presented a fabricated case to the king as a real one: 2 Samuel 14:4-7. Scripture assigns the plan to Joab, who put the words in her mouth (2 Samuel 14:3, 14:19), and passes no judgment on her part in it.

Character Assessment

Scripture calls her a wise woman and shows why. She is an instrument of Joab's manipulation, and she is also the speaker of one of the most striking theological sentences in the historical books - that God devises means so that his banished are not expelled from him. The text records both without weighing them against each other.

Significance

Her intervention brought Absalom back to Jerusalem, which led to the rebellion. Her words in 2 Samuel 14:14 about God devising means for the banished are frequently cited as an Old Testament anticipation of reconciliation.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Samuel 14:20.

Scripture References

2 Samuel 14:1-20
—

Ittai the Gittite

A foreigner from Gath, newly come to David, who refused to leave him in the flight from Absalom and was given command of a third of the army.

Family

A Gittite - a man of Gath (2 Samuel 15:19).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He had come to David only the day before, or shortly before, the rebellion (2 Samuel 15:20).

Life Synopsis

As David left Jerusalem, six hundred Gittites passed on before the king. David said to Ittai, "Wherefore goest thou also with us? return to thy place, and abide with the king: for thou art a stranger, and also an exile... whereas thou camest but yesterday, should I this day make thee go up and down with us? seeing I go whither I may, return thou, and take back thy brethren: mercy and truth be with thee."

Ittai answered, "As the Lord liveth, and as my lord the king liveth, surely in what place my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be." David said, "Go and pass over." He passed over with all his men and all the little ones with him (2 Samuel 15:19-22). When the army was divided for battle, David put a third part under Ittai's command alongside Joab and Abishai (2 Samuel 18:2).

What They Did Right

  • Refused the king's own permission to leave, and bound himself to him in life or death: 2 Samuel 15:21.
  • Was trusted with a third of the army within days of that declaration: 2 Samuel 18:2.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His declaration is the more striking for his position: a Philistine from Goliath's own city, an exile with no stake in Israel's dynastic quarrel, who had been with David a matter of days, committing himself to a king in flight. It is set in the narrative immediately alongside Ahithophel's defection.

Significance

His loyalty, like the Gittites' generally, is part of a pattern in David's reign in which foreigners - Uriah the Hittite, Ittai the Gittite, the Cherethites and Pelethites - show conspicuous fidelity while Israelites rebel. He commanded a third of the force that defeated Absalom.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Samuel 18:12.

Scripture References

2 Samuel 15:18-22; 2 Samuel 18:2, 18:5, 18:12
—

Shimei (son of Gera)

A Benjamite of the house of Saul who cursed David and threw stones at him during the flight from Absalom; pardoned, then executed under Solomon for breaking his parole.

Family

Son of Gera, a Benjamite of Bahurim, of the family of the house of Saul (2 Samuel 16:5).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He was executed early in Solomon's reign, after three years under restriction (1 Kings 2:39).

Life Synopsis

As David fled, Shimei came out cursing, casting stones at him and at all his servants, and crying, "Come out, come out, thou bloody man, and thou man of Belial: the Lord hath returned upon thee all the blood of the house of Saul" (2 Samuel 16:5-8). Abishai asked to take off his head; David refused: "Let him alone, and let him curse; for the Lord hath bidden him. It may be that the Lord will look on mine affliction, and that the Lord will requite me good for his cursing this day" (2 Samuel 16:9-12).

When David returned in triumph, Shimei hurried down with a thousand Benjamites to meet him, fell before him, and confessed: "Let not my lord impute iniquity unto me... for thy servant doth know that I have sinned." Abishai again asked to kill him; David again refused and swore he would not die (2 Samuel 19:16-23).

David's dying charge to Solomon named him: he had cursed with a grievous curse, and though David had sworn not to kill him, Solomon was to bring his hoar head down to the grave with blood (1 Kings 2:8-9). Solomon confined him to Jerusalem on pain of death; three years later he went to Gath to recover runaway servants, and Solomon had him executed (1 Kings 2:36-46).

What They Did Right

  • Came down and confessed his fault before David when the king returned, and did so first of all the house of Joseph: 2 Samuel 19:16-20. Scripture records the confession without stating whether it was sincere.
  • Beyond this, no specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Cursed the king and threw stones at him and his servants: 2 Samuel 16:5-6.
  • Charged David with the blood of Saul's house, a charge Scripture elsewhere does not support: 2 Samuel 16:8.
  • Broke the terms of his confinement after swearing to them: 1 Kings 2:42-43.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the cursing, the pardon, and the eventual execution, and never states whether his repentance was genuine. David's own reading at the time was that God might be in it, which is why he forbade reprisal twice. His death came not for the cursing but for breaking an oath he had sworn before the Lord, which is how Solomon framed it.

Significance

David's refusal to answer his cursing is one of the clearest instances in Scripture of a man leaving vengeance with God under provocation. His execution is part of the settling of accounts by which Solomon secured the kingdom.

Death / Outcome

Executed by Benaiah at Solomon's command for breaking the terms of his confinement (1 Kings 2:46).

Scripture References

2 Samuel 16:5-14; 2 Samuel 19:16-23; 1 Kings 2:8-9, 2:36-46
—

Amasa

David's nephew; commanded Absalom's army, was pardoned and appointed captain in Joab's place, and was murdered by Joab.

Family

Son of Ithra (or Jether) by Abigail, David's sister (2 Samuel 17:25; 1 Chronicles 2:17); cousin of David, Joab, and Absalom.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Absalom made him captain of the host in place of Joab (2 Samuel 17:25). After the rebellion failed, David sent word to him: "Art thou not of my bone, and of my flesh? God do so to me, and more also, if thou be not captain of the host before me continually in the room of Joab" (2 Samuel 19:13).

When Sheba revolted, David ordered him to assemble Judah in three days. He took longer than the set time, and David sent Abishai ahead lest Sheba escape. At the great stone in Gibeon Joab met him. "And Joab said to Amasa, Art thou in health, my brother? And Joab took Amasa by the beard with the right hand to kiss him. But Amasa took no heed to the sword that was in Joab's hand: so he smote him therewith in the fifth rib, and shed out his bowels to the ground." He was left wallowing in the highway until a man moved him out of the road and covered him with a cloth, because everyone who came by stood still (2 Samuel 20:4-12).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. Scripture records his commands and his death but no assessment of his conduct.

What They Did Wrong

  • He commanded the army of a rebellion against the Lord's anointed: 2 Samuel 17:25. Scripture records this without a separate condemnation, and David pardoned him and promoted him.
  • He exceeded the time set for assembling Judah: 2 Samuel 20:5. The text records the delay without explaining it.

Character Assessment

Scripture offers no verdict on him. He is chiefly the occasion of two decisions by others: David's remarkable pardon of the rebel commander, and Joab's murder of the man appointed over him. David's dying charge names his blood along with Abner's as a debt unsettled (1 Kings 2:5).

Significance

David's appointment of him was an attempt to break Joab's hold on the army and to reconcile the men who had followed Absalom. Joab's murder of him ended both.

Death / Outcome

Murdered by Joab at the great stone in Gibeon, struck under the fifth rib while being greeted with a kiss (2 Samuel 20:9-10).

Scripture References

2 Samuel 17:25; 2 Samuel 19:13; 2 Samuel 20:4-12; 1 Kings 2:5, 2:32; 1 Chronicles 2:17
—

Sheba (son of Bichri)

A Benjamite, a man of Belial, who raised a revolt against David after Absalom's defeat and was beheaded by the people of Abel.

Family

Son of Bichri, a Benjamite (2 Samuel 20:1).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

In the quarrel between Judah and Israel over bringing the king back, "there happened to be there a man of Belial, whose name was Sheba, the son of Bichri, a Benjamite: and he blew a trumpet, and said, We have no part in David, neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse: every man to his tents, O Israel." All the men of Israel went up after him (2 Samuel 20:1-2). David judged that he would do more harm than Absalom had.

Amasa was sent to gather Judah and was slow; Joab murdered him on the way and took command. Sheba was pursued to Abel of Bethmaachah and besieged there. A wise woman called from the wall and negotiated with Joab, who said he wanted only the one man. "Then the woman went unto all the people in her wisdom. And they cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri, and cast it out to Joab" (2 Samuel 20:14-22).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Raised revolt against the king, calling Israel away from David: 2 Samuel 20:1. Scripture calls him a man of Belial in introducing him.

Character Assessment

Uniformly negative in the brief record. His slogan - "We have no part in David... every man to his tents, O Israel" - is recorded verbatim, and it matters: the same words are used again when the northern tribes finally break with the house of David under Rehoboam (1 Kings 12:16).

Significance

His revolt was the last crisis of David's reign, and his rallying cry became the formula of the northern secession a generation later. The episode also occasioned Joab's murder of Amasa.

Death / Outcome

Beheaded by the people of Abel of Bethmaachah and his head thrown over the wall to Joab (2 Samuel 20:22).

Scripture References

2 Samuel 20:1-22; compare 1 Kings 12:16
—

The wise woman of Abel

Unnamed. A woman of Abel of Bethmaachah who negotiated with Joab from the city wall and saved the city by having Sheba beheaded.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

Joab was battering the wall to throw it down. "Then cried a wise woman out of the city, Hear, hear; say, I pray you, unto Joab, Come near hither, that I may speak with thee." She reminded him of the city's standing: "They were wont to speak in old time, saying, They shall surely ask counsel at Abel: and so they ended the matter. I am one of them that are peaceable and faithful in Israel: thou seekest to destroy a city and a mother in Israel: why wilt thou swallow up the inheritance of the Lord?"

Joab denied wanting to destroy anything and named his terms: only Sheba. She answered, "Behold, his head shall be thrown to thee over the wall." She went to the people in her wisdom, they beheaded Sheba, and Joab blew the trumpet and withdrew (2 Samuel 20:16-22).

What They Did Right

  • Opened a negotiation instead of waiting for the wall to fall: 2 Samuel 20:16-19.
  • Argued from the city's reputation and from the inheritance of the Lord, and moved a man not easily moved: 2 Samuel 20:18-19.
  • Persuaded the whole city to act, and saved it: 2 Samuel 20:22.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture calls her a wise woman and records nothing against her. She is the second unnamed woman in the books of Samuel whose intervention prevents a slaughter, the first being Abigail, and like Abigail she argues rather than pleads.

Significance

Her negotiation ended the last revolt of David's reign without the destruction of a city. Her description of Abel as "a mother in Israel" and her appeal to the inheritance of the Lord preserve a glimpse of how a settled Israelite town understood itself.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Samuel 20:22.

Scripture References

2 Samuel 20:16-22
—

Barzillai

A very great and aged Gileadite of Rogelim who provisioned David at Mahanaim and declined the king's offer of a place at court.

Family

A Gileadite of Rogelim (2 Samuel 17:27). His son Chimham went with David in his place (2 Samuel 19:37-40).

Chronology

"Barzillai was a very aged man, even fourscore years old" (2 Samuel 19:32).

Life Synopsis

When David reached Mahanaim in flight, Barzillai with Shobi and Machir brought beds, basons, earthen vessels, wheat, barley, flour, parched corn, beans, lentiles, honey, butter, sheep, and cheese, "for they said, The people is hungry, and weary, and thirsty, in the wilderness" (2 Samuel 17:27-29).

He came down to conduct the king over Jordan on the return. David invited him to Jerusalem: "Come thou over with me, and I will feed thee with me in Jerusalem." He declined: "How long have I to live, that I should go up with the king unto Jerusalem? I am this day fourscore years old: and can I discern between good and evil? can thy servant taste what I eat or what I drink? can I hear any more the voice of singing men and singing women? wherefore then should thy servant be yet a burden unto my lord the king?" He asked only to go back and die in his own city by the graves of his parents, and offered Chimham to go instead. David kissed him and blessed him (2 Samuel 19:31-39).

What They Did Right

  • Provisioned David and his people generously and at his own risk while the outcome of the rebellion was still uncertain: 2 Samuel 17:27-29.
  • Declined reward for it, asking nothing for himself: 2 Samuel 19:34-37.
  • David remembered him on his deathbed and charged Solomon to show kindness to his sons: 1 Kings 2:7.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His refusal of the king's table is one of the most self-aware speeches in the Old Testament: he declines not from modesty but because at eighty he would not be able to enjoy it and would only be a burden. He supported the king when supporting him was dangerous, and asked for nothing when it was safe.

Significance

His provisioning sustained David's forces through the campaign against Absalom. David's dying charge to Solomon to let his sons be among those who eat at the king's table is one of only two positive charges in that speech (1 Kings 2:7). Ezra 2:61 records priests who took their name from his daughters.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded; he returned to his own place to die there (2 Samuel 19:37-39).

Scripture References

2 Samuel 17:27-29; 2 Samuel 19:31-40; 1 Kings 2:7; Ezra 2:61
—

Zadok

Priest under David alongside Abiathar; stayed loyal in Absalom's rebellion, anointed Solomon, and became sole high priest.

Family

Son of Ahitub, of the line of Eleazar (2 Samuel 8:17; 1 Chronicles 6:8, 6:53); father of Ahimaaz (2 Samuel 15:27).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He served through David's reign and into Solomon's.

Life Synopsis

Zadok served as priest with Abiathar throughout David's reign (2 Samuel 8:17; 2 Samuel 20:25). He was among those who brought up the ark to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 15:11).

When David fled from Absalom, Zadok and the Levites carried the ark out of the city. David sent it back: "Carry back the ark of God into the city: if I shall find favour in the eyes of the Lord, he will bring me again, and shew me both it, and his habitation." Zadok returned with it and, with Abiathar, acted as David's intelligence in Jerusalem, sending word by their sons Ahimaaz and Jonathan at considerable risk (2 Samuel 15:24-36; 2 Samuel 17:15-21).

When Adonijah moved for the throne, Zadok was not with him (1 Kings 1:8). David sent him with Nathan and Benaiah to anoint Solomon at Gihon, and Zadok took the horn of oil out of the tabernacle and anointed him (1 Kings 1:32-39). After Abiathar was removed, "Zadok the priest did the king put in the room of Abiathar" (1 Kings 2:35).

What They Did Right

  • Carried the ark out of the city and obeyed at once when told to carry it back: 2 Samuel 15:24-29.
  • Served as David's informant in occupied Jerusalem at risk to himself and his son: 2 Samuel 15:35-36; 2 Samuel 17:15-21.
  • Refused to join Adonijah's attempt on the throne: 1 Kings 1:8.
  • Anointed Solomon at David's command: 1 Kings 1:39.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him across a long career spanning two reigns and two attempted usurpations. His loyalty was tested twice, under Absalom and under Adonijah, and held both times.

Significance

His appointment in Abiathar's place transferred the high priesthood from the line of Ithamar to the line of Eleazar and fulfilled the word against Eli's house (1 Kings 2:27, 2:35). The priesthood remained in his line, and Ezekiel's vision of the restored temple assigns the priestly service to "the sons of Zadok" (Ezekiel 44:15).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Kings 4:4.

Scripture References

2 Samuel 8:17; 2 Samuel 15:24-36; 2 Samuel 17:15-21; 2 Samuel 19:11; 1 Kings 1:8-45; 1 Kings 2:35; 1 Kings 4:4; 1 Chronicles 6:8, 6:53; 1 Chronicles 15:11; Ezekiel 44:15
—

Araunah

A Jebusite whose threshingfloor David bought as the site of the altar that stayed the plague. Called Ornan in Chronicles.

Also called Ornan

Family

A Jebusite (2 Samuel 24:16); he had four sons (1 Chronicles 21:20).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. At the end of David's reign, after the numbering of Israel.

Life Synopsis

The angel of the Lord was by the threshingfloor of Araunah when the plague was stayed, and Gad told David to rear an altar there. Araunah looked out, saw the king coming, and bowed himself to the ground. Told why David had come, he offered everything free: "Let my lord the king take and offer up what seemeth good unto him: behold, here be oxen for burnt sacrifice, and threshing instruments and other instruments of the oxen for wood... All these things did Araunah, as a king, give unto the king."

David refused: "Nay; but I will surely buy it of thee at a price: neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the Lord my God of that which doth cost me nothing." He bought the threshingfloor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver, built the altar, and the plague was stayed (2 Samuel 24:16-25). 1 Chronicles 21:25 gives six hundred shekels of gold by weight for the place - a difference from the fifty shekels of silver in 2 Samuel 24:24 that Scripture does not explain and that is noted here rather than harmonized.

What They Did Right

  • Offered his threshingfloor, his oxen, and his implements to the king without charge, and freely: 2 Samuel 24:22-23.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records generosity and nothing against him. He is a Jebusite - a member of the people who held Jerusalem before David took it - and the last recorded act of David's reign takes place on his land, with his agreement, and at his suggestion refused.

Significance

His threshingfloor became the site of the temple: "Then Solomon began to build the house of the Lord at Jerusalem in mount Moriah, where the Lord appeared unto David his father, in the place that David had prepared in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite" (2 Chronicles 3:1). David's refusal to offer God what cost him nothing is one of the most frequently cited sentences in the historical books.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 3:1.

Scripture References

2 Samuel 24:16-25; 1 Chronicles 21:15-28; 2 Chronicles 3:1

Solomon and the Divided Kingdom

—

Adonijah

Fourth son of David; attempted the throne in David's old age and again after Solomon's accession, and was executed.

Family

Son of David by Haggith (2 Samuel 3:4); "his father had not displeased him at any time in saying, Why hast thou done so? and he also was a very goodly man" (1 Kings 1:6).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He acted at the end of David's reign and was killed early in Solomon's.

Life Synopsis

"Then Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, I will be king," and prepared chariots, horsemen, and fifty men to run before him - exactly as Absalom had done (1 Kings 1:5). Joab and Abiathar supported him; Zadok, Benaiah, Nathan, and the mighty men did not. He held a sacrificial feast at Enrogel and invited all the king's sons except Solomon (1 Kings 1:7-10).

Nathan and Bathsheba went to David, who swore that Solomon should reign. Solomon was anointed at Gihon, and the noise reached Adonijah's feast. His guests scattered, and he fled and caught hold of the horns of the altar. Solomon said, "If he will shew himself a worthy man, there shall not an hair of him fall to the earth: but if wickedness shall be found in him, he shall die," and sent him home (1 Kings 1:41-53).

Afterward he came to Bathsheba and asked her to request Abishag the Shunammite for him as wife, prefacing it: "Thou knowest that the kingdom was mine, and that all Israel set their faces on me, that I should reign: howbeit the kingdom is turned about, and is become my brother's." Solomon understood the request as a claim on the throne - "ask for him the kingdom also" - and sent Benaiah to kill him (1 Kings 2:13-25).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Exalted himself to be king while his father lived and against David's oath concerning Solomon: 1 Kings 1:5, 1:13.
  • Excluded Solomon, Nathan, Zadok, and Benaiah from his feast, which shows the attempt was known to be illegitimate: 1 Kings 1:9-10, 1:26.
  • Asked for Abishag after being spared, which Solomon judged a renewed claim on the kingdom: 1 Kings 2:17, 2:22.

Character Assessment

Scripture offers no verdict in words, but supplies two damning observations: he copied Absalom's method exactly, and his father had never once in his life asked him why he did anything (1 Kings 1:6). That note about David's parenting is among the sharpest asides in the historical books. He was given a plain condition for his life and did not keep it.

Significance

His attempt forced the succession into the open and produced Solomon's anointing. His second request occasioned the removal of Abiathar and the deaths of Joab and Shimei, by which Solomon secured the kingdom (1 Kings 2:12-46).

Death / Outcome

Killed by Benaiah at Solomon's command (1 Kings 2:25).

Scripture References

2 Samuel 3:4; 1 Kings 1:5-53; 1 Kings 2:13-25; 1 Chronicles 3:2
—

Abishag

A Shunammite virgin brought to cherish David in his old age; afterward the occasion of Adonijah's death.

Family

A Shunammite (1 Kings 1:3).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

David was old and could get no heat, so his servants sought a fair young virgin to cherish him and lie in his bosom. "So they sought for a fair damsel throughout all the coasts of Israel, and found Abishag a Shunammite, and brought her to the king. And the damsel was very fair, and cherished the king, and ministered to him: but the king knew her not" (1 Kings 1:1-4). She was present when Bathsheba and Nathan came about the succession (1 Kings 1:15).

After David's death Adonijah asked for her in marriage through Bathsheba, and Solomon treated the request as a bid for the throne and had Adonijah killed (1 Kings 2:17-25).

What They Did Right

  • Cherished and ministered to the king: 1 Kings 1:4, 1:15. Scripture records the service without further comment.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Nothing she said is recorded, and no verdict is offered. Scripture is careful to state that David did not know her, which is what makes her position ambiguous afterward - and that ambiguity cost Adonijah his life.

Significance

A wife or concubine of a dead king carried a claim on his throne, which is why Solomon read Adonijah's request as he did (compare 2 Samuel 3:7; 2 Samuel 16:21-22). Her name is the hinge of the last act of David's succession.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Kings 2:22.

Scripture References

1 Kings 1:1-4, 1:15; 1 Kings 2:17-25
—

Benaiah

Son of Jehoiada; a mighty man of David's; captain of the guard, and made captain of the host by Solomon; executor of Solomon's judgments.

Family

Son of Jehoiada, a valiant man of Kabzeel (2 Samuel 23:20).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He served under David and Solomon.

Life Synopsis

"He slew two lionlike men of Moab: he went down also and slew a lion in the midst of a pit in time of snow." He also killed an Egyptian of great stature, plucking the spear out of his hand and killing him with it. He was honourable among the thirty and was set over David's guard (2 Samuel 23:20-23).

He refused to join Adonijah (1 Kings 1:8), and when David gave the order for Solomon's anointing he answered, "Amen: the Lord God of my lord the king say so too" (1 Kings 1:36). He went down with Zadok and Nathan and set Solomon on the mule.

Under Solomon he executed Adonijah, Joab, and Shimei, and was set over the host in Joab's place (1 Kings 2:25, 2:34-35, 2:46).

What They Did Right

  • Performed exceptional acts of courage recorded in detail: 2 Samuel 23:20-21.
  • Stayed loyal to David's declared succession when Joab and Abiathar did not: 1 Kings 1:8, 1:36.
  • Was set over the host and over the guard by two kings: 2 Samuel 23:23; 1 Kings 2:35.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He carried out three executions at Solomon's command, including Joab at the altar (1 Kings 2:29-34). Scripture presents these as the king's judgments and records no fault in the executioner.

Character Assessment

Scripture records courage and unbroken loyalty and nothing against him. He is one of the few men to serve at the top of both David's and Solomon's administrations.

Significance

His loyalty at the moment of Adonijah's attempt was decisive for Solomon's accession, and his appointment over the host ended the house of Zeruiah's grip on the army.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 1 Chronicles 27:5-6.

Scripture References

2 Samuel 8:18; 2 Samuel 23:20-23; 1 Kings 1:8-44; 1 Kings 2:25-46; 1 Kings 4:4; 1 Chronicles 11:22-25; 1 Chronicles 27:5-6
—

Solomon

Son of David and Bathsheba; third king of Israel; builder of the temple; granted wisdom beyond any before or after, and turned away in his old age.

Also called Jedidiah

Family

Son of David and Bathsheba (2 Samuel 12:24); named Jedidiah by Nathan (2 Samuel 12:25). Married Pharaoh's daughter and many strange women; "he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines" (1 Kings 11:1-3). Father of Rehoboam by Naamah an Ammonitess (1 Kings 14:21).

Chronology

Reigned forty years in Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:42). The temple was begun in the fourth year of his reign, four hundred and eighty years after the Exodus (1 Kings 6:1).

Life Synopsis

Solomon was anointed while David lived, after Adonijah's attempt, and secured the kingdom by executing Adonijah, Joab, and Shimei and removing Abiathar (1 Kings 1:32-2:46).

At Gibeon God appeared to him in a dream and offered him whatever he asked. He asked for "an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad," and God gave him wisdom and also the riches and honour he had not asked (1 Kings 3:5-13). The judgment of the two harlots and the living child followed, "and they saw that the wisdom of God was in him, to do judgment" (1 Kings 3:16-28). He spoke three thousand proverbs and a thousand and five songs, and people came from all kings of the earth to hear him (1 Kings 4:29-34).

He built the temple in seven years with Hiram's timber and craftsmen, and his own house in thirteen. At the dedication he stood before the altar, spread out his hands to heaven, and prayed one of the longest prayers in Scripture - and it is largely about foreigners, sin, exile, and the plea that God would hear from heaven and forgive (1 Kings 8:22-53). The glory filled the house.

The queen of Sheba came and found the half had not been told her. Silver was as stones in Jerusalem. He had ships, horses out of Egypt, and forty thousand stalls (1 Kings 10:1-29).

"But king Solomon loved many strange women... his wives turned away his heart after other gods: and his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God, as was the heart of David his father." He went after Ashtoreth and Milcom and built high places for Chemosh and Molech on the hill before Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:1-8). God was angry, having appeared to him twice, and told him the kingdom would be rent from his son, with one tribe left for David's sake (1 Kings 11:9-13). Adversaries were raised up: Hadad, Rezon, and Jeroboam. He sought to kill Jeroboam, who fled to Egypt (1 Kings 11:14-40). He reigned forty years and died.

What They Did Right

  • Loved the Lord and walked in David's statutes at the beginning of his reign: 1 Kings 3:3.
  • Asked for an understanding heart to judge the people rather than long life, riches, or the lives of his enemies: 1 Kings 3:5-12.
  • Judged the case of the two harlots with the discernment that made his wisdom famous: 1 Kings 3:16-28.
  • Built the temple according to the charge given to David: 1 Kings 6:1-38.
  • Prayed at the dedication for God to hear the stranger who came from a far country for God's name's sake: 1 Kings 8:41-43.
  • Blessed the congregation and acknowledged that not one word of God's promise had failed: 1 Kings 8:56.
  • Christ cites his wisdom and his glory as real, while declaring both surpassed: Matthew 6:29; Matthew 12:42.

What They Did Wrong

  • Made affinity with Pharaoh and married his daughter: 1 Kings 3:1.
  • Sacrificed and burnt incense in high places: 1 Kings 3:3.
  • Multiplied horses out of Egypt, and silver and gold, against the law given for kings: 1 Kings 10:26-29; compare Deuteronomy 17:16-17.
  • Loved many strange women of the nations God had forbidden, taking seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines: 1 Kings 11:1-3.
  • His wives turned away his heart, and he went after Ashtoreth and Milcom: 1 Kings 11:4-6. Scripture's verdict is explicit: "Solomon did evil in the sight of the Lord."
  • Built high places for Chemosh and Molech on the hill before Jerusalem: 1 Kings 11:7-8.
  • Sought to kill Jeroboam after God had told him the kingdom would be divided: 1 Kings 11:40.
  • Laid a heavy yoke and grievous service on Israel, which his son's refusal to lighten split the kingdom: 1 Kings 12:4.
  • Nehemiah names him as the standing warning: "did not Solomon king of Israel sin by these things?... nevertheless even him did outlandish women cause to sin": Nehemiah 13:26.

Character Assessment

No life in Scripture has a steeper descent from a higher point. He asked for wisdom rather than wealth and was given both; he built the house of God and prayed a prayer of extraordinary depth at its dedication; and he ended building shrines to Chemolch and Molech on a hill overlooking that same temple. Scripture attributes the fall to a specific and mundane cause repeated three times - his wives turned away his heart - and notes with particular weight that God had appeared to him twice (1 Kings 11:9). His wisdom did not preserve him, which is a point the narrative makes without needing to state it.

Significance

Builder of the first temple, and the king under whom Israel reached its greatest extent and wealth. Traditionally the author of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Solomon, and of Psalms 72 and 127 by their titles. His reign is the high point of the united kingdom, and his idolatry is the stated cause of its division (1 Kings 11:11-13). Christ invokes both his glory and his wisdom, and declares a greater than Solomon present (Matthew 12:42).
