His recorded acts are many: he healed the waters of Jericho with salt (2 Kings 2:19-22); cursed the youths of Bethel who mocked him, and two she bears tore forty-two of them (2 Kings 2:23-24); provided water for three armies in the desert (2 Kings 3:14-20); multiplied a widow's oil to pay her creditor (2 Kings 4:1-7); promised the Shunammite a son and afterward raised him from the dead (2 Kings 4:8-37); healed the poisoned pottage (2 Kings 4:38-41); fed a hundred men with twenty loaves with some left over (2 Kings 4:42-44); sent Naaman to wash in Jordan (2 Kings 5:1-14); made an axe head swim (2 Kings 6:1-7); repeatedly told the king of Israel where the Syrians would camp (2 Kings 6:8-12); prayed his servant's eyes open to see the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire, then prayed the Syrian army blind and led them into Samaria - and told the king to feed them and send them home (2 Kings 6:13-23); foretold the end of the siege of Samaria within a day (2 Kings 7:1-2); wept before Hazael, knowing what he would do to Israel (2 Kings 8:11-13); and sent a young prophet to anoint Jehu (2 Kings 9:1-10).

He fell sick of the sickness whereof he died, and Joash king of Israel came down and wept over him with Elisha's own words for Elijah. He had the king shoot an arrow eastward - the arrow of the Lord's deliverance - and told him to smite the ground; he smote three times and stopped, and the man of God was wroth: he should have smitten five or six times and consumed Syria (2 Kings 13:14-19). After his death a body cast into his sepulchre revived on touching his bones (2 Kings 13:20-21).

What They Did Right

  • Left his oxen and his household to follow the call, burning his plough and his oxen behind him: 1 Kings 19:19-21.
  • Refused to leave Elijah on the last day, three times: 2 Kings 2:2-6.
  • Asked for a double portion of the Spirit rather than any other thing: 2 Kings 2:9.
  • Refused Naaman's reward outright: "As the Lord liveth, before whom I stand, I will receive none": 2 Kings 5:16.
  • Told the king of Israel to feed the blinded Syrian army and send them home rather than kill them, and the bands came no more: 2 Kings 6:21-23.
  • Wept before Hazael over what he would do to Israel's children: 2 Kings 8:11-12.
  • Ministered faithfully to kings who did evil, through four reigns, without ever holding office.

What They Did Wrong

  • Cursed the youths who mocked him at Bethel in the name of the Lord, and two she bears tore forty-two of them: 2 Kings 2:23-24. Scripture records the act and its consequence without commending or condemning it, and gives no comment on the proportion. The passage is much debated and the text offers no explanation.
  • Beyond this, no specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him except an episode it declines to interpret. His ministry is marked throughout by provision rather than confrontation: where Elijah called down fire, Elisha healed water, multiplied oil, fed a hundred men, raised a child, and sent an enemy army home fed. He refused payment when it was pressed on him and served kings who mostly did evil. His last recorded act was a rebuke for a king's half-hearted obedience.

Significance

He is the prophet of the Old Testament with the most recorded miracles, many of which anticipate the pattern of Christ's: multiplied food, healed leprosy, raised the dead, and cleansed at a distance. Christ names him in the synagogue at Nazareth alongside the widow of Zarephath: "many lepers were in Israel in the time of Eliseus the prophet; and none of them was cleansed, saving Naaman the Syrian" (Luke 4:27). Through him Hazael and Jehu came to their thrones, fulfilling the commission given at Horeb.

Death / Outcome

Died of sickness after Joash visited him; a dead man cast into his sepulchre revived on touching his bones (2 Kings 13:14-21).

Scripture References

1 Kings 19:16-21; 2 Kings 2:1-8:15; 2 Kings 9:1-3; 2 Kings 13:14-21; Luke 4:27
—

Naaman

Captain of the host of the king of Syria; a great man and a leper; healed by washing seven times in Jordan and confessed the God of Israel.

Family

Not recorded. He had a wife and a household (2 Kings 5:2-3).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. In the days of Elisha.

Life Synopsis

"Now Naaman, captain of the host of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honourable, because by him the Lord had given deliverance unto Syria: he was also a mighty man in valour, but he was a leper" (2 Kings 5:1).

A little captive maid of Israel who waited on his wife said, "Would God my lord were with the prophet that is in Samaria! for he would recover him of his leprosy." He went with a letter, ten talents of silver, six thousand pieces of gold, and ten changes of raiment (2 Kings 5:2-6).

Elisha did not come out, but sent a messenger: go wash in Jordan seven times. "But Naaman was wroth, and went away, and said, Behold, I thought, He will surely come out to me, and stand, and call on the name of the Lord his God, and strike his hand over the place, and recover the leper. Are not Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel?" His servants reasoned with him: if the prophet had asked some great thing, would he not have done it? He went down and dipped seven times, "and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean" (2 Kings 5:9-14).

He returned and said, "Behold, now I know that there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel." Elisha refused all reward. Naaman asked for two mules' burden of earth, to sacrifice to the Lord alone thereafter, and asked pardon for bowing in the house of Rimmon when he supported his master's hand. Elisha said, "Go in peace" (2 Kings 5:15-19).

What They Did Right

  • Listened to a captive servant girl and then to his own servants when they contradicted him: 2 Kings 5:3-4, 5:13-14.
  • Went down and dipped seven times as the prophet commanded, having nearly refused: 2 Kings 5:14.
  • Confessed that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel: 2 Kings 5:15.
  • Resolved to offer neither burnt offering nor sacrifice to any other god but the Lord: 2 Kings 5:17.
  • Christ names him as the one leper cleansed in Israel in Elisha's day: Luke 4:27.

What They Did Wrong

  • Was wroth at the manner of the cure and nearly went away, having decided in advance how it should be done: 2 Kings 5:11-12.

Character Assessment

Scripture records a proud man's anger, his correction by servants, and a confession of faith fuller than anything recorded from Israel's kings in the same period. His question about bowing in the house of Rimmon is answered with three words and no ruling, which the text leaves exactly as it is.

Significance

His healing is one of the two examples Christ used at Nazareth to show that God's mercy had always reached beyond Israel, and it was that sermon which made the synagogue try to kill him (Luke 4:27-29). The account also turns on the witness of a nameless captive Israelite girl in a foreign household.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He departed from Elisha a little way (2 Kings 5:19).

Scripture References

2 Kings 5:1-19; Luke 4:27
—

The captive maid of Israel

Unnamed. A little girl taken captive from Israel who served Naaman's wife and told her of the prophet in Samaria.

Family

Not recorded. Taken by the Syrians in a raid (2 Kings 5:2).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"And the Syrians had gone out by companies, and had brought away captive out of the land of Israel a little maid; and she waited on Naaman's wife. And she said unto her mistress, Would God my lord were with the prophet that is in Samaria! for he would recover him of his leprosy" (2 Kings 5:2-3). Her words were reported to the king of Syria, and the whole chain of events followed.

What They Did Right

  • Wished healing for the master of the household that had carried her away captive: 2 Kings 5:3.
  • Spoke with confidence of the prophet in Samaria, and was proved right: 2 Kings 5:3, 5:14.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture gives her one sentence and no name, and that sentence sets in motion the healing of a Syrian general and one of the clearest Gentile confessions of faith in the Old Testament. There is no record of resentment in it.

Significance

The account of Naaman turns entirely on her testimony. She is the smallest figure in the chapter and the cause of everything in it.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Kings 5:4.

Scripture References

2 Kings 5:2-4
—

Gehazi

Elisha's servant; ran after Naaman for the reward his master had refused, and was struck with Naaman's leprosy.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

He served Elisha and suggested that the Shunammite's need was a son, since her husband was old (2 Kings 4:14). He was sent ahead with Elisha's staff to lay on the dead child, but "there was neither voice, nor hearing," and the child was raised only when Elisha came himself (2 Kings 4:29-35).

After Elisha refused Naaman's gifts, Gehazi said within himself, "Behold, my master hath spared Naaman this Syrian, in not receiving at his hands that which he brought: but, as the Lord liveth, I will run after him, and take somewhat of him." He told Naaman that two young men of the sons of the prophets had just come and needed a talent of silver and two changes of garments. Naaman pressed two talents on him. He hid them and stood before his master (2 Kings 5:20-24).

Elisha asked where he had been, and he said nowhere. Elisha answered, "Went not mine heart with thee, when the man turned again from his chariot to meet thee? Is it a time to receive money, and to receive garments, and oliveyards, and vineyards, and sheep, and oxen, and menservants, and maidservants? The leprosy therefore of Naaman shall cleave unto thee, and unto thy seed for ever. And he went out from his presence a leper as white as snow" (2 Kings 5:25-27).

He appears once more, recounting Elisha's great deeds to the king, at the moment the Shunammite came to appeal for her house and land (2 Kings 8:4-6).

What They Did Right

  • Suggested to Elisha that the Shunammite had no son, which led to the promise: 2 Kings 4:14.
  • Recounted Elisha's acts to the king, at the moment that secured the Shunammite's restoration: 2 Kings 8:4-6.

What They Did Wrong

  • Ran after Naaman to take what his master had deliberately refused: 2 Kings 5:20-21.
  • Lied to Naaman, inventing two young men and a need: 2 Kings 5:22.
  • Lied to Elisha, saying he had gone nowhere: 2 Kings 5:25.
  • Elisha's charge names the fault precisely - it was not a time to receive money and garments and land - and the sentence was Naaman's leprosy: 2 Kings 5:26-27.

Character Assessment

Scripture records a servant who stood close to the greatest prophet of his generation and could not resist two talents of silver. The gravity of the account lies in what he undid: Elisha had refused payment specifically so that a Gentile would know Israel's God was not for sale, and Gehazi sold him the impression within the hour.

Significance

His case sits directly beside Naaman's: the Syrian leper went home clean and the Israelite servant went out leprous. The reversal is the point of the chapter's ending.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Kings 8:5.

Scripture References

2 Kings 4:12-37; 2 Kings 5:20-27; 2 Kings 8:4-6
—

The Shunammite woman

Unnamed. A great woman of Shunem who built a chamber for Elisha, was promised a son, and saw him raised from the dead.

Family

Married to an older husband (2 Kings 4:14); mother of one son (2 Kings 4:17).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Her land was restored in the days of Jehoram of Israel (2 Kings 8:1-6).

Life Synopsis

She constrained Elisha to eat bread whenever he passed, and said to her husband, "Behold now, I perceive that this is an holy man of God, which passeth by us continually. Let us make a little chamber, I pray thee, on the wall; and let us set for him there a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick" (2 Kings 4:8-10).

Asked what could be done for her - whether she wanted a word spoken to the king or the captain - she answered, "I dwell among mine own people." Gehazi observed she had no child. Elisha promised a son within the year, and she said, "Nay, my lord, thou man of God, do not lie unto thine handmaid." She bore a son (2 Kings 4:11-17).

The child grew, and one day cried to his father, "My head, my head," and died on his mother's knees at noon. She laid him on the prophet's bed, shut the door, asked her husband for a servant and an ass, and said to the servant, "Drive, and go forward; slack not thy riding for me, except I bid thee." To her husband and to Gehazi she said only, "It shall be well." Reaching Elisha she caught him by the feet and said, "Did I desire a son of my lord? did I not say, Do not deceive me?" She would not leave him. Elisha came, shut the door, prayed, stretched himself on the child twice, and the child sneezed seven times and opened his eyes (2 Kings 4:18-37).

Warned of a seven-year famine, she went to the land of the Philistines and returned to appeal for her house and land - arriving as Gehazi was telling the king how Elisha had raised her son. The king restored all, and the fruits of the field since the day she left (2 Kings 8:1-6).

What They Did Right

  • Perceived Elisha to be a holy man of God and provided for him at her own expense: 2 Kings 4:9-10.
  • Asked nothing for herself when offered access to the king: 2 Kings 4:13.
  • Went straight to the prophet when her son died, saying only "It shall be well" to everyone in her way: 2 Kings 4:22-26.
  • Refused to leave Elisha until he came: 2 Kings 4:30.
  • Obeyed the warning about the famine and left the land for seven years: 2 Kings 8:2.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her and shows a woman of unusual composure and independence. She initiated the hospitality, declined the favour offered in return, and in the crisis said nothing to anybody until she reached the one person who could help. Her reproach to Elisha - did I ask for a son? - is not rebuked.

Significance

The raising of her son is one of the three resurrections in the Old Testament, and Hebrews 11:35 refers to women who received their dead raised to life again. Her restoration under Jehoram shows Elisha's standing at court long after the events.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Kings 8:6.

Scripture References

2 Kings 4:8-37; 2 Kings 8:1-6; Hebrews 11:35
—

Hazael

A servant of Benhadad; anointed by Elisha's word to be king over Syria; murdered his master and oppressed Israel severely.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He reigned from the murder of Benhadad into the reign of Jehoahaz (2 Kings 13:22).

Life Synopsis

God told Elijah at Horeb to anoint Hazael king over Syria (1 Kings 19:15). Years later, Benhadad being sick, sent Hazael to Elisha with forty camels' burden of presents to ask whether he would recover.

"And Elisha said unto him, Go, say unto him, Thou mayest certainly recover: howbeit the Lord hath shewed me that he shall surely die. And he settled his countenance stedfastly, until he was ashamed: and the man of God wept." Hazael asked why he wept, and Elisha answered, "Because I know the evil that thou wilt do unto the children of Israel: their strong holds wilt thou set on fire, and their young men wilt thou slay with the sword, and wilt dash their children, and rip up their women with child." Hazael said, "But what, is thy servant a dog, that he should do this great thing?" Elisha replied that the Lord had shown him he would be king over Syria (2 Kings 8:7-13).

"And it came to pass on the morrow, that he took a thick cloth, and dipped it in water, and spread it on his face, so that he died: and Hazael reigned in his stead" (2 Kings 8:15). He afterward smote Israel in all their coasts, took Gath, and was bought off from Jerusalem by Jehoash of Judah with the hallowed treasures (2 Kings 10:32-33; 2 Kings 12:17-18; 2 Kings 13:3, 13:22).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Murdered his master by smothering him: 2 Kings 8:15.
  • Did to Israel exactly what Elisha had foretold and he had denied he would do: 2 Kings 8:12; 2 Kings 10:32; 2 Kings 13:7.
  • Amos names his house for judgment for threshing Gilead with instruments of iron: Amos 1:3-4.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his protest - is thy servant a dog? - and then records him doing precisely what he protested he would never do, beginning the next morning. It offers no separate verdict; the sequence is the verdict. Note that the text does not present Elisha's word as causing the murder: Elisha wept over it.

Significance

He was the instrument of God's judgment on Israel over decades, so that Jehoahaz was left fifty horsemen and ten chariots (2 Kings 13:7). Yet Scripture also holds Syria guilty for it, and Amos pronounces judgment on his house.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded directly; 2 Kings 13:24 states that Hazael king of Syria died and Benhadad his son reigned.

Scripture References

1 Kings 19:15, 19:17; 2 Kings 8:7-15, 8:28-29; 2 Kings 9:14-15; 2 Kings 10:32-33; 2 Kings 12:17-18; 2 Kings 13:3-25; Amos 1:3-4
—

Jehoram (king of Israel)

Son of Ahab; king of Israel; put away the image of Baal but held to Jeroboam's sins; killed by Jehu in Naboth's field. Not to be confused with Jehoram king of Judah.

Also called Joram

Family

Son of Ahab and Jezebel (2 Kings 3:1-2); brother of Ahaziah of Israel and of Athaliah.

Chronology

Reigned twelve years over Israel in Samaria (2 Kings 3:1).

Life Synopsis

"And he wrought evil in the sight of the Lord; but not like his father, and like his mother: for he put away the image of Baal that his father had made. Nevertheless he cleaved unto the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which made Israel to sin; he departed not therefrom" (2 Kings 3:2-3).

He went with Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom against Moab and ran out of water; Elisha, saying he would not have looked toward him but for Jehoshaphat's presence, gave the word for the ditches and the water (2 Kings 3:4-20).

During the siege of Samaria, hearing the woman's account of eating her own child, he rent his clothes and had sackcloth beneath - and swore to take Elisha's head that day (2 Kings 6:26-31). He was wounded at Ramothgilead fighting Hazael and went to Jezreel to be healed (2 Kings 8:28-29).

When Jehu came, he rode out with Ahaziah of Judah to meet him and asked, "Is it peace, Jehu?" Jehu answered, "What peace, so long as the whoredoms of thy mother Jezebel and her witchcrafts are so many?" He turned to flee and Jehu shot him between the arms; the arrow went out at his heart. Jehu had the body cast into the portion of the field of Naboth the Jezreelite, recalling the word spoken there (2 Kings 9:14-26).

What They Did Right

  • Put away the image of Baal that his father had made: 2 Kings 3:2.
  • Rent his clothes and wore sackcloth under his garments during the famine in Samaria: 2 Kings 6:30. Scripture records this without stating whether it was repentance.

What They Did Wrong

  • Wrought evil in the sight of the Lord and cleaved to the sins of Jeroboam, departing not therefrom: 2 Kings 3:2-3.
  • Swore to kill Elisha and blamed God for the famine: "this evil is of the Lord; what should I wait for the Lord any longer?": 2 Kings 6:31-33.

Character Assessment

A partial reformer with no change of direction. Scripture is careful to say he was not like his father and mother, and equally careful to say he did not depart from Jeroboam's sins. His response to national catastrophe was sackcloth and a threat against the prophet in the same breath.

Significance

His death in Naboth's field completed the word Elijah spoke there against Ahab's house (2 Kings 9:25-26), and with it the dynasty of Omri ended in Israel.

Death / Outcome

Shot through the heart by Jehu and cast into the portion of Naboth's field (2 Kings 9:24-26).

Scripture References

2 Kings 1:17; 2 Kings 3:1-27; 2 Kings 6:8-7:20; 2 Kings 8:16, 8:25-29; 2 Kings 9:14-29
—

Jehoram (king of Judah)

Son of Jehoshaphat; king of Judah; married Ahab's daughter, killed his own brothers, and died of an incurable disease unlamented. Not to be confused with Jehoram king of Israel.

Family

Son of Jehoshaphat (2 Kings 8:16); husband of Athaliah the daughter of Ahab (2 Kings 8:18); father of Ahaziah (2 Kings 8:24).

Chronology

"Thirty and two years old was he when he began to reign; and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 8:17).

Life Synopsis

"And he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as did the house of Ahab: for the daughter of Ahab was his wife: and he did evil in the sight of the Lord. Yet the Lord would not destroy Judah for David his servant's sake, as he promised him to give him alway a light" (2 Kings 8:18-19).

Chronicles records that when he was risen up to the kingdom he strengthened himself and slew all his brethren with the sword, and various princes of Israel (2 Chronicles 21:4). Edom revolted and Libnah revolted from under his hand (2 Kings 8:20-22). He made high places in the mountains of Judah and caused Jerusalem to commit fornication (2 Chronicles 21:11).

A writing came to him from Elijah the prophet, charging him with walking in the ways of the kings of Israel and killing his brethren who were better than himself, and announcing a great plague on his people and a disease of his bowels (2 Chronicles 21:12-15). The Philistines and Arabians carried away his substance, his wives, and his sons except the youngest. Then he was struck in his bowels with an incurable disease, and after two years his bowels fell out. "And he departed without being desired. Howbeit they buried him in the city of David, but not in the sepulchres of the kings" (2 Chronicles 21:16-20).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as did the house of Ahab: 2 Kings 8:18.
  • Married Athaliah the daughter of Ahab: 2 Kings 8:18.
  • Slew all his brethren with the sword: 2 Chronicles 21:4.
  • Made high places and caused Jerusalem to commit fornication and compelled Judah thereto: 2 Chronicles 21:11.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned. Scripture records that he departed without being desired, which is among the bleakest epitaphs in the Old Testament, and that he was denied burial in the sepulchres of the kings. The one thing that preserved Judah in his reign was not anything in him but God's promise to David.

Significance

His marriage to Athaliah carried the house of Ahab into the royal line of Judah, and after his son's death she seized the throne and destroyed the seed royal. He stands in the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:8).

Death / Outcome

Died of an incurable bowel disease after two years, unlamented, and was buried in the city of David but not in the sepulchres of the kings (2 Chronicles 21:18-20).

Scripture References

2 Kings 8:16-24; 2 Chronicles 21:1-20; Matthew 1:8
—

Ahaziah (king of Judah)

Son of Jehoram and Athaliah; king of Judah one year; walked in the ways of the house of Ahab and was killed by Jehu.

Family

Son of Jehoram of Judah and Athaliah, the daughter of Omri's house (2 Kings 8:25-26); nephew of Jehoram of Israel.

Chronology

"Two and twenty years old was Ahaziah when he began to reign; and he reigned one year in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 8:26).

Life Synopsis

"And he walked in the way of the house of Ahab, and did evil in the sight of the Lord, as did the house of Ahab: for he was the son in law of the house of Ahab" (2 Kings 8:27). Chronicles adds that his mother was his counsellor to do wickedly, and that the house of Ahab were his counsellors after his father's death to his destruction (2 Chronicles 22:3-4).

He went with Jehoram of Israel against Hazael at Ramothgilead, and went down to Jezreel to see him when he was wounded - arriving exactly as Jehu came. He fled and Jehu's men shot him; he died at Megiddo. His servants carried him in a chariot to Jerusalem and buried him in the city of David (2 Kings 8:28-29; 2 Kings 9:27-28). Chronicles adds that his destruction was of God, in coming to Jehoram (2 Chronicles 22:7).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. Chronicles records that they buried him, "Because, said they, he is the son of Jehoshaphat, who sought the Lord with all his heart" - a commendation of his grandfather, not of him: 2 Chronicles 22:9.

What They Did Wrong

  • Walked in the way of the house of Ahab and did evil in the sight of the Lord: 2 Kings 8:27.
  • Took his mother and the house of Ahab as counsellors to his destruction: 2 Chronicles 22:3-4.

Character Assessment

One year, and Scripture attributes his conduct almost entirely to counsel - his mother's and Ahab's house. The only reason given for his honourable burial is his great-grandfather's faithfulness.

Significance

His death left Judah without an adult king and gave Athaliah her opportunity to destroy the seed royal, bringing the Davidic line to a single surviving infant.

Death / Outcome

Shot by Jehu's men at Ibleam and died at Megiddo; buried in the city of David (2 Kings 9:27-28).

Scripture References

2 Kings 8:24-29; 2 Kings 9:16-29; 2 Chronicles 22:1-9
—

Jehu (king of Israel)

Son of Jehoshaphat son of Nimshi; anointed to destroy the house of Ahab; executed the whole judgment with zeal and then kept Jeroboam's calves.

Family

Son of Jehoshaphat, son of Nimshi (2 Kings 9:2).

Chronology

Reigned twenty-eight years over Israel in Samaria (2 Kings 10:36).

Life Synopsis

Elisha sent a young prophet to Ramothgilead to pour oil on his head with the commission to smite the house of Ahab and avenge the blood of the prophets and of all the Lord's servants at Jezebel's hand. His fellow captains put him on the top of the stairs and blew the trumpet (2 Kings 9:1-13).

He drove to Jezreel - "the driving is like the driving of Jehu the son of Nimshi; for he driveth furiously" - killed Jehoram in Naboth's field and Ahaziah of Judah in flight, and had Jezebel thrown from a window (2 Kings 9:16-37). He wrote to the rulers of Samaria and had the seventy sons of Ahab beheaded, their heads laid in two heaps at the gate (2 Kings 10:1-8). He killed Ahab's great men, kinsfolks, and priests, and forty-two brethren of Ahaziah (2 Kings 10:11-14).

Meeting Jehonadab son of Rechab, he said, "Come with me, and see my zeal for the Lord" (2 Kings 10:15-16). He then gathered all the worshippers of Baal by proclaiming a great sacrifice, filled the house of Baal, set eighty men outside, and destroyed them all; the house of Baal was broken down and made a draught house (2 Kings 10:18-27).

God said to him, "Because thou hast done well in executing that which is right in mine eyes, and hast done unto the house of Ahab according to all that was in mine heart, thy children of the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel." And immediately: "But Jehu took no heed to walk in the law of the Lord God of Israel with all his heart: for he departed not from the sins of Jeroboam, which made Israel to sin" (2 Kings 10:30-31). In his days Hazael began to cut Israel short (2 Kings 10:32).

What They Did Right

  • Executed the judgment on the house of Ahab as commissioned: 2 Kings 9:1-10:17.
  • Destroyed Baal worship out of Israel and broke down the house of Baal: 2 Kings 10:26-28.
  • God's own commendation: "thou hast done well in executing that which is right in mine eyes," with a promise of four generations on the throne: 2 Kings 10:30.

What They Did Wrong

  • Took no heed to walk in the law of the Lord with all his heart, and departed not from the sins of Jeroboam: 2 Kings 10:31.
  • Left the golden calves in Bethel and Dan standing: 2 Kings 10:29.
  • Hosea names the blood of Jezreel as a charge against his house: "I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu": Hosea 1:4. Scripture therefore both commends the execution and later holds his house accountable for it, and does not reconcile the two.

Character Assessment

A commission carried out with total efficiency and no personal reformation. God commends the act and promises four generations for it, and in the very next verse states that he did not walk in God's law with all his heart. His invitation to Jehonadab - come and see my zeal for the Lord - is recorded without comment and reads uncomfortably given what he left standing. Hosea's later charge against his house is a real difficulty and is noted rather than resolved.

Significance

He ended the dynasty of Omri, destroyed organised Baal worship in Israel, and founded the longest dynasty of the northern kingdom, lasting four generations exactly as promised. Under him Israel's territorial decline under Hazael began.

Death / Outcome

Slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria after twenty-eight years (2 Kings 10:35-36).

Scripture References

1 Kings 19:16-17; 2 Kings 9:1-10:36; 2 Kings 15:12; 2 Chronicles 22:7-9; Hosea 1:4
—

Jehonadab

Son of Rechab; joined Jehu's chariot in the purge of Baal; ancestor of the Rechabites, whose obedience to his command Jeremiah later held up to Judah.

Also called Jonadab son of Rechab

Family

Son of Rechab (2 Kings 10:15); father of the Rechabites (Jeremiah 35:6).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He met Jehu at the beginning of his reign.

Life Synopsis

Jehu met him on the way and said, "Is thine heart right, as my heart is with thy heart?" He answered, "It is." Jehu said, "If it be, give me thine hand," took him up into the chariot, and said, "Come with me, and see my zeal for the Lord." He went with Jehu to Samaria and was with him at the destruction of the house of Baal, where the two of them told the worshippers to make sure no servants of the Lord were among them (2 Kings 10:15-23).

Generations later Jeremiah set pots of wine before the Rechabites, who refused: "Jonadab the son of Rechab our father commanded us, saying, Ye shall drink no wine, neither ye, nor your sons for ever: neither shall ye build house, nor sow seed, nor plant vineyard." God used their obedience against Judah, and promised, "Jonadab the son of Rechab shall not want a man to stand before me for ever" (Jeremiah 35:6-19).

What They Did Right

  • Joined in the destruction of Baal worship in Israel: 2 Kings 10:23-28.
  • Laid on his descendants a command they kept for centuries, and God commended their obedience: Jeremiah 35:6-10, 35:18-19.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. He is unusual in that his significance is almost entirely posthumous: a rule he laid on his family was still being obeyed generations later, and God used it to shame a nation that would not obey him.

Significance

The Rechabites' fidelity to his command is the object lesson of Jeremiah 35, and carries a promise that his line would never want a man to stand before God.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention (of him personally): 2 Kings 10:23.

Scripture References

2 Kings 10:15-23; Jeremiah 35:1-19
—

Athaliah

Daughter of the house of Ahab; queen of Judah; destroyed the seed royal and reigned six years until Jehoiada raised up Joash and had her killed.

Family

Daughter of Ahab and granddaughter of Omri (2 Kings 8:18, 8:26); wife of Jehoram of Judah; mother of Ahaziah.

Chronology

She reigned over the land six years (2 Kings 11:3).

Life Synopsis

"And when Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the seed royal" (2 Kings 11:1). But Jehosheba, the daughter of king Joram and sister of Ahaziah, took Joash, the infant son of Ahaziah, from among the king's sons that were slain, and hid him and his nurse in the bedchamber, and afterward in the house of the Lord for six years (2 Kings 11:2-3).

In the seventh year Jehoiada the priest brought out the child, set the guard, put the crown on him and gave him the testimony, and they anointed him and clapped their hands and said, "God save the king." Athaliah heard the noise and came into the temple, "and when she looked, behold, the king stood by a pillar, as the manner was, and the princes and the trumpeters by the king, and all the people of the land rejoiced, and blew with trumpets: and Athaliah rent her clothes, and cried, Treason, Treason" (2 Kings 11:12-14). Jehoiada had her taken out between the ranks so that she should not be slain in the house of the Lord, and she was killed at the entering in of the horse gate (2 Kings 11:15-16). Chronicles records that her sons had broken up the house of God (2 Chronicles 24:7).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Destroyed all the seed royal of the house of Judah: 2 Kings 11:1.
  • Usurped the throne of David and reigned over the land six years: 2 Kings 11:3.
  • "That wicked woman" and her sons had broken up the house of God and bestowed its hallowed things upon Baalim: 2 Chronicles 24:7.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned. She is the only woman to reign over Judah, and she took the throne by killing her own grandchildren. Scripture records no motive and no words except her cry of treason at the moment she lost it.

Significance

Her purge brought the house of David to a single hidden infant, and is the closest the Davidic line ever came to extinction - which makes the survival of Joash the preservation of the messianic promise. Her end was the restoration of the covenant between the Lord, the king, and the people (2 Kings 11:17).

Death / Outcome

Killed at the horse gate by the king's house, at Jehoiada's order (2 Kings 11:16).

Scripture References

2 Kings 8:18, 8:26; 2 Kings 11:1-20; 2 Chronicles 22:2-23:21; 2 Chronicles 24:7
—

Jehosheba

Daughter of king Joram and sister of Ahaziah; hid the infant Joash from Athaliah and so preserved the line of David.

Also called Jehoshabeath

Family

Daughter of Joram of Judah, sister of Ahaziah (2 Kings 11:2); wife of Jehoiada the priest (2 Chronicles 22:11).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"But Jehosheba, the daughter of king Joram, sister of Ahaziah, took Joash the son of Ahaziah, and stole him from among the king's sons which were slain; and they hid him, even him and his nurse, in the bedchamber from Athaliah, so that he was not slain. And he was with her hid in the house of the Lord six years. And Athaliah did reign over the land" (2 Kings 11:2-3).

What They Did Right

  • Stole the infant heir from among the murdered king's sons and hid him for six years, at the risk of her life: 2 Kings 11:2-3.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records one act and nothing else, and that act preserved the house of David. Nothing she said is recorded.

Significance

Her rescue of Joash is the reason the Davidic line survived Athaliah, and therefore the reason there was a house of David to which the promise of Christ could run. She is one of very few women in Scripture recorded as both a king's daughter and a priest's wife.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 22:11.

Scripture References

2 Kings 11:2-3; 2 Chronicles 22:11
—

Jehoiada

High priest in Judah; hid and raised Joash, overthrew Athaliah, renewed the covenant, and guided the king while he lived.

Family

Husband of Jehosheba (2 Chronicles 22:11); father of Zechariah (2 Chronicles 24:20).

Chronology

"But Jehoiada waxed old, and was full of days when he died; an hundred and thirty years old was he when he died" (2 Chronicles 24:15).

Life Synopsis

He sheltered Joash in the house of the Lord six years while Athaliah reigned. In the seventh year he sent for the captains and the guard, showed them the king's son, set them in order with the spears and shields that had been David's, brought out the child, put the crown on him, gave him the testimony, and anointed him (2 Kings 11:4-12). He ordered Athaliah taken out of the temple before she was killed, so that the house of the Lord should not be defiled (2 Kings 11:15).

"And Jehoiada made a covenant between the Lord and the king and the people, that they should be the Lord's people; between the king also and the people." The people went to the house of Baal, broke it down, broke his images, and slew Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars (2 Kings 11:17-18).

He instructed Joash in repairing the temple and devised the chest with a hole in the lid to collect money for the work (2 Kings 12:4-16). "And Jehoash did that which was right in the sight of the Lord all his days wherein Jehoiada the priest instructed him" (2 Kings 12:2). He died at a hundred and thirty and was buried among the kings, "because he had done good in Israel, both toward God, and toward his house" (2 Chronicles 24:15-16).

What They Did Right

  • Sheltered the heir of David for six years in the house of the Lord: 2 Kings 11:3.
  • Restored the rightful king and overthrew a usurper without defiling the temple: 2 Kings 11:4-16.
  • Made a covenant between the Lord, the king, and the people: 2 Kings 11:17.
  • Led the destruction of the house of Baal in Jerusalem: 2 Kings 11:18.
  • Instructed Joash so that he did right all the days of that instruction: 2 Kings 12:2.
  • Was buried among the kings in the city of David because he had done good in Israel, both toward God and toward his house: 2 Chronicles 24:16.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him and gives him an honour granted to no other priest: burial among the kings, with the reason stated. He held the kingdom together through a minority, restored lawful worship, and the record explicitly ties the king's faithfulness to the years of his instruction - and Joash's collapse follows immediately on his death.

Significance

He preserved and restored the Davidic monarchy after Athaliah's purge. The immediate apostasy of Judah after his death, and Joash's murder of his son Zechariah, make his life the clearest case in Chronicles of a nation's health resting on one man's influence.

Death / Outcome

Died at a hundred and thirty years and was buried in the city of David among the kings (2 Chronicles 24:15-16).

Scripture References

2 Kings 11:4-12:16; 2 Chronicles 22:11-24:16
—

Joash (king of Judah)

Son of Ahaziah; hidden as an infant and crowned at seven; repaired the temple, then turned away after Jehoiada's death and murdered his son Zechariah. Not to be confused with Joash king of Israel or Joash father of Gideon.

Also called Jehoash

Family

Son of Ahaziah (2 Kings 11:2); his mother was Zibiah of Beersheba (2 Kings 12:1).

Chronology

"Seven years old was Jehoash when he began to reign... forty years reigned he in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 12:1).

Life Synopsis

Hidden from Athaliah as an infant and raised in the house of the Lord, he was crowned at seven by Jehoiada (2 Kings 11:1-12). "And Jehoash did that which was right in the sight of the Lord all his days wherein Jehoiada the priest instructed him. But the high places were not taken away" (2 Kings 12:2-3).

He ordered the repair of the temple, and when the priests had not done it by the twenty-third year of his reign he called Jehoiada and asked why. The chest was set beside the altar, and the work was done, the workmen dealing faithfully (2 Kings 12:4-15).

After Jehoiada's death the princes of Judah came and made obeisance to the king, "then the king hearkened unto them. And they left the house of the Lord God of their fathers, and served groves and idols." God sent prophets, who were not heard. The Spirit of God came upon Zechariah the son of Jehoiada, who said, "Why transgress ye the commandments of the Lord, that ye cannot prosper? because ye have forsaken the Lord, he hath also forsaken you. And they conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of the house of the Lord. Thus Joash the king remembered not the kindness which Jehoiada his father had done to him, but slew his son. And when he died, he said, The Lord look upon it, and require it" (2 Chronicles 24:17-22).

A small Syrian army came and executed judgment against him, and he was left in great diseases. His own servants conspired against him for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada and killed him on his bed. He was buried in the city of David but not in the sepulchres of the kings (2 Chronicles 24:23-25).

What They Did Right

  • Did right in the sight of the Lord all the days of Jehoiada's instruction: 2 Kings 12:2.
  • Took the initiative in repairing the house of the Lord when the work had lapsed: 2 Kings 12:4-8.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did not take away the high places: 2 Kings 12:3.
  • Hearkened to the princes after Jehoiada's death and forsook the house of the Lord for groves and idols: 2 Chronicles 24:17-18.
  • Commanded the stoning of Zechariah the son of Jehoiada in the court of the house of the Lord: 2 Chronicles 24:21.
  • Remembered not the kindness of Jehoiada, who had saved his life and his throne: 2 Chronicles 24:22.
  • Took the hallowed things of the temple and sent them to Hazael to buy him off: 2 Kings 12:17-18.

Character Assessment

One of the sharpest before-and-after records in Scripture, and it turns on a single funeral. The text ties his faithfulness precisely to the years of Jehoiada's instruction, and his collapse begins in the verse after Jehoiada is buried. That he repaid the man who hid him as an infant by murdering his son in the temple court is stated by Chronicles in exactly those terms.

Significance

His preservation as an infant kept the Davidic line alive. His murder of Zechariah is likely the killing Christ refers to as the last in the Hebrew canon's order: "the blood of Zacharias son of Barachias, whom ye slew between the temple and the altar" (Matthew 23:35), though the patronymic differs and the identification is disputed. He stands in the genealogy of Christ.

Death / Outcome

Killed on his bed by his own servants for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada; buried in the city of David but not in the sepulchres of the kings (2 Chronicles 24:25).

Scripture References

2 Kings 11:1-12:21; 2 Chronicles 22:11-24:27; Matthew 23:35
—

Zechariah (son of Jehoiada)

A priest, son of Jehoiada; rebuked Judah for forsaking the Lord and was stoned at the king's command in the court of the temple.

Family

Son of Jehoiada the priest and, by 2 Chronicles 22:11, of Jehosheba (2 Chronicles 24:20).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. After Jehoiada's death, in the reign of Joash.

Life Synopsis

"And the Spirit of God came upon Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest, which stood above the people, and said unto them, Thus saith God, Why transgress ye the commandments of the Lord, that ye cannot prosper? because ye have forsaken the Lord, he hath also forsaken you."

"And they conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of the house of the Lord... And when he died, he said, The Lord look upon it, and require it" (2 Chronicles 24:20-22). Within a year a Syrian force came against Judah and executed judgment on Joash, and his servants killed him for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada (2 Chronicles 24:23-25).

What They Did Right

  • Spoke God's word to the whole nation and to the king who had been raised in his father's house: 2 Chronicles 24:20.
  • Died committing his cause to God rather than cursing: "The Lord look upon it, and require it": 2 Chronicles 24:22.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His last words are the counterpart of Stephen's - where Stephen asked that the sin not be laid to their charge, Zechariah asked God to require it - and both are recorded without comment.

Significance

His murder is very likely the one Christ names as the last in the sequence of shed innocent blood, "from the blood of righteous Abel unto the blood of Zacharias" (Matthew 23:35; Luke 11:51) - Chronicles being the last book in the Hebrew ordering, so that the phrase spans the whole canon. The patronymic in Matthew differs and the identification is debated; this reference notes it without deciding.

Death / Outcome

Stoned in the court of the house of the Lord at the commandment of Joash (2 Chronicles 24:21).

Scripture References

2 Chronicles 24:20-25; Matthew 23:35; Luke 11:51
—

Joash (king of Israel)

Son of Jehoahaz; king of Israel; wept over the dying Elisha, defeated Syria three times, and defeated Amaziah of Judah.

Also called Jehoash (king of Israel)

Family

Son of Jehoahaz, grandson of Jehu (2 Kings 13:10); father of Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:16).

Chronology

Reigned sixteen years over Israel in Samaria (2 Kings 13:10).

Life Synopsis

"And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord; he departed not from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel sin" (2 Kings 13:11).

When Elisha lay dying he came down and wept over him and said, "O my father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof" - the very words Elisha had cried when Elijah was taken. Elisha had him shoot an arrow eastward and then smite the ground; he smote three times and stopped, and the man of God was wroth: he should have smitten five or six times and destroyed Syria, but now would beat Syria only three times (2 Kings 13:14-19). He recovered the cities of Israel from Benhadad three times, according to that word (2 Kings 13:25).

Amaziah of Judah challenged him. He answered with a parable of a thistle in Lebanon that sent to a cedar for a wife and was trodden down by a wild beast, and told him to glory in his victory and stay home. Amaziah would not hear, and Joash broke down four hundred cubits of the wall of Jerusalem, took the treasures of the temple and the palace and hostages, and returned to Samaria (2 Kings 14:8-14).

What They Did Right

  • Wept over Elisha and honoured him with Elisha's own words for Elijah: 2 Kings 13:14.
  • Warned Amaziah of Judah and urged him not to meddle to his own hurt: 2 Kings 14:9-10.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did evil in the sight of the Lord and departed not from the sins of Jeroboam: 2 Kings 13:11.
  • Smote the ground only three times and stayed, which the prophet took as a want of resolve, and so left Syria undestroyed: 2 Kings 13:18-19.
  • Broke down the wall of Jerusalem and plundered the temple after defeating Amaziah: 2 Kings 14:13-14.

Character Assessment

A mixed record within the usual northern condemnation. He honoured a prophet genuinely and gave sound advice to a rival king, and he is the one man in Scripture rebuked specifically for stopping short in an act of obedience he did not understand. Scripture does not explain why three strokes were not enough; it records only the prophet's anger and the consequence.

Significance

The arrow of the Lord's deliverance and the three strokes have become the standing biblical illustration of partial obedience limiting what God gives. Under him and his son the northern kingdom recovered territory before its final decline.

Death / Outcome

Slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel (2 Kings 13:13; 2 Kings 14:16).

Scripture References

2 Kings 13:9-25; 2 Kings 14:8-16; 2 Chronicles 25:17-24
—

Amaziah

Son of Joash; king of Judah; did right but not with a perfect heart; hired and dismissed Israelite mercenaries, worshipped the gods of Edom, and was defeated and later murdered.

Family

Son of Joash of Judah (2 Kings 12:21); father of Azariah, called Uzziah (2 Kings 14:21).

Chronology

"Twenty and five years old when he began to reign, and reigned twenty and nine years in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 14:2).

Life Synopsis

"And he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, yet not like David his father" (2 Kings 14:3); Chronicles puts it, "but not with a perfect heart" (2 Chronicles 25:2). He executed the servants who had killed his father but spared their children, according to the law of Moses that fathers should not die for children nor children for fathers (2 Kings 14:5-6).

He hired a hundred thousand men of Israel for a hundred talents. A man of God told him not to let Israel go with him, and when he asked what to do about the hundred talents, was answered, "The Lord is able to give thee much more than this." He sent them home and they went in great anger (2 Chronicles 25:6-10). He then smote ten thousand of Seir - and brought back the gods of the children of Seir, set them up as his gods, and bowed before them. A prophet asked, "Why hast thou sought after the gods of the people, which could not deliver their own people out of thine hand?" The king cut him off: "Art thou made of the king's counsel? forbear; why shouldest thou be smitten?" (2 Chronicles 25:14-16).

He then challenged Joash of Israel, was warned off with the parable of the thistle, refused to hear, and was defeated at Bethshemesh; Jerusalem's wall was broken and the temple plundered (2 Kings 14:8-14). "Now after the time that Amaziah did turn away from following the Lord they made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem; and he fled to Lachish; but they sent to Lachish after him, and slew him there" (2 Chronicles 25:27).

What They Did Right

  • Did that which was right in the sight of the Lord: 2 Kings 14:3.
  • Spared the children of his father's murderers in obedience to the written law of Moses: 2 Kings 14:6; Deuteronomy 24:16.
  • Sent home the hired Israelite army at the word of a man of God, forfeiting a hundred talents: 2 Chronicles 25:7-10.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did not do right with a perfect heart, and the high places were not taken away: 2 Kings 14:4; 2 Chronicles 25:2.
  • Brought back the gods of Seir, set them up, and bowed himself before them - the gods of the people he had just defeated: 2 Chronicles 25:14.
  • Silenced the prophet sent to rebuke him with a threat: 2 Chronicles 25:16.
  • Refused Joash's warning and provoked a war that cost Jerusalem its wall and the temple its treasures: 2 Kings 14:8-14.

Character Assessment

A reign of obedience without conviction, which is how Chronicles states it - right, but not with a perfect heart. He obeyed the law about the murderers' children and obeyed the prophet about the mercenaries, and then worshipped the gods of a nation he had beaten, which the prophet's question exposes as absurd on its own terms. His refusal to hear correction is recorded twice.

Significance

His defeat by Joash broke Jerusalem's defences and stripped the temple, and his turning from the Lord is explicitly linked by Chronicles to the conspiracy that killed him. He stands in the genealogy of Christ under the name Amaziah is omitted; the line runs through his son Azariah (Uzziah).

Death / Outcome

Fled to Lachish from a conspiracy and was slain there; brought back on horses and buried with his fathers in Jerusalem (2 Kings 14:19-20).

Scripture References

2 Kings 12:21-14:22; 2 Chronicles 25:1-28
—

Azariah

Son of Amaziah; king of Judah fifty-two years; prospered greatly, then presumed to burn incense in the temple and was struck with leprosy until his death.

Also called Uzziah

Family

Son of Amaziah (2 Kings 14:21); father of Jotham (2 Kings 15:5). Called Azariah in Kings and Uzziah in Chronicles and the prophets.

Chronology

"Sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned two and fifty years in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 15:2). Isaiah's call came in the year of his death (Isaiah 6:1).

Life Synopsis

"And he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord... save that the high places were not removed" (2 Kings 15:3-4).

Chronicles gives the fuller account. He sought God in the days of Zechariah, who had understanding in the visions of God, "and as long as he sought the Lord, God made him to prosper." He warred against the Philistines and Arabians, built towers, dug wells, had husbandmen and vine dressers, and made engines in Jerusalem to shoot arrows and great stones, "and his name spread far abroad; for he was marvellously helped, till he was strong" (2 Chronicles 26:5-15).

"But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction: for he transgressed against the Lord his God, and went into the temple of the Lord to burn incense upon the altar of incense." Azariah the priest and eighty priests withstood him: "It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the Lord, but to the priests the sons of Aaron." He was wroth with a censer in his hand, and the leprosy rose up in his forehead. They thrust him out, "yea, himself hasted also to go out, because the Lord had smitten him." He was a leper to the day of his death and dwelt in a several house, his son Jotham judging the people (2 Chronicles 26:16-21).

What They Did Right

  • Did that which was right in the sight of the Lord: 2 Kings 15:3.
  • Sought God in the days of Zechariah, and as long as he sought the Lord God made him prosper: 2 Chronicles 26:5.
  • Built, fortified, and strengthened Judah, and was marvellously helped: 2 Chronicles 26:6-15.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did not remove the high places: 2 Kings 15:4.
  • When he was strong his heart was lifted up to his destruction: 2 Chronicles 26:16.
  • Went into the temple to burn incense, which belonged to the priests alone: 2 Chronicles 26:16-18.
  • Was wroth with the priests who withstood him, censer in hand: 2 Chronicles 26:19.

Character Assessment

A long and largely successful reign undone by one act, and Chronicles states the mechanism plainly: he was helped till he was strong, and when he was strong his heart was lifted up. He is one of the clearest biblical cases of prosperity itself becoming the danger. His leprosy was immediate, public, and permanent.

Significance

His fifty-two years were among Judah's most prosperous. Isaiah dates his call to the year of Uzziah's death - "In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up" (Isaiah 6:1) - setting a leprous king's death against the vision of the true King. Amos, Hosea, and Zechariah also date by him. He stands in the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:8-9).

Death / Outcome

Died a leper and was buried in the field of the burial which belonged to the kings, for they said, He is a leper (2 Chronicles 26:23).

Scripture References

2 Kings 14:21; 2 Kings 15:1-7; 2 Chronicles 26:1-23; Isaiah 1:1; Isaiah 6:1; Amos 1:1; Zechariah 14:5; Matthew 1:8-9
—

Jeroboam II

Son of Joash; king of Israel forty-one years; restored Israel's borders as Jonah had prophesied, while doing evil in the sight of the Lord.

Family

Son of Joash king of Israel, great-grandson of Jehu (2 Kings 14:23).

Chronology

Reigned forty-one years over Israel in Samaria (2 Kings 14:23).

Life Synopsis

"And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord: he departed not from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin."

"He restored the coast of Israel from the entering of Hamath unto the sea of the plain, according to the word of the Lord God of Israel, which he spake by the hand of his servant Jonah, the son of Amittai, the prophet, which was of Gathhepher. For the Lord saw the affliction of Israel, that it was very bitter... and there was not any helper for Israel. And the Lord said not that he would blot out the name of Israel from under heaven: but he saved them by the hand of Jeroboam the son of Joash" (2 Kings 14:24-27).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. His military restoration is attributed by Scripture to God's compassion on Israel's affliction rather than to any merit of his own: 2 Kings 14:26-27.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did evil in the sight of the Lord and departed not from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat: 2 Kings 14:24.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the longest and most successful reign in the northern kingdom and gives it no credit to the king. The salvation of Israel in his day is explicitly attributed to God seeing their bitter affliction, not to the man he used. Amos and Hosea, prophesying in these years, describe a prosperous society rotten with injustice.

Significance

Under him Israel reached its greatest extent since Solomon, and it is the setting of Amos and Hosea, whose oracles show what that prosperity concealed. Amos 7:9-11 records Amaziah of Bethel reporting Amos to him for conspiracy. His death was followed by the rapid collapse of the northern kingdom.

Death / Outcome

Slept with his fathers, with the kings of Israel, and Zachariah his son reigned (2 Kings 14:29).

Scripture References

2 Kings 13:13; 2 Kings 14:16, 14:23-29; Hosea 1:1; Amos 1:1; Amos 7:9-11
—

Ahaz

Son of Jotham; king of Judah; sacrificed his son in the fire, stripped the temple to buy Assyrian help, and copied a pagan altar from Damascus.

Family

Son of Jotham (2 Kings 15:38); father of Hezekiah (2 Kings 16:20).

Chronology

"Twenty years old was Ahaz when he began to reign, and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 16:2).

Life Synopsis

"And he did not that which was right in the sight of the Lord his God, like David his father. But he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, yea, and made his son to pass through the fire, according to the abominations of the heathen" (2 Kings 16:2-4).

When Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel besieged Jerusalem, he sent to Tiglathpileser of Assyria: "I am thy servant and thy son: come up, and save me." He took the silver and gold of the house of the Lord and of the palace and sent it as a present (2 Kings 16:5-8). Isaiah met him and offered him a sign, and he refused it with a show of piety - "I will not ask, neither will I tempt the Lord" - and received the sign of Immanuel anyway (Isaiah 7:1-14).

He went to Damascus to meet Tiglathpileser, saw an altar there, sent the pattern to Urijah the priest, and had one built like it. He offered on it, moved the brasen altar aside, and altered the temple furniture for the king of Assyria's sake (2 Kings 16:10-18). Chronicles adds that in his distress he trespassed yet more, sacrificing to the gods of Damascus "which smote him," saying, "Because the gods of the kings of Syria help them, therefore will I sacrifice to them, that they may help me. But they were the ruin of him, and of all Israel" (2 Chronicles 28:22-23). He shut up the doors of the house of the Lord (2 Chronicles 28:24).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Walked in the way of the kings of Israel and made molten images for Baalim: 2 Kings 16:3; 2 Chronicles 28:2.
  • Made his son to pass through the fire, after the abominations of the heathen: 2 Kings 16:3.
  • Stripped the house of the Lord to hire the king of Assyria rather than trust God: 2 Kings 16:8; 2 Chronicles 28:20-21.
  • Copied a pagan altar from Damascus and rebuilt the temple's arrangement around it: 2 Kings 16:10-16.
  • Sacrificed to the gods of Damascus because they had defeated him: 2 Chronicles 28:22-23.
  • Shut up the doors of the house of the Lord and made altars in every corner of Jerusalem: 2 Chronicles 28:24.

Character Assessment

One of the worst kings of Judah, and the record is unusual in giving his reasoning. He sacrificed to the gods of the nation that had beaten him on the explicit theory that their gods were helping them - and Chronicles adds the verdict, "they were the ruin of him." He refused Isaiah's offered sign with language borrowed from piety.

Significance

It was to Ahaz that the sign of Immanuel was given - "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel" (Isaiah 7:14) - which Matthew applies to the birth of Christ (Matthew 1:22-23). His submission made Judah a vassal of Assyria. He stands in the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:9).

Death / Outcome

Slept with his fathers and was buried in Jerusalem, but not brought into the sepulchres of the kings of Israel (2 Chronicles 28:27).

Scripture References

2 Kings 15:38-16:20; 2 Chronicles 28:1-27; Isaiah 7:1-25; Matthew 1:9
—

Hoshea

Son of Elah; the last king of Israel; conspired with Egypt, was imprisoned by Shalmaneser, and saw Samaria taken and Israel carried away.

Family

Son of Elah (2 Kings 17:1).

Chronology

Reigned nine years over Israel in Samaria (2 Kings 17:1).

Life Synopsis

He conspired against Pekah and killed him and reigned in his stead (2 Kings 15:30). "And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, but not as the kings of Israel that were before him" (2 Kings 17:2).

Shalmaneser of Assyria came up and Hoshea became his servant and paid tribute. Then the king of Assyria found conspiracy in him, for he had sent messengers to So king of Egypt and brought no present as he had done year by year. He was shut up and bound in prison. The king of Assyria besieged Samaria three years and took it in the ninth year of Hoshea, and carried Israel away to Assyria (2 Kings 17:3-6).

The historian then gives the reason at length: Israel had sinned against the Lord who brought them out of Egypt, feared other gods, walked in the statutes of the heathen, built high places, set up images and groves, served idols, caused their children to pass through the fire, used divination and enchantments, and sold themselves to do evil - and God had testified against them by all the prophets and all the seers, and they would not hear (2 Kings 17:7-23).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded. Scripture records that he did evil "but not as the kings of Israel that were before him" (2 Kings 17:2), which is a comparative statement rather than a commendation.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did evil in the sight of the Lord: 2 Kings 17:2.
  • Conspired with Egypt against Assyria and withheld the tribute: 2 Kings 17:4.
  • Murdered Pekah to take the throne: 2 Kings 15:30.

Character Assessment

Scripture gives him nine verses and spends the rest of the chapter explaining that the fall of Israel was not really about him. The comparative note that he was not as bad as his predecessors, placed in the account of the kingdom's destruction, makes the point that judgment had been long accumulating.

Significance

The last king of the northern kingdom. Samaria fell in his ninth year and the ten tribes were deported, and 2 Kings 17:7-23 is Scripture's fullest single explanation of why - naming the sin of Jeroboam as the root and the rejection of the prophets as the immediate cause.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He was shut up in prison by the king of Assyria (2 Kings 17:4).

Scripture References

2 Kings 15:30; 2 Kings 17:1-23; 2 Kings 18:9-12
—

Hezekiah

Son of Ahaz; king of Judah; removed the high places and the brasen serpent, trusted God against Sennacherib, and was given fifteen added years.

Also called Ezekias

Family

Son of Ahaz; his mother was Abi the daughter of Zachariah (2 Kings 18:2). Father of Manasseh (2 Kings 20:21).

Chronology

"Twenty and five years old was he when he began to reign; and he reigned twenty and nine years in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 18:2).

Life Synopsis

"And he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, according to all that David his father did. He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan." The assessment that follows is one of the strongest in Kings: "He trusted in the Lord God of Israel; so that after him was none like him among all the kings of Judah, nor any that were before him" (2 Kings 18:3-5).

He reopened and cleansed the temple his father had shut, restored the Levites and the service, and kept a great passover, inviting even the remnant of the northern tribes; some mocked, but many came, and there was great joy in Jerusalem, the like of which had not been since Solomon (2 Chronicles 29:1-30:27).

Sennacherib came up against all the fenced cities of Judah. Hezekiah first paid tribute, stripping the temple doors (2 Kings 18:13-16). Rabshakeh came to the wall and mocked God to the people in their own language. Hezekiah took the letter into the house of the Lord and spread it before him, praying, "Now therefore, O Lord our God, I beseech thee, save thou us out of his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that thou art the Lord God, even thou only." Isaiah sent word, and the angel of the Lord smote a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp (2 Kings 19:1-36).

Sick unto death, he turned his face to the wall and wept, and was given fifteen more years and a sign (2 Kings 20:1-11). Afterward the ambassadors of Babylon came, and he showed them all his treasures. Isaiah asked what they had seen, and told him all would be carried to Babylon and his sons made eunuchs there. Hezekiah answered, "Good is the word of the Lord which thou hast spoken" - and added, "Is it not good, if peace and truth be in my days?" (2 Kings 20:12-19).

What They Did Right

  • Did right according to all that David did, and removed the high places, which no king before him had done: 2 Kings 18:3-4.
  • Broke the brasen serpent that Moses had made, because Israel had made it an idol: 2 Kings 18:4.
  • Trusted in the Lord God of Israel, so that there was none like him among all the kings of Judah before or after: 2 Kings 18:5.
  • Clave to the Lord and departed not from following him, and kept his commandments: 2 Kings 18:6.
  • Reopened and cleansed the house of the Lord which his father had shut: 2 Chronicles 29:3-19.
  • Kept a great passover and invited the remnant of Israel, praying for those who came unprepared: 2 Chronicles 30:1-20.
  • Spread Sennacherib's letter before the Lord and prayed that all the kingdoms of the earth might know God alone: 2 Kings 19:14-19.
  • Accepted Isaiah's word of judgment without protest: 2 Kings 20:19.

What They Did Wrong

  • Stripped the gold from the temple doors and pillars to pay Sennacherib's tribute: 2 Kings 18:15-16.
  • Showed all his treasures to the ambassadors of Babylon: 2 Kings 20:13-18. Chronicles states the cause: "his heart was lifted up," and that God left him to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart: 2 Chronicles 32:25-31.
  • His response to the sentence on his sons - "Is it not good, if peace and truth be in my days?" - is recorded without comment and reads as relief that judgment would fall after him: 2 Kings 20:19.

Character Assessment

Scripture gives him the highest comparative verdict of any king of Judah: none like him before or after in trusting the Lord. It records his failures anyway, and Chronicles names the cause of the last one exactly - his heart was lifted up after the deliverance, and God left him to try him. The reform was genuine and thorough, reaching even to a relic of Moses that had become an idol.

Significance

His reform and passover were the most thorough since Solomon, and his deliverance from Assyria preserved Jerusalem when Samaria had fallen. His added fifteen years produced Manasseh, who undid the reform. His prayer and Isaiah's answer occupy two of the longest narrative passages in the prophets (Isaiah 36-39). He stands in the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:9-10).

Death / Outcome

Slept with his fathers and was buried in the chiefest of the sepulchres of the sons of David; all Judah and Jerusalem did him honour at his death (2 Kings 20:21; 2 Chronicles 32:33).

Scripture References

2 Kings 16:20; 2 Kings 18:1-20:21; 2 Chronicles 29:1-32:33; Isaiah 36:1-39:8; Matthew 1:9-10
—

Sennacherib

King of Assyria; took the fenced cities of Judah, besieged Jerusalem and blasphemed the God of Israel, and lost a hundred and eighty-five thousand men in a night.

Family

Father of Adrammelech and Sharezer, who killed him (2 Kings 19:37).

Chronology

He came against Judah in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:13).

Life Synopsis

He came up against all the fenced cities of Judah and took them, and Hezekiah paid three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold (2 Kings 18:13-16). He then sent Rabshakeh with a great host to Jerusalem.

His letter and his messenger's speech both rested on one argument: no god of any nation had delivered its land out of his hand, therefore neither would the Lord (2 Kings 18:33-35; 2 Kings 19:10-13). Isaiah's answer to him is one of the longest prophetic addresses to a foreign king in Scripture, and it turns the argument around: he was the axe in God's hand and had boasted against him who used it, and God would put a hook in his nose and a bridle in his lips and turn him back the way he came (2 Kings 19:20-28).

"And it came to pass that night, that the angel of the Lord went out, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians an hundred fourscore and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead corpses. So Sennacherib king of Assyria departed, and went and returned, and dwelt at Nineveh." As he worshipped in the house of Nisroch his god, two of his sons killed him with the sword (2 Kings 19:35-37).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Reproached and blasphemed the living God, and lifted up his eyes on high against the Holy One of Israel: 2 Kings 19:22.
  • Reckoned the God of Israel among the gods of the nations, which were the work of men's hands: 2 Kings 19:17-18.
  • Boasted of his own conquests as though the axe could boast against him that hewed with it: 2 Kings 19:23-24; Isaiah 10:15.

Character Assessment

Scripture treats him as the type of imperial arrogance. Isaiah's oracle grants that he was genuinely an instrument in God's hand and condemns him precisely for not knowing it. His death, murdered by his own sons in his god's temple, is recorded in one verse without comment.

Significance

The destruction of his army delivered Jerusalem when every other fortified city of Judah had fallen, and it is the single greatest recorded deliverance in the history of the divided kingdom. Isaiah 10:5-19 uses him as the standing illustration of a nation used by God and judged for its pride.

Death / Outcome

Killed by his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer with the sword while worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god (2 Kings 19:37).

Scripture References

2 Kings 18:13-19:37; 2 Chronicles 32:1-22; Isaiah 10:5-19; Isaiah 36:1-37:38
—

Rabshakeh

A chief officer of Sennacherib sent to demand Jerusalem's surrender; addressed the people on the wall in Hebrew and mocked their God.

Family

Not recorded. Rabshakeh is an Assyrian office-title rather than a personal name; Scripture uses it as his designation.

Chronology

In the fourteenth year of Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:13, 18:17).

Life Synopsis

Sent with Tartan and Rabsaris and a great host, he stood by the conduit of the upper pool and addressed Hezekiah's officers. His argument was systematic: Egypt was a bruised reed that would pierce the hand; if they said they trusted in the Lord, was it not his high places Hezekiah had taken away? He offered two thousand horses if they could set riders on them, and claimed he had come up by the Lord's own word (2 Kings 18:19-25).

Eliakim asked him to speak in Syrian and not in the Jews' language in the ears of the people on the wall. He answered that his master had sent him precisely to the men on the wall, and raised his voice in Hebrew, telling them not to let Hezekiah deceive them, offering them their own vines and fig trees under Assyrian resettlement, and finishing: "Who are they among all the gods of the countries, that have delivered their country out of mine hand, that the Lord should deliver Jerusalem out of mine hand?" The people held their peace and answered not a word, for the king's commandment was not to answer him (2 Kings 18:26-36).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Deliberately addressed the people over their officers' heads to break their morale: 2 Kings 18:27-28.
  • Ranked the God of Israel with the gods of the nations he had conquered: 2 Kings 18:33-35.
  • Claimed the Lord had sent him, using God's name to serve his own siege: 2 Kings 18:25.
  • Hezekiah and Isaiah both identify his words as reproaching and blaspheming the living God: 2 Kings 19:4, 19:6.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his speech at unusual length, which is itself significant - it is preserved because it is the most articulate case for despair anywhere in the historical books. He knew the political situation, knew about Hezekiah's reform, and turned both against the defenders. The people's silence is recorded as obedience to their king rather than as having no answer.

Significance

His speech is the occasion of Hezekiah's prayer and Isaiah's greatest oracle. It states the question the whole episode answers: whether the God of Israel is one god among the nations or the Lord of all the kingdoms of the earth.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He returned and found the king of Assyria warring against Libnah (2 Kings 19:8).

Scripture References

2 Kings 18:17-37; 2 Kings 19:4-8; Isaiah 36:2-37:8
—

Manasseh (king of Judah)

Son of Hezekiah; king of Judah fifty-five years; the most idolatrous of Judah's kings, who was carried to Babylon in chains and humbled himself there.

Family

Son of Hezekiah; his mother was Hephzibah (2 Kings 21:1). Father of Amon (2 Kings 21:18).

Chronology

"Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and reigned fifty and five years in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 21:1) - the longest reign of any king of Judah.

Life Synopsis

"And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, after the abominations of the heathen, whom the Lord cast out before the children of Israel." He rebuilt the high places his father had destroyed, reared altars for Baal, made a grove, worshipped all the host of heaven, built altars in the house of the Lord and in its two courts, made his son pass through the fire, observed times, used enchantments, and dealt with familiar spirits and wizards. He set a graven image of the grove in the house of which God had said, "In Jerusalem will I put my name" (2 Kings 21:2-7).

"So Manasseh made Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem to err, and to do worse than the heathen." God spoke by his prophets and they would not hearken. "Moreover Manasseh shed innocent blood very much, till he had filled Jerusalem from one end to another" (2 Kings 21:9-16).

Chronicles alone records the sequel: the king of Assyria's captains took him among the thorns, bound him with fetters, and carried him to Babylon. "And when he was in affliction, he besought the Lord his God, and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers, and prayed unto him: and he was intreated of him, and heard his supplication, and brought him again to Jerusalem into his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the Lord he was God." He took away the strange gods and the idol out of the house of the Lord, repaired the altar, and commanded Judah to serve the Lord - though the people still sacrificed in the high places (2 Chronicles 33:11-17).

What They Did Right

  • In affliction he besought the Lord, humbled himself greatly, and prayed - and God was intreated of him: 2 Chronicles 33:12-13.
  • Knew after his restoration that the Lord was God: 2 Chronicles 33:13.
  • Removed the strange gods and the idol from the house of the Lord, repaired the altar, and commanded Judah to serve the Lord: 2 Chronicles 33:15-16.

What They Did Wrong

  • Rebuilt the high places Hezekiah had destroyed and reared altars for Baal: 2 Kings 21:3.
  • Built altars for all the host of heaven in the two courts of the house of the Lord: 2 Kings 21:5.
  • Made his son pass through the fire, observed times, used enchantments, and dealt with familiar spirits and wizards: 2 Kings 21:6.
  • Set a graven image in the house of the Lord: 2 Kings 21:7.
  • Made Judah to do worse than the heathen God had cast out: 2 Kings 21:9.
  • Shed innocent blood very much, till he had filled Jerusalem from one end to another: 2 Kings 21:16.
  • 2 Kings 24:3-4 names his sins as the reason God would not pardon Judah, and Jeremiah 15:4 says Judah would be removed into all kingdoms of the earth because of him.

Character Assessment

The most striking single case in the Old Testament of both extremes in one life. Kings records only the evil and names it as the cause of Judah's eventual destruction; Chronicles alone preserves the repentance, and records that God heard him. Both are Scripture. What Chronicles does not claim is that the repentance undid the consequences - Judah's course was not reversed, and his own son Amon returned to his father's idols without his father's repentance.

Significance

His reign is named twice as the reason for the exile (2 Kings 24:3-4; Jeremiah 15:4), which raises the hardest question in the historical books: a man personally forgiven whose national damage stood. He stands in the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:10).

Death / Outcome

Slept with his fathers and was buried in the garden of his own house, in the garden of Uzza (2 Kings 21:18).

Scripture References

2 Kings 20:21-21:18; 2 Kings 23:26; 2 Kings 24:3-4; 2 Chronicles 32:33-33:20; Jeremiah 15:4; Matthew 1:10
—

Amon

Son of Manasseh; king of Judah two years; followed his father's idolatry without his repentance and was murdered by his servants.

Family

Son of Manasseh; his mother was Meshullemeth (2 Kings 21:19). Father of Josiah (2 Kings 21:26).

Chronology

"Amon was twenty and two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned two years in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 21:19).

Life Synopsis

"And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, as his father Manasseh did. And he walked in all the way that his father walked in, and served the idols that his father served, and worshipped them: and he forsook the Lord God of his fathers, and walked not in the way of the Lord" (2 Kings 21:20-22). Chronicles adds, "and Amon trespassed more and more," and that unlike his father he did not humble himself before the Lord (2 Chronicles 33:23).

His servants conspired against him and slew him in his own house. The people of the land slew all who had conspired, and made Josiah his son king in his stead (2 Kings 21:23-24).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did evil as his father Manasseh did, and served and worshipped his father's idols: 2 Kings 21:20-21.
  • Forsook the Lord God of his fathers: 2 Kings 21:22.
  • Did not humble himself before the Lord as his father had done, but trespassed more and more: 2 Chronicles 33:23.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned, and Chronicles draws the comparison that defines him: he inherited his father's sins and not his father's repentance. Two years, and the whole record is a contrast with the man before him.

Significance

His murder brought the eight-year-old Josiah to the throne, under whom Judah's last reform took place. He stands in the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:10).

Death / Outcome

Slain in his own house by his servants (2 Kings 21:23).

Scripture References

2 Kings 21:18-26; 2 Chronicles 33:20-25; Matthew 1:10
—

Josiah

Son of Amon; king of Judah from the age of eight; found the book of the law, carried out the most thorough reform in Judah's history, and was killed at Megiddo.

Also called Josias

Family
