Son of Amon; his mother was Jedidah the daughter of Adaiah of Boscath (2 Kings 22:1). Father of Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah (2 Kings 23:30-34; 2 Kings 24:17).

Chronology

"Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty and one years in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 22:1). He was named by a prophet some three centuries before his birth (1 Kings 13:2).

Life Synopsis

"And he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, and walked in all the way of David his father, and turned not aside to the right hand or to the left" (2 Kings 22:2). Chronicles records that in the eighth year of his reign, while still young, he began to seek after the God of David, and in the twelfth began to purge Judah and Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 34:3).

In his eighteenth year he sent Shaphan to Hilkiah about the money for repairing the temple, and Hilkiah said, "I have found the book of the law in the house of the Lord." When it was read to the king, "he rent his clothes," and sent to enquire of the Lord, "for great is the wrath of the Lord that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book" (2 Kings 22:8-13). Huldah the prophetess answered that the evil would come, but not in his days, because his heart was tender and he had humbled himself.

He gathered all the people, read the book in their ears, and made a covenant to walk after the Lord with all his heart and soul (2 Kings 23:1-3). He then purged the land: the vessels of Baal and the grove burned at Kidron, the idolatrous priests put down, the houses of the sodomites broken, the high places defiled, Topheth in the valley of the son of Hinnom defiled so that no man could make his son pass through the fire, the horses of the sun taken away, and the altar at Bethel broken down and its bones burned on it - fulfilling the word of the man of God from Judah, whose sepulchre he spared (2 Kings 23:4-20). He kept a passover such as had not been held since the days of the judges (2 Kings 23:21-23).

"And like unto him was there no king before him, that turned to the Lord with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his might, according to all the law of Moses; neither after him arose there any like him" (2 Kings 23:25).

Pharaohnechoh went up against Assyria, and Josiah went out against him. Nechoh sent word that God had sent him and that Josiah should not meddle - and Chronicles states that Josiah "hearkened not unto the words of Nechoh from the mouth of God." He disguised himself and fought in the valley of Megiddo, was shot by the archers, and died (2 Kings 23:29; 2 Chronicles 35:20-24). Jeremiah lamented for him, and all Judah mourned.

What They Did Right

  • Did right and walked in all the way of David, turning not aside to the right hand or to the left: 2 Kings 22:2.
  • Began to seek after God while still young: 2 Chronicles 34:3.
  • Rent his clothes at the reading of the law and sent to enquire of the Lord: 2 Kings 22:11-13.
  • Made a covenant before the Lord and had the whole people stand to it: 2 Kings 23:3.
  • Carried out the most thorough purge of idolatry in Judah's history, extending into Israel's territory: 2 Kings 23:4-20.
  • Kept a passover unlike any since the days of the judges: 2 Kings 23:21-23.
  • Scripture's verdict: no king before or after turned to the Lord with all his heart, soul, and might as he did: 2 Kings 23:25.
  • Huldah's word: his heart was tender and he humbled himself before the Lord: 2 Kings 22:19.

What They Did Wrong

  • Went out against Pharaohnechoh and would not hear his warning; Chronicles states that Nechoh's words were from the mouth of God: 2 Chronicles 35:21-22. Kings records the campaign without comment, and Chronicles alone frames it as a failure to hear.

Character Assessment

Scripture gives him the highest personal verdict of any king in either kingdom - none like him before or after in turning to the Lord with all his heart, soul, and might. The one failure recorded is at the very end and is recorded only by Chronicles. His reform was the most thorough ever carried out, and it did not avert the judgment: 2 Kings 23:26 states that the Lord turned not from the fierceness of his wrath because of Manasseh's provocations.

Significance

Named by a prophet three centuries before his birth (1 Kings 13:2), and the fulfilment recorded in 2 Kings 23:15-18. His reform and his passover were Judah's last, and his death at Megiddo began the twenty-two-year collapse to the exile. Jeremiah lamented him, and the mourning for him became a proverb (2 Chronicles 35:25; Zechariah 12:11). He stands in the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:10-11).

Death / Outcome

Shot by archers at Megiddo fighting Pharaohnechoh; brought to Jerusalem and buried in his own sepulchre, and lamented by Jeremiah and all Judah (2 Kings 23:29-30; 2 Chronicles 35:23-25).

Scripture References

1 Kings 13:2; 2 Kings 21:24-23:30; 2 Chronicles 34:1-35:27; Jeremiah 1:2; Zephaniah 1:1; Matthew 1:10-11
—

Hilkiah

High priest in Josiah's reign; found the book of the law in the house of the Lord.

Family

The high priest (2 Kings 22:4); father of Azariah in the priestly line (1 Chronicles 6:13).

Chronology

In the eighteenth year of Josiah (2 Kings 22:3).

Life Synopsis

Josiah sent Shaphan the scribe to him about the money gathered for repairing the temple. "And Hilkiah the high priest said unto Shaphan the scribe, I have found the book of the law in the house of the Lord. And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it" (2 Kings 22:8). He was among those sent to Huldah the prophetess to enquire of the Lord (2 Kings 22:12-14), and afterward carried out the removal of the vessels of Baal and the grove from the temple (2 Kings 23:4).

What They Did Right

  • Reported the finding of the book of the law and handed it over at once rather than concealing it: 2 Kings 22:8.
  • Went with the king's officers to enquire of the Lord by Huldah: 2 Kings 22:14.
  • Carried out the cleansing of the temple at the king's command: 2 Kings 23:4.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. The account does not explain how the book came to be lost in the house of the Lord, nor what he thought of finding it; it records only that he found it and immediately gave it to the king's scribe.

Significance

The book he found produced the reform, the covenant, and the passover of Josiah's reign, and its reading is one of the pivotal moments in Judah's history. His descendant Ezra is traced through the same line (Ezra 7:1).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 35:8.

Scripture References

2 Kings 22:4-23:24; 1 Chronicles 6:13; 2 Chronicles 34:9-22; 2 Chronicles 35:8; Ezra 7:1
—

Shaphan

Scribe to Josiah; carried the found book to the king and read it before him; head of a family that repeatedly protected the prophets.

Family

Son of Azaliah the son of Meshullam (2 Kings 22:3). Father of Ahikam, who protected Jeremiah (Jeremiah 26:24), and grandfather of Gedaliah (Jeremiah 39:14).

Chronology

In the eighteenth year of Josiah (2 Kings 22:3).

Life Synopsis

Sent by Josiah to Hilkiah about the temple repairs, he received the book of the law, read it himself, and reported to the king: "Hilkiah the priest hath delivered me a book. And Shaphan read it before the king" (2 Kings 22:8-10). When the king rent his clothes, Shaphan was among those sent to Huldah (2 Kings 22:12-14).

What They Did Right

  • Read the book to the king rather than summarising or suppressing it: 2 Kings 22:10.
  • Went with the delegation to enquire of the Lord: 2 Kings 22:14.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His significance is largely in what his family did afterward: his son Ahikam saved Jeremiah's life, another son Gemariah had a chamber in the temple from which Baruch read the scroll, and his grandson Gedaliah was made governor after the fall of Jerusalem.

Significance

He read the law that started Josiah's reform. Three generations of his household appear in Jeremiah as protectors of the prophet and of the word - one of the clearest instances in Scripture of a family's continuing influence.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Jeremiah 39:14, by reference to his grandson.

Scripture References

2 Kings 22:3-14; 2 Chronicles 34:8-20; Jeremiah 26:24; Jeremiah 36:10-12; Jeremiah 39:14
—

Huldah

A prophetess in Jerusalem, consulted by Josiah's officers about the found book of the law; confirmed the judgment and promised Josiah he would be gathered to his grave in peace.

Family

Wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, keeper of the wardrobe; she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college (2 Kings 22:14).

Chronology

In the eighteenth year of Josiah (2 Kings 22:3).

Life Synopsis

Hilkiah the high priest, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asahiah went to her. She answered without softening: "Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, Tell the man that sent you to me, Thus saith the Lord, Behold, I will bring evil upon this place, and upon the inhabitants thereof, even all the words of the book which the king of Judah hath read: because they have forsaken me, and have burned incense unto other gods... therefore my wrath shall be kindled against this place, and shall not be quenched."

To the king she sent a separate word: "Because thine heart was tender, and thou hast humbled thyself before the Lord, when thou heardest what I spake against this place... and hast rent thy clothes, and wept before me; I also have heard thee, saith the Lord. Behold therefore, I will gather thee unto thy fathers, and thou shalt be gathered into thy grave in peace; and thine eyes shall not see all the evil which I will bring upon this place" (2 Kings 22:15-20).

What They Did Right

  • Gave God's word without softening it, to the high priest and the king's officers: 2 Kings 22:16-17.
  • Distinguished the judgment on the nation from God's answer to the king's own tenderness of heart: 2 Kings 22:18-20.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against her. She is consulted by the high priest and the king's secretary at the most significant moment of Josiah's reign, while Jeremiah and Zephaniah were both prophesying - and the text offers no explanation of why she was chosen, nor any comment on her being a woman. Her answer is the whole of her record and it is entirely direct.

Significance

One of the small number of women called prophetess in Scripture, with Miriam, Deborah, Noadiah, and Anna. Her word authenticated the found book, set the reform in motion, and defined its limits: the reform would be genuine and the judgment would still come.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 34:22-28.

Scripture References

2 Kings 22:14-20; 2 Chronicles 34:22-28
—

Jehoahaz (king of Judah)

Son of Josiah; king of Judah three months; deposed by Pharaohnechoh and died in Egypt.

Also called Shallum

Family

Son of Josiah; his mother was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah (2 Kings 23:31). Called Shallum in Jeremiah 22:11.

Chronology

"Jehoahaz was twenty and three years old when he began to reign; and he reigned three months in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 23:31).

Life Synopsis

The people of the land took him and made him king after his father's death. "And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his fathers had done" (2 Kings 23:30-32).

Pharaohnechoh put him in bands at Riblah, put the land to a tribute, made his brother Eliakim king in his place and changed his name to Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz to Egypt, "and he came to Egypt, and died there" (2 Kings 23:33-34).

Jeremiah's word concerning him: "Weep ye not for the dead, neither bemoan him: but weep sore for him that goeth away: for he shall return no more, nor see his native country" (Jeremiah 22:10-12).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his fathers had done: 2 Kings 23:32.

Character Assessment

Three months, one verdict. Scripture's fuller comment comes through Jeremiah, who told Judah to mourn not for Josiah who had died but for this son who would never see his country again.

Significance

His deposition by Egypt ended Judah's independence. Every king after him was installed by a foreign power.

Death / Outcome

Died in Egypt (2 Kings 23:34).

Scripture References

2 Kings 23:30-34; 2 Chronicles 36:1-4; Jeremiah 22:10-12
—

Jehoiakim

Son of Josiah; installed by Pharaohnechoh; taxed the land for tribute, burned Jeremiah's scroll, and shed innocent blood.

Also called Eliakim

Family

Son of Josiah; his mother was Zebudah the daughter of Pedaiah (2 Kings 23:36). Originally Eliakim; renamed by Pharaohnechoh. Father of Jehoiachin (2 Kings 24:6).

Chronology

"Jehoiakim was twenty and five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 23:36).

Life Synopsis

Made king by Pharaohnechoh, he taxed the land to give the tribute, exacting silver and gold of the people of the land, every man according to his taxation. "And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his fathers had done" (2 Kings 23:35-37).

Nebuchadnezzar came up and he became his servant three years, then rebelled (2 Kings 24:1). Bands of Chaldees, Syrians, Moabites, and Ammonites were sent against Judah, "according to the word of the Lord, which he spake by his servants the prophets" (2 Kings 24:2).

Jeremiah dictated a scroll to Baruch and it was read in the temple and then before the princes and finally to the king in his winter house. "And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed... Yet they were not afraid, nor rent their garments, neither the king, nor any of his servants, that heard all these words." He ordered Baruch and Jeremiah arrested, but the Lord hid them (Jeremiah 36:21-26). Jeremiah also records that he killed the prophet Urijah, having him fetched back from Egypt (Jeremiah 26:20-23).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his fathers had done: 2 Kings 23:37.
  • Taxed the people of the land to pay tribute to Egypt: 2 Kings 23:35.
  • Cut Jeremiah's scroll with a penknife and burned it, and neither he nor his servants were afraid nor rent their garments: Jeremiah 36:23-24.
  • Sought to seize Jeremiah and Baruch: Jeremiah 36:26.
  • Had the prophet Urijah brought back from Egypt and killed with the sword: Jeremiah 26:20-23.
  • Jeremiah's charge: his eyes and heart were for covetousness, for shedding innocent blood, for oppression and violence: Jeremiah 22:17.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned, and given one of the harshest prophetic sentences in Scripture: "He shall be buried with the burial of an ass, drawn and cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem" (Jeremiah 22:19). The burning of the scroll is the defining act - deliberate, unhurried, page by page, and without fear.

Significance

His rebellion brought Nebuchadnezzar against Judah and began the deportations. The burning of the scroll and its rewriting with many like words added (Jeremiah 36:32) is Scripture's clearest statement that the word cannot be destroyed by destroying the copy. He stands in the genealogy of Christ under Josiah's line (Matthew 1:11).

Death / Outcome

"So Jehoiakim slept with his fathers" (2 Kings 24:6). Jeremiah 22:18-19 and Jeremiah 36:30 pronounce that he would be buried with the burial of an ass and his body cast out; Scripture does not narrate the manner of his death.

Scripture References

2 Kings 23:34-24:7; 2 Chronicles 36:4-8; Jeremiah 22:13-19; Jeremiah 26:20-23; Jeremiah 36:1-32; Daniel 1:1-2; Matthew 1:11
—

Jehoiachin

Son of Jehoiakim; king of Judah three months; carried to Babylon with the treasures and the craftsmen, and released from prison thirty-seven years later.

Also called Jeconiah, Coniah, Jechonias

Family

Son of Jehoiakim; his mother was Nehushta the daughter of Elnathan (2 Kings 24:8).

Chronology

"Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned in Jerusalem three months" (2 Kings 24:8). He was released in the thirty-seventh year of his captivity (2 Kings 25:27).

Life Synopsis

"And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his father had done" (2 Kings 24:9). Nebuchadnezzar's servants besieged Jerusalem, and he went out to the king of Babylon with his mother, his servants, his princes, and his officers.

Nebuchadnezzar carried out all the treasures of the house of the Lord and of the king's house, cut in pieces the vessels of gold that Solomon had made, and carried away all Jerusalem - the princes, the mighty men of valour, the craftsmen and smiths, ten thousand captives - leaving none save the poorest sort of the people of the land (2 Kings 24:10-16).

Jeremiah's word against him was severe: "Write ye this man childless, a man that shall not prosper in his days: for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah" (Jeremiah 22:30).

In the thirty-seventh year of his captivity Evilmerodach king of Babylon lifted up his head out of prison, spoke kindly to him, set his throne above the throne of the kings with him, changed his prison garments, and gave him a daily allowance all the days of his life (2 Kings 25:27-30). These are the closing verses of 2 Kings.

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his father had done: 2 Kings 24:9.

Character Assessment

Three months as king and thirty-seven years in prison, and Scripture's verdict on him is a single formula. What the account gives him instead is the last word of the book: a king of Judah alive, released, honoured at a foreign table. The historian ends there without comment, and the placement is not accidental.

Significance

His deportation is the exile Ezekiel dates by (Ezekiel 1:2). Jeremiah's sentence that none of his seed should prosper on David's throne stands alongside his appearance in Matthew's genealogy of Christ as Jechonias (Matthew 1:11-12) - a tension long noted and variously explained, and recorded here without resolution. His release in the closing verses of Kings leaves the Davidic line alive at the end of a book that has just recorded its destruction.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He ate bread before the king of Babylon continually all the days of his life (2 Kings 25:29-30).

Scripture References

2 Kings 24:6-16; 2 Kings 25:27-30; 2 Chronicles 36:8-10; Jeremiah 22:24-30; Jeremiah 52:31-34; Ezekiel 1:2; Matthew 1:11-12
—

Zedekiah (king of Judah)

Son of Josiah; last king of Judah; installed by Nebuchadnezzar, rebelled, and saw his sons killed before his eyes were put out.

Also called Mattaniah

Family

Son of Josiah; his mother was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah (2 Kings 24:18); uncle of Jehoiachin. Originally Mattaniah; renamed by Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kings 24:17).

Chronology

"Zedekiah was twenty and one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem" (2 Kings 24:18).

Life Synopsis

Nebuchadnezzar made him king in Jehoiachin's place and changed his name. "And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that Jehoiakim had done" (2 Kings 24:17-19). Chronicles adds that he humbled not himself before Jeremiah the prophet speaking from the mouth of the Lord, and rebelled against the king who had made him swear by God (2 Chronicles 36:12-13).

He consulted Jeremiah repeatedly and in secret, asking, "Is there any word from the Lord?" and was told plainly to surrender and live. He answered that he was afraid of the Jews that had fallen to the Chaldeans, lest they mock him, and would not do it (Jeremiah 37:17; Jeremiah 38:14-23). He allowed the princes to put Jeremiah into the dungeon and then allowed Ebedmelech to draw him out (Jeremiah 38:4-13).

In the ninth year of his reign Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem. In the eleventh year the famine was severe and the city was broken up. He fled by night by the way of the gate between two walls and was overtaken in the plains of Jericho, his army scattered. "And they slew the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, and put out the eyes of Zedekiah, and bound him with fetters of brass, and carried him to Babylon" (2 Kings 25:1-7).

What They Did Right

  • Sent repeatedly to Jeremiah to enquire of the Lord: Jeremiah 37:3, 37:17; Jeremiah 38:14.
  • Permitted Ebedmelech to draw Jeremiah out of the dungeon: Jeremiah 38:10.
  • Protected Jeremiah from the princes who wanted him dead, though weakly: Jeremiah 38:5, 38:24-27.

What They Did Wrong

  • Did evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that Jehoiakim had done: 2 Kings 24:19.
  • Rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar, breaking an oath sworn by God: 2 Chronicles 36:13; Ezekiel 17:15-19.
  • Humbled not himself before Jeremiah speaking from the mouth of the Lord: 2 Chronicles 36:12.
  • Knew what God required and would not do it, for fear of being mocked: Jeremiah 38:19.
  • Told Jeremiah to conceal their conversation from the princes: Jeremiah 38:24-27.

Character Assessment

A weak man rather than a defiant one, and Scripture records the weakness precisely. He enquired of the prophet again and again, in secret, and received the same plain answer each time, and could not act on it because he feared what people would say. The princes overruled him at will - "the king is not he that can do any thing against you" (Jeremiah 38:5). His last recorded sight was the death of his sons.

Significance

The last king of Judah. With him the throne of David ended until Christ, and the temple, the city, and the walls were destroyed in his eleventh year. Ezekiel treats his broken oath to Nebuchadnezzar as an oath despised against God himself (Ezekiel 17:15-19).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He was blinded, bound with fetters of brass, and carried to Babylon; Jeremiah 52:11 adds that he was put in prison till the day of his death.

Scripture References

2 Kings 24:17-25:7; 2 Chronicles 36:11-21; Jeremiah 21:1-10; Jeremiah 34:1-22; Jeremiah 37:1-38:28; Jeremiah 52:1-11; Ezekiel 17:11-21
—

Nebuchadnezzar

King of Babylon; destroyed Jerusalem and the temple and carried Judah into exile; humbled until he acknowledged that the most High rules in the kingdom of men.

Also called Nebuchadrezzar

Family

Father of Evilmerodach (2 Kings 25:27); Belshazzar is called his son in Daniel 5:2.

Chronology

He reigned over Babylon through the last years of Judah; his first year corresponds to the fourth of Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 25:1).

Life Synopsis

He came against Jehoiakim, who served him three years and rebelled (2 Kings 24:1). He besieged Jerusalem in Jehoiachin's reign, took the treasures and ten thousand captives, and set Zedekiah on the throne (2 Kings 24:10-17). When Zedekiah rebelled he besieged the city, and in the eleventh year it was broken up. Nebuzaradan burned the house of the Lord, the king's house, and every great house, and broke down the walls of Jerusalem (2 Kings 25:1-10).

Daniel records another side of him: he dreamed of a great image and Daniel interpreted it, and he fell on his face and said, "Of a truth it is, that your God is a God of gods, and a Lord of kings" (Daniel 2:47). He then set up a golden image and threw three men into a furnace for refusing it, and on seeing them unharmed decreed that no one should speak against their God (Daniel 3:1-30). Warned in a second dream to break off his sins by righteousness, he said twelve months later, "Is not this great Babylon, that I have built...by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?" and was driven from men to eat grass as oxen until seven times passed over him (Daniel 4:29-33).

"And at the end of the days I Nebuchadnezzar lifted up mine eyes unto heaven, and mine understanding returned unto me, and I blessed the most High... Now I Nebuchadnezzar praise and extol and honour the King of heaven, all whose works are truth, and his ways judgment: and those that walk in pride he is able to abase" (Daniel 4:34-37).

What They Did Right

  • Acknowledged the God of Daniel as a God of gods and a Lord of kings: Daniel 2:47.
  • Decreed that no one should speak amiss against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego: Daniel 3:28-29.
  • After his humbling, blessed, praised, extolled, and honoured the King of heaven, and confessed that those who walk in pride he is able to abase: Daniel 4:34-37.
  • Dealt kindly with Jeremiah, charging Nebuzaradan to look well to him and do him no harm: Jeremiah 39:11-12.

What They Did Wrong

  • Destroyed Jerusalem and burned the house of the Lord: 2 Kings 25:9.
  • Set up a golden image and commanded all to worship it on pain of the burning furnace: Daniel 3:1-6.
  • Said in pride, "Is not this great Babylon, that I have built by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?": Daniel 4:30.
  • Slew Zedekiah's sons before his eyes and blinded him: 2 Kings 25:7.

Character Assessment

Scripture treats him in two registers that must be held together. In Kings, Chronicles, and Jeremiah he is the destroyer of Jerusalem, and also God's own servant used for that purpose (Jeremiah 25:9; Jeremiah 27:6). In Daniel he is a man brought through repeated warnings to a confession of God's sovereignty stated in his own words. The confession in Daniel 4:34-37 is one of the fullest in the Old Testament, and it is spoken by the man who burned the temple.

Significance

He carried Judah into the seventy years of exile that Jeremiah foretold (Jeremiah 25:11-12), destroyed Solomon's temple, and is the head of gold in the image of Daniel 2. God repeatedly calls him "my servant" in Jeremiah, which is Scripture's plainest statement that God governs through rulers who do not know him.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Daniel 4:36 records his restoration to his kingdom with added majesty.

Scripture References

2 Kings 24:1-25:22; 2 Chronicles 36:6-21; Jeremiah 25:9; Jeremiah 27:6-8; Jeremiah 39:1-14; Jeremiah 52:1-30; Daniel 1:1-4:37; Ezekiel 26:7
—

Nebuzaradan

Captain of Nebuchadnezzar's guard; burned the temple and Jerusalem, carried away the captives, and freed Jeremiah with a remarkable speech.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

In the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kings 25:8).

Life Synopsis

He came to Jerusalem and burned the house of the Lord, the king's house, and every great house, and his army broke down the walls round about. He carried away the rest of the people and the deserters, but left of the poor of the land to be vinedressers and husbandmen (2 Kings 25:8-12). He took the pillars, the sea, and the vessels, and brought the chief priests and officers to Riblah, where they were slain (2 Kings 25:13-21).

Jeremiah records that he took Jeremiah, bound in chains among the captives at Ramah, and released him with these words: "The Lord thy God hath pronounced this evil upon this place. Now the Lord hath brought it, and done according as he hath said: because ye have sinned against the Lord, and have not obeyed his voice, therefore this thing is come upon you." He gave him victuals and a reward and let him go where he would, and committed him to Gedaliah (Jeremiah 40:1-5).

What They Did Right

  • Left the poor of the land vineyards and fields: 2 Kings 25:12; Jeremiah 39:10.
  • Released Jeremiah, gave him provisions and a reward, and let him choose where to go: Jeremiah 40:1-5.

What They Did Wrong

  • Burned the house of the Lord and the city, and broke down the walls: 2 Kings 25:9-10. Scripture records these as acts of judgment carried out by Babylon and offers no separate condemnation of the man.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the destruction he executed and, in Jeremiah, a speech in which a Babylonian officer states the theology of the exile more clearly than most of Judah's kings had: God said this would happen because of your sin, and now he has done it. The text passes no verdict on him.

Significance

He carried out the destruction of the temple and the final deportation. His release of Jeremiah preserved the prophet through the fall of the city.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Jeremiah 52:30.

Scripture References

2 Kings 25:8-21; Jeremiah 39:9-14; Jeremiah 40:1-5; Jeremiah 52:12-30
—

Gedaliah

Son of Ahikam; made governor over the remnant left in Judah by Nebuchadnezzar; refused to believe a warning of assassination and was murdered.

Family

Son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan (2 Kings 25:22); his father had protected Jeremiah (Jeremiah 26:24).

Chronology

After the fall of Jerusalem, in the seventh month (2 Kings 25:25).

Life Synopsis

Nebuchadnezzar made him governor over the people left in the land. He sware to the captains of the forces and their men: "Fear not to be the servants of the Chaldees: dwell in the land, and serve the king of Babylon; and it shall be well with you" (2 Kings 25:22-24). Jews returned from Moab, Ammon, and Edom, and gathered wine and summer fruits in abundance (Jeremiah 40:11-12).

Johanan warned him that Baalis king of the Ammonites had sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to kill him, and offered to kill Ishmael secretly. "But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam said unto Johanan the son of Kareah, Thou shalt not do this thing: for thou speakest falsely of Ishmael" (Jeremiah 40:13-16).

In the seventh month Ishmael came with ten men and they ate bread together at Mizpah, and Ishmael rose up and killed him, with the Jews and the Chaldeans that were with him (2 Kings 25:25; Jeremiah 41:1-3). The people fled to Egypt for fear of the Chaldeans (2 Kings 25:26).

What They Did Right

  • Reassured the frightened remnant and urged them to settle and serve peaceably: 2 Kings 25:24.
  • Refused to have a man killed on suspicion: Jeremiah 40:16. Scripture records the refusal and its fatal outcome without calling it either virtue or folly.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. He disbelieved a true warning, and it cost him his life and scattered the remnant. Scripture states the fact and passes no verdict.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents a decent man in an impossible position, killed at his own table by a guest. His refusal to strike first is recorded plainly, along with the fact that the warning was true. The text does not tell the reader what he should have done.

Significance

His murder ended the last organised Jewish community in the land and drove the remnant into Egypt, taking Jeremiah with them against his counsel (Jeremiah 43:5-7). The fast of the seventh month, mentioned in Zechariah 7:5 and 8:19, is traditionally associated with his death.

Death / Outcome

Murdered by Ishmael the son of Nethaniah at Mizpah while eating bread with him (2 Kings 25:25; Jeremiah 41:2).

Scripture References

2 Kings 25:22-26; Jeremiah 39:14; Jeremiah 40:5-41:18
—

Ishmael (son of Nethaniah)

Of the seed royal; murdered Gedaliah at his own table, killed eighty pilgrims, and fled to the Ammonites.

Family

Son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama, of the seed royal (2 Kings 25:25; Jeremiah 41:1).

Chronology

In the seventh month after the fall of Jerusalem (2 Kings 25:25).

Life Synopsis

He came to Gedaliah at Mizpah with ten men, and they ate bread together. "Then arose Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and the ten men that were with him, and smote Gedaliah... and slew him, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land." He killed all the Jews and the Chaldean soldiers with him (Jeremiah 41:1-3).

The next day, before anyone knew, eighty men came from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria with offerings and incense for the house of the Lord, their beards shaven and their clothes rent. He went out weeping to meet them and said, "Come to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam." When they were in the city he killed them and cast them into a pit, sparing ten who offered him hidden stores of wheat, barley, oil, and honey (Jeremiah 41:4-9). He carried away the king's daughters and the remnant captive toward the Ammonites, but Johanan overtook him and recovered them; Ishmael escaped with eight men (Jeremiah 41:10-15).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Murdered the governor at his own table after eating bread with him: Jeremiah 41:1-2.
  • Killed the Jews and the Chaldeans at Mizpah: Jeremiah 41:3.
  • Enticed eighty mourning pilgrims into the city with a pretence of weeping and killed them: Jeremiah 41:4-7.
  • Carried the remnant, including the king's daughters, captive toward Ammon: Jeremiah 41:10.

Character Assessment

Uniformly condemned by the record. His crime is aggravated at every point: the man he killed had sworn to protect the people, the killing followed a shared meal, and the eighty men he murdered were coming to worship. Scripture records that he was acting for Baalis king of the Ammonites (Jeremiah 40:14).

Significance

His murder of Gedaliah destroyed the last Jewish administration in the land and drove the remnant to Egypt in fear of Babylonian reprisal, taking Jeremiah with them.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He escaped with eight men to the Ammonites (Jeremiah 41:15).

Scripture References

2 Kings 25:25; Jeremiah 40:8, 40:13-16; Jeremiah 41:1-18
—

Evilmerodach

King of Babylon after Nebuchadnezzar; released Jehoiachin from prison and gave him a place at his own table.

Family

Son of Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kings 25:27, by succession).

Chronology

In the year that he began to reign, the thirty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's captivity (2 Kings 25:27).

Life Synopsis

"And it came to pass in the seven and thirtieth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the seven and twentieth day of the month, that Evilmerodach king of Babylon in the year that he began to reign did lift up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah out of prison; and spake kindly to him, and set his throne above the throne of the kings that were with him in Babylon; and changed his prison garments: and he did eat bread continually before him all the days of his life. And his allowance was a continual allowance given him of the king, a daily rate for every day, all the days of his life" (2 Kings 25:27-30).

What They Did Right

  • Lifted a captive king out of prison after thirty-seven years, spoke kindly to him, set his throne above the other kings, changed his garments, and provided for him daily for the rest of his life: 2 Kings 25:27-30.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records one act of kindness and nothing else about him, and places it at the very end of the books of Kings. Nothing is said of his motive.

Significance

His kindness supplies the last four verses of 2 Kings, which end a history of national destruction with a king of David's line alive, out of prison, and eating at a table. The historian offers no comment, and the placement is the comment.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture References

2 Kings 25:27-30; Jeremiah 52:31-34

Further Figures of the Kingdom Period

—

Jabez

A man of Judah, more honourable than his brethren, whose prayer God granted.

Family

Of the tribe of Judah; his mother named him (1 Chronicles 4:9). His brethren are mentioned but not named.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. He appears in the genealogies of Judah without chronological anchor.

Life Synopsis

"And Jabez was more honourable than his brethren: and his mother called his name Jabez, saying, Because I bare him with sorrow."

"And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested" (1 Chronicles 4:9-10). Nothing else is recorded of him. The two verses interrupt a long genealogy and then it resumes.

What They Did Right

  • Was more honourable than his brethren - the Chronicler's own assessment: 1 Chronicles 4:9.
  • Called on the God of Israel, asking for blessing, enlargement, God's hand with him, and to be kept from evil: 1 Chronicles 4:10.
  • God granted him that which he requested: 1 Chronicles 4:10.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Two verses, and both are favourable. Scripture does not say what made him more honourable than his brethren, does not describe the sorrow of his birth, and does not record what the granted request produced. His prayer includes a petition to be kept from evil that it might not grieve him - a man named for sorrow asking not to cause it.

Significance

His prayer is one of very few in Scripture recorded together with the explicit statement that God granted it. The town of Jabez, where families of scribes dwelt, bears the same name (1 Chronicles 2:55), though Scripture does not connect the two.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture References

1 Chronicles 4:9-10; compare 1 Chronicles 2:55
—

Adino the Eznite

Chief of David's captains, who lifted his spear against eight hundred at one time.

Also called Josheb-basshebeth, The Tachmonite

Family

Called "the Tachmonite that sat in the seat" (2 Samuel 23:8). 1 Chronicles 11:11 calls him Jashobeam, an Hachmonite, and gives the number as three hundred.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. In David's reign.

Life Synopsis

"These be the names of the mighty men whom David had: The Tachmonite that sat in the seat, chief among the captains; the same was Adino the Eznite: he lift up his spear against eight hundred, whom he slew at one time" (2 Samuel 23:8). The parallel in 1 Chronicles 11:11 reads: "Jashobeam, an Hachmonite, the chief of the captains: he lifted up his spear against three hundred slain by him at one time." The difference in name and number between the two passages is a well-known textual question and is noted here rather than resolved.

What They Did Right

  • Chief among David's captains, credited with an exceptional feat of arms: 2 Samuel 23:8; 1 Chronicles 11:11.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records his rank and one feat, with no moral evaluation. He heads the list of David's mighty men.

Significance

First named in the roll of David's mighty men, the record of the soldiers who established the kingdom.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture References

2 Samuel 23:8; 1 Chronicles 11:11
—

Eleazar (son of Dodo)

One of the three mighty men; fought the Philistines until his hand clave to the sword. Not to be confused with Eleazar the son of Aaron.

Family

Son of Dodo the Ahohite (2 Samuel 23:9).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"And after him was Eleazar the son of Dodo the Ahohite, one of the three mighty men with David, when they defied the Philistines that were there gathered together to battle, and the men of Israel were gone away: he arose, and smote the Philistines until his hand was weary, and his hand clave unto the sword: and the Lord wrought a great victory that day; and the people returned after him only to spoil" (2 Samuel 23:9-10).

What They Did Right

  • Stood and fought when the men of Israel had gone away, until his hand clave to the sword: 2 Samuel 23:9-10.
  • The text credits the outcome to God: "the Lord wrought a great victory that day": 2 Samuel 23:10.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records one action, and the detail that the army had already retreated is what gives it weight. The victory is attributed to the Lord and the people are recorded as returning only to gather spoil.

Significance

One of the three chief of David's mighty men. He is among the three who broke through the Philistine host to bring David water from the well of Bethlehem, which David poured out to the Lord rather than drink (2 Samuel 23:13-17).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture References

2 Samuel 23:9-17; 1 Chronicles 11:12-19
—

Shammah (son of Agee)

One of the three mighty men; stood alone in a field of lentiles and defended it against the Philistines.

Family

Son of Agee the Hararite (2 Samuel 23:11).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture.

Life Synopsis

"And after him was Shammah the son of Agee the Hararite. And the Philistines were gathered together into a troop, where was a piece of ground full of lentiles: and the people fled from the Philistines. But he stood in the midst of the ground, and defended it, and slew the Philistines: and the Lord wrought a great victory" (2 Samuel 23:11-12).

What They Did Right

  • Stood in the midst of a field when the people fled, and defended it: 2 Samuel 23:11-12.
  • The victory is attributed to the Lord: 2 Samuel 23:12.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records one stand over a field of lentiles - a piece of ground of no obvious strategic value - and calls the outcome a great victory wrought by the Lord. The account is included in the roll of the mighty men without further comment.

Significance

One of the three chief mighty men of David.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture References

2 Samuel 23:11-12; 1 Chronicles 11:12-14
—

Amasai

Chief of the captains; the Spirit came upon him and he declared for David at Ziklag.

Family

Chief of the captains (1 Chronicles 12:18).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. While David was still a fugitive at Ziklag.

Life Synopsis

Men of Benjamin and Judah came to David in the hold, and David went out to meet them and said that if they came peaceably his heart would be knit to them, but if to betray him, God would rebuke it.

"Then the spirit came upon Amasai, who was chief of the captains, and he said, Thine are we, David, and on thy side, thou son of Jesse: peace, peace be unto thee, and peace be to thine helpers; for thy God helpeth thee. Then David received them, and made them captains of the band" (1 Chronicles 12:18).

What They Did Right

  • Declared for David under the Spirit's coming upon him, and credited the help to David's God: 1 Chronicles 12:18.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

One verse, entirely favourable, and unusual for recording that the Spirit came upon a soldier for the purpose of an oath of allegiance.

Significance

His declaration secured a body of men for David during the years of flight, and is one of the clearest statements of loyalty in Chronicles.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture References

1 Chronicles 12:16-18
—

Uzzah

A son of Abinadab who put out his hand to steady the ark and was struck dead.

Also called Uzza

Family

Son of Abinadab, in whose house the ark had rested (2 Samuel 6:3); brother of Ahio.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Early in David's reign over all Israel.

Life Synopsis

David brought the ark from the house of Abinadab on a new cart, driven by Uzzah and Ahio, with all Israel playing before the Lord on all manner of instruments.

"And when they came to Nachon's threshingfloor, Uzzah put forth his hand to the ark of God, and took hold of it; for the oxen shook it. And the anger of the Lord was kindled against Uzzah; and God smote him there for his error; and there he died by the ark of God" (2 Samuel 6:6-7). Chronicles adds that his hand was on the ark (1 Chronicles 13:9-10).

David was displeased and afraid, called the place Perezuzzah, and would not bring the ark further, leaving it in the house of Obededom for three months (2 Samuel 6:8-11). Three months later he brought it up properly, by the Levites, and said, "For because ye did it not at the first, the Lord our God made a breach upon us, for that we sought him not after the due order" (1 Chronicles 15:13).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • Put forth his hand and took hold of the ark: 2 Samuel 6:6-7. Scripture calls it his error and records that God's anger was kindled. The law had forbidden touching the holy things on pain of death and required the ark to be carried by the Levites on staves (Numbers 4:15; Exodus 25:14-15). David afterward identified the fault as failing to seek God after the due order (1 Chronicles 15:13), which places responsibility on the whole undertaking and not on Uzzah alone.

Character Assessment

One of the hardest passages in the historical books, and Scripture offers no softening. The act looks instinctive and protective, and the text calls it error and records the death without elaboration. What it does supply is David's later verdict: the fault lay in transporting the ark on a cart at all, contrary to the law, and the whole company bore that.

Significance

His death stopped the procession for three months and caused David to study how the ark was to be moved, so that the second attempt was made by Levites bearing it on their shoulders as Moses had commanded (1 Chronicles 15:2, 15:13-15). The place was named Perezuzzah, the breach of Uzzah.

Death / Outcome

Struck dead by God beside the ark at the threshingfloor of Nachon, also called Chidon (2 Samuel 6:7; 1 Chronicles 13:10).

Scripture References

2 Samuel 6:1-11; 1 Chronicles 13:1-14; 1 Chronicles 15:11-15; Numbers 4:15
—

Obededom

A Gittite in whose house the ark rested three months, and whose household God blessed; afterward a Levite doorkeeper and singer.

Also called Obed-edom

Family

Called the Gittite (2 Samuel 6:10). 1 Chronicles 26:4-8 names eight sons and records sixty-two of his house as able men for the service.

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. In David's reign.

Life Synopsis

After Uzzah's death David would not carry the ark into the city of David, "but David carried it aside into the house of Obededom the Gittite. And the ark of the Lord continued in the house of Obededom the Gittite three months: and the Lord blessed Obededom, and all his household" (2 Samuel 6:10-11).

David heard of the blessing and went and brought the ark up with gladness (2 Samuel 6:12). Obededom afterward appears among the Levites appointed to minister before the ark and as a porter and singer (1 Chronicles 15:18-24; 1 Chronicles 16:5, 16:38), and his house among the doorkeepers, "for God blessed him" (1 Chronicles 26:4-5).

What They Did Right

  • Received the ark into his house when the king was afraid to take it further: 2 Samuel 6:10.
  • Continued in the service of the ark afterward as porter and singer: 1 Chronicles 15:18-24; 1 Chronicles 16:38.
  • Scripture states twice that the Lord blessed him and his household: 2 Samuel 6:11-12; 1 Chronicles 26:5.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him and states the blessing on his house twice. The contrast with the preceding verses is deliberate: the same ark that had just killed a man blessed a household for three months, and the difference lay in how it was approached rather than in the ark itself.

Significance

The blessing on his house is what moved David to bring the ark to Jerusalem, and his family became a permanent part of the temple service.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 25:24.

Scripture References

2 Samuel 6:10-12; 1 Chronicles 13:13-14; 1 Chronicles 15:18-25; 1 Chronicles 16:5, 16:38; 1 Chronicles 26:4-8, 26:15
—

Asaph

A Levite appointed by David as chief of the singers before the ark; a seer, and named in the titles of twelve psalms.

Family

Son of Berachiah, of the sons of Gershom (1 Chronicles 6:39-43). His sons formed a continuing order of temple singers (1 Chronicles 25:1-2).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Appointed in David's reign.

Life Synopsis

David appointed Levites to minister before the ark, "Asaph the chief, and next to him Zechariah," and Asaph was to make a sound with cymbals (1 Chronicles 16:4-5). On the day the ark came up, David delivered a psalm into the hand of Asaph and his brethren (1 Chronicles 16:7).

He and his sons prophesied with harps, psalteries, and cymbals "according to the order of the king" (1 Chronicles 25:1-2). He is called "Asaph the seer" (2 Chronicles 29:30), and his words were used in Hezekiah's restoration of worship. The sons of Asaph continued as temple singers through the monarchy and returned from exile (Ezra 2:41; Nehemiah 7:44).

What They Did Right

  • Appointed chief of those who ministered in song before the ark: 1 Chronicles 16:4-5.
  • Prophesied with instruments in the service of the house of God: 1 Chronicles 25:1-2.
  • Called a seer, and his words used in the reformation of worship under Hezekiah: 2 Chronicles 29:30.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him and gives him an unusual double designation: chief musician and seer. His psalms include some of the most searching in the Psalter.

Significance

Twelve psalms carry his name in their titles - Psalm 50 and Psalms 73 to 83 - including Psalm 73, which sets out the problem of the prosperity of the wicked more directly than any other psalm. His order of singers outlasted the monarchy and the exile.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. His descendants are named as late as Nehemiah 11:17.

Scripture References

1 Chronicles 6:39; 1 Chronicles 15:17-19; 1 Chronicles 16:4-7, 16:37; 1 Chronicles 25:1-9; 2 Chronicles 29:30; Ezra 2:41; Nehemiah 7:44; Psalms 50 title; Psalms 73-83 titles
—

Heman

A Levite singer, grandson of Samuel; the king's seer in the words of God; named in the title of Psalm 88.

Family

Son of Joel, son of Samuel (1 Chronicles 6:33). He had fourteen sons and three daughters (1 Chronicles 25:5).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Appointed in David's reign.

Life Synopsis

He was appointed with Asaph and Ethan to sound with cymbals of brass (1 Chronicles 15:17-19), and with Jeduthun to give thanks with trumpets and instruments (1 Chronicles 16:41-42).

"All these were the sons of Heman the king's seer in the words of God, to lift up the horn. And God gave to Heman fourteen sons and three daughters. All these were under the hands of their father for song in the house of the Lord, with cymbals, psalteries, and harps, for the service of the house of God" (1 Chronicles 25:5-6). He is named among those whose descendants served under Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 29:14).

What They Did Right

  • Appointed to the service of song in the house of the Lord and named the king's seer in the words of God: 1 Chronicles 25:5.
  • His whole household - fourteen sons and three daughters - served in the temple music under his direction: 1 Chronicles 25:5-6.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. He is a grandson of Samuel serving in David's temple arrangements, which quietly links the last judge to the ordering of worship.

Significance

Psalm 88 carries his name in its title, and it is the darkest psalm in the Psalter, ending without resolution. That the man Scripture calls the king's seer, with seventeen children and a place in the temple choir, is credited with that psalm is worth noting and is not explained by the text.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture References

1 Chronicles 6:33; 1 Chronicles 15:17-19; 1 Chronicles 16:41-42; 1 Chronicles 25:1-6; 2 Chronicles 5:12; 2 Chronicles 29:14; Psalms 88 title
—

Jeduthun

A Levite appointed with Asaph and Heman over the service of song; named in the titles of three psalms.

Family

His sons are named among the singers and porters (1 Chronicles 25:3; 1 Chronicles 16:38).

Chronology

Date not established by Scripture. Appointed in David's reign.

Life Synopsis

He was appointed with Heman to give thanks to the Lord, with trumpets and cymbals and instruments of God (1 Chronicles 16:41-42). "Of Jeduthun: the sons of Jeduthun; Gedaliah, and Zeri, and Jeshaiah, Hashabiah, and Mattithiah, six, under the hands of their father Jeduthun, who prophesied with a harp, to give thanks and to praise the Lord" (1 Chronicles 25:3). He is called "the king's seer" (2 Chronicles 35:15).

What They Did Right

  • Appointed over the service of song and named as one who prophesied with a harp to give thanks and praise the Lord: 1 Chronicles 25:3.
  • Called the king's seer: 2 Chronicles 35:15.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. With Asaph and Heman he forms the third of the three orders of temple singers established by David.

Significance

Psalms 39, 62, and 77 name him in their titles. His order of singers continued through the monarchy and appears again after the return from exile (Nehemiah 11:17).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture References

1 Chronicles 16:41-42; 1 Chronicles 25:1-6; 2 Chronicles 5:12; 2 Chronicles 35:15; Nehemiah 11:17; Psalms 39 title; Psalms 62 title; Psalms 77 title
—

Shemaiah (the man of God)

A prophet in Rehoboam's reign; forbade the war against Israel and interpreted Shishak's invasion.

Family

Called the man of God (1 Kings 12:22) and the prophet (2 Chronicles 12:5).

Chronology

In the reign of Rehoboam (1 Kings 12:22).

Life Synopsis

When Rehoboam assembled a hundred and eighty thousand men to fight Israel, the word of the Lord came to Shemaiah: "Ye shall not go up, nor fight against your brethren the children of Israel: return every man to his house; for this thing is from me. They hearkened therefore to the word of the Lord, and returned" (1 Kings 12:22-24).

When Shishak came up, Shemaiah came to Rehoboam and the princes and said, "Ye have forsaken me, and therefore have I also left you in the hand of Shishak." They humbled themselves and said, "The Lord is righteous." The word of the Lord came again: because they humbled themselves, God would not destroy them but would grant them some deliverance, though they would be Shishak's servants (2 Chronicles 12:5-8). He is named as a recorder of Rehoboam's acts (2 Chronicles 12:15).

What They Did Right

  • Delivered God's word forbidding a civil war, and was obeyed by a king and an army of a hundred and eighty thousand: 1 Kings 12:22-24.
  • Told Rehoboam and the princes plainly why Shishak had come: 2 Chronicles 12:5.
  • Brought back the word of mercy when they humbled themselves: 2 Chronicles 12:7.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him, and records that he was heard on both occasions - an unusual outcome for a prophet in the historical books.

Significance

His first word prevented a war between Judah and Israel at the moment of the division, and his second turned a national judgment into a partial one. He recorded the acts of Rehoboam.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 12:15.

Scripture References

1 Kings 12:22-24; 2 Chronicles 11:2-4; 2 Chronicles 12:5-8, 12:15
—

Shishak

King of Egypt; sheltered Jeroboam and later invaded Judah, taking the treasures of the temple and the palace.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

He came up in the fifth year of Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:25).

Life Synopsis

Jeroboam fled to him from Solomon and stayed in Egypt until Solomon's death (1 Kings 11:40).

"And it came to pass in the fifth year of king Rehoboam, that Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem: and he took away the treasures of the house of the Lord, and the treasures of the king's house; he even took away all: and he took away all the shields of gold which Solomon had made" (1 Kings 14:25-26). Rehoboam made shields of brass in their place. Chronicles records twelve hundred chariots, sixty thousand horsemen, and people without number, and states that Judah became his servants, "that they may know my service, and the service of the kingdoms of the countries" (2 Chronicles 12:2-9).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records his invasion as God's response to Judah's transgression (2 Chronicles 12:2) and offers no separate verdict on him.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents him as an instrument of judgment rather than as a man assessed. The detail it dwells on is the loss of Solomon's gold shields and their replacement with brass - the visible measure of how much had been lost in five years.

Significance

His invasion stripped the temple within five years of Solomon's death and made Judah a tributary. God's stated purpose was that they should learn the difference between his service and the service of the kingdoms of the countries (2 Chronicles 12:8).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He departed from Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 12:9).

Scripture References

1 Kings 11:40; 1 Kings 14:25-28; 2 Chronicles 12:2-9
—

Azariah (son of Oded)

A prophet on whom the Spirit of God came; met Asa returning from battle and called Judah to reform.

Family

Son of Oded (2 Chronicles 15:1).

Chronology

In the reign of Asa (2 Chronicles 15:1).

Life Synopsis

"And the Spirit of God came upon Azariah the son of Oded: and he went out to meet Asa, and said unto him, Hear ye me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin; The Lord is with you, while ye be with him; and if ye seek him, he will be found of you; but if ye forsake him, he will forsake you." He recited a period when Israel had been without the true God, without a teaching priest, and without law, and said, "Be ye strong therefore, and let not your hands be weak: for your work shall be rewarded" (2 Chronicles 15:1-7).

"And when Asa heard these words, and the prophecy of Oded the prophet, he took courage, and put away the abominable idols out of all the land," renewed the altar, and gathered Judah, Benjamin, and those from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon to a covenant to seek the Lord (2 Chronicles 15:8-15).

What They Did Right

  • Delivered a word that produced the most thorough reform of Asa's reign: 2 Chronicles 15:1-8.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His message contains one of the clearest conditional statements in the Old Testament - the Lord is with you while you are with him - and it was acted on immediately.

Significance

His word set off Asa's covenant renewal, which drew people from the northern tribes into Judah. The sentence "if ye seek him, he will be found of you" is among the most quoted in Chronicles.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 15:8.

Scripture References

2 Chronicles 15:1-8
—

Zerah the Ethiopian

Commander of a host of a thousand thousand who came against Asa and was overthrown.

Family

An Ethiopian (2 Chronicles 14:9).

Chronology

In the reign of Asa (2 Chronicles 14:9).

Life Synopsis

"And there came out against them Zerah the Ethiopian with an host of a thousand thousand, and three hundred chariots; and came unto Mareshah." Asa cried to the Lord: "Lord, it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power: help us, O Lord our God; for we rest on thee, and in thy name we go against this multitude."

"So the Lord smote the Ethiopians before Asa, and before Judah; and the Ethiopians fled" (2 Chronicles 14:9-12).

What They Did Right

  • No specific commendation is recorded.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Scripture records his invasion and defeat without moral evaluation of him.

Character Assessment

Scripture records the size of his host and its overthrow, and gives its attention entirely to Asa's prayer. He is the occasion of the clearest statement of dependence in Asa's reign.

Significance

His defeat is the victory Hanani later reminded Asa of, when the king had turned to Syria instead of God (2 Chronicles 16:8).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. His host fled and was destroyed (2 Chronicles 14:12-13).

Scripture References

2 Chronicles 14:9-15; 2 Chronicles 16:8
—

Hanani (the seer)

A seer who rebuked Asa for hiring Syria instead of relying on the Lord, and was imprisoned for it.

Family

Father of Jehu the prophet (1 Kings 16:1; 2 Chronicles 19:2).

Chronology

In the thirty-sixth year of Asa's reign (2 Chronicles 16:1, 16:7).

Life Synopsis

"And at that time Hanani the seer came to Asa king of Judah, and said unto him, Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the Lord thy God, therefore is the host of the king of Syria escaped out of thine hand. Were not the Ethiopians and the Lubims a huge host... yet, because thou didst rely on the Lord, he delivered them into thine hand. For the eyes of the Lord run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to shew himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him. Herein thou hast done foolishly: therefore from henceforth thou shalt have wars" (2 Chronicles 16:7-9).

"Then Asa was wroth with the seer, and put him in a prison house; for he was in a rage with him because of this thing" (2 Chronicles 16:10).

What They Did Right

  • Rebuked a king who had been faithful for decades, and did so by reminding him of his own earlier faith: 2 Chronicles 16:7-9.
  • Accepted imprisonment rather than soften the message: 2 Chronicles 16:10.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His rebuke is notable for its method: he did not accuse Asa of a general failure but pointed to the single decision and set it against the king's own past.

Significance

His words in 2 Chronicles 16:9 - that the eyes of the Lord run to and fro throughout the whole earth to show himself strong for those whose heart is perfect toward him - are among the most quoted in the Old Testament. His son Jehu continued the same ministry to the next generation of kings.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. He was put in a prison house (2 Chronicles 16:10).

Scripture References

2 Chronicles 16:7-10; 1 Kings 16:1, 16:7; 2 Chronicles 19:2; 2 Chronicles 20:34
—

Jahaziel

A Levite of the sons of Asaph on whom the Spirit of the Lord came in the congregation, telling Judah the battle was God's.

Family

Son of Zechariah, son of Benaiah, son of Jeiel, son of Mattaniah, a Levite of the sons of Asaph (2 Chronicles 20:14).

Chronology

In the reign of Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 20:14).

Life Synopsis

As all Judah stood before the Lord with their little ones, their wives, and their children, the Spirit of the Lord came upon Jahaziel in the midst of the congregation. He said, "Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God's... Ye shall not need to fight in this battle: set yourselves, stand ye still, and see the salvation of the Lord with you" (2 Chronicles 20:14-17).

Jehoshaphat and all Judah bowed with their faces to the ground, the Levites stood to praise, and in the morning they went out with singers before the army; the enemy destroyed one another (2 Chronicles 20:18-24).

What They Did Right

  • Delivered God's word to a frightened nation under the Spirit's coming upon him, and it was obeyed: 2 Chronicles 20:14-18.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. He speaks once, in the middle of an assembly, and his words redirect a national crisis.

Significance

His word - the battle is not yours, but God's - is among the most quoted sentences in Chronicles, and it produced the unique spectacle of an army going into battle led by singers.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 20:14.

Scripture References

2 Chronicles 20:14-19
—

Eliezer (son of Dodavah)

A prophet of Mareshah who foretold the destruction of Jehoshaphat's ships because of his alliance with Ahaziah of Israel.

Family

Son of Dodavah of Mareshah (2 Chronicles 20:37).

Chronology

Late in the reign of Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 20:35-37).

Life Synopsis

Jehoshaphat joined himself with Ahaziah king of Israel to make ships to go to Tarshish. "Then Eliezer the son of Dodavah of Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat, saying, Because thou hast joined thyself with Ahaziah, the Lord hath broken thy works. And the ships were broken, that they were not able to go to Tarshish" (2 Chronicles 20:36-37).

What They Did Right

  • Told a good king that his alliance had destroyed his own enterprise, and was proved right immediately: 2 Chronicles 20:37.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

One verse of prophecy and its immediate fulfilment. Scripture records nothing else about him.

Significance

His word is the third recorded rebuke of Jehoshaphat for allying with the house of Ahab, after Micaiah's warning and Jehu son of Hanani's rebuke - a pattern the Chronicler makes unmistakable.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded.

Scripture References

2 Chronicles 20:35-37
—

Oded

A prophet of the Lord in Samaria who confronted the returning army of Israel and secured the release of two hundred thousand captives of Judah.

Family

Not recorded. Not to be confused with Oded the father of Azariah (2 Chronicles 15:1).

Chronology

In the reign of Ahaz of Judah and Pekah of Israel (2 Chronicles 28:5-9).

Life Synopsis

Israel had taken two hundred thousand women, sons, and daughters of Judah captive, with much spoil, and brought them to Samaria.

"But a prophet of the Lord was there, whose name was Oded: and he went out before the host that came to Samaria, and said unto them, Behold, because the Lord God of your fathers was wroth with Judah, he hath delivered them into your hand, and ye have slain them in a rage that reacheth up unto heaven. And now ye purpose to keep under the children of Judah and Jerusalem for bondmen and bondwomen unto you: but are there not with you, even with you, sins against the Lord your God?" (2 Chronicles 28:9-10).

Certain heads of Ephraim stood with him. The armed men left the captives and the spoil before the princes and the congregation. Men rose up, clothed the naked among them from the spoil, shod them, gave them to eat and drink, anointed them, carried the feeble on asses, and brought them to Jericho to their brethren (2 Chronicles 28:12-15).

What They Did Right

  • Confronted a victorious army alone and told them their victory did not license what they intended: 2 Chronicles 28:9-11.
  • Reminded Israel of their own sins rather than only Judah's: 2 Chronicles 28:10.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. His intervention is one of the most remarkable in Chronicles: a single prophet turned an army back from enslaving two hundred thousand people, and the men who had captured them then clothed, fed, and carried them home. Nothing in the northern kingdom's record resembles it.

Significance

The treatment of the captives - clothed from the spoil, fed, anointed, and the feeble carried on asses to Jericho - is a striking Old Testament parallel to the parable of the good Samaritan, which Christ set on the same road (Luke 10:30-35). Scripture draws no connection, and none is asserted here.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: 2 Chronicles 28:9.

Scripture References

2 Chronicles 28:5-15

The Exile, the Return, and the Persian Court

—

Cyrus

King of Persia; issued the decree permitting the Jews to return and rebuild the house of the Lord; named by Isaiah long before his birth.

Family

Not recorded.

Chronology

The decree came in the first year of his reign over Babylon (Ezra 1:1).

Life Synopsis

"Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the Lord by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom, and put it also in writing, saying, Thus saith Cyrus king of Persia, The Lord God of heaven hath given me all the kingdoms of the earth; and he hath charged me to build him an house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Who is there among you of all his people? his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem" (Ezra 1:1-3).

He brought out the vessels of the house of the Lord which Nebuchadnezzar had taken, and numbered them to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah - five thousand four hundred vessels in all (Ezra 1:7-11). His decree was later found at Achmetha and confirmed by Darius when the work was challenged (Ezra 6:1-5).

Isaiah had named him: "That saith of Cyrus, He is my shepherd, and shall perform all my pleasure: even saying to Jerusalem, Thou shalt be built; and to the temple, Thy foundation shall be laid." And: "Thus saith the Lord to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have holden... I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me" (Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:1-5).

What They Did Right

  • Issued the decree for the return and the rebuilding of the house of the Lord: Ezra 1:1-4.
  • Restored the vessels of the temple that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away, numbered and delivered: Ezra 1:7-11.
  • Acknowledged the Lord God of heaven as the one who had given him his kingdoms and charged him to build: Ezra 1:2.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. Isaiah's word about him is among the most remarkable in the Old Testament: God calls him his shepherd and his anointed, and says plainly "thou hast not known me" - a man used and named by God without knowing him.

Significance

His decree ended the seventy years of exile that Jeremiah had foretold, and Ezra opens by saying it happened so that Jeremiah's word might be fulfilled. Isaiah named him roughly a century and a half before the event. He is the only foreign ruler in Scripture called God's anointed.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Daniel 10:1.

Scripture References

2 Chronicles 36:22-23; Ezra 1:1-11; Ezra 3:7; Ezra 4:3-5; Ezra 5:13-17; Ezra 6:1-14; Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:1-13; Daniel 1:21; Daniel 6:28; Daniel 10:1
—

Zerubbabel

Son of Shealtiel; governor of Judah at the return; led the first company home and rebuilt the altar and the temple.

Also called Zorobabel, Sheshbazzar

Family

Son of Shealtiel (Ezra 3:2; Haggai 1:1); of the line of David through Jehoiachin (1 Chronicles 3:17-19, which calls him the son of Pedaiah). Named in both genealogies of Christ (Matthew 1:12-13; Luke 3:27).

Chronology

He returned under Cyrus and the temple was finished in the sixth year of Darius (Ezra 6:15).

Life Synopsis

He came up with the first company from the captivity (Ezra 2:2). "Then stood up Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and his brethren the priests, and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and his brethren, and builded the altar of the God of Israel, to offer burnt offerings thereon, as it is written in the law of Moses... for fear was upon them because of the people of those countries" (Ezra 3:2-3). They kept the feast of tabernacles and laid the foundation of the temple, and the old men who had seen the first house wept while others shouted (Ezra 3:8-13).

When the adversaries offered to help build, he answered, "Ye have nothing to do with us to build an house unto our God; but we ourselves together will build unto the Lord God of Israel" (Ezra 4:1-3). The work was stopped by opposition until the second year of Darius, when Haggai and Zechariah prophesied and Zerubbabel and Jeshua rose up and began to build again (Ezra 5:1-2).

Zechariah's word to him: "Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts. Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain... The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also finish it" (Zechariah 4:6-9). Haggai's closing word makes him a signet: "I will take thee, O Zerubbabel, my servant, the son of Shealtiel, saith the Lord, and will make thee as a signet: for I have chosen thee" (Haggai 2:23).

What They Did Right

  • Built the altar first, before the foundation of the temple was laid, despite fear of the surrounding peoples: Ezra 3:2-3.
  • Refused the offer of help from those who did not worship the Lord alone: Ezra 4:1-3.
  • Resumed the work at the word of Haggai and Zechariah after years of delay: Ezra 5:1-2.
  • Finished the house, as Zechariah had said his hands would: Zechariah 4:9; Ezra 6:14-15.
  • God's own word: "I will make thee as a signet: for I have chosen thee": Haggai 2:23.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Haggai rebuked the people, including the leaders, for dwelling in ceiled houses while the house of God lay waste (Haggai 1:2-4), and Zerubbabel obeyed the word when it came (Haggai 1:12-14).

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him. He led the first return, restored the altar in a hostile land, and completed a temple that took over twenty years against sustained opposition. Zechariah's word to him - not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit - is spoken to a governor with no army and no independence.

Significance

He rebuilt the temple, and he stands in both genealogies of Christ, carrying the Davidic line through the exile. Haggai's naming of him as a signet reverses the word spoken against his ancestor Jehoiachin, whom God had said he would pluck off as a signet (Jeremiah 22:24).

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. Last mention: Zechariah 4:9-10.

Scripture References

1 Chronicles 3:17-19; Ezra 2:2; Ezra 3:2-13; Ezra 4:1-3; Ezra 5:1-2; Nehemiah 7:7; Nehemiah 12:1; Haggai 1:1-2:23; Zechariah 4:6-10; Matthew 1:12-13; Luke 3:27
—

Jeshua (the high priest)

Son of Jozadak; high priest at the return; built the altar with Zerubbabel and was shown in Zechariah's vision clothed in filthy garments and given change of raiment.

Also called Joshua the high priest, Jozadak's son

Family

Son of Jozadak, of the high priestly line (Ezra 3:2; Haggai 1:1). Called Joshua in Haggai and Zechariah.

Chronology

He returned with the first company under Cyrus and was still serving in the second year of Darius (Ezra 3:2; Haggai 1:1).

Life Synopsis

He came up with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:2) and stood up with his brethren the priests to build the altar and offer burnt offerings as written in the law of Moses (Ezra 3:2). He set the priests in their apparel and appointed the Levites to the work (Ezra 3:8-9). With Zerubbabel he refused the adversaries' offer of help (Ezra 4:3), and rose up to build again when Haggai and Zechariah prophesied (Ezra 5:2).

Zechariah saw him "standing before the angel of the Lord, and Satan standing at his right hand to resist him. And the Lord said unto Satan, The Lord rebuke thee, O Satan... is not this a brand plucked out of the fire? Now Joshua was clothed with filthy garments, and stood before the angel. And he answered and spake unto those that stood before him, saying, Take away the filthy garments from him. And unto him he said, Behold, I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee, and I will clothe thee with change of raiment" (Zechariah 3:1-4). Crowns were set on his head as a sign concerning the man whose name is The BRANCH (Zechariah 6:11-13).

What They Did Right

  • Built the altar and restored the burnt offerings before the temple was begun: Ezra 3:2-6.
  • Refused the compromised offer of help: Ezra 4:3.
  • Rose up to build again at the prophets' word: Ezra 5:2.
  • Obeyed the voice of the Lord through Haggai and feared before the Lord: Haggai 1:12.

What They Did Wrong

  • No specific wrongdoing is recorded. Zechariah's vision shows him clothed in filthy garments before the angel, which the passage treats as needing removal by God rather than as a specific charge; the iniquity is caused to pass from him and he is clothed with change of raiment: Zechariah 3:3-4.

Character Assessment

Scripture records nothing against him directly. The vision of Zechariah 3 is not an accusation but a picture of a priest accused by Satan and cleared by God, and its point is the clothing rather than the filth.

Significance

He restored the priesthood after the exile. Zechariah's vision of his cleansing and crowning points beyond him to "the BRANCH," who would build the temple of the Lord and be a priest upon his throne (Zechariah 6:12-13) - one of the clearest Old Testament statements of a combined priesthood and kingship.

Death / Outcome

Not recorded. His descendants are traced in Nehemiah 12:10-11.

Scripture References

Ezra 2:2; Ezra 3:2-9; Ezra 4:3; Ezra 5:2; Nehemiah 7:7; Nehemiah 12:1, 12:10; Haggai 1:1-14; Haggai 2:2-4; Zechariah 3:1-10; Zechariah 6:11-13
—

Ahasuerus

King of Persia who reigned from India to Ethiopia over a hundred and twenty-seven provinces; deposed Vashti, made Esther queen, and reversed Haman's decree.

Family

Husband of Vashti and afterward of Esther (Esther 1:9; Esther 2:17).

Chronology

The events span from the third year of his reign to the twelfth (Esther 1:3; Esther 3:7).

Life Synopsis

He made a feast of a hundred and eighty days and then seven days more, and on the seventh day, when his heart was merry with wine, sent for Vashti to show her beauty. She refused, and on Memucan's advice she was deposed and a decree sent out that every man should bear rule in his own house (Esther 1:1-22).

Esther was chosen from the gathered virgins and made queen, and he made a great feast (Esther 2:17-18). Mordecai discovered a plot by Bigthan and Teresh and it was written in the book of the chronicles (Esther 2:21-23).

He promoted Haman above all the princes, and when Haman offered ten thousand talents for permission to destroy a certain people, he took his ring off his hand and gave it to him: "The silver is given to thee, the people also, to do with them as it seemeth good to thee." The decree went out and "the king and Haman sat down to drink; but the city Shushan was perplexed" (Esther 3:1-15).

On a sleepless night he had the chronicles read and learned that Mordecai's service had gone unrewarded, and had Haman lead him through the city in royal apparel (Esther 6:1-11). At Esther's banquet he learned of the plot against her people, went in wrath into the garden, returned to find Haman fallen on the queen's bed, and had him hanged on the gallows he had prepared (Esther 7:1-10). He gave Haman's house to Esther and his ring to Mordecai, and granted a second decree allowing the Jews to defend themselves (Esther 8:1-14).

What They Did Right

  • Rewarded Mordecai for saving his life, once he was reminded of it: Esther 6:1-11.
  • Granted Esther's petition and permitted the Jews to defend themselves: Esther 8:7-11.

What They Did Wrong

  • Sent for his queen to display her beauty before the princes when his heart was merry with wine: Esther 1:10-11.
  • Handed the fate of an entire people to Haman without asking who they were: Esther 3:8-11.
  • Sat down to drink while the city was perplexed by the decree he had just sealed: Esther 3:15.

Character Assessment

Scripture presents him as impulsive, easily advised, and largely unaware. He deposes a queen on a courtier's counsel, signs away a nation on a favourite's word without asking its name, and reverses himself when the facts reach him. The book never mentions God, and the king's obliviousness is part of how the account works: everything turns on a sleepless night and a book read aloud.
